News.title: US terrorist set to be executed on LIVESTREAM by military firing squad after gunning down 13 at army base
News.content:
MEET HIS MAKER US terrorist set to be executed on LIVESTREAM by military firing squad after gunning down 13 at army base







Next

A TERRORIST will be executed on livestream after killing 13 people at an army base in a shooting rampage.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan will be a “public event” as he wants to make sure people are able to watch it.



President Donald Trump officially approved the execution of Hasan on Monday, according to Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell.

The sentence will be carried out on December 3 at 1pm CST (7PM GMT) with more details to follow.



If the sentence goes ahead, he will be the first member of the US Armed Forces to be executed since John A. Bennett was hanged for rape and attempted murder in 1961.

When asked if Hasan had made any final requests or reached out to the Trump administration, Hegseth simply replied “Don’t care. We’ll see him on December 3rd.”

Hasan, an Army psychiatrist who held the rank of major, was convicted of killing 13 people and injuring 32 others in a shooting at Fort Hood military base in 2009.

On November 5 he entered a medical building and opened fire with a laser-sighted handgun on long lines of soldiers, who were waiting for routine immunizations and deployment clearances.

Before discharging his weapon he bowed his head several times and shouted Allahu Akbar, which is Arabic for “God is great!”

The former psychiatrist was later found with a Smith & Wesson .357 Magnum revolver, but it was not used during the shooting.



During the trial, prosecutors uncovered that Hasan spent weeks planning the deadly attack, often visiting an outdoor shooting range in Florence, Texas, where he allegedly became extremely skilled at hitting silhouette targets up to 100 yards away.

He allegedly entered the Guns Galore store in Killeen, Texas, on July 31, 2009 and asked for “the most technologically advanced weapon on the market and the one with the highest standard magazine capacity”.

Witnesses said Hasan initially “sprayed bullets at soldiers in a fanlike motion” before aiming at individual soldiers.



Sergeant Michael Davis, an eyewitness, said: “The rate of fire was pretty much constant shooting. When I initially heard it, it sounded like an M16.”

Investigators recovered 146 shell casings inside the building and 68 more outside, where Hasan shot at the backs of soldiers fleeing toward the parking lot.

Hasan said he carried out the twisted ten-minute shooting because he wanted to stop the soldiers from going to Afghanistan and “killing his fellow Muslims”.

A military judge did not allow him to use this defence during his trial, where the convicted terrorist made almost no effort to defend himself.

He told jurors that the evidence would show he was the shooter, describing himself as a “soldier who had switched sides”.



Duane Reasoner, a convert to Islam whom Hasan was mentoring in the religion, said: “[Hasan] said Muslims shouldn’t be in the US military, because obviously Muslims shouldn’t kill Muslims. He told me not to join the Army.”

Hasan was convicted on all charges during his trial, including 13 counts of premeditated murder and 32 counts of attempted murder.

Several military law experts said that Hasan could choose to appeal his execution and file a habeas petition in civilian court, which would significantly delay the execution.

Eugene R. Fidell, a visiting lecturer at Yale Law School specialising in military law, said: “It frankly might outlast the current administration, and who knows if the next one will have the same penchant for executions.”

The U.S. military has not executed a service member by firing squad since World War II.



The last military execution took place on April 13, 1961, when Army Pvt. John Bennett was executed by hanging.

It comes after the botched execution of Christa Pike, 50, who survived two rounds of lethal injection on September 30.

The convicted killer was charged with the murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer after luring her into a wooded area and brutally killing her.

She carried out the murder with her then-boyfriend, 17-year-old Tadaryl Shipp, in a satanist ritual, carving a pentagram onto Colleen’s chest.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Shipp narrowly avoided the death penalty as he was under 18.



Instead he was handed a life sentence for first-degree murder and given 25 years for conspiracy to commit first-degree murder.

News.title: Missing cat’s severed tail posted through owners’ letterbox as woman distraught following death of tabby & 3 arrested
News.content:
FELINE AGONY Missing cat’s severed tail posted through owners’ letterbox as woman distraught following death of tabby & 3 arrested







Next

A MISSING cat’s severed tail was posted through its owners’ letterbox – as cops arrest three people in connection with the incident.

The suspects – a 37-year-old woman and two men, aged 47 and 75 – are currently in custody being questioned.



They were arrested on suspicion of malicious communications and failing to prevent causing unnecessary harm to an animal.

The younger man was arrested on suspicion of assault and criminal damage, while the other man was arrested on suspicion of witness intimidation and harassment.



It follows the tragic death of beloved tabby Max, who went missing from his home in Hull last month.

The pair said Max had become a real “homebody” after the family moved into the property last July and rarely left the premises.





Owners Louise, 45, and Lisa, 47, had put Max out in the front lawn at around noon on September 14 when he suddenly vanished.

By 7pm the following day, Louise was starting to panic and the two of them put up missing posters around the village.

When Lisa went to collect the mail from their shared post area later on, she discovered the distinctive white-tipped tail inside.

“I just heard Lisa screaming and crying,” said Louise.

“That is something I will never forget.”



Max’s tail was later sent to a specialist vet in Liverpool for forensic analysis.

His body was found in the nearby woods by a dog walker six days later, not far from Lisa and Louise’s home.

The pair feared Max might have been alive when his tail was cut off.

The couple held a candelit vigil for their cherished tabby outside their flat, near to his favourite tree.

Dozens of mourners came to show their respects and tie yellow ribbons around the branches.



Lisa and Louise – who have been together for nine years – said the disturbing ordeal had cast a shadow over their wedding plans.

They cancelled a pub celebration and buffet because they said could not stomach it after Max’s devastating death.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Insp Lucy Kevan, of Humberside Police, said: “I understand a report of this nature causes concern amongst the community.

“However, I would like to provide reassurance that we believe this to be an isolated incident.”

News.title: Most freed lags who breach their electronic tag are let off with no punishment, warns Sir Mark Rowley
News.content:
Next

ALMOST every freed prisoner who breaches their electronic tag is let off without punishment, the Met Police chief has warned.

Sir Mark Rowley said that 95 per cent of criminals who fall foul of their licensing conditions receive “zero sanction”.



The Scotland Yard boss’ intervention is a rebuke to ministers who claim tagging helps soften the impact of the early release scheme.

Many lags are currently being let out of jail having served just a third of their sentence to help ease overcrowding.



Labour has insisted that fitting a tag – which can monitor someone’s location and alcohol level – helps prevent reoffending.

But Sir Mark told LBC: “I’m worried, though, about the number of offenders being released into communities.”

He said that more than 100 criminals were being arrested in London alone every day for breaking their tagging conditions.

He added: “So we take them to court. We’re seeing 95 per cent plus of the tagging breaches that we arrest are simply being bailed back into the community on the same condition, so there is zero sanction.”

Justice Secretary Alex Norris was last week unable to say how many freed criminals had been tagged.

While the government has a “presumption of tagging”, it is not guaranteed each convict will be fitted with one.



A Government spokesperson said: “We inherited a prison system on the brink of collapse. If we had failed to act, the police would have been forced to halt arrests, putting communities at untold risk.

“To manage offenders out on licence, we are rolling out the toughest-ever controls, including world-first restriction zones, the largest expansion of electronic tagging, and giving victims a say in licence conditions.”

News.title: Burnham must resist Germany’s advances on pulling Britain closer to EU, warn Tories and Reform UK
News.content:
Next

ANDY Burnham must resist Germany’s advances after its Chancellor said he would “do anything” to pull Britain closer to the EU, the Tories and Reform UK warn.

The PM came under fire after the two leaders’ first face-to-face meeting in Berlin.



Chancellor Friedrich Merz said he would do whatever is necessary for the UK to forge closer ties with the bloc.

Shadow Cabinet minister Alex Burghart said: “Our people-pleaser PM should be wary of these overtures.



Closer alignment with the EU comes with a cost.”

“Labour’s flawed EU reset is already showing that.



“We should not reopen settled arguments about Brexit when the priority must be tackling the structural problems holding back our economy.

“From Labour’s ballooning welfare bill to weak growth.”

And Reform’s deputy leader Richard Tice added: “The British public had their say in 2016 and chose Brexit.

“They don’t want a return to free movement.



“And they definitely don’t want billions being sent to Brussels in return for suffocating rules and regulations.

“Regardless of what the French or Germans say.”

News.title: Dramatic moment French riot cops charge student protesters as dozens of officers injured in worsening violence
News.content:
Next

THIS is the dramatic moment cops charge student protesters as dozens of cops are injured in escalating clashes.

Shocking videos show students and feared riot police doing battle on the streets of the French capital, as protests about school conditions explode into violence.



Masked pupils hang off railings as huge projectiles are hurled at police – including fireworks, plants ripped straight out of the ground and the protesters’ own shoes.

Others drape themselves with the tricolour as they face off with armed police.



One video shows the moment teens yell at police before the riot police charge en masse at the demonstrators.

Protesters and police then lock in close combat, pinning each other to the ground in Paris’ historic Place de Bastille, where the famed prison was stormed by revolutionaries on July 14, 1789.

The square saw some of the worst of the violence on Thursday, as kids climbed the iconic monument in its centre and did bitter battle with cops.

Many also protested peacefully, some waving the French flag and singing the national anthem.



One student was seen sitting on the top of a bus stop, clutching a sign reading: “Reason for absence: Too busy fighting for our future.”

More than 71,000 took part in marches across the country today, the French interior ministry said, including some 24,500 in Paris.



The ministry spokesperson warned that violence at the demos is ramping up.

He said there was “an increase in urban violence, on the fringes of the peaceful mobilisations of sixth form students, which has marred their legitimate expression”.

504 people were arrested and 48 police officers injured today alone.

Students from Lycees – the French equivalent of sixth form colleges, for pupils aged 15 – 18 – have been revolting for weeks, initially over conditions in schools.



Students are now demanding more teachers, shorter school hours, and an end to racial discrimination.

On Thursday France‘s education minister promised 3,000 substitute teachers for the country’s worst-off sixth forms.

Education Minister Edouard Geffray said the supply teachers would be deployed in just days to replace absent staff at the 114 worst-affected schools.

Violence exploded this week, with thousands of schools shut as students have barricaded entrances and set bins on fire in the street.

Riot police have responded with force, trying to control the chaos by firing tear gas and water cannons at crowds to break up violent fringes on the edge of protests.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

A baby in a pram has been hit with a firework, a teen’s hand has been blown off and college set alight as pupils raged at school conditions.

The 15-year-old who lost a hand after police fired a stun grenade caused the French government to suspend the use of the weapon.

News.title: Britain’s nuclear-armed submarines being protected by a glorified car wash shows why PM must boost defence spending
News.content:
In reel trouble







Next

BRITAIN’S nuclear-armed submarines carry enough firepower to wipe out 40 major cities — yet they rely on fire hoses to protect themselves from drone attack.

That’s the sorry state of our hollowed-out Armed Forces today.



Our brave, highly skilled crews are literally being trained to point and squirt high-pressure water at lethal airborne threats.

It would be funny if it weren’t so deadly serious. It’s a symptom of a crippling, decade-long failure to invest in our defences.



The Royal Navy has shrunk to its smallest size in 500 years and Top Brass have warned the submarine fleet is in a “parlous state”.

Yet, despite a clear and present danger from known enemies, the dithering PM wants to delay any decision to boost defence spending until next year.

It’s an insult to our military personnel and a betrayal of the British public.

We expect our last line of defence to be protected by military-grade muscle — not a glorified car wash.

Stopped trying

HAS the Government simply given up on even pretending to do anything to stop the boats?

Illegal migrants are currently landing on Britain’s shores at the rate of one every six minutes.



That is the shocking reality of our broken borders after 1,739 people made the perilous Channel crossing in the first week of October.

But what have we heard from Labour? Absolute silence.

While the traffickers treat the Channel like a motorway, spineless ministers have been missing in action.

Labour promised to smash the gangs and stop the boats. But statistics show the complete opposite, with 23 dinghies arriving in the past week alone.

This isn’t just a failure of leadership — it’s a dereliction of duty.



Lag free-for-all

LABOUR’S soft-touch early release scheme has handed hardened criminals a free pass to terrorise our communities.

Probation chiefs warned the system would be unable to cope with such a surge in freed offenders — and now we are witnessing the results.

More than 5,000 lags who were supposed to be electronically tagged were freed without the device being fitted.

And a staggering 95 per cent of those who breached their tagging conditions were simply bailed back into the community with “zero sanction”.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

That means thousands of potentially dangerous crooks — including domestic abusers and stalkers — are on the loose and nobody knows where they are.



This rash scheme has opened the prison gates while locking thousands of crime victims in a cage of fear.

News.title: From ‘brain dead’ to walking & talking – the ‘poison paradox’ that helped Christa Pike beat executioner’s needle
News.content:
Next

CHRISTA Pike may have survived two rounds of lethal injection drugs because of a bizarre paradox that saw the drug fail to kill her while potentially helping protect her brain, a medical expert has claimed.

Death row inmate Pike, 50, was administered pentobarbital during her botched execution in Tennessee before the procedure was called off.



Her attorneys have since revealed she is now awake, talking and walking after spending days unconscious and on a ventilator in the hospital.

The U.S. Sun spoke exclusively to Dr. Kenneth Katz, a medical toxicologist who has published case reports involving two women who survived severe pentobarbital poisoning, including a 94-year-old woman who spent days unresponsive before fully recovering.



Katz believes the execution team may have blown Pike’s veins, causing pentobarbital to leak into the tissue of her arms and form what he described as a localized “poison depot.”

Instead of the lethal drug rapidly flooding her bloodstream, he said it may then have been absorbed more slowly into her system — potentially helping explain why she became profoundly unconscious but survived.

And the pentobarbital that did reach her bloodstream may have had another unexpected effect — suppressing her brain’s demand for oxygen and potentially protecting it while she was unconscious.

“It appeared that both of her forearms, her arms were swollen and injured, probably because the drug had extravasated or leaked either from a blown vein or the catheter didn’t function properly,” Katz said.

“So I think what happened was she got some of the dose in the vein, probably, because she was comatose at that what it appeared to be, but probably not enough to be lethal,” he said.

The pentobarbital that leaked into her arms may then have remained trapped in the surrounding tissue rather than immediately circulating through her body.



“The drug is an alkaline drug, so it can cause swelling, burning, inflammation, pain,” Katz said.

“It sort of acted like a little depot in the tissue. The paradox is that [the drug] can actually make that tissue less demanding of oxygen.

“It’s almost neuroprotective at the same time.”



Katz said that creates a remarkable paradox in cases of severe pentobarbital poisoning, where the drug can profoundly suppress the body without necessarily causing permanent neurological damage if the dose is survived.

“So you have a drug that in extreme amounts can obviously kill you,” he said.

“But at the same time, if it’s not to that degree, it can cause coma but also be neuroprotective at the same time.”

The 94-year-old patient Katz studied had ingested pentobarbital alongside another barbiturate and became completely unresponsive before waking on the third day with no memory of what had happened.

She was discharged from hospital 11 days later.



Katz said the drug’s effects can mimic the signs of brain death, despite a patient later regaining consciousness and neurological function.

That could shed light on what happened in Pike’s case, after her lawyers believed she was brain dead and expected her to be taken off life support before she suddenly woke up and began talking.

Asked if he thinks Pike could eventually walk out of the hospital, Katz said, “If she received adequate ventilation, oxygenation, in theory, I would not be stunned if she has a complete neurologic recovery.”

But he said the crucial question for Pike’s long-term recovery is whether her brain was deprived of oxygen at any point during the failed execution.

“The brain does not tolerate that for very long, for only a few minutes or so,” he said. “And that can cause what we call anoxic brain injury.”



Katz said doctors can use MRI scans to look for evidence of damage caused by a lack of oxygen, while Pike now being awake, speaking and beginning to walk are encouraging signs.

The other case Katz studied involved a 48-year-old woman who injected a veterinary euthanasia solution containing pentobarbital.

Discussing the case, Katz said, “One woman was out cold, out in a coma for several days, and then just woke up and we took the tube out, we extubated.

“She didn’t recall all the events, but she understood generally what had happened.”

The woman also suffered severe damage to her arm where the drug was injected and required emergency surgery, but ultimately woke up neurologically normal and recovered.



Katz said there could be similarities to the severe arm injuries Pike suffered after around seven needles were reportedly used in attempts to establish IV access.

The 48-year-old woman developed compartment syndrome, where pressure builds inside the arm and begins restricting blood flow to the muscles and surrounding tissue.

If the pressure becomes severe enough, surgeons can perform an emergency operation known as a fasciotomy, cutting open the tissue surrounding the affected compartment to release it.

Katz likened the procedure to “popping a balloon,” allowing blood to properly flow through the affected tissue again.

“Once you relieve that pressure, now the blood flow can improve, perfuse the tissue, and then there’s a recovery from the physical fasciotomy,” he said.



“It can be limb saving and people can recover fairly well from that.”

But Katz said severe compartment syndrome would generally be identified relatively quickly.

If Pike has avoided that complication, he said her treatment could instead involve pain control, elevation, gentle movement and allowing the swelling to subside.

“She’s dealing with sort of a liquid burn, if you will, a chemical burn,” he said.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Despite Pike’s injuries, Katz said, “The human body is remarkably resilient. That is one thing I have seen over the years, and it can take a lot of beating.”



To watch Dr. Katz’s full interview on Christa Pike’s recovery, visit The U.S. Sun’s YouTube channel.

News.title: Body found in search for missing ‘family friend’ of Marcus Rashford who disappeared in Colombia two months ago
News.content:
TRAGIC FIND Body found in search for missing ‘family friend’ of Marcus Rashford who disappeared in Colombia two months ago







Next

A BODY has been found in the search for a “family friend” of Marcus Rashford after he disappeared in Colombia two months ago.

Anton Green, from Manchester, moved to the South American country three years ago before his loved ones lost contact with him in August.



His family have now been told a body has been discovered and it is believed to be the 43-year-old, reports BBC.

They told the broadcaster they were “trying to come to terms with what’s happened”.



They have been tortured by weeks of radio silence from the Brit and had last heard from him on August 6.

Anton’s family had launched a desperate plea for help finding him, urging anyone with information about his whereabouts to come forwards.



Even footballer Marcus Rashford joined the search for Anton, calling him “a family friend”.

Anton’s mum Nyla Green, 64, said Rashford had played with her youngest son, ex-Manchester United youth team defender Ro-shaun Williams, both at the academy and at junior football club Fletcher Moss.



She told The Sun it was “very nice of him” to share the appeal for Anton, adding: “We’ve known Marcus since they were six, seven years old. So he’s like a son to us.”

Anton, originally from Whalley Range, Manchester, settled near Colombia‘s capital Bogotá, three years ago.

He was staying around the Fontibón and Mesitas del Colegio areas before he vanished and may have been planning a trip to neighbouring Ecuador.

He spoke Spanish and Dutch fluently, and had moved out to Colombia three years ago, where he works remotely.

But his loved ones hadn’t heard from the Brit since August 6.



Nyla, a teaching assistant, said when she last spoke to Anton they ended the call saying: “We’ll speak next week.”

Anton’s dad last spoke to him on August 5 and a friend in Colombia reportedly heard from him the next day.

Neither reported anything unusual at the time but his family said his phone had been switched off since August 8.



And his friends in Colombia had not heard from him either.

Anton’s sister, Sian Tuohey, 40, told The Sun her worst fear would be him “not being alive”.

Sian described her older brother as a “great uncle” with a “love of learning languages”.

Mum Nyla said Anton grew up as a “typical young boy, really mischievous, funny, really bright”.

He travelled around Europe before moving to South America.



She said: “He was keen on learning languages. He liked to know about the world and loved animals as well.”

The family said this time last year he started struggling with his mental health, and had been suffering with low mood.

Nyla said it was difficult to see her son suffer from far away, adding: “I continued to talk to him and reassure him that he’s loved and that we’re here for him.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Anton’s sister said it was particularly hard that he was missing more than 5,000miles away from family.

The family said previously the UK police were limited in what they could do, but that working with Colombian cops had been difficult, with Nyla saying the search process had been “extremely slow”.

News.title: ADHD and autism at risk of over-diagnosis, says government review
News.content:
There is a risk of people being over-diagnosed with ADHD and autism, an official review in England has found.

Experts said a rise in diagnoses over the past 25 years meant cases now appear to be outstripping the expected number in the population for some younger age groups.

The review called for tougher regulation of private firms offering assessments for the NHS, saying they had concerns about quality and consistency, and a ban on advertising.

It concluded economic uncertainty combined with social media was driving an increase in mental health problems among young people and said there needed to be better support in place for all conditions.

The review - led by leading doctors in the field - was ordered 10 months ago by Wes Streeting after the then-health secretary claimed in an interview that young people were over-diagnosed and "written off".

It looked at people of all ages, but particularly focused on young people and children who have the highest rates of diagnoses.

It is likely to feed into government policies on everything from NHS services and benefits to support for young people who are not in education, employment or training.

News.title: Polanski failed to show leadership over Zionism motion, ex-Green leader says
News.content:
Zack Polanski failed to show leadership over a motion passed by Green Party members declaring Zionism a form of racism, the party's former leader Caroline Lucas has told the BBC.

Lucas told Newsnight that the party's current leader, who did not attend the debate on the motion at the Green Party's annual conference in Brighton, "should have been there and he should have voted".

She described the motion, which defined Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state", as "dangerous" and "divisive".

In the wake of the vote, Polanski has said he will not accept anyone being excluded from the Green Party "because of the religious or communal body they are part of".

Lucas's comments came after polls closed in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election, where Polanski is standing as a candidate.

Polanski did not vote on the motion after leaving the party's conference early to campaign in the north London constituency.

The Green leader has declined media interviews since the motion was passed on Sunday and did not answer questions from a BBC reporter about the motion earlier on Thursday.

The motion also backed a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine", which includes modern-day Israel.

Under Green Party rules, motions supported by members become official party policy, but will not necessarily be included in the party's manifesto at the next general election.

Lucas, who voted against the motion, said: "I would have hoped [Polanski] would have been a very strong critic of this motion."

She added that it was "flawed from top to bottom".

Asked if Polanski should stand down, she told Newsnight: "I think let's just see what happens in the coming days and weeks. Obviously he has been completely taken up with this by-election.

"I want him to speak now about what's happened, I want him to show the leadership that was frankly missing on Sunday.

"I think the jury is out about whether he will do that - but I very much hope he will."

In response to Lucas's comments, a Green Party source said: "There are ups and downs in politics and when people are passionate they disagree in the heat of a campaign.

"We do things differently - unlike Labour who use anonymous sources and resort to factionalism."

News.title: Warrants used to search Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor's homes were unlawful, court says
News.content:
Thames Valley Police has accepted warrants it used to search Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor's homes at the time of his arrest in February were unlawful, the High Court has been told.

Following Thursday's hearing, items seized in the raid continue to be held by the police, with a further hearing to take place in 2027 to decide whether the material can be used as evidence.

Meanwhile, the criminal investigation into Mountbatten-Windsor is ongoing.

The former prince, who denies any wrongdoing, was arrested by police on 19 February on suspicion of misconduct in public office, after which he launched a legal challenge over the legality of the search warrants.

The force said it accepted that the "initial court's decision to issue warrants under the specific piece of legislation used was incorrect" before they searched the properties.

On Thursday at the High Court, judge Mr Justice Hilliard said Mountbatten-Windsor and the police had agreed that the search warrants had been unlawful.

However, he added: "The fact that the search warrants were quashed does not bring the investigation to an end or mean that the whole of the investigation is unlawful."

Mountbatten-Windsor opposes the police's bid to retain the evidence, the judge said, and another hearing is expected in 2027.

News.title: Emotions run high at the round table as Celebrity Traitors banish two players
News.content:
Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from the third episode of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.

We normally expect raised voices, conflicting theories and a dramatic showdown from the Celebrity Traitors. But as this year's first round table got under way, the writing was on the castle wall.

Viewers who often get frustrated with the faithful and root for them to uncover a traitor had their wish firmly Richard E Grant-ed on Thursday, as the actor was banished in a landslide vote.

His questionable strategy of revealing he was a traitor to the other celebrities in the bar led to the first time in the UK version of the show that a traitor has been identified at the opening round table.

"Thank you for giving me an almost bingo full-house of votes," Grant told his fellow players. "I have always wanted to be a traitor, and sometimes in life your dreams do come true."

There was jubilation from the other celebrities as Grant confirmed his identity, waving his hands in the air. Ross Kemp was so happy it came out as borderline anger, with a vein-popping "get in there!"

Other players seemed genuinely shocked. "This is me with men all the time," joked comedian Joanne McNally, who hadn't voted for Grant. "I completely believed him!"

But although the faithful had successfully found a traitor, and even managed to spell his name correctly on their slates, the first round table saw some other players behave in ways that immediately aroused suspicion.

News.title: Mark Zuckerberg has an image problem - so why is Meta's business booming?
News.content:
Mark Zuckerberg was just three minutes into his keynote speech at the company's annual Meta Connect product event last month when his tone turned almost wistful.

"Building is an act of love," he said, glancing down at the ground with his hands in his pockets. "It's how we impart what we believe, and we pour our hearts and our souls into what we make."

Speaking to hundreds of analysts and developers, Zuckerberg proceeded to share news about Meta's latest AI products: its new agentic chatbot Muse, a slew of smart glasses, as well as a Tamagotchi-like AI gadget users can attach to their wrists.

It was a conference focused on new technologies - but still, it's perhaps notable that during a presentation lasting nearly an hour, Zuckerberg did not mention two of his most popular products, Instagram and Facebook, the social media platforms that have helped Meta become a $2tn company.

For much of the past year, Meta has been embroiled in a series of legal actions, accused of deliberately designing products that are addictive to young users.

That has led to the release of internal emails, corporate documents and whistleblower testimony that personal injury lawyers and prosecutors across the country have wielded to make their case.

And Zuckerberg is unpopular: last year, a Pew Research Center poll found that two-thirds of Americans had an unfavourable opinion of him.

News.title: 'Add me to WhatsApp' scam calls to be investigated
News.content:
The UK's data watchdog is investigating a spike in complaints about "robo calls" - where a recorded voice asks you to add them on WhatsApp - that are suspected to lead to a recruitment scam.

The Information Commission's Office (ICO) had more than 3,600 complaints about automated calls in September - a five-year high and nearly three times the number it had in July.

But it suspects millions of people are getting these calls and told BBC Radio 4's You and Yours it was "deeply concerned" by the sharp rise.

The ICO advises people to ignore calls from numbers they don't recognise, and to block and report any suspicious calls to the watchdog.

The automated calls typically come from what appears to be a UK mobile number.

Some of the recorded messages mention an offer of part-time work.

Simon Fell, from the Communications Crime Strategy Group, a telecoms industry body set up to tackle fraud, said he couldn't be sure exactly what form the scam would take as he hadn't followed up on the messages.

"Mostly likely it would be a recruitment scam," he said.

News.title: Two Latvian men arrested on suspicion of trespass at RAF base in Cambridgeshire
News.content:
Two Latvian men were arrested after a fence was breached at an RAF base used by the US military and Nato for intelligence operations, counter-terrorism police have said.

The alert was raised when a Ministry of Defence Police (MDP) security patrol at RAF Molesworth identified an abandoned vehicle at about 22:00 BST on Wednesday.

Searches revealed a small breach of the fence at the site in Cambridgeshire, and a few hours later, police said the pair were arrested inside the perimeter.

The two men are aged 36 and 32 and live in the UK, the Met Police said.

The force's Counter Terrorism Policing London is investigating and commander Helen Flanagan said officers were not currently linking it to the high-profile incident in Gloucestershire.

"We're very aware of the recent heightened interest and concern around military sites, but at this stage there is nothing to suggest this incident is connected to the events at RAF Fairford last week," said Flanagan.

However, she stressed the inquiry was in its "very early stages".

They were initially arrested on suspicion of trespass on a prohibited site and criminal damage - after Cambridgeshire Police officers joined the search - and were taken to a local station.

The pair were later arrested on suspicion of an offence under Section 4 of the National Security Act 2023, external â namely entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK.

RAF Molesworth is home to the US's intelligence operations centres for Europe and Africa, as well as a Nato intelligence hub.

It is not used as a flying station.

News.title: Harry says he 'slipped into depression' after leaving UK
News.content:
The Duke of Sussex has said he "slipped into depression for about two weeks" after relocating to Canada in 2019 ahead of his move to the US.

Prince Harry, who recently returned to the UK with his wife Meghan and their two children, said he had originally left the country to "get some space."

The duke also discussed feeling "emotionally numb" after the death of his mother Diana, Princess of Wales, because he felt "disloyal and guilty for the possibility of being happy and joyful without her".

He opened up about his mental health with a neuroscientist in a session for a video learning platform.

He and his brother, the Prince of Wales, have previously been candid about their mental health struggles, including over their mother's death, and both are involved in mental health charities.

Prince Harry, who stepped back from royal duties to move to California with Meghan, made the latest comments as part of a paid-for online masterclass on dealing with grief.

"Being in Canada, away from the stressful environment where presumably my body was just pumped full of adrenaline, within two or three days, I experienced this adrenaline crash, something that I'd never experienced before," he recalled.

"It was as if I needed stress in order to get the adrenaline to make my brain function because I became useless around the house.

"I actually slipped into depression for about two weeks and I felt like I couldn't function without adrenaline."

News.title: Three sisters who drowned in sea off Brighton took own lives, inquest finds
News.content:
Three sisters who drowned in the sea off Brighton took their own lives, a coroner has ruled.

Jane Adetoro, 36, Christina Walters, 32, and Rebecca Walters, 31, had been living "very secluded lives" following the death of their mother, who drowned in 2010, senior coroner Penelope Schofield said.

On 11 May, the women - who had all been living together in Greenford, London - visited an area of Birmingham close to where their mother died before travelling the next day to Brighton beach, where they drowned in adverse sea conditions in the early hours of 13 May. The coroner said they could not swim.

Their father Joseph Jacobsen said it was heartbreaking to lose "all three of my precious daughters".

He was among family members who followed proceedings via video link.

In an emotional statement read out on his behalf, he said he watched his daughters grow from little girls to beautiful, intelligent women "with a special place in my heart".

He said: "There are no words that can adequately express the pain of losing a child.

"To lose all three of my precious daughters is a heartbreak beyond anything I could ever have imagined."

He could not understand why his daughters' lives ended so suddenly, and hoped they were reunited with their mother "in God's eternal care", he added.

If you are experiencing emotional stress, help and support is available via the BBC Action Line here.

The coroner told the court: "These three sisters lived very secluded lives, they were incredibly private, we don't know why they took this course of action or indeed why they chose to do it in Brighton.

"It is not for the court to speculate and sadly these reasons may never be known."

News.title: Royal Navy sailor in court accused of preparing to spy for Russia
News.content:
A junior Royal Navy sailor accused of preparing to spy for Russia has appeared in court.

Able Seaman Teddy Young, who specialised in warfare intelligence, allegedly retained UK defence and intelligence material that he had access to and made preparations to disclose sensitive information, a court was told.

The 24-year-old appeared at Westminster Magistrates' Court on Thursday after being charged under the National Security Act.

The BBC understands that the allegations against Young include translating a message into Russian and looking for a web portal that invited people to submit information to Russia.

Wearing a police-issue grey sweatshirt, Young spoke in court to confirm his name, date of birth and his address in Clapham, near Bedford.

He is formally charged with engaging in conduct in preparation for disclosing protected information, and obtaining, copying, recording or retaining protected information, intending the conduct to benefit a foreign power.

The charges cover a period between 26 November 2024 and 21 May 2025.

"The allegation is that while serving as a Royal Navy warfare intelligence rating with high level security clearance and intelligence-system access, Teddy Stanley Greenidge Young accessed and retained sensitive UK defence and intelligence material and engaged in activity consistent with preparing to pass protected information to a foreign power," the Crown Prosecution Service told the court in a written summary of the allegations.

Police said the alleged offences were not related to the recent RAF Fairford incident that resulted in a number of arrests after suspicious activity was reported near the base.

In total, seven men have been arrested and later released on bail in connection with the incident, which is being investigated by counter-terror police.

Young was arrested at his home address in Bedfordshire on Tuesday.

He is the first member of the armed forces to be charged under the new National Security Act 2023.

Cdr Helen Flanagan, head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, said: "These are very serious charges against a serving member of the armed forces.

"We have worked extremely closely with relevant operational colleagues within the Ministry of Defence as our investigation has progressed to ensure appropriate measures could be taken to mitigate any potential risks linked to this matter."

A Royal Navy spokesperson confirmed a service member had been charged and added: "As legal proceedings are ongoing, it would be inappropriate to comment further at this stage."

Judge Annabel Pilling remanded Young in custody. He will next appear at the Old Bailey on 16 October.

News.title: Death prompts call for allergy management ratings
News.content:
Assistant coroner Briony Ballard listened to evidence at London Inner South Coroner's Court before publishing a narrative conclusion on Mia's death.

In a statement read after the conclusion of the inquest, Mia's parents Adrian St Hilaire and Chanel Spence said families with food allergies should not be "at risk" when eating out.

"We hope that lessons will be learned from Mia's death and that changes will be made to prevent other families enduring the devastation that we now have to live with," they said.

"Consumers rely on food hygiene ratings when deciding where it is safe to eat, but they do not tell us anything about the way a food business runs allergy management systems.

"There should be a separate, clearly displayed rating dedicated to the allergy management, like the food hygiene rating.

"This would mean that people with allergies could make more informed choices about where they eat."

Natasha's Foundation founder Tanya Ednan-Laperouse, whose daughter died aged 15 from an allergy to sesame in a Pret A Manger baguette, said allergies were "a serious, unpredictable medical condition".

"The inquest into Mia's death illustrates just how far we still have to go to improve awareness, understanding and regulation of food allergies," she said.

"Natasha's Foundation is working hard with business, schools, communities and the government to increase awareness and understanding of food allergies to try to prevent other families from having to go through the terrible loss that Mia's family endure."

Rebecca Sudworth, director of food policy at the Food Standards Agency, said her "deepest sympathies" were with Mia's family.

"Food businesses must take allergen risks seriously, every time," she said. "People have the right to know exactly what is in their food and drink, and it is a business's legal duty to provide accurate allergen information.

"We recently produced new guidance for businesses to make sure they understand their responsibilities to inform consumers about allergens, including the risk of cross-contact, and we are keeping this policy under review. We also have free allergy training and practical tools that businesses can use."

News.title: Forty five Scottish police officers suspended over alleged crimes against women
News.content:
Police Scotland has said 45 serving officers are currently suspended over allegations of violence against women and girls.

Chief constable Jo Farrell said she expected more would face sanctions over their behaviour following a spate of former officers being convicted for sexual offences.

Farrell said a review into the handling of the case surrounding officer Alan Greer â who was exposed as a serial rapist after taking his own life â was under way.

She added about 8,000 members of staff were still to be "re-vetted" for their roles after a change in regulations earlier this year.

First minister John Swinney said he had "full confidence" in Police Scotland and the renewed vetting process.

In an interview with BBC Scotland News, Farrell described the scale of violence against women and girls in Scotland as an "epidemic", and that police forces were not immune to the problem.

She said: "We've got in the order of between currently 40 and 50 people currently suspended, so not at work, who are being investigated for offences that relate to violence against women and girls.

"Those investigations are at various stages."

News.title: Asos hackers took more personal details than first revealed, BBC finds
News.content:
Asos has told its customers that hackers are in possession of detailed profiles of potentially millions of the online store's users.

It issued the update after BBC News told the retailer it had been contacted by cyber criminals who said this week's breach went beyond the "basic contact details" Asos previously said might have been accessed.

Names, addresses, phone numbers, emails, customer numbers and dates of birth are now in the hands of criminals.

One victim told the BBC it was "very unsettling" that the hackers now know these things about her.

The criminals also have access to the searches customers have made on the website. Terms like "reclaimed vintage", "glamorous wide fit" and "Asos petite" are visible in the data.

Harriet has been using Asos since 2019 - another detail the hackers now know.

"What I find particularly worrying is the possibility that stolen data can be used as a tool for for future attacks, meaning the impact of a breach could extend well beyond the initial incident," she said.

With the stolen information, scammers may be able to create convincing phishing attack emails or phone calls.

The risk to individuals is now higher and customers are being warned about potential impersonation scams.

In its email to customers, Asos confirmed data profiles were taken but said no bank details or passwords were accessed.

"Please remain cautious of unexpected messages or calls claiming to be from Asos," it said.

"We will never ask you to share passwords, security codes or payment details through an unsolicited message or call."

The company did not respond to questions about the scale of the breach.

News.title: Birmingham Airport announces £2bn expansion
News.content:
Birmingham Airport has announced a Â£2bn expansion plan which bosses say could more than double passenger numbers and create thousands of jobs.

The draft plan, a spokesperson said, sets out the use of existing runway capacity alongside "significantly enhanced" passenger facilities over the next 15 years.

Unveiling an eight-week public consultation, chief executive Nick Barton said the scheme aims to ensure the airport was "ready for the future" but needed a "fair and stable taxation environment".

Transport secretary Heidi Alexander said the government was "backing our aviation sector to continue growing, right across the country".

In 2025, the airport said it had seen a record year with more than 13 million passengers travelling through it. Bosses want to see this rise by more than double, up to 30 million a year.

Airport chiefs said the proposals set out a "clear commitment" to continue serving the region and create more than 50,000 jobs, including 3,800 at the airport site.

They added that they wanted to make sure the growth was "delivered responsibly and sustainably" for the people living closes to the site.

The first stage of development could start in 2027, with significant investments in areas such as baggage and terminal facilities, additional aircraft stands and improvements in surface access.

Hundreds of passengers were affected by issues with the airport's baggage system in August, with many left without their luggage.

People can give feedback on the plans online, by post or attend any of the 20 events, which start in Hampton on Arden on 16 October, external.

News.title: E-bike battery in fatal fire had repairs - inquest
News.content:
An e-bike battery linked to a fire which killed a mother and two children had issues prior to the blaze, an inquest has heard.

Gemma Germeney, 31, and children Lilly, eight, and Oliver, four, lost their lives in the fire on Sackville Close in Cambridge on 30 June 2023. The children's father, Scott Peden, survived.

Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service said at the time the most probable cause of the fire was an e-bike that was charging.

Scott Peden told the inquest he had bought a replacement battery after the previous one had been stolen and the bike later cut out, and had visited a repairman twice for work done.

Peden told the inquest he had purchased the bike online for Â£900 and it was in "perfect working order", apart from an incident where he lost the key on a fairground ride.

He said the battery was stolen a few months later and they researched a new one, but it would have been "quite a lot of money and I couldn't afford it at the time".

News.title: Woman told PC 'get off me' 300 times as he raped her
News.content:
A woman told a police officer to "get off me" more than 300 times as he subjected her to an 82-minute violent rape in a Liverpool hotel room.

Former Merseyside Police constable Ryan Theaker, 30, was secretly recorded by the victim after a night out in 2023.

The woman, who cannot be named to protect her anonymity, read an emotional statement at Liverpool Crown Court and faced the dock as she told Theaker "monsters never win".

He was designated a "dangerous" offender by a judge and jailed for 11 years with an extended five-year licence period.

Warning: This story contains distressing details of sexual violence.

Theaker, from Park Lane in Netherton, had been convicted of rape, sexual assault and assault by penetration after a trial last month.

Gareth Roberts, prosecuting, said the audio recordings captured Theaker demanding the woman let him take naked pictures of her, despite her saying she did not want him to.

He also assaulted her with sex toys he had brought to the hotel, the court heard.

News.title: A former SSPX priest embraces life as a gay man and tattoo artist
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

In March 2024, Francis Palmquist bent over his right calf and carefully tattooed the tear rolling down Mary’s cheek as depicted in the famous image. It was six years after he left Catholic priesthood and the ultra-traditionalist Society of St. Pius X.

“Happy Mary doesn’t resonate with me, but Mary in front of the cross feeling so much sorrow — a sword going through her heart — that’s where I relate,” Palmquist said. “Our Lady of Sorrows” was the first piece he tattooed on himself in the realism style, which has quickly become his signature.

In some traditionalist circles, Palmquist’s story — from SSPX priest to his two-year stint on YouTube discussing the faith and being gay — is already infamous. Unlike in more mainstream branches of Catholicism, there aren’t other former members of the society, which rejects many Second Vatican Council reforms, who are talking on the internet about coming out. But in the last four years, Palmquist’s online presence has reflected his new vocation: a dedication to his clients and tattooing craft through his business, St. Francis Tattoo.

In some traditionalist circles, Palmquist’s story — from SSPX priest to his two-year stint on YouTube discussing the faith and being gay — is already infamous. Unlike in more mainstream branches of Catholicism, there aren’t other former members of the society, which rejects many Second Vatican Council reforms, who are talking on the internet about coming out. But in the last four years, Palmquist’s online presence has reflected his new vocation: a dedication to his clients and tattooing craft through his business, St. Francis Tattoo.

“He’s a prophet for authenticity,” said C., a fan who asked to be identified by an initial only to maintain relationships with his family. A former older Latin Mass attendee, C. said the vulnerability Palmquist shares, still without attacking the church, helped him to be more authentic and less ideologically defensive.

The journey to this point — where Palmquist, 37, is fully “being myself,” living with his partner and throwing himself into his art — has not been easy, he recalled to RNS during an August interview at the tattoo studio in Exton, Pennsylvania where he works. Leaving the priesthood in 2017 was so traumatic that his brain “shut off religion,” he said. He’s not sure he’d remember the steps of the Mass. But he has also spent his years since then inscribing symbols from his former life all over his body — an owl carrying the Sacred Heart of Jesus on his chest, the Immaculate Heart of Mary just below it and Mary Magdalene above the devil on his right arm. He has asked himself, “Why the heck am I getting all these religious tattoos?”

Growing up in Belmont, North Carolina, a Charlotte suburb, Palmquist doesn’t remember being interested in religion when his family attended the most common Catholic liturgy, known to traditionalists as the Novus Ordo. But after his mother decided the family would attend an SSPX chapel when he was a preteen, he threw himself in head first.

“ There was almost like this silent competition for who could be holier,” said Ryan Arcia, a lifelong friend whose family switched to the same SSPX parish around the same time.

The SSPX is known for celebrating the older Latin Mass, a liturgy used before the modernizing reforms of the Second Vatican Council. The reforms that the SSPX rejects include celebrating Mass in local languages and embracing dialogue with other religions. After ordaining bishops in July without the pope’s approval, the group and the lay Catholics who formally participate in it were excommunicated.

he SSPX, which says there are approximately 25,000 lay people attending its chapels in the U.S., represents just a fraction of the Catholics in the U.S. who attend the older Latin Mass.

But Palmquist’s priest went beyond typical early 2000s SSPX traditionalism. He recommended parishioners get rid of their televisions and rock-and-roll albums, Arcia remembers. Palmquist said the priest reinforced a version of masculinity that felt inaccessible.

Arcia said he never wondered whether Palmquist might be gay — even when he was “sticking up” for his friend when other boys called him feminine. “That’s the very last thing you think about your best friend” in that world, Arcia said.

But Palmquist said he always felt a “natural attraction” to men. Confused, he found “peace” and “order” at Mass and looked for every opportunity to be in the church. Like many SSPX young men, he began to consider becoming a priest.

Massimo Introvigne, a sociologist at the Center for Studies on New Religions based in Italy, who interviewed SSPX founder Archbishop Marcel Lefebvre, said Lefebvre’s goal was to “freeze the priesthood as it was in the 1950s,” placing heightened importance on the role.

Palmquist referred to his seven years in a Winona, Minnesota, seminary as “militaristic.” He thought he was “getting over” his attraction to men, but he now recognizes that was “a facade.” Looking back, he believes his spiritual director, with whom he was “100% open,” should have cautioned him against getting ordained.

But instead, in June 2016, he laid face down outside the seminary chapel and was ordained. The back of Palmquist’s ordination card reads, “I thirst,” chosen because of his intense spirituality.

Instead of joining his classmates in English-language ministries, he moved to Guadalajara, Mexico, to hear confessions, give homilies and teach philosophy in Spanish — a language he barely knew.

"Back then, I just bulldozed through my limitations, and I couldn’t do enough. I couldn’t be enough,” Palmquist said. “Once you’re known for being that person who goes the extra mile, then that’s the expectation, especially for yourself.”

Soon, his situation began spiraling out of control, he said. His superiors seemed to dislike him because he was American, and he struggled to connect with the other priests. Missing community, he downloaded an anonymous chat app and connected with other gay men.

Many of the conversations were “normal,” Palmquist remembers, “ but it was the first time I heard someone say, like, ‘You’re really handsome.’”

“ This was like the beginning of my little double life,” he said.

He struggled with sleep and disordered eating, going from 180 to 140 pounds. He began drinking as his mental health worsened. “It got to the point where I looked in the mirror and it was like I was a shell of who I was before,” he said.

Palmquist said his seminary rector suggested he pray more. But he also told Palmquist, “ I don’t think you were ever supposed to be a priest.” Eventually Palmquist asked his Mexican superiors for a therapist — help that Palmquist said never arrived. (The director of communications for the SSPX District of the USA did not respond to a request for comment.)

Rather, in December 2017, his superior told Palmquist he’d be going to a house in Kansas City known to take problem priests. He contacted a friend he met at a gay bar, “freaking out,” he recalled. The next night, hours before he was supposed to leave for Kansas City, he met that friend and disappeared in the middle of the night.

Arcia, who also left SSPX, learned about Palmquist’s exit from his mother. “ Francis was kind of a celebrity within the SSPX — a lot of people knew who he was — so when he left, it was a bigger thing than it needed to be,” Arcia said.

Palmquist spent the next seven years in Mexico, trying to find financial stability, reinventing himself and going to therapy. A month after he left the priesthood, he got his first tattoo — the owl carrying a Sacred Heart across his chest. It was a nod to the idea that owls “see the clearest in the dark.” In that dark period of his life, he felt he could see clearly, but he wanted to move forward with “the heart” of his past, he said.

“ I’m going to live this new life, but as close to being a Catholic as possible,” he said of his mindset. He added, these “were ideas that I had meditated hours on, that I had dissected, that I had attacked and tried to refute."

Through his first gay relationship, Palmquist met a tattoo artist and realized it was a career in which he could incorporate his longtime love of art. He also began to write a book about his experience leaving the priesthood.

His therapist suggested he try making YouTube videos before releasing the book to test out dealing with public exposure, creating his channel, “ I am Judas Project, ” in 2020. Palmquist said he wanted to prevent others in similar situations from “feeling so alone.”

During his two years on YouTube, he felt ready to move back to the U.S. and started to put down roots in Philadelphia. And as his focus shifted toward tattooing, Palmquist gave up the channel.

His business, St. Francis Tattoo, is a nod to his religious past. “I definitely don’t think I’m a saint,” he said, laughing. But he works below a San Damiano crucifix, the image of Christ that spoke to St. Francis and eventually led him to renounce worldly goods to serve the church.

"The Franciscans in general, their whole lives were given to the poor — just complete self-dedication for others. And that’s how I want to live my life,” Palmquist said.

Now, he channels his impulse for service into his work with tattoo clients, he said. Doing excellent work isn’t enough — Palmquist finds himself checking in on and caring for them, “kind of being a priest to them in a sense.”

Lindsay Healey, a client, said her experience working with Palmquist has been different from other artists she has worked with. For her first tattoo with him, Palmquist is creating an arm sleeve that brings the figures on playing cards to life.

“ I’m actually a pretty shy person, but he made me feel really comfortable, and through the sessions, he’s constantly checking on me” to make sure she can tolerate the pain, Healey said. “He’s a great artist, but honestly, he is an even better friend.”

Palmquist hopes to have the opportunity to mentor other tattoo artists. “ Art has always been about passing down the knowledge that was given to you,” he said. “ There’s so much good with what we’ve been given from the past.”

His skepticism of modernity impacts his feelings about LGBTQ+ Catholic Masses. He said he attended a few and felt like he was being pandered to.

At seminary, Palmquist said he learned Catholic doctrine cannot change without becoming “unrecognizable.” Of proponents of LGBTQ-affirming Catholicism, Palmquist asked, “ Are they doing it because it’s the truth, or are they doing it because it’s just the modern thing now?”

Still, Palmquist said he feels at peace and sees his gay relationships as confirmation he made the right decision to leave the priesthood. “I think I am where I should be,” he said.

And, right now, he doesn’t feel the need to work out the conflict between the doctrine of his former faith and his current life. “I’m not at my destination yet,” he said. “I never want to come across like I’m some beacon of whatever. It’s just a very human experience.”

News.title: Man shot during apparent ICE operation in NYC, Gov. Hochul demands explanation
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

A man has been shot, apparently by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents during an operation in New York City, prompting Gov. Kathy Hochul to demand an explanation.

The shooting occurred at around 4 p.m. ET on Thursday in the Marble Hill neighborhood of the Bronx, the New York City Police Department wrote on X.

The NYPD said the shooting involved “federal law enforcement agents,” but didn’t specify which agency the officers were working under.

A city official told local outlet WABC that multiple shots were fired during what was believed to be an ICE operation. The official said the man was in a car when he was shot and a boy, believed to be 5 years old, was in the back seat unharmed.

open image in gallery A man has been shot by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents during an operation in New York City, according to officials ( AFP via Getty Images )

“The NYPD was not involved in the incident and was not on scene at the time of the shooting,” the department said. “The individual who was shot is at a nearby hospital and is currently conscious and receiving medical attention.”

One woman who witnessed the shooting said she initially thought the four shots she heard were a car backfiring.

She then thought, “‘No, that's definitely gunshots.’ So I ran to my window and all of a sudden I saw cops running – not walking — down the street, and followed shortly thereafter by more cops, and then more cops and ICE agents.

“Everybody was running. A lot of the ICE agents were, of course, masked,” the woman told WABC. “I think it's horrifying."

“It was really quick,” another witness told the outlet. “It was boom, boom, boom, boom, boom.” He said that others told him ICE was responsible for the shooting.

open image in gallery A city official told local news that the man was in a car when he was shot and a boy, believed to be 5 years old, was in the back seat unharmed ( AFP via Getty Images )

The Independent has reached out to the Department of Homeland Security and ICE for comment.

Hochul has demanded federal authorities explain what happened.

“I’ve been briefed on this afternoon’s shooting involving federal law enforcement agents in the Bronx,” Hochul wrote on X. “We expect federal authorities to provide a full and transparent accounting of the circumstances surrounding this incident.

“New Yorkers deserve to know exactly what happened and why.”

open image in gallery President Donald Trump’s massive deportation campaign has been criticized as too aggressive, with multiple shootings involving federal immigration agents making headlines ( AFP via Getty Images )

President Donald Trump’s massive deportation campaign has been criticized as too aggressive, with multiple shootings involving federal immigration agents making headlines.

In July, the Trump administration received fierce pushback after ICE agents fatally shot a 52-year-old Mexican man, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, in Houston and a 25-year-old Colombian native, Joan Sebastian Guerrero, in Maine at traffic stops less than a week apart.

DHS said an ICE officer fired his weapon at Guerrero because he feared for “public safety,” and Salgado Araujo was shot in “self-defense.”

About half of Americans, 49 percent, believe Trump’s mass deportations targeting illegal immigrants have been too aggressive, according to a Poliitco/Public First poll released in August.

Meanwhile, 30 percent of respondents said his immigration crackdown has been about right, 11 percent said it hasn’t been aggressive enough, and 10 percent were unsure.
