News.title: Carney says Canadians will decide their future after Elon Musk expresses support for separatism
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Thursday that Canada’s future will be decided by Canadians, pushing back on Elon Musk's call for Quebec, Alberta and Saskatchewan to separate from Canada.

“The future of Canada will be decided by Canadians and the priorities of Canadians, the priorities of the people of Quebec,” Carney said when asked about Musk’s comments.

Carney said Canadians should be free to live according to their languages and cultures, without interference "from foreign governments and large tech firms that think they can tell us what to do."

Musk weighed in on Canada’s separatist debates Wednesday in a post on X about Quebec Premier-designate Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, whose separatist Parti Québécois won Monday’s provincial election.

The PQ’s victory was not a mandate for independence. The party won about 28% of the popular vote and fell short of a majority of the seats in the Quebec legislature. Support for Quebec independence remains at about 30%, said Daniel Béland, a political science professor at McGill University in Montreal. He said the election was driven more by a desire to oust the Coalition Avenir Québec government than by support for separation.

“Good. Quebec should separate,” Musk wrote, adding that “They would be better off. Alberta and Saskatchewan should separate too.”

Alberta is scheduled to hold a vote Oct. 19 on whether the province should remain in Canada or move toward a future referendum on separation. Alberta Premier Danielle Smith has said she will vote to remain in Canada.

Smith said Thursday that separatist sentiment in her province has weakened as her government and Carney’s have worked to address Albertans’ concerns.

“The federal government has changed. Their approach to us has changed and they’re willing to work together on addressing those issues,” Smith said in Edmonton.

Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe responded to Musk on X with a single word: “No.”

Musk, the world’s richest man and first-ever trillionaire, is a South African-born Canadian-American.

News.title: JD Vance rebukes selling access to government officials after Kimberly Guilfoyle’s ‘unseemly’ texts revealed
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Vice President JD Vance has rebuked anyone selling access to government officials following a bombshell report that accused Kimberly Guilfoyle, the U.S. ambassador to Greece, of texting a donor to President Donald Trump to ask for money.

Days before her Senate confirmation hearing on July 9, 2025, Guilfoyle, the former fiancée of Donald Trump Jr., pleaded with Eric Deters, who was trying to get the Trump administration’s attention for personal tax and legal issues, to send $100,000 to pay off her American Express card, according to a Wall Street Journal report published Wednesday.

Guilfoyle disputed the authenticity of the texts between her and Deters, her lawyer, Jesse Binnall, told the Journal.

When asked about a hypothetical situation that strongly hinted towards Guilfoyle’s scandal, Vance said, “Obviously, I don’t love that.”

open image in gallery Vice President JD Vance has rebuked anyone selling access to government officials following a bombshell report that accused Kimberly Guilfoyle, the U.S. ambassador to Greece, of texting a donor to President Donald Trump to ask for money ( Getty Images )

“Do you have any reaction to a U.S. government official, in this case a U.S. ambassador, asking someone to pay off debt in exchange for access to other government officials?” CBS News’ Jennifer Jacobs asked the vice president during a press conference on the administration’s crackdown on alleged fraud in work visa programs Thursday.

“I don’t know exactly who you are talking about; I don’t know the full details,” Vance said.

“Of course I don't like anybody selling access to another government official, certainly a high-level government official, but I assume you are talking about a specific case and I can’t say with confidence that the case you’re talking about is actually reflective of the way you’re describing it,” the vice president continued.

“I’d like to get the full story before offering a real opinion.”

open image in gallery Guilfoyle, the former fiancée of Donald Trump Jr., reportedly asked the donor, who wanted access to the Trump administration, to send $100,000 to pay off her American Express card ( Pool/AFP via Getty Images )

Guilfoyle told Deters that she needed her credit card balance to be paid down before her confirmation hearing.

“Honey, please I need you to get this done for me today,” she said, according to a text message sent July 3, 2025, that was reviewed by the Journal.

Deters reportedly didn’t end up giving Guilfoyle the money, telling her it would cost him his marriage.

CNN Senior Political Contributor Scott Jennings, who has routinely defended the Trump administration on air, trashed Guilfoyle’s reported texts, calling them “unseemly.”

“It's extremely unseemly, these text messages. There's no other way to read it. Again, may not be illegal. Has to be investigated. I assume that at the State Department, that is the next thing that will happen,” he told his fellow panelists on The Arena with Kasie Hunt Thursday.

open image in gallery When asked about a hypothetical situation that strongly hinted towards Guilfoyle’s scandal, Vance said, “Obviously, I don’t love that.” ( Pool/Getty Images )

While on a trip to Greece, Secretary of State Marco Rubio lashed out at reporters when asked about the scandal.

"You guys somehow walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it’s the gospel. It’s not the gospel. It’s not the gospel for me," he said Thursday.

Jennings gave some advice to Guilfoyle: “If I were in her shoes right now, I would be considering what I wanted to tell the president, the secretary of state about my future.”

“Because when you're in an appointed position like this, and you hold a position of trust with the government, and then you become a distraction or an embarrassment to your principles, that's a problem,” the political pundit said.

“And if this story continues to spiral, or more bad information were to come out — only she would know that — and she needs to be transparent with her principles about that.”

News.title: Federal agents involved in a shooting that wounds a person in New York, police say
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Federal law enforcement agents shot and wounded a person in New York City on Thursday, city police said.

Few details were immediately available about the shooting, which happened around 4 p.m. The person who was shot is conscious and being treated at a hospital, the New York Police Department said in a post on X, noting that its officers didn’t witness the shooting and weren’t involved.

Messages seeking further information were sent to federal authorities.

An FBI spokesperson said an evidence response team was responding to the scene “to support our partners at the Department of Homeland Security,” but offered no other details.

The shooting happened in the Marble Hill neighborhood, a small part of Manhattan attached to the Bronx.

Pedro Almaraz, an employee at a nearby restaurant, said he heard about three or four gunshots and saw a man on the ground surrounded by several officers wearing face masks and vests with Department of Homeland Security branding. Witnesses, he said, were screaming.

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul, a Democrat, said in a post on social media that she had been briefed on the shooting.

“We expect federal authorities to provide a full and transparent accounting of the circumstances surrounding this incident. New Yorkers deserve to know exactly what happened and why,” she said.

News.title: Rent review – Gaten Matarazzo succeeds but his co-stars dazzle in a rock-solid musical revival
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Increasingly, Hollywood actors seem to arrive on London’s theatre scene to a blare of look-at-me fanfare: through press releases and tube posters, we are made acutely aware that these are big fishes splashing around in our somewhat smaller pond. For Gaten Matarazzo, there was no real splashing to speak of. When it was announced earlier this year that Jonathan Larson’s seminal rock musical Rent was returning to the West End after nearly three decades, the casting of 24-year-old Stranger Things star Matarazzo was never really pushed as the selling point. No, the big draw here is the material: a chance to see what has proven to be one of the most enduring musicals in decades, staged with a careful fidelity to its origins.

Here at the Tom Stoppard Theatre (recently renamed from the Duke of York’s), Matarazzo is Mark, budding filmmaker and somewhat nebbishy hanger-on to New York’s young, queer, bohemian milieu. It is Christmastime in the height of the AIDs crisis, and the virus has already torn through this social set: at the start of the play, several characters are already HIV positive, including the scared, pugnacious musician Roger (Travis Ross), and Mimi (Alexa Lopez), a troubled, vulnerable stripper with a drug problem. As Roger and Mimi indulge a fraught will-they/won’t-they/oh-for-the-love-of-God-just-do-it-already courtship, we see an easier, kinder love affair develop between gentle giant Collins (Billy Nevers) and Angel (Jeevan Braich), a flamboyant drag queen, both of whom have AIDs.

When Rent came out, it was transgressive in its candour, particularly in its handling of issues around AIDs; in the years since, this has almost become a reductive pigeonholing. In the puppet satire Team America: World Police, it was lampooned with the musical number “Everyone Has AIDS” – crass, yes, but indicative of just how Rent was perceived by the wider culture. Thirty years on from its original debut, though, it’s remarkable just how relevant the production still feels in places, how unlike anything else on stage at the moment. Even this year’s musical Pride, which explores similar themes and owes some of its DNA to Rent, feels less striking, less urgent.

It works, then, that Luke Sheppard’s production opts to reiterate more than reimagine, in everything down to the costumes (designed by Gabriella Slade, they have that familiar shabby, chic Rent look). There have been some technological advances since its original staging in 1993 – a judiciously used rotating floor works wonders as Ross sings the mournful “One Song Glory” early on, while live footage from Mark’s video camera is frequently fed through live to a constellation of retro TV screens dotted around the peripheries. But by and large, this is Rent as you’ve seen it before; the musical’s fresh relevance is supplied, by the audience, and the changed world that lurks outside the theatre.

open image in gallery Braich and Nevers in ‘Rent’ ( Pamela Raith )

Matarazzo doesn’t quite shine here, but it’s a hard role to shine. Mark is inherently, constitutionally passive, serving mostly as an outside observer and conduit for the audience. The former child star is affable and slightly dweeby in the role – there are shades of a young, pre-Seinfeld Jason Alexander – and sings well, though most of the other singers here, particularly Ross, Braich, and Nevers, are absolutely exceptional.

Larson’s death – at the age of 35, the day of Rent’s first preview – has always cast a strange light over this musical’s legacy. Unlike many of his characters, Larson did not know he was destined to die young (he didn’t have AIDs, but died suddenly, of a cardiovascular malfunction known as an aortic dissection), but he seemed to write as if he knew his time was up. Rent is a musical about finding ways to live life in the shadow of death – a theme that is, at the end of the day, universal. At the end of the day, the big question facing a revival like this is whether it can fundamentally justify its own existence. Rent manages that, and then some.

‘Rent’ is at the Tom Stoppard Theatre until May 2027

News.title: Not everyone with ADHD and autism traits needs a diagnosis, major review finds
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

ADHD and autism are at increased risk of overdiagnosis and misdiagnosis, a major government-ordered review has found, which calls for “radical reform” to support patients as waiting lists spiral.

The review, ordered by former health secretary Wes Streeting as part of Labour’s plans to tackle welfare spending, found the current system in England “falls short”, with people waiting years in some cases because help is “locked behind waiting for a diagnosis”.

While the authors said they “cannot conclude that overdiagnosis is occurring at scale”, they warned of an “increased risk of misdiagnosis and overdiagnosis”.

They called for a move away from needing a diagnosis to access help, saying a diagnosis can “do harm” when it is inaccurate by directing someone towards the wrong treatment. And they said overdiagnosis can lead to “over-medicalisation” when other support might be more suitable.

They gave an example of a student experiencing “marked loneliness but not major depression” being prescribed antidepressants “when a better option would be anything that increases their social networks”.

“Having ADHD- or autism-related traits does not necessarily mean someone has a diagnosable condition,” the authors said.

Mr Streeting commissioned the review last year after waiting lists for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder assessments hit 560,000 in December 2025 – more than 17 times the number recorded in 2019. More than 254,000 people had an open autism referral in December last year.

open image in gallery The report authors said there was a risk of ‘over-medicalisation’ of many who do not need it ( Alamy/PA )

The proportion of working-age adults with a common mental health disorder, such as anxiety or depression, has increased by almost half over the past 30 years, from 15.5 per cent of adults aged 16 to 64 diagnosed in 1993 rising to 22.6 per cent in 2024.

“The rise in mental health problems is real, is affecting everyday functioning, and cannot be explained by greater awareness alone,” the authors wrote.

At a briefing, report chair Dr Peter Fonagy said the report came as young people faced struggles such as increased uncertainty, financial pressures, and unaffordable housing and “a lack of hope among young people that their lives will be better than their parents”.

Meanwhile, awareness of ADHD and autism has “risen dramatically”, leading to hundreds of thousands of people waiting for an assessment.

The audit, also chaired by Sir Simon Wessley, concluded that people waiting years to access help was unsustainable and called for a shift away from a “diagnosis-dependent system”, which is needed to access education support and some benefits. They also called for a clinical review of those on waiting lists to to prioritise those with the highest needs.

Although the review highlights the risk of overdiagnosis occurring in the future, the reviewers said current data on the prevalence of ADHD and autism is too old and have called for new evidence to be gathered.

The review also raised concerns about the “consistency and quality” of private ADHD and autism providers, which conduct more than half of NHS-funded ADHD and a third of autism assessments.

The cost of private ADHD diagnosis has soared by 252 per cent in three years, but there is no consistent oversight, transparency or quality assurance over the sector, the authors said.

Experts have welcomed the review and its recommendation to move away from a diagnosis-dependent system.

Thea Stein, chief executive for The Nuffield Trust, said: “Moving towards a system based on people’s needs is sensible, but it can only work if support is actually there for people who need it. The knotty question for policymakers is how we decide who needs clinical care and diagnosis and who can be better helped through support in work, school and wider society.”

She added: “Today’s report marks an important step in moving the debate on from unhelpful caricatures like the ‘snowflake generation’.

“But change comes with a price tag. The over 400 pages of findings and recommendations are at risk of gathering dust if the government doesn’t work quickly to make hard choices and commit the funding to invest in the new service models Fonagy has outlined.”

However, Dr Rachel Moseley, principal academic in psychology at Bournemouth University, cautioned against the suggestion in the report that patients with the most severe needs should be prioritised.

She said: “It is inarguable that neurodivergent people with obvious, complex difficulties need and deserve support and diagnosis. However, we have observed a growing trend calling into doubt the legitimacy of needs in autistic and ADHD people whose differences are less extreme – people who attend mainstream schools, sustain employment for prolonged periods, yet suffer excess morbidity and mortality, particularly through suicide.

“There is, as such, a threat that diagnosis and support will be rationed to the detriment of these groups, who find a diagnosis "life-saving" for the explanation it gives them, but who also have significant need for support.”

News.title: What is the XFG Covid strain? Symptoms and what to know as the variant hits the UK
News.content:
Cases of Covid-19 have risen sharply across the UK this month, driven largely by a variant of the virus known as ‘XFG’.

Sometimes referred to as ‘Stratus’ and the ‘American strain’, owing to the fact that it is now the most common strain in North America, it was first identified in January 2025 and has since spread worldwide.

Between August and September, Covid cases in Britain jumped 230 per cent, from 1,374 to 4,589 new infections, half of which were caused by the XFG strain.

Hospitalisation rates have also increased by 15 per cent in the same period, according to the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA).

The true number of cases is likely to be much higher, as most people who contract Covid-19 experience a milder illness and will not visit hospital or receive an official diagnosis via their GP.

What are the symptoms, and how is it different from other variants?

Symptoms of XFG are similar to other variants of Covid-19 like Delta and Omicron, and typically begin with a sore throat, before developing into a cough and fever.

However, experts have noted that patients diagnosed with XFG tend to present with a characteristic hoarse, croaky voice, which is distinctive from older strains.

More than 30 other symptoms have been known to be associated with XFG and other Covid strains, including diarrhoea, vomiting, loss of taste and smell, shortness of breath, headache, and muscle aches.

Why are cases rising?

Current data does not suggest that XFG leads to more severe illness than any other variant in circulation, according to the UKHSA.

As the UK moves into winter, colder and wetter weather naturally influences the rise in respiratory illnesses like Covid-19 and the flu, given people spend more time indoors and in closer proximity to each other, where viruses can more easily transmit between them.

It has also been roughly a year since the last significant wave of Covid-19 cases, meaning that the population-wide immunity has somewhat waned, making people more susceptible to the disease, the UKHSA said.

Can you be vaccinated against XFG?

The current Covid-19 vaccine is designed to protect against XFG and related strains specifically, after modelling suggested it would become the dominant variant this season.

Those eligible for a Covid-19 autumn booster include adults over the age of 75, residents in care homes, and anyone over six months old with a weakened immune system, due to a health condition or treatment.

Covid vaccines are also available to buy privately for those who are not eligible for a free jab, and typically cost around £98 per dose.

What should you do if you suspect you have XFG?

The NHS no longer advises that people with symptoms of Covid-19 take a test, unless they want to do so.

If you feel unwell or have a high temperature, health authorities advise you to try and stay home and avoid contact with people until you feel better.

They also recommend avoiding contact with vulnerable people, like those undergoing chemotherapy or the elderly, for at least 10 days.

Protect yourself and your family by learning more about Global Health Security

News.title: Harry’s Invictus Games challenge in Kenya is helping veterans battle physical and mental scars
News.content:
Wounded veterans from 10 countries have gathered in Kenya’s Great Rift Valley for a week of endurance challenges, organised by the charity behind Prince Harry’s Invictus Games.

Twenty-five serving and former personnel, among them a Ukrainian who survived a direct bomb hit in Donetsk and a Danish combat engineer who cleared roadside bombs in Afghanistan, will run, hike or cycle up to 120km across the area on Saturday October 10, World Mental Health Day.

The Invictus Games Foundation, the charity the Duke of Sussex founded in 2014 for wounded, injured and sick service personnel, has organised the event.

For Vasyl, a Ukrainian soldier, it will be his first time in Africa and his first long-distance challenge.

After three weeks of military training in the UK, the 34-year-old joined a brigade in Donetsk as a reconnaissance squad commander, spending more than 19 months on the front line. He was wounded when a drone dropped a grenade three metres from him, and the shrapnel still causes frequent pain in his leg which can sometimes make walking difficult.

But he said the physical injury was easier to bear than the loss of the friends he made in the trenches.

“There is a level of kindness between comrades in a trench that you will never find in civilian life,” he said. “If someone made a mistake or said something wrong, we immediately forgave them and thought nothing more of it.

“For me, the pain of loss is the hardest thing the war has left behind.”

News.title: From Yale to the Congo: The mathematician who became one of Africa’s most intrepid reporters
News.content:
Sundaram has a lot of experience with the Rwandan methods of control. After spending 17 months in DRC, he moved to Kigali and he is eloquent about the convoluted effects of dictatorship. “Living in Rwanda taught me so much about how dictatorships function internally and how counter-intuitive they can be. A friend of mine who was working in public health told me ‘When we ask people in India to wash their hands we get a 30 per cent success rate from a campaign, but when we need people in Rwanda to wash their hands, we just need to slip a line in one of Kagame’s speeches and we get a 90 per cent success rate. That’s fantastic isn’t it?’

“And I said, ‘well is it? It’s great for short term health outcomes but what does that say about society? Isn’t democracy about people choosing freely? What if the government tells them to do something bad – like what happened in the genocide when people were told to kill all the Tutsis?’

“Kagame and his army stopped the genocide, and he has restored peace, but he governs using the same system that was used to perpetrate the genocide.”

In Bad News: Last Journalists in a Dictatorship, the book Sundaram went on to write about his time in Rwanda teaching journalists, he describes a more extreme version of this phenomenon, recalling how Kagame once commented that thatched roofs on huts were primitive. “And the local authorities took that as a sign that he didn’t like thatched roofs, and that they should get rid of them. And without replacements being built, people climbed up and dismantled their own thatched roofs. And I saw these villages with houses which just had mud walls without roofs, and the families were sitting outside with their children and their goats, the thatch strewn on the ground. In the rain, quite often. The children would get sick, and it was like a war zone.

“At the end of my time in Congo, I was at a UN base and they were digging latrines, when they found some human bones. They stopped digging and alerted the press, and I happened to be in Goma nearby.” He subsequently found out that it was one of a series of mass graves containing the bodies of Congolese killed by forces controlled by Kagame. “And so when I arrived I had a sense of what Rwanda had done in Congo, but I didn’t fully appreciate the extent to which it was totalitarian. I’d heard that the country was a shining example of progress – aid programs were successful, and poverty reduction programs. The streets were clean, public services functioned. I was living in a nice house with a big garden provided by the journalism programme I was working in.”

Many European governments, including Britain, are enamoured with Rwanda, because, says Sundaram, “dictatorships can be very efficient”. But it is a “mirage of a country”, he says.

The teaching programme he was running was briefed not to challenge the government on any level, and an embassy official told him that if any of the journalists mentioned repression they would be expelled.

“Layer by layer, as I began to talk to the journalists I was training, the true story unravelled. The first instance was when one of them left the programme, and I heard him on the radio one day praising the president, but with a degree of flattery that was completely exaggerated, and I didn’t understand why. The rest of the class were reluctant to talk about it but eventually I learned that another student had been beaten to a coma on the day he criticised the president.

“I started to realise that my class contained some of the most courageous journalists in the country.” As a foreigner, if he transgressed, Sundaram could have his visa cancelled or get kicked out, or even locked up for a couple of days, but for the Rwandan journalists, everything was at stake. They could be killed or their families threatened.

“But still they persisted, and they took me around the country and showed me all the things the government didn’t want anyone to see – things they couldn’t report on because it was too dangerous, so they wanted to show me because they wanted somebody to speak up. It’s really a book about them – they’ve been my greatest teachers in journalism.”

News.title: I tried Amazon’s new iPad rival – and there’s one standout feature
News.content:
Amazon says that this tablet has three times the computing power and nine times the graphics power of any previous Amazon tablet, so this is a significant boost in performance to previous models.

That will make light tasks, such as crunching through emails, browser-based activity like online shopping and document work. With a keyboard factored in, it could work as a laptop alternative for some. The same could be said of the iPad Air, although with recent price increases from Apple and the matte screen, for my money, this is a better proposition.

The premium makeover that comes with the Alexa Tablet Pro includes a slim aluminium design, with flattened edges, so it looks like an iPad or Samsung tablet, only 6.5mm thick. The Pro version only comes in the Graphite colour seen here. All models in the new line-up feel more grown-up and less like kid’s tablets than the Fire range. Plus the switch to proper Android over Fire OS is welcome and will result in better app compatibility (although I noticed that these tablets were running Android 16, which is now an old version).

It has a battery that’s good for 16 hours of video playback and supports 27W charging. There are cameras front and rear although like any tablet, these won’t be as good as your phone, while there’s support for Dolby Atmos from the speakers, so your movies will sound decent.

The AI capabilities are a step up

As the name suggests, Amazon is keen to promote the AI element here. It has customised the interface slightly with access to Alexa+ meaning you can utilise Amazon’s AI at any time to ask about what’s on the screen, to control smart home devices or search for content. If you are a keen Alexa user, then that will be a plus, but for me it’s not the headline news.

News.title: Kenyan authorities scramble to find passengers on Ebola flight
News.content:
Authorities are racing to track down passengers who boarded a flight from Uganda to Kenya on Saturday alongside a man infected with Ebola.

The man travelled by bus from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), the epicentre of an Ebola outbreak that has killed 4,000 people, to Kampala, Uganda. He then boarded a flight to Nairobi on Saturday, October 3, which was operated by the African airline Jambojet.

The patient went to a hospital in Nairobi and died just 48 hours later, meaning the journey took place in the final days of infection, the stage at which patients who die of the disease are most contagious. By October 6 authorities had tracked down 28 contacts, including family members of the deceased, but said they urgently needed to track down 23 passengers and crew who had travelled on the same flight.

The man is Kenya’s first ever case of the disease. Ebola does not typically spread through the air like Covid-19 or measles, requiring close contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person to spread. However, an aeroplane cabin significantly intensifies these risks because passengers share cramped spaces for prolonged periods and touch the same surfaces, such as a cabin toilet.

“We are working closely with the Ministry of Health, Port Health Services and other relevant authorities to support the ongoing public health response, including the identification and management of the other guests and crew who may have been in contact with the individual,” a spokesperson for Jambojet said on Tuesday.

After landing in Kenya, airport staff screened the patient, standard protocol for people travelling from at-risk countries during the current Ebola outbreak, but allowed him to continue his journey into Nairobi.

Kenya’s health ministry director-general, Patrick Amoth, said the patient may have passed through airport screening because medication had masked his symptoms.

News.title: Africa embraces ‘Go to Work on an Egg’ to boost maternal health and nutrition
News.content:
The sun is barely up when villagers start queuing for eggs at the metal gate of Shamim Haried’s home.

By noon, all that day’s supply is usually sold out, but people keep coming and asking if there are any left.

Demand is so high that arguments can break out in the queue, says the mother-of-two who lives outside Malawi’s capital, Lilongwe.

Her eggs are cheaper and fresher than those sold in the market.

“The people almost fight for eggs: it’s hard to watch,” she explains.

“Eggs are the cheapest healthy protein that they can get and it’s better for them to buy here than anywhere else.”

Her flock of 1,400 chickens lay around 1,000 eggs each day, but she reckons she could sell three times that.

News.title: What is pneumonic plague? Symptoms and how it spreads
News.content:
The death of a researcher at a plague laboratory in Siberia has prompted the World Health Organization to press Moscow for answers.

Russian officials have yet to share details of what caused the worker’s illness, and this information vacuum has fuelled speculation.

But what is the disease, and how much of a threat does it pose?

What is pneumonic plague?

Plague is a rare and serious infection caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, usually found in small mammals such as rodents and their fleas. Pneumonic plague is the most virulent of plague’s three forms, and is a severe infection of the lungs.

The other types are bubonic plague – the Black Death that laid waste to much of Europe during the Middle Ages – which attacks the lymph nodes, and septicaemic plague, which attacks the blood. Either can develop into the pneumonic form if the infection spreads.

Pneumonic plague is rarer than the bubonic form, but more dangerous.

Each year, the world records an estimated 1,000 to 3,000 plague cases of all types, though the number fluctuates.

Most cases are bubonic, and spread by the bite of an infected flea, and most occur in Madagascar and the Democratic Republic of Congo. But infections are also found in countries including Russia, India, China and the United States.

Sports.title: Chelsea double winner, 35, announces retirement and reveals tears in emotional statement after EFL club released him
Sports.content:
Next

CHELSEA cult hero Fabio Borini announced his retirement from football with a touching statement four months after his release from Salford.

Borini, 35, was among nine players axed by the Ammies by club co-owners and Manchester United legends Sir David Beckham and Gary Neville.



And the now former striker decided to roll credits on a 17-year journeyman career that saw him playing for a whopping 11 clubs, including Chelsea, Liverpool, Sunderland, Roma, AC Milan and Swansea.

The ex-Italy international looked back at his journey that he revealed started with a tearful flight from his hometown of Bologna to west London where he would kick his career off with the Blues.



And the ex-Parma star is adamant that despite the jitters he felt in that plane back in 2007, he never gave up and is very grateful with his achievements.

The former Sampdoria star took to Instagram to make the big announcement along with photos of him playing for all the clubs he represented, which also included Hellas Verona and Fatih Karagumruk.

Borini posted: “It all started with a flight. Thank you @chelseafc. I was 16 years old.

“A flight I spent entirely with tears in my eyes, beginning the journey of my career with no real destination, other than the dreams I wanted to achieve.

“From that day on, I started building myself, without knowing what would become of that kid with such a strong mindset. I started building my dreams in my head, and somehow, I ended up turning them into my reality.

“The same reality that today will change forever. The reality that has shaped my past, my present and my future. Today, just like that day when I sat on a plane to London, I feel those same emotions about what lies ahead.

Borini was promoted to Chelsea’s first team just two years after joining their academy and won the Premier League as well as the FA Cup in his maiden season where he amassed eight appearances.



That led to a short but impressive loan stint at Swansea where he registered six goals and four assists in 12 appearances before a transfer to Parma, who immediately loaned him out to Roma where he signed a permanent deal soon after.

The Italian’s stint in Rome didn’t last long as he returned to the Premier league in 2012 for Liverpool where he registered three goals and as many assists in 38 appearances during his three-year spell.

That led to a move to Sunderland, who signed him after short loan, where he amassed 17 goals and five assists in 93 appearances.

A loan to AC Milan followed in 2017 and that led to another permanent move as well as eight goals and six assists in 75 appearances.

Borini’s journeyman career was extended in 2020 when he went on to play for the likes of Verona, Fatih, Sampdoria and ultimately Salford.



The ex-forward played only once for Italy but was part of the team that made it to the final of Euro 2012.

Sports.title: Man City fans accuse Premier League of already airbrushing them from history after guilty verdict for serious breaches
Sports.content:
Next

MANCHESTER CITY fans have accused the Premier League of already trying to erase them from the history books in the wake of their financial scandal.

City were last month found guilty of over 100 breaches of the Prem’s financial rules during a nine-year period.



The Etihad club have appealed the bombshell verdict but will likely receive the harshest-ever Prem punishment should they fail to overturn it.

The prospect of City being stripped of the three titles they won during their period of breaches is a real possibility.



And some of the Etihad faithful reckon the Prem has already tried to airbrush their achievements after seeing one of the latest videos on their official YouTube channel.

The video in question was a compilation of goals over the years which have sent stadiums into a “frenzy”.

And conspicuous by it’s absence was Sergio Aguero‘s iconic title-clinching goal for City against QPR on the final day of the 2011/12 season.

Also absent from the highlight reel was Vincent Kompany‘s thunderbolt against Leicester City late in the 2018/19 season.

The omissions didn’t go unnoticed by City fans, one of whom wrote on X: “The erasure has begun.”

Another said in YouTube comments: “NOTICE HOW THE AGUERO MOMENT WASN’T IN THE VIDEO!!!”



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

And another said: “Not a single City moment: propaganda.”

One remarked: “Not one city goal???

Declan Rice‘s winner for Arsenal against Manchester United in the 2023/24 season kicked off the video and was followed up by Dejan Kulusevski‘s 100th-minute strike for Tottenham against Sheffield United in the same season.



Cole Palmer‘s winner for Chelsea against United in the same season was the next goal and was followed up by Jamie Vardy‘s wonder strike for Leciester against Liverpool in the 2015/16 season.

Other notable goals included Jermaine Defoe’s stunner for Sunderland in the Tyne-Wear derby in the 14/15 campaign, Reiss Nelson‘s last-gasp winner for Arsenal against Bournemouth in March 2023 and James Tarkowski‘s last-gasp equaliser for Everton in the last-ever Merseyside derby at Goodison Park.

Michael Owen’s dramatic Manchester derby winner in 2009 was also included, as was England youngster Rio Ngumoha‘s winner for Liverpool against St James’ Park last season.

The late Cheick Tiote’s stunning equaliser for Newcastke against Arsenal also featured, as did Thierry Henry’s stunning solo goal in the North London derby in 2002.

The compilation video was preceded by a video titled “The most emotional moments in Premier League history.”



The video included a host of teary-eyed goodbyes, including Mohamed Salah and Trent Alexander-Arnold‘s respective Anfield farewells.



Mikel Arteta‘s emotional retirement also featured, as did that of West Ham icon Mark Noble.

Christian Eriksen‘s stunning return to football with Brentford following his cardiac arrest at Euro 2020 also featured, as did Manchester United icon Sir Alex Ferguson‘s retirement from management in the summer of 2013.

The video closed out with Andrea Bocelli’s singing of ‘Time to Say Goodbye’ at the King Power in Leicester’s celebration of their shock title win in the 15/16 season.



The Premier League’s official Facebook account also got the tears rolling by sharing a compilation of some memorable departures.

The clip, which included the caption, “We’re not crying, you are”, featured Steven Gerrard and John Terry‘s respective farewells to fans at Anfield and Stamford Bridge in 2016 and 2017, respectively,

It also featured Arteta and Salah’s respective goodbyes to the Emirates and Anfield faithful, as well as Wayne Rooney‘s Old Trafford swansong.



And it signed off Alan Shearer’s goodbye to Newcastle fans at St James’ Park after their relegation to the Championship.

Sports.title: How Man Utd’s cheat code and ‘shadow-boxing’ strategy will expose Tottenham – as long as they unleash two stars
Sports.content:
Next

MANCHESTER UNITED host Tottenham at Old Trafford this weekend in a mouth-watering Prem clash that is crucial for both teams.

United are off to a poor start under Michael Carrick with just one win from their first five, while Roberto De Zerbi‘s side are winless and rock bottom.



Carrick’s side enter the fixture searching for tactical clarity after a mixed start, but the international break has given the United boss a golden opportunity to recalibrate his blueprint.

And the major key to victory lies in whether Carrick is ready to unleash big-money summer signing Carlos Baleba alongside Kobbie Mainoo, while handing returning fan-favourite Amad Diallo the keys to unlock United’s bogged-down attack.



Bizarrely, both sides come into this fixture suffering from the exact same structural defect: possessing plenty of the ball, but taking their shots from absurdly long range.

United lead the Premier League with a staggering 113 shots this season – 18 more than any other team – yet sit right near the bottom with Spurs for average shot distance (17.7m and 17.9m respectively), over five metres further out than the league’s most clinical side Sunderland (12.7m).

Tottenham under De Zerbi are top of the charts for total carries, carry distance, and progressive take-ons, yet sit an abysmal 18th in expected goals (xG) because they struggle desperately to penetrate inside the opposition box.

So how can Carrick fix United’s complete lack of a central focal point, survive Spurs’ dangerous baiting press, and launch a devastating counter-attacking masterclass in front of the Stretford End?

SunSport’s tactical guru Dean Scoggins reveals the three key battles ahead of Saturday’s crunch fixture.

BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

DIAL AMAD FOR ATTACK

United’s biggest headache this season has been how utterly disconnected their front four looks when building attacks from deep.



With Marcus Rashford, Bruno Fernandes, Matheus Cunha, and Bryan Mbeumo starting together, both Fernandes and Cunha repeatedly drop deep into midfield to hunt for the ball.

That leaves Mbeumo floating isolated without support and completely strips United of a central focal point, forcing players to resort to low-probability shots from distance.

Bringing Amad Diallo onto the right wing changes the entire dynamic of Carrick’s frontline.



With Marcus Rashford dropping out of the starting XI, Mbeumo can move centrally into the main striker role — especially given the uncertainty surrounding Benjamin Sesko‘s fitness — while Cunha shifts to his preferred left wing position and Bruno stays in the No10.

Diogo Dalot can then push up the right-hand flank, allowing Amad to float inside into the half-spaces and giving United a lethal 3-2-5 attacking shape.

THE BOXER AND THE SHADOW BOXER

Having Mbeumo operating between the lines while Amad stays wide acts as a genuine tactical “cheat code” — leaving opposition centre-backs completely baffled over whether to step up or sit deep, opening up crucial space in the penalty area.

In the engine room, inserting £70m summer signing Carlos Baleba alongside Kobbie Mainoo is exact catalyst required to unlock United’s full potential.



Youri Tielemans has done a steady job in midfield, but he is best suited for matches where United dominate 70 per cent possession against a park-the-bus low block. Baleba, yet to feature after arriving from Brighton, brings the raw power and defensive bite needed for intense, physical encounters.

Think of Baleba as the heavy-hitting boxer in the ring, going 2v1 in central clusters to smash through opposition lines and win back possession.

Mainoo acts as the shadow boxer — positioning himself as the instant relief pass to bounce the ball straight into counter-attacking runners like Cunha, Mbeumo, and Amad.

With Baleba providing a solid steel shield behind him, Mainoo can be released to charge forward from midfield and attack the open spaces between the lines.



Crucially, United’s possession stats have jumped from 48 per cent under Carrick last season to 58 per cent this year, yet their overall win rate has dropped because opposition teams are happily sitting behind the ball.

Carrick must be brave at Old Trafford: instead of bowing to home crowd demands to dominate the ball, United should sit back, absorb Spurs’ play, and use Baleba and Mainoo to launch lightning-fast turnover attacks.

BEWARE THE DE ZERBI BAIT

Tottenham will arrive at Old Trafford desperate to exploit any lingering flaws in Manchester United’s pressing setup.



De Zerbi’s side specialize in goading opposition players forward — goalkeeper Antonin Kinsky will literally stand with his foot on top of the ball to invite you on before Spurs play rapid forward passes through the broken press.

United’s high press has been sloppy and disconnected at times this season, with Rashford previously taking heavy criticism for leaving gaping spaces on the left wing that opponents easily played through.

If United jump out with an intense but uncoordinated press, Spurs have the elite ball-carriers to slice straight through the middle of the pitch into dangerous territory.

However, Spurs’ high-risk build-up leaves them with only two defenders back when they push into their wide triangular attacking shape, leaving their central midfielders heavily split.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

If Carrick instructs United to drop into a compact low block on the edge of their own penalty box, it turns Spurs’ entire gameplan on its head.



Deprived of space inside the box where they have already struggled to score, Tottenham will be sucked high up the pitch, leaving vast, empty oceans of space behind them for United’s rapid front line to exploit on the break.

CRISTIANO RONALDO’S mother Dolores Aveiro has admitted she cried after her son quit the Portugal camp “through the back door”.

Ronaldo, 41, dramatically walked out on his national team after being an unused substitute in their 4-2 win over Denmark.



The five-time Ballon d’Or winner lashed out at boss Jorge Jesus in a stunning 1,996-WORD statement and accused him of breaking promises.

But the Portugal captain stopped short of retiring and insisted he would remain available.



Question marks continue over his immediate future with the team and his mother has been left devastated by the row.

Dolores told TV 7 Dias she “cried a little” when she found out Ronaldo had fallen out with Jesus.

She claimed the news was a “shock” but insisted God would “take care of it”.

She said: “I feel sad, it’s normal. It was a shock, my son could have left through the main door and instead he left through the [back] door, but it’s okay, God will take care of it.

Dolores added: “He has always been Portugal’s hero. They are not valuing him as they should.”

Ronaldo did apologise for leaving the camp and insisted he should be punished.

But he doubled down on his criticism towards Jesus, as he said: “Despite the absolute breach of trust in the coach’s word, as those who witnessed these conversations can attest, I should not have done it.“

He also revealed he had already written his retirement letter before being convinced to push it back by Portuguese FA chiefs.

Ronaldo added: “After the 2026 World Cup I prepared a letter to the Portuguese people, which I still keep, with the words I want to address to them when I leave our team for good.

“At the end of the competition, already on the flight back from the United States, the President of the Federation asked and insisted that I reconsider the decision to leave, because the FPF wanted me to continue.”



Ronaldo – who helped Portugal win Euro 2016 and two Nations League titles – has picked up 234 caps for his country.

According to reports in Portugal, he is aiming to score his 1,000th career goal while playing for the national team – he’s currently 21 away.

And after his explosive feud with Jesus, the coach has appeared to extend an olive branch to mend it.

Jesus said: “Cristiano Ronaldo will be called up for the next international break, if he wants to return.

“It’s his decision. I am ready to call him if he will play with Al-Nassr. In my opinion, you can’t hold a one-year friendship against someone over a situation that is difficult to understand.

MIKEL ARTETA “destroyed” a room on his first day at Arsenal — to illustrate the chaos at the club.

The Spaniard has been rewarded for leading the Gunners to their first Premier League title in 22 years with a bumper three-year deal worth £80million, extending his stay at the Emirates until 2030.



Arteta, 44, has become renowned for his unusual methods since quitting as Pep Guardiola’s No 2 at Manchester City — including hiring a pickpocket to teach his players a lesson.

And the former Arsenal midfielder has revealed his first steps at sorting them out when he returned to North London as boss in December 2019.



Arteta admitted: “I just destroyed the office and put everything on the floor — the computers, the laptops, cables. Then brought everybody in.

“I said, ‘Listen, this is what I heard. I don’t know if it’s true but from a lot of different people, the sentiment is that this is how they feel about working in the organisation.

“I’m here to help you enjoy your profession and life, and the passion we all share. If you want me to help you do that, you have two minutes to put this in order and at least to be ready to work together’. And I left.”

Arteta had the pickpocket steal personal items off players during a team dinner in order to hammer home the importance of staying alert on the pitch.

He also sabotaged pre-season games by delaying meals, diverting transport and cranking up the heating in the dressing room.

His unorthodox methods were used as a stick to beat him with during Arsenal’s struggles to end their title drought.

BENIN’s manager has accused Argentina of snubbing his players’ attempts to commemorate their part in Lionel Messi’s international swansong.

The Cheetahs were chosen as the final opponent of Messi’s historic Argentina career.



After Wednesday’s match, footage of the footie icon seemingly deliberately snubbing Benin players’ attempts to take a post-match selfie with him spread like wildfire on social media.

And manager Gernot Rohr has now claimed his troops were prevented from exchanging shirts with the opposition.

Sports.title: Everton striker Martin Sherif admits to breaching FA betting rules and is handed major punishment by football chiefs
Sports.content:
Next

EVERTON star Martin Sherif has been fined £5,000 after he admitted breaching the FA’s betting rules.

The forward, 20, was found to have “caused, permitted or enabled” 61 bets on matches between November 20, 2024 and February 12, 2026.



Sherif did not place any of the bets himself, but they did come out of his bank accounts.

However, the commission said it was “difficult to accept” that he wasn’t aware of the bets.



The ruling found the player had “apologised and expressed remorse for his actions”.

It added he was 18 or 19 at the time and did not receive a financial benefit from the bets.

And Sherif was said to have been left “out of pocket” by them.

The verdict went on to say he had warned Everton youngsters about the dangers of betting and had closed his betting accounts.

An FA statement read: “Martin Sherif of Everton FC has been fined £5,000 for breaching The FA’s betting rules.

“The player admitted breaching FA Rule E1.2 by causing, permitting, or enabling 61 bets to be placed on football matches between 20 November 2024 and 12 February 2026.”



It went on to say: “Having considered all of the above factors, the Commission considered that a fine of £5,000, represents a fair and proportionate sanction for Mr Sherif’s conduct.

“The Commission considered that Mr Sherif’s conduct did not warrant a sporting sanction.”

Sherif was born in Liberia before joining Almere City as a youngster.

He moved to Everton aged 13 before being loaned out to Rotherham and Port Vale last season.



Sherif is yet to make a senior appearance for the Toffees under David Moyes.

He has represented the Netherlands at Under-17 level.

Sports.title: Hunter Bell celebrates in Team GB's 'glam' female track success
Sports.content:
Georgia Hunter Bell has enjoyed quite the year, winning a hat-trick of gold medals at the World Indoor Championships, for England at the Commonwealth Games, and again for Team GB at the European Championships.

But British female track success in 2025 certainly didn't stop there. Sprinter Amy Hunt made headlines with a record four-gold display in the Europeans in Birmingham, while Dina Asher-Smith now tops the all-time medal table at the championships after winning her 11th, eight of which are gold.

Among other successes, Keely Hodgkinson claimed World Indoor gold in the 800m in March - in the second-fastest indoor time in history - and set a new British record at that distance in the summer, though she'd be pipped to gold at the Europeans after sitting out the Commonwealth Games due to muscle tightness.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Keely Hodgkinson reacts after winning the 800m at the London Diamond League in July - but failing in her bid to break the world record

"It's really cool. just being part of this era. It's really fun," Hunter Bell told Sky Sports.

"We all know each other very well. We all travel together, see each other a lot throughout the year, so it's fun to tune in and be like, 'Oh, Amy's racing tonight'.

"We're locked into everyone's goals and what they're trying to do. And when you're on a team together, someone winning or bringing home a medal, it makes you even more keen to do well because you want to contribute."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Amy Hunt reflects on her record-breaking European Championships, after the Great Britain sprinter secured four gold medals in Birmingham

In addition to her statement performances on the track during her record-breaking Europeans, Hunt earned attention for her curated nail art that gave nod to landmarks within Birmingham, like the Bull Ring.

"Everyone knows I love a bit of glam and I love my nails," Hunt told the BBC at the time.

Hunter Bell says it's something the GB squad share, as feeling your best self on the start line can provide "that extra one or two per cent" to make you "feel like you can do anything".

Image: Georgia Hunter-Bell celebrated winning Commonwealth gold in the 800m this summer

"I enjoy the whole process of getting ready. We get ready like we're going to a club, we're quite glammed up," Hunter Bell said.

"We definitely put effort into it, for sure. We want to look nice.

"It's about doing whatever you need to feel confident on the start line - and I just think it makes you race better if you're feeling good about yourself.

"So much of that comes from the training and the lead up, of course. But it's that extra one or two per cent that makes you stand on the start line and feel like you can do anything, feel like you're a winner."

In terms of eye-catching track looks, Hodgkinson dominated the final race of her 2026 season by winning the 800m at Athlos in London last month as she debuted a new full-length, hooded speed suit.

Image: Keely Hodgkinson ran in a special new Nike speed suit at Athlos in London in September

Hodgkinson's outfit reminded people of Australian Cathy Freeman's which she won the women's 400m in at the 2000 Sydney Olympics, and it could be a feature for athletes at the next Olympics in Los Angeles in 2028.

Hunter Bell didn't rule out being one of them to don the suit.

"The first time you see it, it's like, 'Whoa! Haven't seen that before'," she said. "It will be interesting to see whether it becomes the norm.

"They do say it's quicker, so I'm definitely not ruling it out."

Sports.title: 'It's about time!' - F1 drivers excited amid Rwanda GP rumours
Sports.content:
Lewis Hamilton, Max Verstappen and George Russell have expressed their excitement at the possibility of Rwanda hosting a Formula 1 race amid speculation the African nation could soon be added to the sport's calendar.

With Africa not having hosted an F1 race since the 1993 South African Grand Prix, Hamilton has been pushing hard over the last few years for the continent to return to the F1 schedule.

Several reports on Thursday claim an agreement has been struck and that an announcement could be made as soon as next week to confirm Rwanda's addition to the calendar for the 2030 season.

Asked about the speculation ahead of this weekend's Singapore Grand Prix, Hamilton said: "I haven't really got any news for you. I saw something on people posting online, but I've always said that we need to have a Grand Prix in Africa.

"It is, for me, the most important continent, to be honest, the most beautiful continent. We're on all the other continents but that one and there should be no reason for it."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports News reporter Craig Slater talks to the CEO of Formula One Stefano Domenicali about the F1 season so far

Hamilton has repeatedly publicly encouraged F1 president Stefano Domenicali to prioritise adding a race in Africa, and the seven-time world champion is pleased with the Italian's efforts.

"It is something I've been pushing for in the background, and Stefano has been amazing," Hamilton added.

"He's flown to Africa so many times over the last couple of years, speaking to lots and lots of different people, so I hope that he has some news for me soon."

'I would be very excited if rumours were true'

Formula 1 already has a packed 24-race schedule confirmed for 2027, but the hosting deals of several of the circuits on next year's calendar expire before 2030.

Portugal is returning as a host in 2027 but has just a two-year deal, while races in Mexico and Singapore are only currently agreed until 2028, and the Japanese Grand Prix is only confirmed until 2029.

Mercedes driver Russell said: "I would be very excited if these rumours were to come true.

"I was in Africa earlier this year and I really, really loved my time there.

"Formula 1 is a worldwide sport. Africa is the only continent we don't race on, and it's about time we had a race there."

Image: Max Verstappen (left) and Lewis Hamilton are both keen to race in Africa

Four-time world champion Verstappen added: "For sure, if that's possible, it would be great.

"We want to race in a lot of different places in the world, so I really hope that it can be pushed through.

"I've been once to Rwanda.

"We have to wait to see if it's all going to go through, but I think we're all very excited if that would happen."

Sports.title: 'Stick together, enjoy the ride and smile' - Haaland's message to Man City fans
Sports.content:
"Stick together, enjoy the ride and smile," is Erling Haaland's message to Man City fans.

The club have launched an appeal against the verdict of an independent commission finding them guilty of all charges related to serious breaches of Premier League financial rules.

City insist in their statement they are "innocent" and have described the judgement against them as "opinion" and claimed it "contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe".

The independent commission found that between 2009/10 and 2017/18, Man City arranged "sham" contracts with a number of its commercial partners as part of a "disguised funding scheme" to artificially inflate the club's revenues by £830m.

Amid all the off-field news, Haaland and his team-mates go to Anfield on Sunday, live on Sky Sports, to face Liverpool.

Liverpool

Manchester City Sunday 11th October 4:00pm Kick off 4:30pm

Asked what he would say to the City supporters ahead of that game, Haaland said: "They're going to have a good time.

"We have to stick together. We have to stay with each other, and we have to stay positive. No matter what happens in life, we always have to have a smile.

"So we have to stay positive, look ahead, and try to win football games and try to enjoy the situation and win the game.

"We have to stick together; we have to spread the love to each other. So yeah: stick together, and enjoy the ride and smile."

Haaland - the son of former City player Alf-Inge Haaland - says he considers himself a fan of City, too, and referenced his connection with Manchester.

"I care a lot about the city, I have to say. I care a lot about the fans because I'm a fan myself, and I feel with them as well."

City's matches with Liverpool became big rivalry games during the Pep Guardiola and Jurgen Klopp eras at the two clubs and Haaland is looking forward to the occasion.

"It's always special to play against Liverpool. Especially with Pep and Klopp. I remember sitting in Salzburg and Dortmund and watching the games, how much they pushed each other. It's always special games there.

"I won there, I drew there, I lost. So it's always special, and every Premier League game is different, and every game against Liverpool is always special."

Maresca remains 'very calm' and 'trusts club completely'

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Enzo Maresca speaks for the first time in a club interview over the guilty verdict

Man City boss Enzo Maresca has also spoken for the first time since the independent commission's verdict in an interview conducted by the club.

The Italian insists he is "very calm", "completely trusts" the club and that his players "don't care too much about the noise".

He told CityTV: "Personally, I'm very calm, to be honest. The club has been quite clear. We trust completely the club.

"We understand the noise but the focus for us is just what we can control and we can control just the football side.

"The feeling is fantastic, to be honest. The players are excited for the next two games. But especially they are excited because in this moment, we are top of the league.

"The players are just focused on that. They know what we can control is the football side - they are not worried at all about different things.

"They know their profession and they know that the noise is there but they don't care too much about the noise. They are just focused in this moment on how we can beat Liverpool and how, together with the fans, we can try to win at Anfield."

Maresca is set to be quizzed further on the guilty verdict at a pre-match press conference on Friday at 10.30am, which you can follow live on Sky Sports News ​​​​​​and digital platforms.

What did the independent commission find?

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Kaveh Solhekol explains how the other Premier League clubs are reacting to Manchester City's rule breaches ahead of the appeal process

Manchester City arranged "sham" contracts with a number of its commercial partners as part of a "disguised funding scheme" to artificially inflate the club's revenues by £830m.

The club filed accounts that concealed the true state of its finances.

Manchester City were significantly in breach of both the Premier League's and UEFA's spending limits and broke "well over 100" Premier League regulations.

Manchester City failed to co-operate and act in good faith towards the league during the investigation, with three out of four alleged breaches upheld and one charge not proven.

The commission also said it was "regrettable" that a decision had taken so long to reach, with the hearing having taken place between September and December 2024.

City: Process was not impartial

Following the publication of the guilty verdict on September 29, a Manchester City statement read: "Manchester City FC is both disappointed and surprised by the opinion of the Premier League commission, that has been published today.

"The club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case. The club will therefore be relentless, and where necessary proactive, in any and all appropriate regulatory and legal forums.

"The Premier League process remains ongoing, with significant elements uncompleted. Manchester City FC will now pursue the appeal avenues open to it, on the basis that the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe.

"The club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League board and executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence.

"The club is obviously restricted in what it can say further until all future proceedings are complete."

Manchester City's statement erroneously refers to a Premier League commission. It is an independent commission.

Why Man City's appeal could drag into 2027

Latest from Sky Sports News' Kaveh Solhekol and Amar Mehta:

Manchester City's appeal could drag on into next year if they argue that the process should not be run according to Premier League rules which were introduced for this season.

City have filed their appeal and the new rules about appeals state that this part of the disciplinary process has to be concluded within 12 weeks and the appeal hearing can last no longer than five days.

City's lawyers could argue that they were charged in 2023 and a hearing was held in 2024 - when the rules about a speeded-up appeals process were not in the Premier League Handbook.

A legal expert told Sky Sports News Manchester City would have a strong case for arguing that the new rules should not apply in this case.

The new rules were introduced to ensure that clubs, where possible, were punished in the same season as relevant rule breaches.

Sports.title: Campbell would end retirement to fight Benn: 'He was insulting me!'
Sports.content:
Olympic gold medallist Luke Campbell would come out of retirement to fight Conor Benn without hesitation.

Campbell, who took gold at London 2012, fought at the highest level as a pro too, boxing Vasiliy Lomachenko and Ryan Garcia in an impressive professional career.

Benn incurred Campbell's wrath when he disparaged the Olympic champion's performance against Garcia.

Campbell hasn't boxed since that fight in 2021. But goaded by Benn, he would make a return.

"Once it's in your blood, it's in your blood," Campbell told Sky Sports. "I'm not officially making a comeback, but I'm in training as always and if there was an opportunity that presented itself then I would take it."

Image: Campbell won gold at London 2012. (AP Photo/Ivan Sekretarev)

Campbell is now the mayor of Hull and East Yorkshire. But boxing is remains on his mind. "I still think about it. There's combinations flying through my head all the time. Not as much it used to but still," he said.

"I think boxing's one of the only sports that brings you in the present moment. Your mind can't afford to drift backwards or forwards. You've got to be in the moment."

He wouldn't hesitate to fight Benn. "100 percent. If it came my way, definitely," Campbell said. "I haven't called anyone out. He was insulting me and I just responded to that.

"Everything's gone from there really. I would definitely entertain it."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Speaking on Toe2Toe, Barry Jones reflects on Conor Benn's defeat to Ryan Garcia.

Even now, after all these years out, Campbell, who boxed down at lightweight, is convinced he'd take out Benn, a welterweight looking to move back up through the divisions.

"I don't know what was going through his head or what level he thought he was at [when he fought Garcia]. I don't know what the boxing IQ was or what the game plan was," Campbell said.

"It would be the same result [with me as with Garcia], probably a knockout. I don't know if it would be two rounds but it would be the same result."

Sports.title: Russell, Antonelli to race with different specs amid Mercedes upgrade concern
Sports.content:
George Russell will race Mercedes' older-specification car, while Kimi Antonelli will run an upgraded package at the Singapore Grand Prix as the team bid to get to the bottom of why the updates introduced in Malaysia did not deliver the expected performance.

The world championship leaders brought their first big upgrade to their W17 cars since the end of May to last week's race but unexpectedly endured a challenging weekend on F1's return to Sepang, with Max Verstappen instead proving the dominant force and claiming Red Bull's first win of the season.

In an unusual move, Mercedes will now split their packages across their two drivers for the whole Sprint weekend in Singapore, with Russell - who will start at the back of Sunday's main race grid owing to an engine penalty, following his car's failure last Sunday - running the older aerodynamic package last raced in Baku and Antonelli the one that debuted with difficulty at Sepang.

Russell revealed he was the one who first floated such an idea, with the decision to do so ultimately becoming a "no-brainer" once they knew he was going to be starting last for the Grand Prix this weekend anyway.

"Well, actually, I instigated the conversation prior to the race on Sunday," revealed Russell, who slipped a season-high 84 points behind team-mate Antonelli after dropping out of third place with five laps to go at Sepang.

"So when the failure happened, it was kind of a no-brainer because we were kind of 50-50 about it pre-race.

"And I was more in favour to do it, even pre-race. Whereas now, it is a total no-brainer."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Speaking on the F1 Show podcast, Naomi Schiff discusses what George Russell can do now after his 'gut-wrenching' DNF.

It means Russell will again race with the package he took to an impressive victory in Azerbaijan two races ago.

"It is back!" said Russell of the Baku-spec W17.

"Obviously, Malaysia was the worst weekend of the year for us as a team in terms of pace, qualifying result.

"Of course, we probably both would have been on the podium [had his power unit not failed], but it was a difficult one. And we don't know whether that was a Malaysia specific or whether that was anything to do with the upgrade.

"There's no major science telling us there's anything to do with the upgrade, but we don't measure performance in F1 on how much downforce a car produces, you measure it with a stopwatch, and the stopwatch wasn't great in Malaysia.

"So let's see this weekend. I'm very happy to be back on that package and do the compare. I'm not really in any sort of fight this weekend, or the championship for that regard, so it's the right place to do it."

Will front wing addition unlock new package's performance?

Russell also revealed that the newer package running on Antonelli's car will be boosted by the arrival of a front wing in Singapore that had originally been due to be part of the initial package at Sepang.

"I hope the upgrade that is on Kimi's side works as we expect, because as a team, we need that to be the case, and it would be slightly concerning for us if the new package we had in Malaysia is not working as we expected," he added.

"We have a front wing this weekend that Kimi's running that we didn't have in Malaysia. The package was meant to come with the front wing - maybe that was a reason why it wasn't working so well.

"There's nothing telling us it shouldn't work. But of course, the car I had in Baku, I won in Baku, Kimi won in Madrid. It's still a fast car, so hopefully we can have some good fun."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Kimi Antonelli shares hopes that a 'missing piece' will boost Mercedes' upgrades.

Asked about the new front wing, Antonelli said: "I hope [it makes the difference]! That's the question we will try to answer.

"George is going back on the old package, which we know works really well, especially on these kind of tracks. On my side we will try to find and answer for this package and hopefully we will understand it more and finally extract the potential of the package.

"Of course, we will have the front wing, even though it's just one front wing, but let's see. I think Sepang was overall a little bit of an outlier because of the tarmac, the temperatures, but hopefully this weekend we will be able to put the car in a better place and extract more from the package."

Image: George Russell and Kimi Antonelli will be in different-specification Mercedes W17s this weekend

Antonelli said he was happy to be sticking with the updated W17.

"We really want to understand this new package and try to strike the maximum out of it because the team has done a tremendous job," added the Italian

"They've put in so much work on this new package and it would be just a shame to write it off so early.

"I feel like I'm quite comfortable on keeping it and, actually, I really want to help the team out to understand it more and to try to extract the potential."

Antonelli also confirmed that he was "committed to the new package for the whole weekend", with no option to revert to the older-spec during the Sprint event should the older parts on Russell's car be proving more competitive.

Russell expects second grid penalty before season is out

While Antonelli will hope to contend for victory in both the Sprint and main Grand Prix at Marina Bay, Russell's hopes of fighting at the front are set to be restricted to the shorter-form race on Saturday ahead of his engine-change penalty being applied to Sunday's grid.

Russell will be running a fresh power unit all weekend, but it will not feature the ADUO (Additional Development and Upgrade Opportunities) upgrade Mercedes have been working on as that update is not in Singapore.

The ADUO upgrade will instead be introduced at a later race, with the United States GP next up in two weeks' time.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Craig Slater explains why George Russell's Singapore GP grid penalty could end his chances of a world title this season.

Mercedes had hoped to coincide the expected introduction on Russell's car of a penalty-triggering fifth engine of the season at the same race that the ADUO was deployed, but that will now not be possible.

Russell said: "We were waiting to take the engine penalty with the ADUO update but obviously unfortunately we've had to take it here.

"But with seven races remaining, that's longer than the engines are designed for. Unfortunately it means I'll be taking another penalty at some point between the next race and the end of the season.

"So, yeah, it feels a little bit one thing after another right now but that's just how the cookie crumbles."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player George Russell is OUT with a Power Unit failure in the closing stages of the Bahrain GP in Malaysia.

Russell, who won last year in Singapore, has vowed to throw caution to the wind this weekend as he bids to salvage a strong result.

"Yeah, all-out attack, just trying to enjoy the weekend," he added..

"Obviously, if you could choose where to take the penalty in the season, this would be probably second bottom of the list after Monaco. But, unfortunately, we had no choice but to take it here.

"Singapore is a place I love and, yeah, I'll try and carve my way through the pack."
