Sports.title: 'It wasn't good enough' - Hamilton reveals 'huge' talks over Ferrari blunder
Sports.content:
Lewis Hamilton has revealed Ferrari held a "huge discussion" to reflect on a strategic error at the Bahrain Grand Prix that he says "wasn't good enough".

Ferrari fitted both Hamilton and his team-mate Charles Leclerc with slick dry tyres at last weekend's Bahrain Grand Prix, which was being hosted in Malaysia and started on a wet track that the Italian squad anticipated would quickly dry out once the race began.

The decision was proven wrong as Hamilton fell from his starting position of second to almost the back of the field in the opening stages, with the 14 of 22 drivers that started on the intermediate tyre gaining a huge advantage.

Hamilton ultimately produced a stunning fightback to finish on the podium in third, but having fallen 106 points behind championship leader Kimi Antonelli, reiterated his desire to see improvement from his team ahead of this weekend's Singapore Grand Prix.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Watch Lewis Hamilton drop to P15 as Mercedes claim the lead at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia

"It wasn't good enough and we've had a huge discussion about it," Hamilton told Sky Sports F1.

"And we're going to try and work on how we can come to a better conclusion more consistently in the future."

Before revealing those talks, Hamilton had defended Ferrari from what he feels is disproportionate criticism the team receive compared to their F1 rivals.

McLaren also started the race in Sepang on dry tyres and suffered the same fate as Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri slid towards the back of the pack.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia at the Sepang International Circuit

"We do for some reason as a team get far more flack than anybody else," the seven-time world champion said. "McLaren made the same decision and no one even said anything about it.

"You know, they made some excuse of some sort. McLaren made the same mistake and the same call."

'The call didn't come from the strategist'

Hamilton also offered a specific defence of Ferrari's strategists, insisting they alone were not responsible for the starting tyre choice.

He added: "It was ultimately a mistake but it's not the strategists. I think, unfortunately, my strategy team gets the brunt of the (criticism for the) call.

"But in actual fact, the call didn't come from the strategist. The call comes from collectively, us working together.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Lewis Hamilton recovers from P15 to podium places.

"(Team principal) Fred (Vasseur), (head of track engineering) Matteo (Togninalli), myself, my engineer, we make the decision together. And we discuss it and we put our input, we put all our ideas and information into the pot, whether that's good or not…

"I went into the pit lane, I'm like, 'it's wet'. I go to the pit wall, I'm like, 'it's wet'. Come back to the garage, I'm like, 'guys, we should be on the inters'.

"And then they all give a different perspective. And if you've got three people giving you a different perspective, you eventually get convinced by that. And you're like, 'OK, I'll go with what you suggest.' And that's how you work as a team.

"And you hope three are more right than one. But in some scenarios, it's the other way around. And you were right and your gut feeling was right. And then you're like, 'damn, I should have gone with my gut'. But everyone's generally trying to do the best they can."

'We're here to attack' - Hamilton hopeful of Singapore chances

Hamilton is hopeful Ferrari's car will be suited to the Marina Bay Street Circuit this weekend, with the track potentially providing the team with their best chance of victory over the final seven rounds of the season.

"I think with our car, it's generally good on street circuits, particularly when there's not particularly long straights," Hamilton said.

"If you look at the last races, we were quick through corners, not so quick on the straight line. This is a high-drag circuit, so I'm hoping the advantage others have on those long straights kind of comes down a little bit and we can start matching them through keeping up with them on the pace, through corners.

"I think for us, it's just making sure we've got a great, stable platform underneath us, particularly in the bumpy zones because it's bumpy here."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Hamilton defends Vasseur but wants changes to Ferrari's F1 operation

With Singapore hosting a Sprint weekend for the first time, meaning there is only one practice session before Sprint Qualifying on Friday, Hamilton believes quickly finding a strong setup will be crucial.

He added: "We've looked at Monaco, we've looked at Montreal, we've looked at Baku's setup. We're coming here and it is requesting something different.

"I've been pushing the car in a certain direction, and I think we are slowly making gains and improvements.

"We're here to attack. Qualifying is key, and it would be really great if we could start tomorrow on the right foot and then just be attacking in qualifying, but we have to wait and see."

Leclerc: Singapore layout seems good for us

Leclerc is also hopeful Singapore could present an opportunity for he or Hamilton to add to their sole victories this season, but is taking nothing for granted.

Ferrari failed to meet pre-weekend expectations when many considered them favourites for victory in Monaco and Budapest earlier this year, but claimed surprise victories when Hamilton won in Barcelona and Leclerc at Silverstone.

Asked whether Singapore represented Ferrari's best chance to add another victory this season, Leclerc replied: "Maybe. It definitely is one of those tracks where the layout seems to be pretty good for us.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Charles Leclerc says his Ferrari team-mate Lewis Hamilton 'is driving at an exceptional level' and 'is having a great season'

"Whether this will pay off or not… Budapest and Monaco were strong layouts for us on paper and it didn't go well. Silverstone was a bad layout on paper and it went really well.

"I don't know if it tells the full story but we'll give our best. Historically we've been quite strong here but we cannot really rely on the past.

"We've got to do everything we can to be in the best possible situation. It's also true that the tendency lately has been that we've been losing a bit of performance compared to the guys in front, so to win will be very difficult."

Sports.title: Premier League: 10 things to look out for this weekend
Sports.content:
1 Rice rested and refreshed?

Declan Rice’s future role in England’s midfield was questioned by Gary Lineker after Alex Scott’s impressive first senior international start in the 7-0 thrashing of Croatia. But the decision to withdraw from Thomas Tuchel’s squad in an attempt to manage his workload made sense after Rice had only three weeks off post-World Cup before returning to pre-season training. The 27-year-old has struggled with persistent back problems after suffering a hamstring injury last December and Mikel Arteta will hope that the rest has done Rice – who is thought to be close to agreeing a lucrative new contract at the Emirates – the world of good as they prepare to resume the defence of their Premier League title against Leeds on Saturday. Ed Aarons

Arsenal v Leeds, Saturday 12.30pm (all times BST)

2 Ready? Garnacho’s time to shine

Several Aston Villa players shone for their countries during the international window but one of those who stayed with the club may have made the biggest impression on Unai Emery. Villa’s remaining squad went to Spain for a mid-season training camp, including Alejandro Garnacho, whose last cap for Argentina was almost two years ago. Garnacho has been lesser-spotted in a Villa shirt, playing just 31 minutes as a substitute, but scored in both of Villa’s friendlies during the break, against Southampton and Sevilla. The 22-year-old, who joined Villa on loan from Chelsea in the summer with a conditional obligation, was an unused substitute for their past matches but is he now primed to affect games? Villa are hopeful Emery has unlocked Garnacho, who has struggled for form since leaving Manchester United. “Ready now!” Garnacho posted on social media last weekend and Villa will hope that is the case. Ben Fisher

Aston Villa v Brentford, Saturday 3pm

3 Toth can soothe pain of Scott’s injury

With Eli Junior Kroupi, Amine Adli, Veljko Milosavljevic and Julián Araujo yet to feature this season due to injury, Marco Rose must have been tearing his remaining hair out upon learning Alex Scott got hurt on England duty and will be out of action for two months. Sitting 17th and still searching for their first league win, the German’s side squandered nine points from winning positions in four of their first five games – and it was the 23-year-old who was central in ensuring Bournemouth had those leads in the first place. With just 55 minutes of football behind him this season, it seems unlikely Alex Toth will get the nod to replace Scott when Bournemouth travel to Chelsea with the older, more experienced Ryan Christie available and in good form. But having forced his way into the Hungary starting lineup during the international break it would be no surprise to see the 20-year-old get more minutes with a view to being used far more often given his side’s gruelling schedule of nine matches in the next month. Barry Glendenning

Chelsea v Bournemouth, Saturday 3pm

View image in fullscreen Alex Toth impressed for Hungary during the international break and will look to make his mark for Bournemouth. Photograph: Peter Morrison/AP

4 Ipswich’s calm an obstacle for Fulham

Ipswich’s place in mid-table, their total of six points, came via victories over Sunderland and Crystal Palace. Gary O’Neil’s team were presented with a tough opening schedule, and while defeated by Manchester United, Liverpool and Arsenal, their manager has not allowed those reverses to dilute team spirit. Speaking to the media following the home defeat by Liverpool, O’Neil painted an ultra-positive picture that defied most observers’ view of a game beyond his team’s reach from the early stages. Thus far, a successful strategy, certainly by comparison to early season at winless Fulham. Like O’Neil, Álvaro Arbeloa is new to his job. An improved performance in the draw against United did not result in a victory Fulham deserved, though there were signs of the progressive, attacking football the arrival of the former Real Madrid interim promised. Much of the burden has fallen on Josh King, the teenager building on last year’s breakthrough season. John Brewin

Ipswich v Fulham, Saturday 3pm

5 Ballard’s absence a boon for Brighton

Still in the Carabao Cup, with a Europa League campaign to negotiate and just four points acquired from their opening five Premier League excursions, the games are about to start coming thick and fast for a Sunderland side whose ability to cope with such a hectic schedule remains to be seen. Having lost Dan Ballard and Brian Brobbey to hamstring injuries during the international break, Régis Le Bris will have to reshuffle his pack against a free-scoring Brighton side who make the 700-mile round trip to Wearside for their first game since embarrassing Arsenal three weeks ago. While Wilson Isidor will almost certainly deputise for Brobbey, Ballard’s centre-back berth will be filled by either Omar Alderete or Nordi Mukiele. Having shipped five last time out against Manchester City, a Sunderland defence that had looked conspicuously porous in the early stages of this season will need all their focus if they are to stop the gallop of a team that have already scored 16 goals. BG.

Sunderland v Brighton, Saturday 3pm

6 Crisis talk lingers in air at Old Trafford

If “Dr Tottenham” is a thing, Manchester United possess their own healing powers for opponents. Self-harm is a factor too. They rolled out the welcome mat to Premier League newcomers Hull on opening day and Brighton were ushered back into a Carabao Cup tie. In United’s final game before the international break flagging Fulham were able to restore some faith, their goal via slapstick defending from Lisandro Martínez and Senne Lammens. Can Old Trafford, where fans will have regulatory matters at City to celebrate, lift the gloom for Tottenham? This season, like last season and the one before that, Spurs have assumed the mantle of crisis club, a status Michael Carrick’s January arrival temporarily removed from United. Lose to Tottenham, and the crisis prefix is likely to be reattached. Tottenham have done damage before. In September 2024, a 3-0 Spurs win at Old Trafford began Erik ten Hag’s hurtle towards the exit. Losing the Europa League final started Ruben Amorim’s downward spiral. Carrick beware? JB

Manchester United v Tottenham, Saturday 5.30pm

7 Fiery reception for Glasner at Palace

All eyes will be on Oliver Glasner as he returns to Selhurst Park with Nottingham Forest on an afternoon that will be emotionally charged for both sets of supporters and in the boardroom. The Crystal Palace chair, Steve Parish, sought to defuse tensions last week when he urged fans to “buck the trend” by welcoming the manager who led the south London club to the first three major trophies in their history in the space of 12 months. “I would be mortified if he gets anything other than the roof blown off,” said Parish. But given the strength of feeling towards Forest and their owner, Evangelos Marinakis – who is still blamed by some for Palace’s demotion to the Conference League at the expense of Forest last season – many have still not forgiven Glasner for joining their rivals and could still make their feelings known when the Austrian takes his seat in the dugout before kick-off. EA

Crystal Palace v Nottingham Forest, Sunday 2pm

View image in fullscreen Was this the calm before the storm for Oliver Glasner? Photograph: Ritchie Sumpter/Nottingham Forest FC/Getty Images

8 Aerial battle of the dead-ball bosses

In Sergej Jakirovic and David Moyes, Hull City and Everton boast two of the more “pragmatic” managers in the Premier League. Renowned for their safety-first defensive styles, both teams are happy to surrender possession, rank among the top flight’s lowest sides in pass completion rates, and rely on rapid transitions and set pieces for a major share of their total expected goals. A game featuring two defences that pride themselves on their obduracy may well be settled by a well-delivered dead ball into a packed penalty area. While it may not be aesthetically pleasing, expect to see the massed ranks of defenders on both sides spending much of Sunday afternoon bracing themselves for rearguard action while peering towards the sky. The last time these sides met in the Premier League, Everton ran out easy 4-0 winners. A decade on, the aerial traffic is unlikely to be quite so one-way. BG

Hull City v Everton, Sunday 2pm

9 Anfield to turn up heat on besieged City

Manchester City resume playing under the darkest of clouds, with a visit to their greatest rivals of a golden period now shrouded by a guilty verdict. Five Premier League wins from five under Enzo Maresca had offered hopes of success in a post-Pep Guardiola era. The dial has since moved on what constitutes success for a club where minds are consumed by legal issues but the band must play on. Can Maresca summon a siege mentality? City lifted a treble, including the Champions League, when the 100-plus charges first came to public light in 2023. The Anfield crowd will readily remind City of the infamy their club faces down. That Guardiola’s now-disputed dominance came at the cost of Jürgen Klopp’s great team will add to the ire, and very probably the pyro greeting to Anfield. Cool heads may be required in the policing and on the field, to which a return to focusing on football may offer welcome relief. JB

Liverpool v Manchester City, Sunday 4.30pm

10 Will Coventry build on first win?

International football’s incursions have curbed the adrenaline rush of Coventry’s win at Nottingham Forest and Jay Dasilva’s brilliant goal, his club’s first in the top division since 2001. That gave Frank Lampard foundations to build on, a blueprint, where Forest were allowed to blow themselves out before Dasilva’s strike came on the counter. It was Stephen Mfuni, 18, on loan from Manchester City, who starred in that rearguard effort on his Premier League debut. Coventry now seek a first Premier League goal at a stadium opened in 2005, after the club’s long decline had set in. Newcastle this week passed five years of the ownership of a consortium led by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund. There have been two seasons of Champions League football, a trophy lifted and yet a sense of unfulfilled promise. Matthias Jaissle is leading the second phase of a jagged development process, this season’s positive signs tempered by reverses such as the 4-1 defeat by Leeds, shows how far Coventry must travel. JB

Sports.title: Khaldoon al-Mubarak: the tightrope walker who made rare misstep over City charges
Sports.content:
No one better understands the precarious tightrope Abu Dhabi walks when it tries to balance its relationships with western Europe while weighing the complex geopolitics of the Gulf region than Manchester City’s chair, Khaldoon al-Mubarak. He was eight when his father, ambassador Khalifa Ahmed Abdel Aziz al-Mubarak, left the family’s Paris apartment for work on 9 February 1984, and was assassinated on the street by a Palestinian terrorist.

And no one outside the emirate’s royal family could be more wrapped up in the project of making and maintaining Abu Dhabi as a significant and secure world power and the dominant member of the United Arab Emirates, a nation state still only 55 years old. His paternal grandfather, Ahmad bin Abdul Aziz al-Mubarak, was chair of Abu Dhabi’s Sharia judicial department and senior adviser to Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan al-Nahyan, the founding president of the UAE. As such, Ahmad bin Abdul Aziz was the James Madison of the UAE (the founding father, not the Spurs player) in that he crafted the Islamic legal framework of the new nation in the 1970s.

Khaldoon’s father was assassinated by a group led by Abu Nidal which, according to the CIA, was “the most dangerous and effective of all terrorist groups [and] the best organized of the radical Palestinian terrorist groups” before the emergence of Hamas. The murder was justified in a phone call saying that the UAE “had expelled Palestinian and Arab residents and was linked with American imperialism”. In essence, they were accused of being too soft on the west, not radical enough for Palestinians.

Both al-Mubarak’s grandfather and father have streets named after them in Abu Dhabi, with his father honoured as a martyr of the state. It is fair to say the City chair has honoured the family tradition as chief adviser to the UAE president and Abu Dhabi ruler, Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed al-Nahyan, for whom he first worked after graduating from Tufts University in Massachusetts. Given his father’s martyrdom, the royal family is said to have looked out for al-Mubarak as a quasi-adopted son. According to a source in the Financial Times, al-Mubarak is “diplomatically in charge of the UK file as well as the China file … and he’s the main liaison with the US administration” and has diplomatic immunity in the UK. That said, he appears to have made a rare misstep with his belligerent tone on Manchester City.

According to Manchester City’s lawyer Simon Cliff, it was al-Mubarak who dictated the aggressive, confrontational stance City have taken with football authorities. As far back as 2014, when City were fighting their first Uefa charge, Cliff wrote, according to leaked documents first published by Der Spiegel: “Khaldoon says he would rather spend £30m on the 50 best lawyers in the world and sue them [Uefa] for the next ten years than agree a financial penalty.”

View image in fullscreen Khaldoon al-Mubarak with Pep Guardiola after Manchester City’s Premier League title win in 2021-22. Photograph: Martin Rickett/PA

He backed down on that occasion, along with the co-accused Paris Saint-Germain, both clubs agreeing a small fine and minor transfer restrictions with Uefa. It is extraordinary that City kept fighting thereafter, whereas the Qatar-owned PSG accepted their punishment, cosied up to Uefa – with the club’s president, Nasser al-Khelaifi, becoming chair of the European Club Association (now European Football Clubs) and chief opponent of the breakaway Super League – and built the most exciting and successful team in Europe, bringing admiration for the Qatari brand from observers willing to ignore human rights abuses. Al-Mubarak, in fighting to the end with City, appears to have broken an ambassador’s cardinal law: don’t embarrass your boss. Should City lose their appeal against an independent commission’s finding that they were guilty of multiple breaches of financial rules, al-Mubarak may be instructed to organise the sale of the club.

“I’m sure that’s the case with Man City,” says Christopher Davidson, author of Abu Dhabi, Oil and Beyond. “More than that, I’ve been told by some [in Abu Dhabi] that it will be the case. I can’t see any reason why they would stick around and try to rebuild the reputation after this. It’s embarrassing the royal family now. I can’t think of any example where things have gone wrong [for Abu Dhabi] and they’ve just kept plugging money into it. I think they’ll play out the appeal – nothing to lose with that – but once that’s done, it’s all about how to get out before the owners are declared unfit, a far worse outcome. There are very clever people involved in Abu Dhabi who I’m led to believe will very strongly counsel this needs to be a quiet retreat because the longer they stay in the game, the more damaging it is and it will unravel any kind of soft power Abu Dhabi managed to gain.”

In June al-Mubarak said “these sorts of jewels, you don’t sell” and that there was “only intention to keep growing this”. As for the wider threat to UK-Abu Dhabi relations, Davidson believes it is overstated. “Some of the reporting perhaps has portrayed Abu Dhabi as a bit monolithic. There are entire big and growing sections of Abu Dhabi state economy that are outside al-Mubarak’s remit. Some of Abu Dhabi’s biggest investments in the UK in recent years have been in renewable energy and the windfarms of Scotland from Masdar energy, which is chaired by Sultan al-Jaber, who’s another key lieutenant of the ruler.”

Davidson also cites the International Holding Company (IHC), which has huge biotech, shipping, healthcare and retail investments in the UK, including the Ivy restaurants, and is chaired by Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed al-Nahyan, deputy ruler of Abu Dhabi and brother of the UAE president and Sheikh Mansour. “It’s inconceivable that these investments would be withdrawn,” says Davidson.

View image in fullscreen Khaldoon al-Mubarak (left) alongside City owner Sheikh Mansour at the then City of Manchester Stadium in August 2010. Photograph: Jason Cairnduff/Action Images/Reuters

In May this year the UK signed a free trade agreement with Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the UAE which it said could be worth £3.7bn a year to the UK economy. “The UAE was a major force behind getting that and it was a major accomplishment on both sides, so there’s no prospect any of this is going to be interfered with,” Davidson says.

Al-Mubarak will probably emerge from this fiasco largely untarnished, because City are a tiny part of his portfolio. “He can’t possibly have known what’s going on in every part of his empire,” says Davidson. “My gut feeling would be that it’s the layers below him. It’s all about your legal counsel. I think the Qataris had very clever people working for them. This has been a case of poor advice being given to the senior Emiratis involved, a misreading of UK politics and a misreading of the Premier League and its bigger picture as a rules-based institution.

“I think the statements al-Mubarak has made, including the one early last summer that ‘We will not sell’, are the product of poor advice delivered to him and ultimately to Sheikh Mansour. It may be important to us in the UK but Man City has been a peripheral project [for Abu Dhabi].”

Sports.title: Sergio Camello: ‘Rayo is the last team standing – it’s football from another time’
Sports.content:
An 11-year-old, second-hand VW Beetle with more than 300,000km on the clock pulls over on Clown Fofó Street in the heart of Vallecas. The music goes off, the Smiths silenced and out gets Sergio Camello: movie aficionado with 156 films reviewed, part-time photographer, sometime drummer, Olympic gold medallist and the second-top goalscorer in Europe’s top five leagues. Engulfed in graffiti, stickers covering the glass between metal bars in red, a single step up from the street, the small door into Rayo Vallecano’s ground is locked, but in 64 hours it will open for the first time this season. “It’s my home, it’s Vallecas,” Camello says.

Forced to abandon their place, on Saturday at 2pm the tenants return. With the Madrid council declaring Estadio de Vallecas unsafe, unfit for purpose, Rayo’s home matches have instead been played in Leganés, out of the city to the south and boycotted by fans. Walking the neighbourhood that is proud of its social conscience, its community and its team, Camello can’t wait to be back again. And not just for the football; maybe not even for the football. “It’s the pre-game, the post-game, the people,” he says, passing the bar where they’ll be waiting for him after, same as always.

View image in fullscreen ‘I’m me, Sergio Camello, a normal person from a humble team’ – Sergio Camello at the door to Rayo Vallecano’s Vallecas ground. Photograph: Pablo Garcia/The Guardian

Yet the football is good too, good as it’s ever been. Across the continent’s top five leagues only Raphinha has more goals than Camello’s seven in seven league games and Camello himself has never had so many either. “I try not to think about it but my teammates keep reminding me,” he says. “‘Pichichi! Pichichi!’ It’s not Sergio any more.” Pichichi was the great Athletic Club striker whose name adorns the top-scorer award. No pressure, then. “None, I love it,” Camello replies, “and I love that they’re enjoying it.”

Two months into the season, this is already his best campaign in primera where the previous totals were five, three and three. And although there’s a tactical element, the new coach Beñat San José altering his movement, Camello looks deeper for an explanation. Above all he looks inside, which is where, from the beginning, another conversation starts: a simple question prompts a complex, nuanced and human discussion, the striker talking calmly, thoughtfully and with startling unexpected honesty.

View image in fullscreen Sergio Camello celebrates after scoring against Barcelona in August. Photograph: Pablo Rodriguez/Quality Sport Images/Getty Images

Camello is that most unusual of footballers – prepared to speak on materialism, racism, or homophobia, social media “poison” or the housing crisis, that rare player prepared to use his platform, which he says was born of his upbringing but also learned being here in the barrio. This is personal, but at once universal too, something in his experience that is about everyone. Who knows, maybe there is something in what he has lived that can help, some reason to share it, the goals scored offering tangible proof of an intangible process.

So what has changed? “How I go on to the pitch,” he says. “I thought it would be much harder to change my mindset but I’m seeing that I can be myself: be free, connect with the Sergio I can offer Rayo. To feel liberated, to enjoy it – and it’s been a long time since I enjoyed all this like this.

View image in fullscreen Sergio Camello has been outscored only by Barcelona’s Raphinha so far this season. Photograph: Pablo Garcia/The Guardian

“The first thing was to have many conversations with friends, people who truly know me. Especially my twin brother Gonzalo; there’s a connection that goes beyond the human. He could see I wasn’t enjoying it much, wasn’t myself. We talked and I tried to take that on to the pitch. Above all, to play without the pressure. Because pressure is horrendous. It makes it so that you don’t enjoy absolutely anything, puts you in a position where if things don’t work, that leads to frustration, frustration leads to pity, and suddenly everything is negative. There’s a point in the conversations where it’s: ‘That’s it; it’s done’.

“This is a sport you chose before it was your job, because it’s what made you happiest. It’s about connecting to that kid again. I’d discussed this in therapy too; the idea of getting back to that kid.”

Somewhere that can be lost – not just failure you have to live with but also success. “The pressure can come from everywhere,” Camello says. “We’re young, the change happens so fast, no one prepares you for it. If you can’t manage that it can do a lot of damage and that happened to me. [Early on], I would even get a bit paranoid, have fixations. ‘They’re looking at me.’ The first day in primera, when I scored, the journey there had been normal – scooter, bus, metro, bus – but on the same journey home some kids followed me shouting: ‘Camello! Camello!’ It was a shock. The night we returned from the Olympics I was in the usual bar, people crowded and I had a kind of anxiety attack and had to go. And, look, I’m me, Sergio Camello, a normal person from a humble team. I can’t imagine what it is like for someone at Lamine Yamal’s level. I don’t envy that.”

“But it’s about seeing the balance, understanding,” Camello continues, “and football has given me so, so much. There are so many people who can’t enjoy their job, who don’t have the [financial] freedom. When you have bad moments, when the clouds come, when you feel that cycle of negativity, you talk.”

Camello looks across the room: it’s quiet, 25 chairs sitting empty. “One of my friends [Dani Fernández] is a musician about to do four sellouts at the Wizink [Centre]; when I met him, he wouldn’t have sold out this room,” he says. “We both got ‘caught’ in this about the same time and we talked a lot. When he had doubts, I was there; when I did, he was. A torch in the darkness. You think: ‘I’d love to be a rock star’, and then someone you admire who is tells you how bloody shit it can be behind the scenes. You understand each other, you think: ‘Bloody hell, maybe I don’t have to analyse things so deeply.’ If in even those places you idealise, there is darkness, solitude, maybe I’m not so bad.

View image in fullscreen Sergio Camello says he his thriving by playing without pressure. Photograph: Pablo Garcia/The Guardian

“Otherwise you could go into a very dark place where you feel you have to escape this [football]. Even then the world wouldn’t end. And fortunately, the positive in football has always weighed much more heavily. And that’s been shown to be right. Those conversations give me perspective, make me conscious of how fortunate I am.”

Although Camello says doubts about the game itself are rarely shared in such depth in the dressing room – “football might be the most important thing in the entire world to your teammate” – something about this place helps. The club’s problems are significant, debilitating and should not be romanticised, he insists, and yet somehow they have made a success of it, built through solidarity. Besides, he says, “we’re also here because we want to be” and there is something about Rayo, something about breaking out of the bubble, that has been good for him, for all of them, as people as well as players. There’s a moment when he talks about everything that comes with being a footballer and says “it’s easy to be a dickhead”, but that’s diminished at a club not just in the barrio but of the barrio, one that’s “totally different” to anywhere else he knows, where “your feet are that bit more on the ground and you realise you’re not stars”.

View image in fullscreen Sergio Camello says the club and players have a unique connection with the Vallecas neighbourhood. Photograph: Pablo Garcia/The Guardian

“Rayo is the last team standing from football from another time, that’s what I like,” Camello says. “Even just parking here on the street right in front changes things. The same faces, every time. The least important thing about the football here is the football; it’s what they stand for every weekend, what they believe in, the connection. It’s Isi in the bar on the corner. Unai and his mates in the one down the bottom there. The bar we’ve taken over. That doesn’t exist anywhere else. To have those guys you were watching half an hour ago in the same bars, doesn’t happen. I’ve built relationships that are very sincere that I never expected. I’m a normal bloke who fulfilled mine and many kids’ dream. Like a superhero when they pull on the mask; I come here, I put on the kit, I’m the most competitive, most professional person you can be. But when I leave I take it off and forget about it.”

There is a release, refuge in something else. In the camera. In the drum lessons Camello admits have been slow and the guitar he’s abandoned, the ability God gave his feet denied to his fingers. In the films, in the indie rock music first heard in the family car, and the musician mates he has made. The music discouraged by reggaeton-loving teammates who control the stereo blaring out each morning– and, . They wonder, he says laughing, why he’s not so keen on the gym.

View image in fullscreen Sergio Camello with the Action for Music charity. Photograph: Action for Music

The music that can make a difference, too; if there is anything that moves people, reaches them like football, it may only be that. “There’s something I’ve wanted to do for a long time and it’s really fun,” Camello says. “I joined a charity, Action for Music, which gives opportunities to kids to play music in humble neighbourhoods. They go to four hours of classes a week: percussion, strings, wind. The kids don’t pay a euro, everything’s free: the space, the teachers, the instruments. They have schools in Tetuán and Carabanchel. I’m getting involved, learning, and I want to set up a school in Vallecas next year.” He stops, grins. “Only I’m going to do it my way … with rock.

“I did a session with them the other day, me trying to play the drums after six months. There was a kid on sax: wow, what a vibe he had, he was just loving it. When you don’t know where to go, there’s a place, someone who believes in you, gives you an opportunity. Forty kids: put some drum sticks in their hand, a guitar, a sax, something that will give them so much. Tell them they can be good at something, feel good about themselves. Have fun, maybe find something inside they didn’t know was there. It’s a way of giving back to Vallecas everything it gives me. I’m so excited.”

View image in fullscreen Sergio Camello stops to take a selfie with a fan while walking through the Vallecas neighbourhood. Photograph: Pablo Garcia/The Guardian

Imagine them playing the Wizink. “I can be their manager,” Camello laughs. “The idea is to do concerts at the end of each year. Imagine those kids, coming into their first class … then going on stage. It’s good to see yourself up there, with an instrument. Their family there, people who have bought tickets to see them play, the applause. That feeling: ‘I’m worth it.’”

Sounds like scoring a goal. Camello’s eyes light up. “Yes, it is,” he says. “I’m still the same guy as I was when I didn’t score, eh. But at that moment when you’re standing there, there’s nothing else in your head, just a feeling that all this makes sense. When the ball hits the net, when you get a ground on its feet, all together, when they’re celebrating, it’s like it’s all worth it. You feel important, you’re good at something.”

Sports.title: Maresca believes City players ‘don’t care about the noise’ as Haaland calls for unity
Sports.content:
Enzo Maresca says his players “don’t care about the noise” surrounding Manchester City, while Erling Haaland has called for unity after the club were found guilty of serious breaches of Premier League financial rules.

The manager and players reconvened on Thursday after spending the international break apart when the news of the club’s predicament was made public.

City maintain their innocence and have launched an appeal against the ruling, but if that fails could face a severe punishment. In the meantime, the staff and players are showing a strong front as they prepare for their first game in three weeks when they face Liverpool on Sunday.

“Personally I’m very calm to be honest,” Maresca told the club’s official website. “The club has been quite clear. We trust completely the club. We understand the noise but the focus for us is just what we can control and we can control just the football side.”

City have started life under Maresca with five straight Premier League wins and sit top of the table but the on-field success has been overshadowed by the off-field matters. Players have sought reassurance about the future of the club and were able were to sit down collectively for the first time since the news was announced, as they begin preparations for what is expected to be a fiery visit to Anfield.

“The feeling is fantastic, to be honest,” said the Italian. “The players are excited for the next two games. But especially they are excited because in this moment we are top of the league. The players are just focused on that. They know what we can control is the football side – they are not worried at all about different things.

“They know their profession and they know that the noise is there but they don’t care too much about the noise. They are just focused in this moment on how we can beat Liverpool and how, together with the fans, we can try to win in Anfield.”

Haaland, meanwhile, has spoken of the need for everyone associated with City to unite in this difficult period for the embattled club.

“We have to stick together,” the striker told Sky Sports News. “We have to stay with each other, and we have to stay positive. No matter what happens in life, we always have to have a smile. So we have to stay positive, look ahead, and try to win football games and try to enjoy the situation and win the game. We have to stick together; we have to spread the love to each other. So yeah: stick together, and enjoy the ride and smile.”

The Norwegian is following in the footsteps of his father, Alf-Inge, who played for City in a less successful era, so has witnessed the changes that have come since the takeover in 2008. “I care a lot about City, I have to say,” he said. “I care a lot about the fans because I’m a fan myself and I feel with them as well.”

View image in fullscreen Erling Haaland said of Manchester City’s predicament: ‘No matter what happens in life, we always have to have a smile.’ Photograph: Richard Sellers/Getty Images/Allstar

Pep Guardiola is expected to attend City’s first home match since they were found guilty when they face Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League on Wednesday.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

It would be the former head coach’s first return since leaving in the summer after 10 years. Guardiola’s attendance is regarded as a show of support for City’s hierarchy after the guilty verdict that has rocked the club.

Guardiola wrote on social media last week: “I want every single fan to know I am here; more than ever. I am, always have been, always will, be behind my club, my owner, my chairman, Ferran [Soriano, the chief executive], the players, staff, Enzo [Maresca] and you, our unique supporters. Let me be clear: we will get through this together. I love you all.”

The Catalan took on a role as a City Football Group ambassador when he departed as head coach. Guardiola was a close ally of Soriano, who brought him to Manchester, the pair having worked together at Barcelona.

Guardiola faced regular questions during his tenure over City’s financial conduct after they were charged by the Premier League in 2023 and always reiterated his belief in what he was told by those above him.

Meanwhile, his former Real Madrid rival José Mourinho joked that he may not live to see the end of City’s legal battle. Mourinho managed Manchester United from 2016 and led them to a second-placed Premier League finish behind Pep Guardiola’s City in 2018.

“I would rather ‌laugh about it,” Mourinho said, when asked about the case in an interview with Italy’s Corriere dello Sport. “I ​think we will eventually get an ending, but we are both in our 60s [Guardiola is actually 55] and we’ll need to be lucky enough to still be around when the final verdict arrives. There will be a verdict, then appeals, then more appeals.”

Sports.title: Wiegman praises Toone’s attitude after late Lionesses recall for Greece playoff
Sports.content:
Sarina Wiegman heaped praise on Ella Toone for her positive reaction to being left out of England’s initial squad for their Women’s World Cup playoff against Greece, after recalling the Manchester United midfielder for Friday’s first leg in Heraklion, Crete.

An injury sustained by Lucy Bronze, described by Wiegman as “really small”, prompted the England right-back to return to Chelsea and Wiegman called up Toone, who travelled to Greece from Spain, where she had organised a training routine during the international window.

Toone has 69 caps and has scored 24 goals, including in the Euro 2022 final and 2023 World Cup semi-final, but Wiegman said when naming her squad that she had left out Toone and Chloe Kelly because “the levels weren’t what I expect from them on the pitch”. On Saturday, after starting Manchester United’s victory over Liverpool, Toone took ownership of things, telling the BBC: “It’s about me now. I’ve got to keep working hard and use it as fuel to come back even better.”

Wiegman, asked whether she had been impressed with Toone’s response, said: “Yes, very much. I think when I gave her the call, of course that was a hard call. But she took that straight away. Of course [she was] very disappointed, but the first thing she did [was say]: ‘OK, I’m going to get back, I’m going to do that.’ She has the support around her too.”

The head coach referenced Toone’s post-match comments when she said: “That answer in the game, also the way she spoke about it, I thought that was really good. And then getting everything ready to go to Spain instead, but go for training there, I think that really impressed me. Well done, I would say.”

That will be music to the ears of Toone, whose experience is also understood to have been a factor in Wiegman picking her rather than a replacement right-back. She could feature on Friday, when the European champions will hope to build a strong first-leg lead before Tuesday’s reverse fixture in Leicester.

To qualify for next summer’s finals in Brazil, England must overcome Greece and win another two-leg playoff, against Slovakia or Ukraine, in December.

Quick Guide Greece v England: Wiegman's probable team for visitors Show (4-2-3-1) Hampton; Le Tissier, Morgan, Williamson, Greenwood; Stanway, Walsh; Mead, James, Hemp; Russo Greece v England, Pankritio Stadium, Friday, 5.30pm BST Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

The draw for the World Cup will follow on 11 December and it would feel inconceivable for the 2023 runners-up to miss out. They are in the playoffs despite winning five of their six qualifiers in a group with Spain, the defending champions, who pipped England to top spot by virtue of their stronger head-to-head goal difference.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Sarina Wiegman (centre), speaks to the players during a training session in Heraklion, Greece. Photograph: Naomi Baker/The FA/Getty Images

Greece have never qualified for a major tournament and, major underdogs against England, will probably set up in a low, defensive shape. The England defender Esme Morgan said she and her teammates would remain calm even if it takes time to break through: “It’s just [about] persistence and trying not to get drawn into being frustrated by the opposition. I think a really good example of it was the away game we played against Ukraine [in qualifying].

“We couldn’t seem to break through in the first half – the keeper was making saves, I think we struck the woodwork a couple of times – but the messaging at half-time among the players and when Sarina came in to speak to us was just to keep continuing because we were creating opportunities. Not to start snatching or taking hot shots from distance, just trusting in the style of play that we have and in our ability to keep finding gaps in and around the defence. We came out for the second half after that and scored really, really quickly. So it’s just sticking to the gameplan, trusting in what we do and being patient”

Sports.title: Glasner urges quick end to Manchester City saga and fears damage to Premier League
Sports.content:
Oliver Glasner has said Manchester City being found guilty of arranging “sham contracts” has damaged the Premier League brand globally and believes the integrity of the English top flight is under threat.

The Nottingham Forest head coach said the league faces a job to repair its image and suggested supporters might switch off after City were found to have artificially inflated their income by more than £900m.

City have appealed against last week’s seismic judgment of an independent commission that they broke financial rules across a nine-year period. If City’s appeal fails, the panel could determine a range of sporting sanctions, including expulsion from the league and point deductions. Glasner said the case must be finalised “as soon as possible” to protect the competition’s integrity.

Glasner cited his experience of Crystal Palace being demoted from the Europa League at the court of arbitration for sport (Cas) last year for breaking Uefa’s multi-club ownership rules as an example of how legal processes can drag.

“Let’s wait until the final verdict is spoken, but my wish is just that this is quick,” Glasner said. “Because we didn’t know with Palace if we were in the Europa League or Conference League and then it was ‘you will hear on Thursday’ and then that became Monday, because it was always delayed. Then we got the final verdict 10 days before the Conference League started.

“And that’s why I think this must be [completed] as soon as possible. There is still damage for the Premier League, not just in England. It’s a big topic all over the world, especially in Europe. The most important thing is the integrity of the league because as soon as the fans can’t trust it, they won’t watch it any more.”

View image in fullscreen Manchester City are appealing against last week’s seismic judgment of an independent commission that they broke financial rules across a nine-year period. Photograph: Loannis Alexopoulos/Anadolu/Getty Images

Last week Aston Villa’s Unai Emery became the first Premier League manager to discuss the City case. “If other clubs had been artificially inflated and that were now coming to light, there would obviously be some damage,” Emery said, in an interview published with Spanish outlet Diario de Sevilla. “That is something for the courts and the relevant authorities to decide.

“I feel sorry because of the way that [City] team played. Under [Pep] Guardiola, there were times when they were unmatched.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

City deny wrongdoing and formally lodged an appeal last Thursday. “The club’s firm position is that, on multiple grounds, the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact and is unsafe,” a City statement read.

“The club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case. We will continue to respect due process and are necessarily restricted in what we can say further until all proceedings are complete.”

Sports.title: Manchester United offer JJ Gabriel new deal but risk losing prodigy for £350,000
Sports.content:
Manchester United have made JJ Gabriel an official scholarship contract offer, but remain at risk of losing the teenage forward for as little as £350,000.

The prodigy, who turned 16 this week, stunned the club when he asked for his registration to be cancelled last month, setting in motion a scramble among Europe’s elite clubs for his signature.

Under Premier League youth rules, Gabriel would have been able to leave for a rival for nothing in January if the club had not offered him a formal scholarship for next season. The Guardian can reveal that the offer has now been lodged with the player.

Whether he accepts it or not – and it appears unlikely he will stay at Old Trafford – any Premier League club must now negotiate a fee directly with United for the player. If one is not reached, compensation will be set by a Professional Football Compensation Committee tribunal.

At a tribunal, United would expect to receive in excess of £3m, plus a clause in the deal granting them 20% of his next transfer fee. In a previous tribunal for a high-profile academy player, Liverpool were required to pay Chelsea £2.8m up front – with an additional £1.2m in performance-related add-ons – for Rio Ngumoha, and a 20% sell-on clause was inserted in the deal.

A United team photograph released this week featuring Gabriel briefly raised fan hopes of a reconciliation. But a breakdown between his representatives and the club means the forward – who has been at United since he was 11 – is now almost certain to leave.

He was permitted under Premier League rules to sign a pre-agreement after his 16th birthday, but his camp were not prepared to enter discussions after a disagreement over first-team minutes.

His next move is yet to be decided, though it is believed he favours a move to Europe, where compensation would be significantly lower. Real Madrid are favourites to sign him, with Barcelona, Bayern Munich and Paris Saint-Germain all monitoring developments.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

According to official Fifa compensation figures for a Category I academy, United would receive around £350,000 if he moves abroad. He would ordinarily have been prevented from transferring before his 18th birthday, but is eligible for an EU passport through his parents. The club will consider taking legal action if they believe recruitment rules have been breached.

Gabriel has not appeared at training for more than three weeks and, according to sources, the club has made multiple attempts to check on his wellbeing. To fast-track his progression into the first team, Gabriel had worked with specialist staff usually reserved for senior players.

Sports.title: Victor Montagliani eyes re-election at Concacaf that would rule out Fifa presidency run
Sports.content:
Victor Montagliani has told Concacaf staff he intends to stand for re-election as the confederation’s presidentnext year, which will rule him out of going up against Gianni Infantino for the top job at Fifa.

The Canadian businessman is understood to have relayed the message to most of the 41 members of Concacaf, the North and Central American and Caribbean confederation.

Montagliani has been widely touted as a potential candidate to take on Infantino for the Fifa presidency, particularly among Uefa member associations, who are conscious a European candidate would have no chance of beating Infantino in a ballot of Fifa’s 211 members.

At a town hall meeting of Concacaf staff late last month, however, Montagliani is understood to have said that despite the Fifa governance crisis and calls for him to stand, he wants to continue serving members in the region.

Concacaf’s presidential election will take place in the first quarter of next year before the Fifa vote on 18 March in Rabat, with the similar timelines leading Montagliani to clarify his intentions to staff.

The 61-year-old was elected president on a reforming mandate 10 years ago after the corruption scandal that culminated in the arrest of then Concacaf president, Jeffrey Webb, after an FBI investigation. Webb admitted he had taken “bribes and kickbacks”.

Uefa will also hold presidential elections next year, with Aleksander Ceferin confirming his intention to stand at a meeting of Uefa’s 55 member associations in Berlin on Thursday. Ceferin had said in February 2024 that he would not run for a fourth term at the helm but the likelihood that he would, after all, continue had long been an open secret. Previously, changes to the Uefa statutes had been passed that meant his first term, which began midway through the standard four-year cycle, did not count towards the standard three-term limit.

It raises the prospect of Ceferin, who took the presidency in September 2016, holding power for more than 15 years in total. That is seen among most European FAs as a positive amid the turmoil engulfing football’s governance while putting to bed any perception that Ceferin, who would have had a number of proponents, might be tempted to challenge Infantino for the Fifa role

Montagliani and Ceferin are expected to continue working together to bring about governance reform at Fifa after the World Cup sell-off scandal, which will be on the agenda at next Thursday’s Fifa council meeting in Zurich.

Fifa’s council has not met since Infantino’s Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) plan was exposed in July despite repeated calls from members for an extraordinary general meeting, with the summit their first meeting since Fifa congress in Vancouver last March.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Montagliani, Ceferin and the Asian Football Confederation president, Salman bin Ibrahim al-Khalifa, are expected to use the council meeting to demand an independent review of FFE and call for broader governance reforms of Fifa, which would give a greater voice to stakeholders and formalise the council’s role in decision-making.

Previous calls from the trio, expressed in letters sent to Infantino last month, for Fifa to allocate a portion of its $6bn (£4.5bn) cash reserves to members will also be discussed.

Delegates at Uefa’s Berlin meeting discussed a framework for Fifa reform, whose key points were made public during the afternoon. Among the points listed were the need for “a president who leads, not manages”, “stronger ethics, disciplinary, audit and compliance”, and “a clear process for major decisions”.

Azerbaijan was an outlier in refusing to back Uefa’s reform proposals. The Azeri FA’s former general secretary, Elkhan Mammadov, now plays a key role at Fifa as its chief member associations officer and has been instrumental in Infantino’s attempts to keep wavering nations onside during the FFE crisis. Later this month, Azerbaijan will hold the first Fifa Under-15 World Cup, whose contestants will include Russia.

Sports.title: Stats boffins reveal the Premier League side with the TOUGHEST fixtures before the next international break as Man United face tricky tests and City have mixed run after guilty verdict
Sports.content:
Stats boffins reveal the Premier League side with the TOUGHEST fixtures before the next international break as Man United face tricky tests and City have mixed run after guilty verdict

Fans of the Premier League will be filled to the brim with excitement as the top flight returns to our screens following the three-week extended international break this weekend.

However, Liverpool supporters may not share quite the same level of enthusiasm.

That is because Andoni Iraola's Reds have not been blessed with a kind fixture list over the next month. They are deemed to have the trickiest upcoming five league games before the November break arrives, according to Opta.

The sports data wizards have rated the difficulty of every Premier League team's matches over the next four weeks. Fulham are believed to have been handed the easiest run, while a quick glance at the teams Liverpool will face suggests they may be in for a Nemesis Inferno-level rollercoaster ride.

Their rough run begins on Sunday as they take on Manchester City at Anfield in what is set to be a monumental affair. The club's rivalry that has grown over the past decade will come to the fore after City were found guilty of breaking financial rules. Anfield is going to be a cauldron of hostility.

However, despite the noise that is inevitably going to greet Enzo Maresca's side, and could well cause them to crack under the pressure, they still – at this moment in time – have a team filled with quality and sit top of the Premier League with a 100 per cent record.

Liverpool's next five Premier League games have been dubbed the most difficult in the division

The Reds resume their rivalry with Man City on Sunday in their first clash since City were found guilty of breaking financial rules

Iraola's side then face two of the 'Bermuda Triangle' – where social media says points are lost and never seen again – in back-to-back games. Having already faced one of the third team in the dynamic trio, Bournemouth, they will take on Brentford away from home and then host Brighton.

Both sit above Liverpool in the table, with the Seagulls, who beat champions Arsenal in their last game, placed third and the Bees just below them in fourth after electric starts to the campaign.

The 20-time champions then host the side who took their title from them last season, the Gunners, before finishing off their nightmare spell of games away at Crystal Palace, where they were beaten by a dramatic stoppage-time winner last season. Opta has given their five fixtures a difficulty rating of 95.4.

That is one difficulty rating higher than the second-placed team in this graph, Nottingham Forest.

Forest have had a mixed start to the season, earning an impressive draw at Anfield and a win away at Aston Villa, before slipping up at home to Midlands rivals and promoted side Coventry City.

It was not the result Oliver Glasner wanted heading into a three-week break, and things may get worse before they get better with the run of games they have coming up. Forest take on Crystal Palace at Selhurst Park, host Arsenal, travel to Ipswich and Brentford and play City at home in their next five games.

Brighton and Villa are also set for a tricky run of fixtures. In addition to taking on Liverpool, Fabian Hurzeler's side travel to the Etihad and also host one of the first 'Bermuda Triangle' derbies as they face Brentford.

Meanwhile, once their ears have stopped ringing after being subject to raw emotion at Anfield, City players are in for a calmer ride over the next month.

A trip to Anfield is champions Arsenal's trickiest fixture over the course of the next month

Maresca's men will host Ipswich in their first game back at the Etihad following the guilty verdict, before games against Villa, Brighton and Forest.

However, for their rivals across the city, Manchester United, things are not set to get any easier after a difficult start to the season, in which they have only picked up five points from a possible 15.

The Red Devils will be looking for only their second win of the season when they face basement boys Tottenham at Old Trafford on Saturday evening. That blockbuster clash is followed up by a meeting with bitter rivals Leeds United at Elland Road.

A date with bogey team Bournemouth, who United haven't beaten since 2023, follows at the Theatre of Dreams, before a trip to Xabi Alonso's Chelsea. They finish off their run of games by hosting Aston Villa.

Elsewhere, after hosting the Cherries, Alonso's side have a trip to Everton and a derby with Tottenham to contend, in addition to clashes with United and Sunderland.

Champions Arsenal are judged to have a more difficult run than the Blues, but a more reasonable than Liverpool and the two Manchester clubs.

They will look to bounce back from defeat at the Amex before the break as they host Leeds this weekend, before travelling to the City Ground to face Forest. Then, sandwiched either side of the grand clash at Anfield, are dates with Everton and Hull.

The side deemed to have the easiest run is Fulham, with a difficulty rating of 91.1. That is because they face all three promoted sides – Hull, Ipswich and Coventry – in their next three matches.

Alvaro Arbeloa's team then finishes off their run with games against Villa and Newcastle.

Sports.title: Christian Horner's ex-colleagues turn on him as £67m Red Bull pay-out to Geri Halliwell's husband is revealed, calling out 'lying' and how behaviour caused 'constant spicy tension'
Sports.content:
Christian Horner's ex-colleagues turn on him as £67m Red Bull pay-out to Geri Halliwell's husband is revealed, calling out 'lying' and how behaviour caused 'constant spicy tension'

Christian Horner's former Red Bull colleagues have called him out for 'lying' and 'causing spicy tension'.

Earlier on Thursday, it was uncovered that Horner, 52, was paid a staggering £67million in severance after being sacked by Red Bull following a texting scandal.

The Daily Mail's Richard Eden revealed that documents filed this week at Companies House from Red Bull Racing disclose that Horner, 52, banked £33.5m. The husband of former Spice Girl Geri Halliwell was then paid an extra £33.5m from other Red Bull accounts.

The team's superstar driver Max Verstappen has opened up about what life was like in the team under ex-team principal Horner, while the cloud of scandal was hanging over them.

He said: 'To be honest, I like to see that people get on. It is not nice when you constantly have tension between people.

'Of course, from the outside, people like it, but honestly between the teams, it is better when you have just a friendly relationship.

Max Verstappen said their was 'tension' in Red Bull when Christian Horner was in charge

The team principal was axed after a texting scandal, though two investigations cleared him of impropriety

'It is not as spicy, but I obviously quite like how things are going at the moment, with everyone’s behaviour, let’s put it like that.

'It is less stressful. We are all leading a stressful life and, when you can take a bit of stress out of it at times, it is good.'

There were more scathing comments from Helmut Marko, who was a colleague in his role as Red Bull adviser. Horner, in his upcoming autobiography 'Drive', claims Marko did not want Verstappen in the team.

Marko, 83, rubbished that allegation by referring to former F1 driver Ralf Schumacher assessment that Horner's version of events was an 'absolute lie'.

'I'm ignoring it as much as possible. Ralf Schumacher handled it very well,' Marko told Austrian outlet OE24.

On an episode of the Backstage Boxengasse podcast, Schumacher said: 'Marko approached Max when he was just 11-and-a-half years old. At the time, Jos said it was still too early for him. 'The doctor, as you know him, was a bit miffed and said: "Okay, if you don't want to, then so be it."'

And Marko added: 'I brought Max into Formula 1 and had to stand my ground against Horner at his first race for Red Bull in Barcelona. He thought Max was too young, too inexperienced.'

Horner had been the longest reigning team principal in the sport, steering Red Bull for 20 years and winning eight drivers' championships and six constructors' titles, but was sacked in July 2025, a year after the scandal that engulfed him over texts he apparently sent to a female employee.

Horner claims Helmut Marko (right) did not want Max Verstappen at Red Bull, which the Austrian vehemently denies

The settlement payment is disclosed in the small print of Red Bull Racing's latest accounts for last year and is reported as 'compensation for loss of office' in the directors' remuneration section.

Horner has always denied the claims and was twice cleared of any impropriety in internal investigations at Red Bull, despite a tranche of supposedly intimate text exchanges between the pair being made public in an explosive email sent to F1 figures before the 2024 Bahrain Grand Prix.

His wife Geri stood by him throughout the scandal. They live together in a £9.2m mansion near the Oxfordshire border with Northamptonshire.

Last month, it was revealed that the woman who accused him of coercive behaviour had been mysteriously released from her latest role in motor racing.

A source told Daily Mail Sport that she was informed her services were no longer required moments before her scheduled flight to Budapest, a race won by McLaren's British world champion Lando Norris.

Her then employers, who can also not be named, said: 'We do not comment on personnel matters.'

It is understood her latest position was terminated after her new boss, with whom she worked closely, lost confidence in her 'for a lack of discretion'.

The saga that unfolded surrounding Horner's supposedly coercive behaviour was one of the biggest to hit F1 in recent years.

Seventy-nine screenshots of WhatsApp chats between Horner and the female then colleague were leaked in an explosive email sent to F1 figures ahead of the 2024 Bahrain Grand Prix.

The file allegedly containing texts and images was leaked to almost 200 people involved in the sport, including owners Liberty Media, team principals and the media.

Horner had been at the top of Red Bull since its inception in 2005, and led them in two phases to world championship success through Sebastian Vettel and Max Verstappen.

There have been growing rumours of the 52-year-old potentially returning to the grid. He recently told The Times that Ferrari are his 'dream' team to join and the only one he would consider signing up for without an equity stake.

'Would I consider Ferrari? I mean, Ferrari is the biggest brand in Formula 1. It's the dream. And arguably it's the sleeping giant of Formula 1,' he said.

'I've been a hired hand. I did 21 years sitting on the pit wall. I don't need to go back to that.

'At this stage in my life, there's only one team for which I would accept non-participation in ownership [Ferrari].'

A week ago Lewis Hamilton, the seven-time world champion, backed his beleaguered team principal Fred Vasseur as the ‘right guy’ to lead Ferrari amid speculation that Horner might take over.

Hamilton did not elaborate on what changes he wanted to see but his comments were hardly an overwhelming vote of confidence in the organisation he joined last season in search of his eighth world title.

But Horner's hopes of a return took a blow when Ferrari publicly backed current team principal Fred Vasseur.

Ferrari’s chief communications officer Maria Conti led the conversation, saying to a group of some 15 reporters: ‘Ferrari want to end speculation over the leadership of the team.

Horner oversaw eight drivers' titles at Red Bull, including four in a row with Max Verstappen

‘I am officially saying that Ferrari has made its choices and has full confidence in Fred Vasseur and his team. Nothing has changed. So that’s it.’

It remains the case that Vasseur has failed to deliver the results chairman John Elkann would have wished for, never getting close to a world championship despite paying Lewis Hamilton £80million-a-year to race for them.

Vasseur is also widely condemned within the organisation for failing to learn more than a few words of Italian, instead speaking in English, or his native French, since taking over as Scuderia boss in 2023.

As Daily Mail Sport revealed in September, the 58-year-old is also believed to have health problems – relating to his heart and the stress of the job. Furthermore, his elevation to such a senior status in the sport remains scarcely believable given his limp years as Alfa Romeo boss, where he won exactly nothing. They were at the back of the field year after year.

Sports.title: Arsenal were the biggest losers from the three-week international break as team with the most average minutes is revealed - but how did it affect YOUR club?
Sports.content:
Arsenal will return to Premier League action with a much-depleted squad after they were hit hardest by injuries during the dreaded international break. There are several reasons why most football fans dislike international breaks – especially when they last three weeks – but chief among them is the fact they regularly leave their club's best players injured. It is usually the league's top teams that are most affected because they have so many high-quality players at international level. And it is no different this time. Liverpool, Manchester City, Manchester United and the Gunners all ranked in the top four of the Premier League for the most players involved in international fixtures, including at Under-21, Under-20, Under-19, Under-18 and Under-17 level. Meanwhile, Tottenham averaged the highest minutes played per player across all levels during the break. Their 12 players averaged 254.1 minutes of game time across a combined total of 38 matches played. Arsenal left the Amex following a humbling 3-0 defeat last month with just one casualty, with Declan Rice pulling out of the England squad due to 'load management'. Now potentially six of his team-mates are in need of the treatment table. Piero Hincapie was the first to drop, missing the entire break, before Kai Havertz had to leave Jurgen Klopp's first Germany camp after picking up a hamstring problem against the Netherlands. Kai Havertz (pictured) was one of six Arsenal players to get injured during international break Max Dowman, Ezri Konsa, Christos Tzolis and Martin Odegaard also sustained minor issues, but the latter of the trio returned to the pitch with Norway by the end of the break. Liverpool were similarly unfortunate, with four of their big guns picking up knocks during their combined 51 matches played by their top-ranked 17 stars in action. Alexander Isak was forced to take an early leave from Sweden duty after suffering a 'minor injury' during a 2-1 win over Romania, a game in which he scored. But there is hope he will return for the Reds' monster clash with Manchester City on Sunday. Jeremy Jacquet impressed on his full France debut against Italy, with new Les Bleus boss Zinedine Zidane so impressed that he stated the defender was 'very good' four times in a matter of moments. However, a 'hamstring strain' kept him out of their 4-1 win over Belgium this week, which is cause for concern for Andoni Iraola. Fellow starters Cody Gakpo and Milos Kerkez are also doubts for the Anfield affair with City, after leaving their respective international teams early due to injury. City themselves have plenty of scares with three of their stars picking up various problems during the break. The biggest concern for Enzo Maresca is that main man Erling Haaland appeared to hobble off during Norway's defeat to Portugal. Nico O'Reilly missed three of England's four games due to a knock, while Rayan Ait-Nouri withdrew from the Algeria squad after their first game. Neighbours Manchester United also have plenty to attend to, with their treatment tables starting to overflow. Tottenham players averaged the most minutes played for their international teams during the three-week period

Your browser does not support iframes.

Marcus Rashford, Kobbie Mainoo, Benjamin Sesko and Karl Darlow pulled out of international duty due to existing injury issues, and two players, Patrick Dorgu and Noussair Mazraoui, have joined them on the list. Bruno Fernandes also picked up a niggle with Portugal but eventually returned to action. Another among the biggest losers were Sunderland, who could do without injuries due to their first foray into Europe in 53 years, adding extra load onto their already thin squad. Their biggest concern will be the fitness of star striker Brian Brobbey, who bagged a hat-trick away at Manchester City before the break, as he pulled up with a hamstring problem while on duty for the Netherlands. Dan Ballard suffered the same fate while playing for Northern Ireland and could be sidelined until the next international break. Rock bottom Spurs, despite seeing their players feature the most, were one of the big winners during the break. They only lost one additional big star to injury, with Jan Paul van Hecke withdrawing from Netherlands duty after hurting his foot in a Nations League clash with Serbia. However, starting right-back Pedro Porro was already on the injury list and withdrew from meeting up with his fellow Spanish world champion team-mates. He is a major doubt for their upcoming clash with United. Meanwhile, Chelsea lost two further players, Mike Penders and Jamie Gittens, to knocks, while Cole Palmer and Joao Pedro will be hopeful for a return to action after missing international duty despite being called upon. The real winners of the break are Fulham, Nottingham Forest and Ipswich, who lost no further players to injury. That is despite all three being ranked in the top ten for averaging the highest minutes played per player across all levels.

Sports.title: Jose Mourinho aims playful dig at Man City over bombshell guilty verdict - and insists he 'would rather have a laugh' about club's cheating scandal
Sports.content:
Jose Mourinho aims playful dig at Man City over bombshell guilty verdict - and insists he 'would rather have a laugh' about club's cheating scandal

Jose Mourinho says he 'would rather have a laugh' about Man City's cheating verdict than be drawn into a serious discussion of the financial cheating scandal.

The former Man United boss, currently in charge of Real Madrid, was asked for his view of City being judged to have broken competition rules over a nine-year period by illegally pumping in more than £900million.

Speaking to Italian newspaper Corriere dello Sport, the 63-year-old said: 'Manchester City? I’d rather have a bit of a laugh about it.

'I think that we will reach a conclusion but, being in my sixties, I will have to be lucky enough still to be here when the final verdict arrives. Now a ruling will come, then an appeal… I’ll be 80.'

Mourinho has previously said that he may still receive a winners' medal if City are stripped of the prize. The Portuguese led United to second behind City in the 2017-18 season.

If City's appeal fails, debate will continue to swirl over whether the club will be stripped of their titles as severe punishments are decided.

Jose Mourinho joked that he will be in his 80s by the time Man City's case has concluded

City lodged their appeal against the verdict, which found that the club had artificially inflated commercial revenues by over £830million between 2009 and 2018, last Thursday evening.

The independent commission came to their decision over three years after the Premier League first brought charges against the club, with its ten-week hearing taking place in late 2024.

Premier League chief executive Richard Masters claimed in a statement released alongside the bombshell core decision that the club 'systemically broke Premier League Rules for nearly a decade' with their use of 'sham' contracts.

In an interview with club media on a day when chief executive Ferran Soriano is understood to have addressed players returning from the international break, manager Enzo Maresca sounded a defiant note.

'Personally, I'm very calm to be honest,' he said. 'The club has been quite clear. We trust completely the club. We understand the noise but the focus for us is just what we can control and we can control just the football side.'

Maresca added that his squad's concentration remained on the pitch, where they will face Liverpool at Anfield on Sunday.

'The players are just focused on that (football),' he said. 'They know what we can control is the football side - they are not worried at all about different things. They know their profession and they know that the noise is there, but they don't care too much about the noise.'

Police on Merseyside have a plan in place while some fans are planning to provide a 'welcoming party' to the visitors as they arrive for the 4.30pm kick-off.

Meanwhile, Haaland has urged fans to keep the faith and 'enjoy the ride' despite the ruling, which found them guilty of more than 100 breaches of the Premier League's rules.

Enzo Maresca (pictured arriving to training on Thursday morning) insists he is 'very calm' about Manchester City's situation with the Premier League despite being found guilty

The Norwegian told Sky Sports that he believes fans will 'have a good time' at Anfield. 'We have to stick together,' he added.

'We have to stay with each other and we have to stay positive no matter what happens in life - we always have to have a smile. We have to stay positive, look ahead and try to win football games and then try to enjoy the situation and win the game.'

The prolific striker also called for unity within the club. 'We have to stick together and we have to spread the love to each other,' he said. 'Stick together and enjoy the ride and smile.'

Next Wednesday, City will play their first game at the Etihad since they were found guilty and Pep Guardiola will be in attendance in a show of solidarity.

The former manager, who left the club at the end of last season, previously shared a message of support for his ex-employers, telling fans: 'We will get through this together. I love you all.'

Guardiola will be joined at the Etihad Stadium by the City board, including chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak, for the club's first home European match since his summer departure.

Sports.title: Stephen Ireland opens up on 'life-changing' double-leg break while playing for ex-Premier League all-stars, why there's a target on their backs - and the 'f***ing mental' mistake by a Man United cult hero!
Sports.content:
Stephen Ireland opens up on 'life-changing' double-leg break while playing for ex-Premier League all-stars, why there's a target on their backs - and the 'f***ing mental' mistake by a Man United cult hero!

Stephen Ireland cries out in pain as the paramedics try to stabilise the fractured tibia and fibula bones in his right leg.

'It's completely broken,' says the former Manchester City and Aston Villa midfielder as the camera zooms in on the gruesome injury and team-mates gather around him. A sickening snap was audible in the footage.

As Ireland's recovery continues five months on, he is fully focused on managing Wythenshawe FC Veterans, the Sunday League team in South Manchester made up of a growing number of ex-Premier League stars like him.
