The banks the applicant prayed the court to protect from the respondents included Zenith Bank Plc, Naira Account Number: 1007158671; Zenith Bank Plc, Domiciliary Account Number: 507 1511327; Guaranty Trust Bank (GTB) Plc, Account Number: 0023824978; Access Bank, Dollar Account Number: 1396386493; and Access Bank, Naira Account Number: 1396382103.

El-Rufai also sought a declaration that any attempt by the respondents to apply for, obtain or execute any interim or final forfeiture or freezing order, without first establishing a reasonable suspicion supported by credible evidence as required by relevant law, would amount to a breach of his rights.

He relied on Section 17(1) of the Advance Fee Fraud and Other Related Offences Act, 2006, and the Supreme Court decision in Melrose General Services Ltd v. EFCC (2024) SC/1519/2019, to pray the court to declare that, as a citizen of Nigeria, he is entitled to the presumption of innocence and the protection of his fundamental rights.

He argued that any action by the respondents seeking to circumvent his constitutionally guaranteed rights through ex parte applications that conceal material facts would amount to a breach of Section 36(5) of the Constitution and a violation of the principles of fair hearing.

World.title: Bordeaux confirmed in sixth tier of French football
World.content:
Six-time French champions Bordeaux, who were sanctioned in the summer for financial irregularities, will play the current season in the sixth tier of French football, the Nouvelle-Aquitaine league confirmed on Thursday.

Bordeaux were sanctioned for failing to provide the roughly 10 million euros ($11.6 million) needed for the 2025-2026 financial year as well as 2026-2027 and meet debt payments.

Once one of France’s leading football clubs and the team where the country’s new head coach Zinedine Zidane made his name, Bordeaux was sold last month for a symbolic one euro to US-based investment group Park Bench who agreed to take on the remaining debt.

Two days after appearing before the oversight commission of the Nouvelle-Aquitaine league, which approved their recovery budget and issued “a positive opinion on their possible participation in Regional 1,” the club was unanimously approved to play in the top tier.

“Rebuilding can now begin,” said Dominique Delport, the new president chosen by Park Bench, speaking to AFP.

The new owners are due in commercial court on October 20 to ratify the new continuation plan, which now runs over 12 years, with the debt halved from 26 to 13 million euros.

The team is largely amateur although they are permitted five players on professional contracts, one of which will go to former Ligue 1 striker Baptiste Guillaume.

The club has produced many big names of French football including academy products Bixente Lizarazu and Christophe Dugarry who both played alongside Zidane in the 1998 World Cup-winning team.

A decade earlier Alain Giresse and Jean Tigana were part of a celebrated France midfield that won the European championships in 1984.

However, they were relegated to Ligue 2 in 2022 and then placed in judicial restructuring in 2024, which caused them to relinquish their professional status and their highly-rated academy.

AFP

World.title: National Grassroots Sports Summit 2026: Building a New Pathway for Nigeria’s Sporting Future
World.content:
Nigeria’s search for a more sustainable sporting future will take centre stage in Abuja as stakeholders prepare for the National Grassroots Sports Development Summit 2026, a strategic national gathering aimed at strengthening the foundation of sports development and creating a clearer pathway for discovering, nurturing and progressing sporting talents across the country.

Scheduled for November 18 and 19, 2026, at the Banquet Hall, State House, Presidential Villa, Abuja, the Summit is being organised by the Office of the Senior Special Assistant to the President on Grassroots Sports Development, Prince Adeyinka Adegboye, under the theme: “Creating a New Pathway for Sustainable Grassroots Sports Development.”

At the heart of the Summit is a simple but important understanding: grassroots sports is where the journey of most sporting careers begin.

Grassroots sports refers to organised sporting activities at the community, school, local government and other entry-level settings where young people are given the opportunity to participate, develop skills, compete and potentially progress into higher levels of sport.

It is the foundation upon which elite sports is built.

Before an athlete represents Nigeria at the African Games, the Olympics, World Championships or other international competitions, there is usually a starting point—a school field, a community pitch, a local competition, a coach who identified potential, or a young athlete who was simply given an opportunity to participate.

For Nigeria, therefore, grassroots sport is not just about winning medals. It is about creating opportunities for young Nigerians to discover their abilities, receive proper training, stay engaged in productive activities and pursue a structured sporting career.

The Summit comes at a crucial period when the conversation around reforming Nigerian sports has increasingly shifted towards the need for stronger structures, improved facilities, better competitions and sustainable talent-development programmes.

Nigeria has produced generations of exceptional athletes who have distinguished themselves on the continental and global stages. Yet, beneath those successes remains a fundamental challenge: thousands of talented young Nigerians in schools, communities and local government areas still lack structured opportunities to be discovered, trained and properly developed.

The National Grassroots Sports Development Summit seeks to confront this challenge by encouraging a more coordinated approach to grassroots sports development.

Rather than treating grassroots sports as occasional competitions, talent hunts or isolated sporting activities, the Summit will promote a system in which talent identification is connected to coaching, education, facilities, regular competition, athlete welfare and a clear progression pathway to elite sports.

One of the major conversations, “Grassroots Sports Development in Nigeria: Challenges and Way Forward,” will examine the obstacles that have limited the country’s ability to fully harness its enormous sporting population and identify practical solutions for building a stronger grassroots sports system.

Another keynote discussion, “The Game Changer: How Sports Rescues Youth and Builds Nations,” will broaden the conversation beyond medals and trophies to examine sports as an instrument for youth empowerment, employment, education, social inclusion, national unity and economic development.

This is particularly important in a country with a large and youthful population. Properly structured grassroots sports can provide young people with opportunities to develop discipline, teamwork, leadership, confidence and valuable skills, while also opening pathways to education, professional careers and entrepreneurship within the wider sports ecosystem.

The Summit is expected to bring together representatives of government at different levels, sports federations, educational institutions, coaches, athletes, former internationals, academies, corporate organisations, development partners, traditional institutions, community stakeholders and the media.

Corporate Nigeria will also have an important role to play, as sustainable grassroots sports development requires investment beyond government funding. Support is needed for sporting facilities, equipment, competitions, coaching programmes, scholarships, talent identification and athlete development.

The Summit, therefore, presents an opportunity to move the national conversation from “Who are our next champions?” to a more fundamental question: “What system are we putting in place to discover, develop and support those champions?”

Ultimately, the National Grassroots Sports Development Summit is about ensuring that talent does not remain hidden simply because a young Nigerian was born in a community without the necessary facilities, coaching or opportunities.

It is about creating a system where a talented child discovered in a school, community or local government area can be identified, nurtured, educated, trained and given a realistic opportunity to progress—from the grassroots to the national stage and, ultimately, to the world.

The vision is to build a Nigeria where talent is not left to chance, opportunity is not determined by location, and the next generation of sporting stars can emerge from every part of the country.

November 18–19, 2026, therefore represents more than another gathering in Abuja. It is an opportunity to begin building a coordinated national pathway for grassroots sports development and to place the development of Nigeria’s sporting future firmly where it belongs: at the grassroots.

World.title: NIGERIA’S DIPLOMATIC GAINS AT UNGA
World.content:
The UN platform gave an opportunity to articulate our national and continental priorities, contends

SAMSON OLAOLUWA

Nigeria’s participation in the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly has placed several defining questions about the country’s international standing and Africa’s future firmly on the global agenda. Through President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s address, delivered by Vice President Kashim Shettima in New York, Nigeria articulated a broad diplomatic agenda centred on equitable global governance, economic transformation, technological advancement, climate responsibility and collective security.

The significance of the address lies not simply in the issues raised, but in the effort to position Nigeria as a country prepared to participate more actively in shaping solutions to global challenges. At a time when developing countries continue to demand greater influence over institutions that affect their economic and political futures, Nigeria used the UN platform to insist that Africa’s contributions must be matched by meaningful representation and decision-making authority.

These are important diplomatic gains in terms of visibility, agenda-setting and the articulation of national and continental priorities. Their lasting value, however, will depend on how effectively Nigeria translates its international advocacy into partnerships, investment, institutional reforms and measurable domestic benefits.

The most prominent element of Tinubu’s address was Nigeria’s demand for at least two permanent African seats on the United Nations Security Council, with the same rights and responsibilities as other permanent members, including veto powers for as long as the veto remains part of the Council’s structure. Nigeria also called for five non-permanent African seats. This demand goes to the heart of a longstanding debate about the legitimacy and representativeness of global governance.

The Security Council’s permanent membership reflects the distribution of power that emerged from the Second World War. More than eight decades later, African countries remain without permanent representation, despite the continent’s importance to international peace, security, development and diplomacy.

Tinubu argued that the world of 2026 could no longer be governed indefinitely by the power arrangements of 1945. His position aligns with the African Union’s Ezulwini Consensus and Sirte Declaration, which call for stronger African representation in the Council.

The importance of Nigeria’s intervention is that it reinforces the demand for institutional reform from an African country with a longstanding record of participation in peacekeeping and regional diplomacy.

Nigeria has contributed to peacekeeping and stabilisation efforts in Liberia, Sierra Leone, Darfur, Mali and The Gambia. It has also worked through the Economic Community of West African States, the African Union and Gulf of Guinea partnerships on mediation, counter-terrorism, democratic governance and maritime security.

The President’s argument was therefore that Africa should not be expected to shoulder responsibilities for international peace and security while remaining excluded from the Council’s permanent decision-making structure.

This is a significant diplomatic position. Nevertheless, the demand is not itself a reform of the Security Council. Achieving that outcome would require sustained negotiations and the agreement of the relevant UN member states. Nigeria’s immediate contribution is to keep the issue prominent and press for a global governance system that reflects contemporary realities.

Another major theme was reform of international financial architecture. Tinubu identified inadequate financing as a major obstacle to sustainable development and called for wider access to concessional financing and debt-sustainability frameworks that recognise the development needs of poorer countries.

For Nigeria, this issue has direct economic relevance. Governments seeking to expand infrastructure, strengthen healthcare and education, improve energy access and create jobs must balance development spending with debt obligations and competing public priorities.

The President also advocated innovative financing mechanisms, including private capital, blended finance, South-South cooperation and strategic partnerships.

The underlying message was that developing countries need financing arrangements that support growth rather than constrain their capacity to invest in their people.

Nigeria’s diplomatic opportunity is to build coalitions around these proposals and attract partners prepared to finance productive projects. However, international advocacy must be accompanied by sound domestic financial management, credible project preparation, transparency and policies that encourage productive investment.

The gains from the UN engagement will ultimately be measured by whether Nigeria can convert these calls into accessible financing, stronger partnerships and investment that expands economic opportunities.

Tinubu’s position on climate change also sought to reconcile environmental responsibility with the development aspirations of African countries. He rejected what he described as a false choice between climate action and economic development, arguing that countries such as Nigeria must be able to industrialise, reduce poverty and expand energy access while pursuing lower-emission development pathways.

Nigeria’s Energy Transition Plan targets net-zero emissions by 2060, combining renewable energy, clean cooking, gas as a transitional fuel, climate-smart agriculture and nature-based solutions.

At the UN, Tinubu called for technology transfer, capacity building and predictable climate finance. He argued that climate funding should reflect equity and shared responsibility rather than charity.

This position highlights an important challenge for Nigeria: the country needs reliable and affordable energy to support manufacturing, businesses, households and public services, while also managing environmental risks and fulfilling its climate commitments.

The President’s intervention gives international visibility to Nigeria’s demand for a transition that reflects its circumstances and development needs. The next step is to strengthen the policies, infrastructure and financing arrangements required to make that transition practical and inclusive.

Tinubu also addressed artificial intelligence, presenting it as a technology that could either intensify global risks or improve human welfare, depending on how it is developed and deployed.

He identified healthcare, education, agriculture, governance and economic productivity as areas where AI could deliver significant benefits. He also highlighted Nigeria’s investments in digital public infrastructure, broadband connectivity, innovation ecosystems, research institutions and technology entrepreneurship.

His invitation to international partners to collaborate with Nigerian youths is particularly relevant to a country with a large, enterprising young population.

AI presents opportunities for Nigerian businesses and professionals to develop new products, improve services and compete in international markets. Yet those opportunities depend on access to electricity, connectivity, skills, computing resources and appropriate regulatory safeguards.

Nigeria’s participation in this global conversation is valuable because the future of AI should not be determined exclusively by countries that already possess the greatest technological and financial resources.

The diplomatic challenge is to turn that argument into practical cooperation: research partnerships, skills development, technology investment and safeguards that encourage innovation while protecting citizens.

The President’s emphasis on the African Continental Free Trade Area further connected Nigeria’s international agenda to the continent’s economic future.

Tinubu argued that Africa must move beyond exporting raw materials and place greater emphasis on manufacturing, value addition, technological innovation and knowledge-driven growth.

This is a crucial question for Nigeria, whose natural and human resources offer opportunities for stronger domestic production and regional trade.

A more integrated African market could support the development of regional value chains, enable businesses to reach more customers and create incentives for investment in processing and manufacturing. It could also provide Nigerian entrepreneurs with opportunities to expand beyond the domestic market.

Realising these possibilities requires improvements in transport infrastructure, trade facilitation, electricity supply, access to finance and the removal of barriers that impede cross-border commerce.

Nigeria’s UN engagement reinforced the case for treating Africa not merely as a source of commodities or a destination for development assistance, but as a potential driver of global economic growth.

Tinubu’s address also drew on Nigeria’s experience confronting Boko Haram, ISWAP and other armed groups to argue that military action alone cannot guarantee lasting peace.

He emphasised the importance of education, economic opportunity, accountable governance and the protection of communities’ rights and dignity.

The President called for stronger international cooperation against terrorism, organised crime, cyberattacks and illicit finance. He also urged urgent diplomacy in conflicts such as Sudan, alongside protection for civilians and access for humanitarian assistance.

This approach recognises that security challenges increasingly cross national borders and require intelligence-sharing, coordinated law enforcement, effective institutions and regional cooperation.

For Nigeria, which continues to confront security threats, international partnerships can support efforts to combat criminal networks and address the conditions that allow violence to persist. But these partnerships must complement effective domestic institutions and sustained attention to affected communities.

The UN platform gave Nigeria an opportunity to speak not only about its own interests but also about Africa’s place in a changing world. Whether that opportunity becomes a lasting national gain will depend on what the country builds from it.

Ultimately, Nigeria’s ambition should be clear: to move from demanding a stronger voice in global affairs to possessing the economic capacity, institutional credibility and diplomatic partnerships needed to make that voice count.

Olaoluwa writes from Abuja

World.title: THE RULE THAT WORKS FOR EVERYBODY ELSE
World.content:
While FIFA should be consistent with its rules, Nigeria should play to win, argues JOSHUA J. OMOJUWA

In Rabat last November, Lionel Mpasi saved two penalties and denied Nigeria the last pathway to the World Cup. He played all the minutes of that playoff final. The match finished one apiece, Congo won the shootout, and the Super Eagles missed a second consecutive World Cup. It was a clean defeat and most of us accepted it as one.

This week the New York Times and Le Monde published what FIFA’s own officials had already concluded. Mpasi, who holds French and Congolese nationality and played for France at youth level, had not completed the paperwork required to switch his international affiliation. By FIFA’s own finding, he should not have been on that pitch.

FIFA has not denied any of it.

Nigeria filed a complaint in December. FIFA’s internal review considered four courses of action. Award the match to Nigeria. Fine the Congolese federation. Replace Congo with Nigeria in the intercontinental playoff against Jamaica. Or dismiss the complaint on the ground that Nigeria had filed it late.

It chose the fourth. Congo beat Jamaica by a single goal in extra time and went to the World Cup.

Ibrahim Musa Gusau, who led the federation at the time, says he was told the complaint had been dismissed for technical reasons and was never informed that FIFA had found a problem with the goalkeeper’s eligibility.

So the governing body reached a finding on the substance, declined to act on it, and communicated only the procedural outcome to the party that had asked the question. Nigeria discovered the substance from a newspaper ten months later.

Whether the dismissal was correct is arguable. Deadlines exist for good reasons, and the NFF must take responsibility for its own tardiness. What is not arguable is that you cannot find a breach, decline to disclose it to the complainant, and then describe the process as independent.

In September last year, in the same qualifying cycle, FIFA sanctioned South Africa for fielding an ineligible player against Lesotho. Teboho Mokoena had accumulated yellow cards that should have suspended him. FIFA stripped South Africa of the points and awarded Lesotho a three nil victory.

Nigeria, incidentally, was a direct beneficiary of that ruling. It reopened our group and it is part of how we reached the playoff at all. What we are entitled to ask is why the same regulation produced a sanction in one case and a procedural dismissal in the other, and why one of those outcomes was announced while the other was withheld.

FIFA says its committees operate independently and that Gianni Infantino had no role in the decision. I have no evidence to the contrary and I will not manufacture any. The question is not whether he intervened. The question is whether an institution applies its own rules consistently, and on the available record it did not.

On the other hand, we are terrible plaintiffs.

Two days before the semi-final against Gabon, the entire Nigerian squad, players and officials together, refused to train in Morocco because they had not been paid. Not a dispute over bonuses for winning. Money already owed. Our players went into a World Cup knockout tie having spent the preceding week arguing about whether they would be paid for playing it.

They won that match anyway, which tells you something about the players and nothing good about the federation.

After the Congo defeat, the entire NFF board resigned. That is not the action of an organisation that had been running competently and was then robbed. It is the collapse of an administration that had been failing at the basics for years, and the Punch editorial at the time named it: a culture of incompetence, breached contracts and unpaid obligations that undermined the national team at every significant moment.

So both things are true, and Nigerians should be able to hold them at the same time.

FIFA found an ineligible player, said nothing to us about it, and let the result stand. That is a failure of governance at the highest level of world football, and it deserves the investigation the former federation president is now asking for. FIFA is simply bad run and this is one of many proofs of that.

We arrived at that tribunal as a country that cannot pay its own footballers on time, cannot keep a board in place, and filed its complaint late.

There is a longer pattern here. In 2006 we went out of a World Cup on head- to- head, level on points with Angola. In 2022 we went out on away goals, a rule UEFA had already abolished as indefensible. In 2026 we went out on a filing deadline.

Twenty years, three eliminations, and on each occasion the football itself could not separate us from the team that qualified.

That is the uncomfortable lesson, and it is not about FIFA at all. Every one of those exits was decided in a margin so narrow that a clause could fit inside it. A team that wins its group does not need a tie-breaker. A team that wins in Kumasi does not need away goals explained to it. A team that scores in Rabat does not need a lawyer.

The rule should work for everybody. It plainly does not, and that should be pursued. But the surest way to stop losing to paperwork is to stop finishing close enough for paperwork to matter.

Lionel Messi represents the ultimate standard in football. He is proof that one man can focus the world’s attention on a country. He has done this for the most part of the last two decades. This week, he took it to its utmost heights as he closed the chapter on his time with the Albiceleste. He is an example for us as a country and for our players. Glory awaits excellence. Doing things the right way has its reward and whilst success is never guaranteed, repeatedly committing to doing more and doing better has its rewards. FIFA failed us, but did we not already fail ourselves?

Omojuwa is chief strategist, Alpha Reach/BGX Publishing

World.title: SECURING THE 2027 ELECTIONS
World.content:
This requires a convergence of physical and cyber defences, argues KABIR ADAMU

Securing Nigeria’s 2027 elections will require a convergence of physical and cybersecurity defences capable of mitigating threat elements to the elections that span both physical and cyber domains. While physical security has traditionally been the focus of election planning, the digital domain is now equally critical, and the two must be integrated if Nigeria is to maintain a mature level of security preparedness for the elections. Current threat estimates show both physical and cyber threats to be at varying assessed levels that if not adequately mitigated will affect the Independent National Electoral Commission’s ability to conduct free, fair and credible elections in Nigeria come January and February, 2027.

The physical security challenges are complex and multifaceted and include terrorism and insurgency, banditry, gang violence and cultism, armed ethnic militia among others. According to data from Beacon Security and Innovations Limited (BSIL) a company I founded and run, and the international platform, Armed Conflict and Event Location Data (ACLED) from January – September, 2026 an average of 700 people are killed and another 500 abducted monthly across Nigeria, despite ongoing security forces operations that have successfully targeted and killed a significant number of the leadership of the violent actor groups operating in Nigeria. This is even as livelihoods continue to be destroyed by this threat actors with huge humanitarian and development consequences for communities where they remain active.

Similarly, Nigeria’s cyberspace has a multitude of institutional and structural challenges that manifest in diverse threats as the country increasingly digitizes its election infrastructure for the scheduled January and February 2027 national elections.

Nigeria is currently facing an average of 4,906 cyberattacks per organisation every week, more than twice the global average of 2,422, and a 45 per cent year-on-year increase, according to Check Point Research’s August 2026 threat intelligence. That volume eased only slightly from 4,975 weekly attacks in July, and leaves Nigeria second only to Angola among the African markets tracked. Across the continent, INTERPOL’s 2026 African Cyberthreat Assessment estimates at least $5 billion in direct economic damage from cybercrime in 2025, with reported losses more than doubling from $192 million in 2024 to $484 million. The measurable losses are concentrated in payments: banks and customers lost ₦52.26 billion to fraud in 2024 and ₦25.85 billion in 2025, for a cumulative ₦134.48 billion between 2020 and 2025 (CBN/NIBSS). An earlier multi-sector estimate put losses at about ₦1.1 trillion between 2017 and 2023 across banking, telecommunications and government. Nigeria also recorded 5,822 ransomware detections in 2025, including an August 2025 attack on the Nigeria Customs Service that froze cargo clearance and generated an estimated $18 million in storage costs. Critical digital infrastructure is increasingly being probed by state-aligned Advanced Persistent Threats. ngCERT and NCC-CSIRT have flagged SideWinder against maritime, government, telecommunications and financial targets, and a wider espionage pattern, including the UNC2814/GRIDTIDE campaign against telecom and government networks, aimed at long-term access to telecommunications backbones rather than immediate financial gain.

In the aftermath of the 2023 elections, the then Ministry of Communications and Digital Economy issued a statement where it indicated that in the lead up to the 2023 General Elections, its monitoring of threat intelligence revealed what it described as “an astronomical increase in cyber threats to Nigerian cyberspace”. The Ministry noted that “threats to public websites and portals averaged around 1,550,000 daily” and that “this skyrocketed to 6,997,277 on Presidential Election Day”.

These statistics are a glaring warning about the fragility of Nigeria’s physical and digital borders. But as we look toward the 2027 General Elections, the stakes are existential to our democracy. A significant effort has already been achieved in physical election security risk management. INEC has internal capabilities for election risk management. It also has the Inter-Agency Consultative Committee on Election Security, which comprises several security sector players and supports election security functions.

However, the cyber security function is not so mature compared to the physical security functions despite our democratic infrastructure now being almost entirely digitised. The Bimodal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS), the Result Viewing Portal (IReV), the National Register of Voters, and the vast digital communication networks used by political parties and the media are platforms that add additional exposure points and the new battlegrounds. We are no longer just looking at the risk of financial theft; we are looking at the very real potential for state-sponsored disruption, voter data manipulation, and AI-driven disinformation campaigns designed to undermine public trust in the electoral process.

Yet, as a nation, we are still flying with a fragmented radar. Currently, our cybersecurity capabilities and evaluations are trapped in regulatory silos. The Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN) mandates rigorous assessments for banks; the MCIDE supports several initiatives for securing the Nigerian cyberspace, including Cybersecurity Centers such as National Information Technology (NITDA)’s Computer Emergency Readiness and Response Team (CERRT), the Nigerian Communications Commission (NCC)’s Computer Security Incident Response Team (CSIRT), and Galaxy Backbone (GBB)’s Security Operations Centre (SOC).

It is worth noting that in the while these sector-specific efforts are commendable, they do not provide a consolidated, holistic view of our national cyber posture. More critically, there is no unified framework mapping the cross-sector, national threat to our democratic infrastructure.

We cannot secure what we do not comprehensively measure. It is time to institutionalise a unified National Cyber Threat Assessment (NCTA) and specifically tailor our national cyber capabilities to protect the 2027 elections. This requires the Office of the National Security Adviser (ONSA), the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC), and the Federal Ministry of Communications, Innovation and Digital Economy to take the lead and advance a unified capability effort. Ad-hoc task forces and post-incident reactions will not suffice. Here is what intentional, institutionalised action must look like:

First, ONSA must institutionalise the NCTA for electoral security. ONSA, through the National Cybersecurity Coordination Centre (NCCC), must lead the development of an annual National Cyber Threat Assessment that specifically models the threat landscape for our electoral infrastructure. This should utilise a “dual-report” model: a public, unclassified guide to help political parties, media, and civil society combat disinformation, and a classified annex detailing state-sponsored APT tactics for the security architecture.

Second, INEC must elevate electoral technology to Critical National Information Infrastructure (CNII) status. Following the President’s landmark 2024 CNII Order, INEC must treat the BVAS, IReV, and the voter register with the same uncompromising rigor applied to the banking sector. This means mandating continuous, independent red-teaming of electoral systems, enforcing zero-trust architecture, and ensuring that the entire electoral technology supply chain is completely vetted against foreign compromise. It must also set up a similar interagency consultative committee to manage cyber security functions. There must also be a pathway for the two functions to support a secure electoral space in Nigeria.

Third, the Ministry of Communications, Innovation and Digital Economy must harden the underlying digital infrastructure and lead the counter-narrative. The Ministry holds the critical mandate for Nigeria’s digital economy and cybersecurity policy. It must ensure that the foundational digital infrastructure supporting the elections, including broadband networks, data centres, and cloud hosting environments, is structurally resilient and insulated from sabotage. Working in tandem with the Ministry of Information and National Orientation, the Ministry must spearhead a national counter-disinformation framework. This involves deploying AI-detection tools to combat deepfakes, coordinating a unified public communication strategy to maintain voter trust, and ensuring that a dedicated portion of the National Cybersecurity Levy is strategically deployed to fund these electoral tech defences.

Fourth, ONSA, INEC, and the Ministries must establish a dedicated Electoral Cyber Defence Node. Breaking down silos is non-negotiable. ngCERT, INEC, and the relevant ministries must establish a joint, real-time threat intelligence-sharing node specifically for the electoral cycle. This node should actively monitor for infrastructure probing and coordinated bot-network disinformation, sharing anonymised telemetry with telecommunications companies and civil society organisations in real-time to neutralise threats before they reach the public.

National security is economic security, but in 2027, a convergence of physical and cybersecurity will be electoral security. If we do not intentionally secure the physical and security and digital pipes of our democracy, we leave the next general elections vulnerable to the very syndicates and state-sponsored actors currently probing our physical and cyber networks.

Nigeria possesses the talent, the legal frameworks, and the institutional architecture to get this right and ONSA, INEC, the Ministry of Communications, Innovation and Digital Economy, and our entire national security architecture should move from reactive posturing to proactive, unified defence. The time to build the shield that protects our democratic mandate is now, as the threat vectors have already been deployed.

Dr. Adamu is the Managing Director of Beacon Security and Innovations Limited.

World.title: TEACHERS NEED THEIR REWARD ON EARTH
World.content:
In Nigeria, there is a popular saying which states that teachers’ reward is in Heaven. This literarily means that no matter the amount of money one pays to a teacher it will never be enough as compensation to a teacher when compared with the value of the services he or she renders to society.

In my view, teachers should be paid as much as bankers in order to attract the best brains into the profession. They deserve to be well compensated. Indeed, teachers deserve their rewards both “here” on earth and in the “hereafter”.

It is sad to note that, the welfare of the Nigerian teacher is generally poor, especially, at the primary school level. No one is anymore attracted to the profession. Something needs to be done urgently! The profession that used to be the first choice of the best brains in the society is now seen as the last option for the jobless.

In the past the status of a teacher is next to that of the District Head and or a Village Head in the society. Teachers were highly admired and cherished. Sadly, the profession is no longer cherished by the people. It no longer attracts the best brains. Year- in- year- out, teachers’ welfare continues to deteriorate.

It baffles me to note that primary education which is the foundation of education is largely being handled by the most dysfunctional tiers of government. Both the federal and state governments intervention shows little or nothing. No building stands without a sound and or a solid foundation. For us to get it right, we must build a solid foundation in our educational system. We must get well motivated and qualified teachers to manage the system.

Local governments or state governments cannot adequately maintain primary education anymore. The local governments, due to lack of financial autonomy and poor IGR, lack the financial capacity to efficiently and effectively fund primary education.

Primary school teachers in virtually all the states of the federation are among the worst hit in terms poor and unpaid salaries. Their working conditions are poor. Even at that they are not being paid as and when due. Their employers pay little or no attention to their training and retraining. The teaching profession has become an “all- comers job”. It is now a platform for political patronage or compensation to political thugs. The financing model of primary education in Nigeria needs a rethink. It is high time the federal government paid more attention to primary education.

Nurudeen Dauda, Kaduna State

World.title: Marwa Commends Security Agencies Over Rescue of 20 Kidnapped Corps Members
World.content:
Michael Olugbode in Abuja

The Chairman/Chief Executive of the National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA), Brig. Gen. Buba Marwa (rtd.), has commended the Nigerian Army, Nigeria Police Force, Department of State Services (DSS) and other security agencies for the successful rescue of 20 prospective National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) members and another victim abducted in the South-east.

Marwa, in a statement issued on Thursday by the Director, Media and Advocacy, NDLEA, Femi Babafemi, described the rescue operation as a victory for the country and evidence of what coordinated and intelligence-driven operations could achieve in the fight against criminality.

He said the safe return of the prospective corps members to their families demonstrated the courage, professionalism and unity of purpose among Nigeria’s security agencies.

“Our corps members are the nation’s best, serving their fatherland with hope and idealism. Nigeria owes them protection, and today our gallant men and women have delivered,” he said.

Marwa, who is a retired military officer, said it was important to draw public attention to the achievements of security agencies and commend them for their efforts in protecting Nigerians.

He also acknowledged other successful rescue operations conducted by security agencies across the country in recent months, saying the operations had freed abducted victims and restored hope to affected families.

“Every life rescued is a triumph for our collective resolve. These operations show that criminals cannot outrun a determined and united security architecture,” he said.

The NDLEA chairman further pledged the agency’s continued support and cooperation with sister security agencies, noting that illicit drug trafficking and abuse often contributed to violent crimes, kidnapping and banditry.

“Where drugs flow, insecurity thrives. That is why the NDLEA will keep working with sister agencies to dismantle the networks that fund and fuel criminality, and we will deepen intelligence-sharing and joint operations,” Marwa said.

He urged security agencies to sustain the momentum in the fight against criminality and called on Nigerians to support security forces by providing timely and credible information.

Marwa also wished the rescued prospective corps members a speedy recovery and successful reunion with their families.

World.title: Northern Stakeholders Support ACReSAL’s $500m Additional Financing
World.content:
Linus Aleke in Abuja

The proposed $500 million additional financing for the Agro-Climatic Resilience in Semi-Arid Landscapes (ACReSAL) project has received broad support from stakeholders across northern Nigeria, according to the Think Nigeria First Initiative (TNFI).

Speaking during a press conference in Abuja, the Director General of TNFI, Alhaji Abubakar Tsanni, said governors, traditional rulers, farmers, herders and women’s groups had thrown their weight behind the next phase of the project because of the tangible results recorded in their communities.

Tsanni identified the governors of Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Kebbi, Kaduna, Jigawa, Benue and Plateau States as among those who had personally inaugurated, inspected or flagged off ACReSAL interventions.

He added that Bauchi State had publicly committed its counterpart funding to the proposed next phase.

“Traditional institutions, including the palaces of the Shehu of Borno, Emir of Argungu and Emir of Zazzau, work hand-in-hand with the project. In Wurno, a farmer of 27 years on the irrigation scheme says hope has returned. In Nguru, herders and fishermen have returned to a wetland that was dry for 12 years,” Tsanni said.

According to him, women account for 47 per cent of the project’s 4.4 million direct beneficiaries, while university students in Kogi, Kebbi and Plateau States are being trained in modern greenhouse farming on their campuses.

He further said the Federal Ministers of Environment, Water Resources and Agriculture had jointly participated in the project’s mid-term review in Kaduna.

Tsanni maintained that stakeholders were not seeking charity, but sustainable financing built around continuity, shared responsibility and self-reliance.

He disclosed that participating states had so far released N22 billion in counterpart funding, while the $9.5 million Community Revolving Fund disbursed to 381 communities was being repaid and re-lent.

He also noted that Benue and Nasarawa States had established state agencies to ensure the sustainability of the project’s assets.

The TNFI Director General therefore urged governors, traditional rulers, legislators and community leaders across the north who had witnessed the impact of ACReSAL to “say so publicly, and say so now”.

He also called on the Federal Government and the World Bank to conclude the financing arrangement without further delay.

World.title: Humanitarian Worker, Police Inspector Killed as Bandits Raid Sokoto Communities
World.content:
Onuminya Innocent in Sokoto

A humanitarian and field operations professional, Ms Lydia Chinenye Nwankwo, has been killed following an attack by suspected bandits in Sokoto State.

Nwankwo was reportedly attacked alongside members of her team while returning from field operations in Kajiji community, Shagari Local Government Area of the state on Tuesday, October 6, 2026.

The development was confirmed by her sister, Chisom Nwankwo, who announced the tragic incident in a Facebook post on Thursday October 8.

According to the family, the team came under heavy attack from the armed bandits who opened fire on their vehicle, killing the young humanitarian worker on the spot.

The incident has thrown the humanitarian community in Sokoto into mourning, with colleagues describing Lydia as a dedicated field worker committed to serving vulnerable communities in hard-to-reach areas.

Meanwhile, the Sokoto State Police Command has confirmed the attack on communities in Shagari LGA, disclosing that a police inspector also lost his life during the incident.

The Command’s Public Relations Officer, DSP Ahmed Rufai, who confirmed the attack to THISDAY, said the Divisional Police Officer in charge of Shagari LGA had briefed the state headquarters on the development.

Rufai, however, noted that the Command was still collating details of the attack to ascertain the full extent of casualties and damage.

“I just spoke with the DPO in charge of Shagari now, who confirmed the attack on some communities in the local government. We are still on it. I cannot give details now until I gather my information about the incident. I will get back to you on it,” the police spokesman stated.

As at press time, the security situation in the affected communities remained tense, with residents calling on the state government and security agencies to intensify patrols and deploy more personnel to Shagari and its environs to forestall further attacks.

World.title: Reality TV star joins ActionSA – announces bid to become ward councillor
World.content:
The Ultimatum South Africa's Nolla has joined ActionSA as a prospective ward councillor. Images via IG

Two years after enduring a dramatic breakup with his partner, Lebogang Sephaphathi, on the season finale of The Ultimatum South Africa, Lehlohonolo Moseko, also known as Nolla, has returned to the spotlight, this time in politics. In fact, the reality TV star is hoping to secure a position as ward councillor for ActionSA in the Emfuleni Municipality during the upcoming local government elections.

Nolla and Lebo have since wed and welcomed a baby boy together.

THE ULTIMATUM’S NOLLA ANNOUNCES ACTIONSA COUNCILLOR BID

In an Instagram post, Nolla Moseko surprised his followers by announcing his bid to run as ward councillor in his local district.



He shared: “It’s official, we are contesting Local Government Elections, and I’m your Counsellor [councillor] Candidate for ActionSA in Emfuleni Ward 35. Let’s vote for change”.

The news was met with surprise and amusement from his followers, given his career as a businessman and social media influencer.

“Giving South Africans an ultimatum?” asked one. “This country is a joke”, responded another.

ROLLERCOASTER ROMANCE

Three years ago, Nolla and his partner Lebo dramatically split on the reunion episode of The Ultimatum South Africa.

The couple had entered the reality TV show in the hopes of strengthening their relationship – Lebo wanted marriage, but Nolla was not ready to commit.



However, during the show, filmed in 2023, Lebo publicly dumped Nolla and left the reality TV experiment after discovering that he had hooked up with a co-star.

During the 2024 reunion, the duo dropped a bombshell that they had reconciled. It was short-lived, though, as Lebo dumped Nolla for the second time – this time during the finale – after claiming she was “unhappy.”

She said: “He hasn’t changed. I don’t see myself being married to him. I don’t feel like I’m in love with you, and I’ve decided to end our relationship.”

Nolla later described being blindsided as a “betrayal.”

Despite the high-profile split, the couple rekindled their romance and got married last year. They also welcomed a baby boy.

“Our love story is about resilience and forgiveness”, Nolla told Batswadi Magazine.

He added, “We learned to grow up and heal, and now we get to raise love itself”.

ACTIONSA AFFILIATION

Nolla wouldn’t be the first high-profile person to support ActionSA and its leader, Herman Mashaba.

Others include:

Moja Love presenter Xolani Khumalo, who is the mayoral candidate for the City of Ekurhuleni.

Muvhango actor Gabriel Temudzani

Prominent lawyer Tumi Sole

Music and theatre composer Lebo M

World.title: Connie Ferguson returns to ‘Generations’…and Somizi? [video]
World.content:
Connie Ferguson, the renowned South African actress, is set to make her highly anticipated return to SABC 1’s Generations: The Legacy.

However, some fans are now wondering whether the incomparable Somizi Mhlongo could also be joining the popular soapie.

CONNIE FERGUSON RETURNS TO ‘GENERATIONS: THE LEGACY’

The beloved actress marks another riveting comeback to Generations: The Legacy, reprising her role as the elegant Karabo Moroka, an iconic character in South African television history.



Connie joined the soapie when it premiered back in 1994 and left many times over the years to explore her talents, such as establishing Ferguson Films alongside her late husband, Shona Ferguson.

In a clip posted on the soapie’s online pages, Connie, looking youthful as ever, walks through the backstage corridors while happily interacting with staff members.

WAIT, IS SOMIZI JOINING ‘GENERATIONS: THE LEGACY’?

While fans look forward to Connie’s comeback, some are speculating whether Somizi’s brief appearance in the video signals a role on the soapie or even a behind-the-scenes position.

Theories quickly floated around, with some suggesting he could be cast as Karabo’s best friend. While others reckoned he might join the wardrobe department given his new path in fashion design.

Somizi has earned his stripes as a performer in his own right, despite standing on the shoulders of acting giants.

His portrayal of Fire in the 1992 film Sarafina! remains memorable, and he continued to take on other acting roles throughout his career.



FANS WEIGH IN

Hannah Molatelo Morudu: Three times dam***, welcome back, Karabo Moroka.

Aactionn Shanguro: Karabo is back.

Fulu Mphaphuli: Welcome back, Karabo.

Ndumiso Kumalo: She is coming back soon to Generations.

Khanyiso Zazini asked: uSomizi uzobangubani ke ngk [What role will Somizi be playing?]

Donald Màmadi replied: He’s coming on the show as Somizi from Metro FM. Lucy will write to [the] Ask a Man show on Metro FM, and that’s how Somizi will be on Generations.

Dinel Natasha suggested: [As] Karabo’s bestie and Lucy’s new friend.

Sambulo Andy Favor Adams commented: Maybe uyabagqokisa [he will style the actors] [since] he is a fashion designer, I stand to be corrected, mangi [if I’m] wrong.

World.title: Roosevelt High School principal chastises matrics: ‘SAPS are on their way’ [video]
World.content:
Roosevelt High School principal Christel Venter was heard chastising learners after its disastrous matric dance event. Images via Facebook

The principal of Roosevelt High School, Cristèl Venter, is heard chastising learners at its recent matric dance, which was shut down early after it spiralled out of control

The disastrous event made headlines after Ventre penned a lengthy open letter after learners were caught indulging in underage drinking, drug use, and threatening staff with firearms.

Since then, podcaster Penuel Mlothswa has visited the school to encourage learners to become responsible and accountable for their actions.



ROOSEVELT HIGH SCHOOL MATRIC DANCE: VOICE NOTE GOES VIRAL

In a voice note leaked online, Roosevelt High School principal Cristèl Venter was heard scolding learners who had misbehaved during the matric dance, held at Avianto Hotel in Muldersdrift.

The event took place during the third term holidays. Venter – who had initially skipped the matric dance due to poor health said: “I had to drag myself out of my house because I’m shutting down your matric dance – because of guns, drugs and drunk people vomiting all over Avianto

“I don’t care what you do afterwards…I said be quiet! When I have to apologise to the management of Avianto…when one of your drivers pulled a gun on a staff member…when one of you people bumped my staff with a car when they asked you to move along.



She added, “I suggest you finish quickly because SAPS is also on their way”

In her open letter, Venter stated that she had decided to shut down the matric dance celebrations due to unruly behaviour. She added that staff had supervised learners who awaited their parents’ pick-up.

Following the backlash, Roosevelt High School have since disabled their social media platforms



PRAISE FOR PRINCIPAL

On social media, many South Africans have praised Roosevelt High School’s principal for her no-nonsense approach.

Here’s what some had to say…

Peter John Wilsnagh: “Not many principals have the testicular fortitude of this dynamic principal.”



Hilde Lotter: “What a principal..so much guts..so real. Well done. Your parents should be so grateful to have a leader like you heading the school their children attend”.

Satie Raath: “This is leadership!”

Ann Collins-Polglase: “Well done! It’s about time!”

World.title: What beachgoers and anglers need to know as spring tides approach
World.content:
Friday’s high and low tide times for South Africa’s coastal cities as spring tide conditions approach. Image: Pexels

However, tides are only part of the picture. Wind, waves and swell can also affect conditions along the shore and at sea.

Spring tide approaching

Tides can affect surfing, swimming, fishing and other coastal activities. Conditions vary from beach to beach depending on the seabed, swell and wind.



Higher tides can cover rocks and reefs that you might easily spot at low tide, so check when water levels will rise and fall.

The next spring tide coincides with the new moon on Saturday, 10 October. Spring tides bring higher high tides and lower low tides than usual.

Tides to watch along the coast on Friday

Checking the high and low tide times can help beachgoers, anglers and boat users plan their activities around changing coastal conditions.



Check the tide times and the latest weather and marine warnings before you head to the coast.

World.title: Five Sundowns heroes who have delivered heartbreak to Pirates
World.content:
Mamelodi Sundowns have had the better of Orlando Pirates in league meetings for more than a decade.

In cup competitions, however, it has been a different story. The Buccaneers are unbeaten in their two cup finals against Masandawana, and the two giants will meet once again this weekend in the MTN8 final at Moses Mabhida Stadium.

Orlando Pirates are chasing a fifth consecutive MTN8 title, while Sundowns will be looking to end their dominance in the competition.



With another blockbuster clash on the horizon, we look at five Sundowns players who have caused heartbreak for the Buccaneers in the past.

Isaac Shai

Isaac Shai produced a memorable performance against Orlando Pirates in November 1999, scoring a brace for Mamelodi Sundowns in the second leg of the Rothmans Cup semi-final.



His Man of the Match display helped Sundowns book their place in the final while breaking the hearts of a Pirates side that had been hoping to progress.

Shai’s explosive strikes and memorable celebrations remain part of the history of this fixture.

Sundowns last defeated Pirates in a final back in 2007

Brent Carelse



In 2007, former Ajax Cape Town midfielder Brent Carelse became a Sundowns hero when he scored the only goal of the SAA Supa 8 final against Orlando Pirates.

Having joined the Brazilians, Carelse made his mark on the big stage by finding the back of the net early in the first half and handing Sundowns a memorable cup triumph over their rivals.

Lucas Ribeiro Costa

Lucas Ribeiro Costa has also enjoyed some memorable moments against Orlando Pirates since arriving in South Africa.



The Brazilian has scored three goals against the Buccaneers, including a brace in Sundowns’ emphatic 4-1 victory in February last year.

Ribeiro’s explosive performance helped Sundowns extend their advantage over Pirates and contributed to what ultimately became an eighth successive league victory.

Peter Shalulile

Peter Shalulile has been a thorn in Orlando Pirates’ side for years, and one of his best performances against the Buccaneers came in the Nedbank Cup in 2021.



The Namibian striker scored twice as Sundowns thrashed Pirates 4-1, underlining his ability to deliver when it matters most.

Shalulile’s physicality, movement and eye for goal have consistently made him a difficult opponent for the Buccaneers.

Leon could be key if Sundowns are to beat Pirates

Brayan Leon



Since joining Sundowns in January, Brayan Leon wasted little time making an impression, scoring five goals in his first month at the club.

However, his biggest impact came against Orlando Pirates at FNB Stadium in February this year, when he broke the hearts of the Buccaneers with a decisive performance.

Leon will be one of the players Pirates will have to watch closely when the two sides meet again.



With Sundowns desperate to end Orlando Pirates’ dominance in the MTN8, the Colombian could once again play a key role as Masandawana look to finally get one over their rivals in the cup.

Who’s winning the MTN8?

World.title: Gauteng weather: What to expect this weekend
World.content:
Gauteng can expect hot weather and possible thundershowers on Saturday before clearer skies return on Sunday. Image: Unsplash

Gauteng residents can expect a hot Saturday with possible afternoon thundershowers before clearer and drier conditions return on Sunday.

World.title: Criticise but don't encourage public to ignore ConCourt rulings - SAHRC
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Criticise judgments if you must, but undermining the Constitutional Court threatens the foundation of South Africa's democracy.

That is the view of the South African Human Rights Commission following Minister in the Presidency Khumbudzo Ntshavheni's statement.

During a briefing on immigration by the Inter-Ministerial Committee on Migration, Ntshavheni said: "If the Constitution of South Africa does not prioritise South Africans, South Africans have a right to demand the amendment of that Constitution".

READ | Constitution must protect South Africans first - Ntshavheni

But SAHRC commissioner Tshepo Madlingozi reminded members of the executive, including Cabinet ministers, of their constitutional obligations.

“Their oath of office says they will not only respect the Constitution, but they will actively promote the Constitution,” he said, emphasising that it is not only the Constitutional Court that needs to protect the Constitution.

Madlingozi stressed that South Africa is a Constitutional democracy and that rulings by the courts must be respected.

“If we don't do so, we are on our way to a very dangerous slippery slope.”

He said people, including members of government, are free to criticise the judiciary, but must be careful.

World.title: 'There will be consequences' - Dimpane calls for calm after violent protests
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - The South African Police Service (SAPS) have taken a hard stance after protest action against illegal foreign nationals turned violent in Gauteng and KwaZulu-Natal on Thursday.

These scenes were witness both in Soweto and Durban CBD.

Briefing the media on these tensions, Acting National Commissioner of the SAPS, Puleng Dimpane, said they would not tolerate lawlessness.

She said in Soweto, ten vehicles were torched and some shops looted. While in Durban, 14 vehicles were torched.

READ | Shops looted in Soweto as protest turns violent.

Police have arrested three people in KwaZulu-Natal. In Gauteng they are still pursuing those behind the criminality.

“Those responsible for acts of violence and destruction will be identified, investigated, and where sufficient evidence exists, they will be arrested and will be brought to court. There will be consequences for this criminality that is taking place today in Gauteng as well as in KZN,”

Dimpane has urged residents to remain calm and allow government to handle things.

World.title: Constitution must protect South Africans first - Ntshavheni
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Minister in the Presidency Khumbudzo Ntshavheni said if the Constitution fails to prioritise South Africans first, citizens have the right to demanded for it be amended to protect themselves and their own sovereignty.

Ntshavheni was speaking on Thursday as the Inter-Ministerial Committee on Migration outlined the government's response to the Constitutional Court ruling that has reopened the asylum system to new applications.

READ | Court does not confer new rights to asylum seekers - Kubayi

She said they have noted the judgment, but maintain that there are ‘unintended consequences', and as such, the government is receiving legal advice on what options it has.

In July, the apex court ruled that parts of the Refugee Act were unconstitutional and invalid.

The Constitutional Court ruled that parts of the Refugees Act are unconstitutional and invalid.

Ntshavheni warned people who do not qualify for asylum not to clog the system, saying those without the required papers could face legal action.

“This is an opportunity for Home Affairs to find out who is supposed to be in the country and who isn't. And we will apply the laws of the country to those who are not supposed to be in the country."

World.title: Number Of The Day | $105 | 08 October 2026
World.content:
South Africa's fuel-price problem is bigger than the petrol pump

When global oil supplies come under threat, the costs can spread from transport and farming to food prices, inflation and household budgets.

South Africa does not need to experience a physical fuel shortage to suffer the economic consequences of disrupted global oil markets. A shipment delayed in the Middle East, a rise in insurance costs for oil tankers or a weaker rand can eventually translate into higher expenses for businesses and households thousands of kilometres away. The resulting pressure rarely stays confined to motorists filling their vehicles.

The latest warning comes from renewed uncertainty surrounding the Strait of Hormuz, one of the world's most important energy shipping routes. According to the

International Energy Agency (IEA), approximately 20 million barrels of crude oil and petroleum products passed through the strait each day in 2025, representing around a quarter of global seaborne oil trade. The limited alternatives available to exporters mean that even temporary disruptions can unsettle international prices.

For South Africa, the vulnerability is particularly acute because domestic fuel prices are closely linked to international petroleum markets. The country's pricing system considers the cost of imported refined products, shipping and the rand-dollar exchange rate. Local taxes, levies, transport costs and margins are then added. This means a stronger global oil market can increase domestic costs even when fuel continues to arrive and local filling stations remain fully supplied.

Why diesel deserves particular attention

Diesel plays a critical role throughout the productive economy. Tractors and harvesting equipment require fuel. Trucks carry agricultural produce to processors, distribution centres and retailers. Construction equipment, mining operations and backup generators also depend on diesel to varying degrees.

When diesel becomes more expensive, these businesses face a choice: absorb the additional cost, reduce expenditure elsewhere or attempt to recover it through higher prices. None is painless. A farmer may have little control over the price received for a crop, while a transport company operating on a fixed contract may be unable to recover its increased fuel bill immediately.

The consequences can accumulate along a supply chain. Higher costs at the farm can be compounded by transport and distribution expenses before food reaches supermarket shelves. Not every increase will be passed on in full, and the effect varies across products and businesses, but the broader risk is clear: an energy shock can become a food-price and household-budget problem.

That possibility has already featured in the South African Reserve Bank's assessments. In its May 2026 monetary policy statement, the Bank identified higher diesel and fertiliser costs as pressures on agriculture. It also examined scenarios in which a prolonged Middle East crisis could combine with food-price pressures and a weaker rand to produce more persistent inflation.

Why an R38 diesel scenario matters, even if it never happens

In the 8 October edition of Number of the Day, Gareth Edwards and Francis Herd discussed a higher-risk scenario in which crude oil could reach $120–$130 a barrel and diesel could rise to R38 a litre.

That figure is not an announced pump price or an inevitable forecast. Its usefulness lies in illustrating the scale of the risk if the conflict escalates significantly.

For a logistics business, the question is not simply whether diesel reaches that exact number. It is whether fuel expenses might climb far enough to undermine existing delivery contracts. For farmers, it is whether production budgets and seasonal planning can withstand another increase. For households, it is whether additional transport and food costs leave less money available for other necessities.

These concerns also explain why a rise in oil prices can become a monetary policy problem. Higher fuel costs directly affect inflation, but their influence can spread when businesses increase prices to recover operating expenses. If inflation expectations rise and those increases become persistent, the Reserve Bank may face a more difficult interest-rate decision.

What can government actually control?

Calls for fuel-price relief are understandable, but South Africa cannot legislate lower international oil prices. Government has more direct influence over domestic

components of the fuel-price structure, including certain taxes and levies, than over the global cost of crude oil or the exchange rate.

Reducing a levy could provide temporary relief, but it would also create a fiscal trade-off. Revenue would have to be replaced, spending adjusted or borrowing increased. The question is therefore not only whether government can lower the amount paid at the pump, but how any relief would be funded and who would ultimately bear that cost.

A more durable response also requires businesses and public institutions to reduce their exposure to energy volatility. More efficient transport networks, resilient supply chains and reduced dependence on diesel for backup power cannot eliminate international shocks, but they can limit the damage those shocks cause.

South Africa's fuel-price challenge is ultimately about economic resilience. The next oil-price movement will matter, but so will the country's ability to prevent an external energy shock from spreading unchecked through production, transport, food prices and household finances.

References

· International Energy Agency, Strait of Hormuz, February 2026.

· Department of Mineral and Petroleum Resources, Fuel Price Structure.

· South African Reserve Bank, Monetary Policy Committee Statement, May 2026.

· eNCA, Number of the Day, 8 October 2026, Gareth Edwards and Francis Herd.

World.title: SA Explained | Can Politicians Still Fool South African Voters? Conrad Koch and Chester Missing | 08 October 2026
World.content:
Beyond the Ballot: How South Africans Can Hold Their Municipalities Accountable

As South Africa approaches the 2026 local government elections, the real test of political promises may be what residents can measure long after the campaign ends.

A pothole does not know which party controls the municipality. Neither does a broken streetlight or a household waiting for water. For residents living with unreliable services, the politics of local government eventually becomes a practical question: who is responsible, what will be done, and when?

As South Africans prepare to vote on 4 November, campaign speeches and coalition promises are likely to compete for attention. Yet the central challenge of municipal democracy extends beyond choosing a party. It is ensuring that whoever takes office can be held accountable for what happens afterwards.

The promise is not the plan

Election manifestos are designed to win support. Municipal administrations, however, are expected to operate through budgets, development plans and measurable performance systems. A political commitment to improve water supply means little without clarity on the infrastructure involved, the money available, the responsible department and the timetable for delivery.

South Africa's Municipal Systems Act provides for community participation in local government, including municipal planning, performance management and decisions about services. This matters because residents are not meant to remain spectators once the votes have been counted.

A useful starting point is to translate campaign promises into specific questions. If a party promises to repair roads, which roads take priority and how will progress be reported? If it pledges better refuse collection, what happens when scheduled collections are missed? If water interruptions persist, what information should households expect from the municipality?

These are not glamorous questions. They are the ones that reveal whether an election promise has become an operational commitment.

Coalitions complicate the promise

Where no party secures outright control of a council, coalition negotiations introduce another layer of accountability. Parties that criticised one another during an election may later find themselves sharing responsibility for municipal decisions.

For voters, that can create understandable confusion. A party's manifesto may remain unchanged, but its ability to implement particular commitments may depend on compromises negotiated with political partners.

The critical distinction is between compromise that enables government to function and arrangements that obscure responsibility. Coalition agreements should not become an excuse for residents to lose sight of who controls which decisions.

Imagine a municipality where parties jointly promise to improve waste collection. If the service deteriorates, residents need more than competing explanations from coalition partners. They need to know which political leadership is accountable, which officials must implement the programme and how the municipality intends to correct the failure.

A functioning coalition should make responsibility clearer through its agreements and governing arrangements, not harder to identify.

Accountability cannot wait five years

Municipal government affects everyday life through service delivery, planning, infrastructure and decisions about public resources. National government has also identified municipal financial management, performance monitoring and public participation as important parts of strengthening local government.

The opportunity for residents is therefore broader than voting. Communities can follow municipal plans, examine budgets, participate in public consultation processes and demand explanations when published targets are missed.

That participation becomes more effective when questions are specific. A general complaint that a council is failing may be politically powerful, but a documented pattern of missed collections, unresolved maintenance requests or delayed projects can create a stronger basis for sustained scrutiny.

There is a role here for neighbourhood organisations, journalists and community groups. They can keep attention on the same commitments long after campaign posters disappear, compare public promises with municipal plans and ask for progress in language residents can understand.

Political satire can help make this scrutiny accessible. In an SA Explained conversation with Naledi Moleo, Conrad Koch and Chester Missing question the promises, personalities and contradictions of election politics. Humour may encourage audiences to recognise a problem, but recognition alone does not repair the service behind the joke.

South Africa's voters do not have to choose between understanding politics and laughing at its absurdities. They can do both. The more demanding task is turning that attention into consistent oversight.

On election day, the ballot records a choice. In the months and years that follow, the quality of local democracy will depend on whether residents can establish what was promised, see what was delivered and insist on answers when the two do not match.

References

· SA Explained, Episode 2, Naledi Moleo with Conrad Koch and Chester Missing, episode transcript, October 2026. · Local Government: Municipal Systems Act 32 of 2000, South African Government. · Local government: roles, planning and accountability, South African Government. · Electoral Commission: 2026 local government elections campaign, 27 May 2026.
