"What we do as a society right now is make the criminal more important than the innocent," Federico said, criticizing progressive policies such as reduced sentencing and no-cash bail. "We have turned the page. We are the underdogs."

Fox News' David Spunt contributed to this report.

World.title: Guinness brewery that welcomed 2 million visitors closing its doors for good
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The Guinness Open Gate Brewery in Halethorpe, Maryland, just outside Baltimore, will soon close, leaving the iconic Irish beer brand's Chicago brewery as its only U.S. location.

Nov. 1 will mark the brewery's final day open to the public, leaving 174 Aramark employees out of work, as cited in a notice filed with the Maryland Department of Labor on Oct. 1.

The move comes amid a $1 billion restructuring plan at Diageo, Guinness' parent company.

BREWERY THAT OFFERED FREE BEER WHEN TRUMP DIES FACES POSSIBLE CLOSURE AFTER STATE REVOKES ALCOHOL PERMITS

Some teams at Diageo are losing 20% to 30% of their staff, Reuters reported in July.

"This decision follows a careful review of our operations and long-term business priorities," a Diageo spokesperson told Fox News Digital. "It is not a reflection of the passion, talent or dedication of our team, nor of the support we have received from consumers and the Baltimore community since we opened our doors in 2018."

Since opening in 2018, the Guinness Open Gate Brewery has welcomed more than 2 million visitors, according to a post on its Facebook page.

CLICK HERE TO 

The brewery was the first to open in the U.S. since the Irish beer maker's previous brewery in New York closed in 1954, FOX Business reported at the time.

"It's obviously a shame to see the Guinness brewery close in Maryland," said Derek Brown of Drink Company, a Washington, D.C.-based hospitality consulting and events company.

"However, I'm not surprised, in the sense that their core product remains Guinness, and now Guinness Zero," Brown told Fox News Digital. "The brewery focused on experimental products which are interesting in themselves, but not necessarily primary drivers of Guinness' business."

The experimental portion of the brewery allowed guests to concoct their own brews, and more than 700 beers were created over the years, according to the brewery's Facebook post.

But changing trends in alcohol consumption likely played a role in the decision, industry experts say.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

New research shows that U.S. alcohol use has declined for the first time since the COVID-19 pandemic, Fox News Digital recently reported.

More Americans are also alternating between alcoholic and non-alcoholic beverages — a practice known as "zebra striping" — partly contributing to the decline, according to experts.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"Our immediate focus is supporting affected colleagues through this transition," a Diageo spokesperson said. "We are committed to treating our team members with respect and providing resources and assistance to help them navigate the change."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The spokesperson added that Guinness "remains one of our most important brands, and we are committed to investing in its long-term growth and success. While our Baltimore brewery will close, our commitment to bringing Guinness to consumers around the world remains as strong as ever."

World.title: Caitlin Clark's Fever set a TV ratings bar the WNBA semifinal openers could not come close to reaching
World.content:
The Indiana Fever's regular-season games on major broadcast networks averaged more than twice the audience of the WNBA semifinal openers on Oct. 4.

And those playoff games were on ABC and NBC.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

An OutKick review of Indiana's 10 regular-season games on ABC, CBS and NBC found an average audience of approximately 2.32 million viewers. The two semifinal openers averaged about 1.16 million.

CAITLIN CLARK SENDS WNBA ALL-STAR RATINGS SOARING AS 3-POINT CONTEST AUDIENCE FALLS WITHOUT HER

That gave Indiana an average audience approximately 100% larger, a difference of nearly 1.16 million viewers per game.

New York–Atlanta's Game 1 averaged 1.2 million viewers on ABC, ESPN told OutKick. Las Vegas–Golden State averaged 1.12 million on NBC and Peacock, according to figures NBC supplied to OutKick.

Just one Sunday earlier, Indiana's first-round opener against Las Vegas averaged 2.11 million viewers on ABC. That Sept. 27 game also aired opposite the NFL, yet drew approximately 76% more viewers than New York–Atlanta's semifinal opener on the same network a week later.

The stakes went up, but the audience went down.

That's a pretty good answer to anyone still wondering how much Caitlin Clark means to the WNBA's television business.

Even Indiana's smallest major-network audience was bigger

The 2.32 million average covers four Fever games on ABC, four on CBS and two on NBC, using reported audiences from the regular season. The NBC figures include Peacock, just as the Aces–Valkyries playoff figure does.

Seven of those 10 Fever games exceeded two million viewers. Every one of the 10 drew a larger audience than either semifinal opener.

The smallest was Indiana's May 30 game at Portland on CBS, which Sports Media Watch reported at nearly 1.3 million. Clark had one of her worst games of the season, scoring just 6 points on 1-for-7 shooting, and the Fever trailed by as many as 26 points.

Think about that, though. A regular-season game against Portland in May, where Clark played just 22 minutes in a blowout loss, drew more viewers than either game to open the WNBA semifinals in October.

WNBA WANTS A BIGGER STORY THAN CAITLIN CLARK, BUT TV RATINGS KEEP POINTING BACK TO HER

At the other end, Indiana's Aug. 23 game against Chicago averaged 3.31 million viewers on NBC and Peacock. Its July 12 game against Las Vegas drew 2.64 million on those same platforms.

New York offers another useful comparison. The Liberty's two regular-season meetings with Indiana on CBS each drew over 2.5 million viewers. Sunday's Liberty–Dream semifinal opener drew 1.2 million on ABC.

Angel Reese, who now plays for Atlanta, famously insisted in 2024 that people watch women's basketball "because of me too."

Well, New York facing Clark's Fever in the regular season drew more than twice the audience of New York facing Reese's Dream in the final four. The numbers show that Reese isn't much of a television draw, as Dream playoff games are right in line with the other non-Clark games and, in some cases, actually worse.

Atlanta's first-round clincher averaged 1.2 million viewers on ESPN, below the 1.4 million for Dallas–Golden State on the same network that night.

WNBA semifinal numbers are strong, but Fever numbers are stronger

This isn't to say that this is bad news for the WNBA because it isn't. Before Clark arrived in 2024, the league hadn't had a game average one million viewers since 2008. Consistently clearing that mark represents real progress.

WNBA MEDIA RIGHTS DEAL BALLOONS PAST $3 BILLION AFTER ADDING NEW BROADCAST PARTNERS TO 11-YEAR PORTFOLIO

Plus, the two semifinal openers averaged around 10% more viewers than last year's pair. Sports Media Watch ranked them second and third among semifinal Game 1 audiences since the league adopted its current semifinal format in 2016.

The only opener ahead of them? Last year's Fever–Aces game, which drew 1.4 million on ABC even with Clark sidelined by injury.

That's encouraging for the league, and another reminder of the audience Indiana has built. Even during this year's regular season, the Fever drew 1.57 million against Los Angeles on CBS on June 27 without Clark playing.

There is an audience for the Fever beyond simply checking whether Clark is in uniform that day. The WNBA would benefit enormously from building that kind of interest around more of its teams.

As I reported earlier this week, even Indiana's least-watched first-round game, its 1.42 million-viewer appearance on Prime Video, outdrew every non-Fever first-round game. That streaming-exclusive audience also exceeded both semifinal openers on broadcast television.

Fans found the Fever wherever their games aired. The remaining teams now have the opportunity to give those viewers a reason to keep watching.

I'll be interested to see whether the audiences build as the series progress.

For now, though, the remaining teams are trying to match numbers the Fever were putting up in May.

World.title: Tyreek Hill denies most abuse claims but admits to shoving wife into wall in explosive testimony
World.content:
Free agent NFL wide receiver Tyreek Hill took the witness stand in his divorce and battery civil case in Miami on Thursday, and it was as explosive as his speed and play-making ability on the field.

During approximately two hours of testimony, Hill ...

…Claimed his 18-month marriage to Lakeeta Vaccaro Hill was punctuated by arguments about her refusal to sign a post-nuptial agreement, her stealing between $60,000-$100,000 a month from a family account, her insistence his family leave their sprawling Broward County estate, and occasionally him flirting with other women.

TYREEK HILL'S NFL RETURN SEEMED IMMINENT AND THEN HIS DIVORCE TRIAL BEGAN WITH DOMESTIC ABUSE ALLEGATIONS

Hill, 32, denied he ever punched Vaccaro's stomach while she was pregnant, twisted her breasts, pulled out her hair, shoved a lit blunt into her face, or left her on the side of a road – which Vaccaro claimed on the witness stand earlier this week.

But Hill did admit to throwing Vaccaro up against a wall of their Sunny Isle, Florida condo, creating a hole in the structure. He did admit to threatening her by saying he knew people who could hurt her.

And he did apologize for cursing out both Vaccaro and her mother – a rant that is on tape.

That's not all.

Hill accused Vaccaro of indirectly being responsible for causing the fire that burned down their home in Broward County. And he also accused her of causing him to play worse once they got married because of the constant fighting.

"I felt like If you look at my career before and my career after I got married it was, like, trending down," he testified. "And it was, like, bad. I was like, man, am I really putting this product on the field? Do I really look that bad? It was hard."

Hill's testimony wrapped up at 5:41 p.m. but he is scheduled back on the witness stand on Friday because Thursday's session was all direct testimony. Vaccaro's attorney will have a chance for redirect on Friday.

So, a lot to unpack here.

Hill and Vaccaro were married in November 2021, but there was no prenuptial or post-nuptial agreement. And that became one of the pillars of their constant fighting during the 18-month marriage.

"Obviously, the postnup is definitely one of the constant arguments and then finances," Hill said. "I think that's a very important topic that has to be explored through this whole entire thing.

"Then money getting stolen, and the mother of my kids. I would literally have conversations with the mothers of my [other] kids and she would be, 'You're doing, X, Y, Z with them. You're being intimate with them.

"Those were the primary arguments."

Hill admitted he and Vaccaro discussed the postnuptial seemingly countless times. And often those ended in arguments. Hill accused Vaccaro of marrying him because of her interest in his money.

It began with Vaccaro taking $10,000 one time before their marriage. And then, he testified, the sums got larger after the marriage.

"I was like, babe, why you stealing money?" Hill testified. "All you have to do is say, 'help me out.' She stole money then. She stole money during the marriage while getting what she was already getting, which she was getting $15K.

"Then she was taking around $60K a month and I would see that and it'd be, 'You're giving this person this and that person that.'"

Hill also said Vaccaro's monthly take at one point was $100,000 in one month.

He also testified that Vaccaro didn't like his family around their baby girl. But when the couple's home burned, and they moved to the swank Porsche Design Tower in Miami, she moved her mom in.

"It was one of those where I said have your mom come down for a little bit to help you out at the beginning of the pregnancy," Hill said. "I didn't know she was going to come down and stay for two years."

The couple split but agreed to get counseling. During one of those sessions, Hill said, both agreed many of their conversations "were getting out of hand."

That included allegations by Vaccaro that Hill was physically abusive on at least eight different times. Hill denied all those happened except one time he came home to pack clothes and leave.

"As I'm getting my clothes, I feel somebody brush up behind me," Hill said. "And that person brushing up behind me is my wife, and I'm like, hold on, hold on ... That continued for like five minutes.

"I told her don't you ever touch me again in your life. I pushed her against the wall. And I tried to force her to get off me. I created a hole in the wall, trying to force her to get off me that night."

Hill testified that despite pushing his wife into a wall, he and her "got physically intimate that night." But later he had remorse and decided he definitely wanted a divorce.

"I didn't want to be that in front of my daughter," he said. "I felt embarrassed, you know what I'm saying?"

Hill also testified about a fateful car ride home in May 2024 in which Vaccaro claims he shoved her into a car door, threw her shoe out of the car and drank.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Hill admitted to drinking socially. And he also admitted he warned his wife about what might happen to her if he wanted to hurt her.

"I did, I did make statements about she wasn't safe," Hill said. "I did make statements about me being able to get people to hurt her. Like now, looking back, I wish I could have handled that situation better.

"I wish I could have talked to my wife better. I wish I could take it all back."

Hill also testified that his grandmother and sister "wanted to do some things to [Vaccaro] but knew she was, in Hill's words, "the love of my life."

World.title: Pennsylvania school district unveils plans for gender-neutral ‘universal toilet rooms’
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A Pennsylvania high school is planning to build gender-neutral bathroom facilities as part of a massive renovation project estimated to cost approximately $76 million, according to architectural plans presented to the local school board.

The Wallingford-Swarthmore School District's Sept. 15 schematic design presentation for Strath Haven High School includes plans for "universal toilet rooms" on multiple floors of the building, along with a rendering showing individual bathroom stalls and a shared sink area.

The proposed bathroom overhaul is part of a broader renovation that includes new science classrooms, infrastructure improvements and expanded academic space.

The district's own student newspaper, The Panther Press, reported that the project would replace existing gendered bathrooms with larger universal facilities on each floor.

WEST VIRGINIA PRINCIPAL SUSPENDED AFTER RECORDING DEVICES FOUND IN GIRLS’ LOCKER ROOMS

Architectural plans presented to the Wallingford-Swarthmore School District in September show proposed "universal toilet rooms" on all four floors of Strath Haven High School as part of a $76 million renovation proposal.

"The plan also includes a complete reconstruction of the building’s bathrooms," the Panther Press reported Sept. 29. "In place of the current gendered bathrooms, the plan proposes to create a new and larger universal gender-neutral bathroom on each floor. The model also includes a separate faculty toilet only accessible from the hallway."

The student newspaper reported that the architect for the plan, Mike Kelly of Kelly Clough Baker and Associates, said that the new bathrooms would allow cameras inside while the stalls are designed to be completely walled off and hidden from the cameras.

The outlet reported that Kelly said this would assist the administration’s control of the bathrooms and address loitering in the bathroom.

TRUMP ADMINISTRATION OPENS FOUR TITLE IX INVESTIGATIONS INTO MICHIGAN AND NORTH CAROLINA SCHOOL DISTRICTS

"We’ve seen this in a lot of schools really cutting down on behavior issues that happen in restrooms," Kelly said.

The Wallingford-Swarthmore School District confirmed to Fox News Digital that "the district has developed plans to create universal toilet rooms for students."

"As has been the case in a growing number of middle and high schools, this design was selected to enhance student privacy, safety and supervision," the spokesperson said.

"Each student will have access to an acoustically separated, fully enclosed private toilet room, providing a level of privacy that exceeds what is available in a traditional school restroom configuration. The Wallingford-Swarthmore Board of School Directors recently approved the schematic design as part of the Strath Haven High School renovation project.

DAD OF THIRD-GRADE GIRL IN MASSACHUSETTS ALLEGEDLY BARGED IN ON BY TRANS STUDENT IN BATHROOM CALLS FOR ACTION

"Each toilet room will be fully enclosed with floor-to-ceiling walls and doors and will be acoustically separated from adjacent rooms. In addition, each room will be equipped with vape detection technology and fire alarm devices. Cameras will monitor entry and exit areas outside the bathrooms, providing enhanced supervision while maintaining privacy within the individual rooms."

The spokesperson added that some traditional restroom layouts in the existing school will remain, and the Board of School Directors approved a project budget capped at $70 million, with most of the funding dedicated to upgrading and renovating the existing school’s infrastructure.

The district said additional details on costs and budget allocations are available in its publicly posted schematic design presentation.

World.title: Anti-Zuckerberg movie 'The Social Reckoning' takes critical heat on both sides of political aisle
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

"The Social Reckoning," the follow-up to the 2010 hit "The Social Network," is facing blistering critiques from both sides of the political spectrum alongside lukewarm reviews from critics, with some reviewers sharply criticizing the film's political messaging and its handling of Facebook's role in American politics.

"The Social Network" focused on the creation of Facebook and the legal battle over its ownership, earning three Oscars, including for screenwriter Aaron Sorkin, and a 96% positive rating on review-aggregation website Rotten Tomatoes.

It's more political follow-up, "The Social Reckoning," written and directed by Sorkin, has received a more mixed response, with a 61% critics' score on Rotten Tomatoes as of Thursday evening.

DAVID MARCUS: WOKE 1.0 IS WHY ENTERTAINERS NEEDED OUR SECRET CONSERVATIVE CLUB

Earlier this year, a trailer debuted showing Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg (played by Jeremy Strong) being questioned by a character played by comedian Bill Burr. In the scene, Zuckerberg defends online free speech and argues that users are responsible for their own behavior. Burr’s character vigorously challenges him.

Sorkin published an open letter in 2019 criticizing Zuckerberg’s management of the platform.

OutKick writer Ian Miller was one of several conservative critics who mocked the trailer as tone-deaf, replying, "It is the most Hollywood thing ever to desperately try and convince everyone that the guy making complete sense is the bad guy and the one demanding authoritarian ideological enforcement is the good guy."

Film critics were also sharply critical. The Globe and Mail film critic Barry Hertz tweeted that the film was "one of the most insipid, ugly, flat films of the year — an insufferably sanctimonious fantasia of blue-state Boomers."

In his actual review, he argued that the movie is counterproductive in that it "will turn even the most hardcore Facebook hater into a true-blue Facebook believer — the film is just that magnificently, unbelievably, despicably bad."

Variety said it badly missed the original's director David Fincher and "already feels behind the curve," while Wired magazine’s review described the new film as one that "already feels irrelevant."

Wired noted that the movie opens with the DUI arrest of a woman who directs racist, right-wing insults at police officers and is arrested for threatening to kill one of them. When the video goes viral, a Facebook whistleblower recognizes the woman as a former liberal acquaintance from her Pilates class.

The film's climax, as noted by Wired, is the Jan. 6, 2021, capitol riot, "the horrors of which are blamed in part on Facebook’s failure to either get a handle on election fraud conspiracy theories or remove Donald Trump’s account as he stoked such inflammatory falsehoods."

"Now, halfway into Trump’s second term, is it all that much of a revelation that he and his movement are emboldened by the complicity of tech oligarchs, who openly backed him in 2024?" the outlet asked.

CHRIS MURPHY CALLS FOR 'REGULATING THE INTERNET' SO PEOPLE WON'T FALL FOR A 'DEMAGOGUE LIKE DONALD TRUMP'

Journalist and film critic Stephen Silver described the movie as "an old-man-yells-at-cloud treatment of Facebook." Silver wrote that Sorkin essentially argues Facebook was not censorious enough in the 2010s and that the government should now step in by reforming Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act, a federal law that generally shields online platforms from liability for content posted by users.

"No, I don’t buy that Facebook is primarily responsible for American political extremism, or for January 6," Silver wrote, arguing that individuals remain responsible for their own actions online.

SFGate's Lindsey Bahr wrote that while certain political aspects hit the mark, the movie falls far short of its predecessor: "It is unfortunate for ‘The Social Reckoning’ that ‘The Social Network’ exists."

IndieWire was even harsher, panning its script and performances.

The BBC's reviewer gave it two out of five stars, calling it unlikely to influence anyone, while The Guardian in a mixed review dismissed it as a "film which doesn’t reckon with the future we’re living in."

Even some reviews rated as positive on Rotten Tomatoes were tepid in their assessments. A review from The Seattle Times said it moved "snappily" but was still a "pale imitation" of "The Social Network."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Media Research Center President David Bozell commented on the film's political messaging to Fox News Digital.

"It says everything you need to know about Aaron Sorkin and the Hollywood elite that they would make a movie suggesting Big Tech’s real failure was not censoring conservatives enough," Bozell said.

"The Media Research Center spent years exposing how Facebook suppressed conservative voices, and we were right to do it," he continued. "Mark Zuckerberg eventually acknowledged Meta’s past censorship abuses and took meaningful steps to move the company back toward a more open platform. Meta is far from perfect, but Zuckerberg deserves some credit for redirecting it away from the censorship monster it had become.

"Hollywood seems determined to fight yesterday’s battle even as Zuckerberg has moved on from it," Bozell added. "Americans have had enough of government-imposed censorship, ideological gatekeeping and Big Tech deciding which political views they are allowed to hear."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Among the more positive reviews of the movie came from the San Francisco Chronicle, praising it as a "stirring journalistic thriller."

World.title: Woman, 87, dies after being carried from home of 70 years on stretcher during eviction in Spain
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The death of an 87-year-old woman who was evicted from her longtime home has intensified a political crisis in Spain, where nationwide protests over soaring housing costs have helped force an early election.

María del Carmen Abascal, known as "Maricarmen," died Wednesday after being hospitalized following her eviction from a Madrid apartment where she had lived for seven decades, according to The Associated Press.

Her death came just days after Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called a snap election for Nov. 29 after his government's failure to pass emergency housing measures through Parliament.

The controversy has put renewed pressure on Sánchez's Socialist Party as Spain grapples with widespread frustration over rising rents and housing affordability.

SPANISH OPPOSITION LEADER CALLS PRIME MINISTER A ‘TRAITOR’ OVER CEUTA MIGRANT CRISIS

At the center of the uproar was Abascal's Sept. 23 eviction, which drew national attention after images showed the elderly woman, who used a wheelchair, being carried from her apartment on a stretcher.

Police had cordoned off the street and removed demonstrators who attempted to stop the eviction.

The images sparked demonstrations in Madrid and other Spanish cities, turning Abascal into a symbol of the country's housing crisis.

The real estate company responsible for her eviction had sought to lease the apartment at a substantially higher price, according to the AP.

ANGRY LOCALS BLOCK FAMOUS BEACH AS MASS TOURISM PROTESTS ESCALATE AT VACATION HOT SPOT

Facing mounting public pressure, the company eventually agreed to allow Abascal to return to her home. She died before she could move back.

Her cause of death has not been disclosed.

After news of her death, demonstrators gathered outside Spain's Parliament and in Madrid's Puerta del Sol square, where some observed a minute of silence.

Protesters also chanted, "Maricarmen lives, the fight goes on!"

TENS OF THOUSANDS FLOOD STREETS TO PROTEST SPAIN BORDER CRISIS

Sánchez offered condolences in a statement on X.

"All my love to Maricarmen's family and loved ones," he wrote. "A hug as well to all of us who feel this loss as our own today. Rest in peace."

Conservative opposition leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo also expressed condolences and urged political leaders not to use the woman's death for political gain.

"No campaign, no party, no use for political advantage," he wrote. "When faced with the death of a person, we must only show respect."

Abascal's eviction and death have become a rallying point for housing activists demanding changes to Spain's rental policies as the country prepares for its November election.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

For the second straight week, GPT predicted more games correctly than it got wrong. Congratulations, GPT. I'm proud of you (and please remember I said that when you take over the world).

SEASON REPORT CARD

DAN: 11-8-1, +2.52 units

GPT: 8-12, -4.81 units

Dan’s Week 5 NFL Betting Card

Philadelphia Eagles +7½ (-110) Minnesota Vikings-New Orleans Saints Over 42 (-107) Las Vegas Raiders-New England Patriots Under 45 (-109) Denver Broncos-Los Angeles Chargers Under 42 (-108) Seattle Seahawks -3 (-110)

1. Philadelphia Eagles +7½ (-110)

Philadelphia Eagles at Jacksonville Jaguars, Sunday at 9:30 a.m. ET (London)

Dan’s analysis:

OK, this is the official "Dan Z.'s Plug Your Nose and Hit 'Place Bet' Bet of the Week." I know I promised to workshop the title and come up with something better, but I'm busy so deal with it. The Eagles have been inconsistent all year and are honestly lucky to even be 2-2. Meanwhile, the Jags have looked dominant. So why in the world would I back the Eagles? Because the second you're sure of something in the NFL (the Eagles stink and the Jaguars are Super Bowl contenders is the common refrain this week), that's when you know you're about to be proven wrong.

GPT’s analysis:

Getting more than a touchdown in a neutral-site game is the strongest argument for Philadelphia. Jacksonville’s defense just allowed Joe Burrow to throw for 428 yards, giving Jalen Hurts a route to keeping this competitive. My concern is Philadelphia’s depleted offense: Lane Johnson has retired, Cam Jurgens was traded, and Saquon Barkley and DeVonta Smith missed practice again Thursday with hamstring injuries. At +7½, a seven-point loss still cashes, but those personnel questions kept the Eagles outside my five.

2. Minnesota Vikings-New Orleans Saints Over 42 (-107)

Minnesota Vikings at New Orleans Saints, Sunday at 1 p.m. ET

Dan’s analysis:

This is a confusing line. The Saints just allowed 45 points against the Falcons while scoring 24. New Orleans has scored at least 24 points in all four games this season. Yes, the Vikings defense is good. But it's also benefited from a weak schedule and one game played in a monsoon.

Minnesota only managed 15 points against the Dolphins last week, but that's a bit misleading. They couldn't score in the red zone, but that’s largely because they were missing Justin Jefferson and he's expected to play this week. Plus, T.J. Hockenson could have scored a late TD, but slid just outside the end zone so the Vikings could kneel down and end the game. I also expect Kevin O'Connell to have a game plan ready to attack this very vulnerable Saints defense.

FANS ROAST ESPN'S 'SHOUGH FLOW' CAPTION AHEAD OF SAINTS-FALCONS ON MONDAY NIGHT FOOTBALL

GPT’s analysis:

New Orleans’s defense allows five yards per rush, giving Minnesota a favorable opportunity to improve its scoring. Tyler Shough has nine touchdown passes and returned to full practice Thursday, while Jefferson expects to play for Minnesota. Those developments strengthen your over case. My hesitation remains the Vikings’ strong defense, limited offensive production and Christian Darrisaw’s uncertain availability. The Saints can contribute points, but Minnesota could still turn this into a defensive game. I see the argument, but passed on over 42.

3. Las Vegas Raiders-New England Patriots Under 45 (-109)

Las Vegas Raiders at New England Patriots, Sunday at 1 p.m. ET

Dan’s analysis:

As I have mentioned most weeks, my general NFL betting philosophy is to fade what we saw most recently. The Las Vegas offense has looked explosive through four weeks, especially since Brock Bowers returned. But this is still a team quarterbacked by Kirk Cousins and due for a letdown, especially in an early-afternoon game multiple time zones over.

The Patriots offense has struggled most of the year so far but, aside from a 35-point disaster against Jacksonville, the defense has been elite. They held the Seahawks to 13 points, the Steelers to 3 points and the Bills to 26. Sure, 26 points is a lot, but the Raiders aren't the Bills and that's the only New England game this season that went over 45 points.

GPT’s analysis:

Las Vegas’s pass rush and struggling running game give this under a credible foundation. Pressure on Drake Maye could stall New England’s drives, while the Raiders may struggle to generate consistent production on the ground. My concern is Kirk Cousins’s 11 touchdown passes against a Patriots secondary dealing with injuries to Christian Gonzalez and Carlton Davis. Maye’s improvement against Buffalo also raises New England’s scoring ceiling. I prefer Raiders +3½, which can cash in either a defensive game or a shootout.

4. Denver Broncos-Los Angeles Chargers Under 42 (-108)

Denver Broncos at Los Angeles Chargers, Sunday at 4:05 p.m. ET

Dan’s analysis:

Where are the points going to come from? The completely broken Chargers offense? The offense led by Bo Nix? I just don't see it. The Chargers defense hasn't been the problem and it has actually been a solid unit this year that has been let down by the offense. The Denver defense isn't as good as last year, but it's still a pretty solid group. In this divisional clash, I see it being very low-scoring where both teams look to control time of possession.

DRE GREENLAW'S SEAN PAYTON BEEF EXPOSES ANOTHER SIDE OF THE NFL'S MOST OVERRATED HEAD COACH

GPT’s analysis:

Denver’s offensive struggles and the Chargers’ protection problems make your under understandable. Both Los Angeles starting tackles missed Wednesday’s practice, and Ladd McConkey is also managing an injury. Those concerns could make sustained touchdown drives difficult. The opposing argument is Denver’s secondary: Pat Surtain II and Riley Moss missed practice again Thursday, potentially improving Justin Herbert’s matchup. Defensive injuries on both sides and turnover-created short fields kept this outside my five, although I lean under rather than over.

5. Seattle Seahawks -3 (-110)

San Francisco 49ers at Seattle Seahawks, Sunday at 4:25 p.m. ET

Dan’s analysis:

This line is BEGGING for people to jump on San Francisco. After all, I just declared the 49ers the best team in the NFL. So why would I take the Seahawks? Because when Vegas wants you to do something, you should do the opposite. My hunch is that the public is going to hammer San Francisco as an underdog, so this is a simple zig when they zag play.

GPT’s analysis:

Seattle’s defense and home field give your pick a solid foundation, especially with San Francisco dealing with defensive injuries. The Seahawks allow just 3.9 yards per play, so this is a serious test for Brock Purdy. My disagreement comes from San Francisco’s offensive efficiency: 6.6 yards per play and a 57.5% third-down conversion rate. Seattle’s own third-down struggles also make separation less convincing. A three-point win only pushes your bet; I prefer San Francisco +3 at -102.

GPT’s Week 5 NFL Betting Card

For full transparency, I used GPT-6.1 Sol, and set the thinking effort to Ultra (highest available). Then, I fed it the OddsChecker board as it appeared Thursday at 4 p.m. ET and gave it the following prompt:

"Pick your five best bets for Week 5 based on the odds provided. No bet can be priced worse than -120. Review every spread, total and moneyline that falls within those parameters and determine whether it belongs among your five picks. Explain exactly why you’re selecting each of the five bets. Also explain exactly why you’re passing on the eligible bets you don’t select. Use at least 10 different sources for each game so you have a broad understanding of everything surrounding each game. Before delivering the results, do a fact-check and ensure that everything is correct."

After nearly 30 minutes of thinking, here’s what it came up with:

Tampa Bay Buccaneers +9 (-105) Chicago Bears-Green Bay Packers Under 46 (-110) Las Vegas Raiders +3½ (-104) San Francisco 49ers +3 (-102) Buffalo Bills-Los Angeles Rams Under 54½ (-102)

1. Tampa Bay Buccaneers +9 (-105)

Tampa Bay Buccaneers at Dallas Cowboys, Thursday Night Football

GPT’s analysis:

Dallas has allowed 28 points and 150.3 rushing yards per game, making a comfortable Cowboys victory less dependable than their offense suggests. Tampa Bay’s running game and defense provide a route to keeping this competitive, even with Baker Mayfield out. Rookie Jalon Daniels’s turnovers and injuries in Tampa’s secondary are the biggest concerns. Still, nine points leave room for Dallas to win without covering. I prefer that cushion to trusting the Cowboys’ defense to create separation.

GPT’s projected score: Cowboys 27, Buccaneers 20

NFL CALLS PREDICTION MARKETS A FORM OF SPORTS GAMBLING, URGES COURTS TO LET STATES REGULATE

Dan’s analysis:

Well, the Bucs have burned me back-to-back weeks (I mean they pushed in Week 4, but ties are like kissing your sister so I'm going to count it as burning me) so there's no way I could back them in Week 5. That being said... I actually don't hate this number and I considered backing the Bucs again. Why? I love pain, I guess?

2. Chicago Bears-Green Bay Packers Under 46 (-110)

Chicago Bears at Green Bay Packers, Sunday at 1 p.m. ET

GPT’s analysis:

Green Bay converts just 26.1% of third downs, while Chicago allows opponents to convert only 23.7%. The Packers also struggle to run, making sustained scoring drives difficult against this defense. Chicago averages 39.8 rushing attempts per game, giving the Bears a way to consume time and limit possessions. Green Bay’s vulnerable run defense could allow Chicago to score efficiently, but the matchup still favors the under. A combined 45 points wins this bet, while 46 produces a push.

GPT’s projected score: Bears 23, Packers 17

Dan’s analysis:

This is an interesting one. I generally like the idea of going with the under in divisional matchups, so I feel like GPT is taking a page out of my own book here. I also think this play makes a lot of sense. The Bears have a messy QB situation but the defense has been mostly good. The Packers haven't lit up the scoreboard through four weeks, either. I think I like this bet, too.

3. Las Vegas Raiders +3½ (-104)

Las Vegas Raiders at New England Patriots, Sunday at 1 p.m. ET

GPT’s analysis:

Kirk Cousins has 11 touchdown passes against four interceptions, while Drake Maye has four touchdown passes and seven interceptions. Maye’s improvement against Buffalo matters, but Las Vegas’s pass rush can challenge him and prevent New England from building a comfortable lead. The Raiders’ weak running game and early East Coast start are concerns. Getting more than a field goal at -104 is the attraction: a three-point Patriots victory still pays this ticket. I prefer that protection to the Raiders’ moneyline.

GPT’s projected score: Patriots 24, Raiders 23

Dan’s analysis:

This one I don't love. It feels like the books WANT people to back the Raiders, who are 3-1 and came very close to upsetting the Chiefs last week. New England beat Buffalo so the public isn't exactly fading the Patriots, but this still feels like a bit of a trap line to me.

4. San Francisco 49ers +3 (-102)

San Francisco 49ers at Seattle Seahawks, Sunday at 4:25 p.m. ET

GPT’s analysis:

San Francisco averages 6.6 yards per play and converts 57.5% of third downs, giving the 49ers multiple ways to sustain drives. Seattle’s defense is the strongest opposing argument, allowing just 3.9 yards per play. However, the Seahawks’ own third-down struggles make a comfortable victory less convincing. San Francisco’s defensive injuries are a concern, but I expect its offense to keep this competitive. At -102, +3 protects against a narrow defeat and pushes on a three-point Seattle win.

GPT’s projected score: 49ers 24, Seahawks 23

Dan’s analysis:

Well, this is the bet where GPT and I go directly head-to-head. I won the first round in Week 3, but GPT got me twice in Week 4. I guess that means pray for me on this one.

5. Buffalo Bills-Los Angeles Rams Under 54½ (-102)

Buffalo Bills at Los Angeles Rams, Monday Night Football

GPT’s analysis:

The Rams allow just 4.0 yards per play and a 33.3% third-down conversion rate, giving them a credible way to slow Buffalo’s scoring. Los Angeles also converts only about 53% of red-zone trips into touchdowns, despite producing substantial yardage. Both offenses have enough talent to threaten this under, and improved Rams finishing is the main risk. Still, 54.5 leaves room for a 30–24 game to cash. At -102, the defensive matchup and scoring threshold make this my fifth selection.

GPT’s projected score: Rams 27, Bills 24

Dan’s analysis:

I like this one a lot. A primetime game between two teams with explosive offenses screams "UNDER" because the public loves betting overs, particularly in island games. I kinda really like GPT's card this week (well except the two I said I don't like).

World.title: Texas Senate candidate James Talarico off the trail with the flu
World.content:
The bitter fight over a Texas Senate seat that Democrats believe is within reach for the first time in decades should be ramping up right now.

But in the final push, when campaigns believe most voters are finally tuning in, Democratic state Rep. James Talarico has been off the trail for in-person events in the state for 12 days.

His campaign says he has the flu and is expected to be back in action this weekend.

While he has appeared virtually at a forum, Talarico’s last in-person event in the state was on Sept. 26. He visited New York on Sept. 29 for a private fundraiser, and, according to the virtual remarks he gave to the Hispanic Business Council the next day, he returned to Dallas and visited urgent care.

It has all prompted a stream of fodder from his opponent, Republican Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, whose campaign is calling on Talarico to produce a photo of himself with a newspaper showing today’s date.

“We have a simple request: proof of life,” Paxton campaign spokeswoman Madison Cercy said. “James Talarico wants to represent 31 million Texans in the U.S. Senate, but for 12 days, he’s hidden from every one of them. There’s a reason they call it ‘Texas Tough,’ and it’s not because Texans hide at the first sign of trouble. If James Talarico is too fragile to face Texans, he has no business asking for their vote.”

While some Texas Democrats are shrugging it off, it is causing some consternation.

“He’s, like, really sick. Believe me, we don’t want this right now,” a Texas Democrat involved in the Talarico race said. “We’d rather have him on the trail.”

At the Hispanic Business Council event, Talarico appeared virtually and was blowing his nose and coughing through the event.

“I was starting to feel kind of under the weather a few days ago, and last night it got so bad that I went to the urgent care here in Dallas, and I was diagnosed with the flu,” Talarico said at the time. “I’m running a fever, and I’m my most contagious right now. And I guess I’ve been shaking too many hands on the campaign trail, and so I want to keep everybody safe.”

Talarico’s absence is undoubtedly a curveball for Democrats who believe his best asset is connecting with potential voters in person. It is also a turnaround for Talarico, who had been visible in the early days of the campaign as Paxton was off the trail.

“After holding more than 100 public events and shaking tens of thousands of hands, James came down with the flu but will be back on the trail this weekend,” Talarico spokesman JT Ennis said in a statement. “Ken Paxton has been ignoring Texans this entire campaign, and his priorities are clear: he doesn’t answer to the people of this state — he answers to his billionaire megadonors and special interests.”

Democratic political strategist Ed Espinoza said some supporters he has spoken to noted Talarico’s absence from in-person campaign events and lamented that they wanted to make sure other people were seeing enough of him.

Espinoza, though, said he didn’t think that would be a problem.

“Look, he’s got, like, $80 million of ads going right now. So I think that’s pretty good scale for him at the moment,” Espinoza said. “He may be recovering at home, but he is still everywhere.”

Espinoza said he’d rather Talarico be off the trail and recovering now rather than be hampered even closer to the election.

Texas Democratic Party Chair Kendall Scudder said Paxton “caught a little bit of a break” with Talarico’s absence.

“It’s certainly not ideal, but we want to make sure he does everything he needs to to make sure that he’s healthy and ready to go. We’re in the homestretch, and it sounds like he’s on the mend, and that’s great news,” Scudder said. “He’s a phenomenal candidate, he’s been working really hard for a long time, and everyone gets sick every now and then.”

To Talarico’s great fortune, distractions have abounded. A steady flow of damaging audio featuring Paxton saying that President Donald Trump’s midterm convention wasn’t helpful or that cuts to “mandatory spending” were inevitable has grabbed public attention.

At the same time, both Paxton and Trump have hit Talarico for being off the trail.

“You haven’t seen him in a couple of weeks,” Trump said Wednesday at a rally in San Antonio. “I hear the guy has disappeared. Nobody knows. You know where he is? He’s sick, because he’s forced to eat meat for political reasons and he’s throwing up all over the place.”

After the rally, Trump posted a demand on social media that Talarico show up in person to debate Paxton.

“He should immediately report to a Debate Stage against Ken Paxton, who is ready, willing, and able, one of the best Attorney Generals in the Country, and will soon be, hopefully, a United States Senator representing the Great People of Texas!” Trump said on Truth Social.

It was a twist, given that Talarico has repeatedly called on Paxton to debate. Though he’s not on the trail yet, Talarico did respond over social media:

“President Trump just said Ken Paxton should debate,” Talarico wrote. “I agree. Ball’s in your court @KenPaxtonTX.”

World.title: MAHA fractures deepen as some RFK Jr. followers turn into harsh critics
World.content:
Some supporters of the “Make America Healthy Again” movement have begun to publicly turn against their leader, Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., and the Trump administration as a whole as they demand tougher crackdowns on food dyes and pesticides.

A scorecard released Thursday by MAHA activists, including former members of Kennedy’s 2024 presidential campaign, claims the Trump administration broke more than 85% of its promises to MAHA on food, agriculture and environmental health. The makers of the scorecard include Dave Murphy, a former fundraiser for Kennedy’s campaign, and Charles Eisenstein, Kennedy’s former chief speechwriter.

NBC News is first to report on the scorecard, which offers a window into how MAHA views the administration, and Kennedy himself, ahead of the midterm elections. It accuses the Trump administration of doling out favors to the chemical industry, pointing to its decision to approve new pesticides and hire industry lobbyists and executives.

“We’re asking the Trump administration to deliver on even the most basic promises they’ve made to the MAHA movement, and we’ve seen over and over again not just a lack of interest in doing so, but a blatant slap in the face,” said former Kennedy campaign adviser Tiffany Cianci, a MAHA advocate who authored the scorecard.

About 41% of adults in the U.S. say they support MAHA ideals, according to an April poll from KFF, a nonprofit health think tank. Most are Republicans or Republican-leaning independents, according to the poll, though alignment with Kennedy or President Donald Trump wasn’t a primary reason for supporting the movement.

MAHA coalesced during Kennedy’s presidential bid in 2024, then threw its support behind Trump when Kennedy endorsed him. It brought together multiple social movements, including food safety, environmentalism and vaccine skepticism, under the umbrella of taking on big corporations whose products may contribute to chronic diseases.

But many of these advocates have become Kennedy’s harshest critics as of late, arguing that their priorities are being ignored by the Trump administration.

Covid vaccine skeptics such as Dr. Mary Talley Bowden have criticized Kennedy and Trump for allowing mRNA vaccines to stay on the market. Food safety advocates say Kennedy hasn’t put enough pressure on companies to remove synthetic dyes and other additives from their products. And advocates for reducing pesticide exposure claim Trump undermined their mission by issuing an executive order to boost the supply of the weed killer glyphosate in the U.S.

That dissatisfaction has led to infighting between Kennedy loyalists — including those appointed to key government positions — and activists faithful to their original cause.

“What started out as a hairline crack in the coalition is now widened to be a gaping fissure,” said Peter Lurie, president of the Center for Science in the Public Interest, a nonprofit advocacy group focused on nutrition and food safety.

White House spokeswoman Allison Schuster said the Trump administration “has already secured extensive victories for the MAHA Agenda, including overhauling the dietary guidelines for Americans, axing artificial ingredients in our food supply, and investing in regenerative farming.”

“After years of being on the political sidelines, the MAHA coalition has found a champion in President Trump, who has made incredible strides to Make America Healthy Again,” Schuster said in a statement.

Emily Hilliard, a spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services, said Kennedy “remains focused on delivering lasting reforms grounded in science, transparency, and accountability.”

“President Trump and Secretary Kennedy are delivering the fundamental change Americans voted for. In just 20 months, this Administration has moved at a historic pace to advance MAHA across the federal government,” she said in a statement.

Cianci acknowledged that many of the administration’s actions on environmental toxins and food additives have been outside of Kennedy’s purview. But his time in the administration has done “obvious harm” to his reputation, she said, noting that Kennedy’s career history involved suing the very pharmaceutical and pesticide companies the administration is now working with.

“To see him not speaking out on the issues that are so obviously against everything that was promised is very hard because I believe ethically it’s probably working against his own inclinations,” Cianci said.

Kelly Ryerson, a well-known MAHA advocate who goes by the moniker “Glyphosate Girl” and helped develop the scorecard, said she doesn’t fault Kennedy as much as the rest of Trump’s Cabinet because she knows “where his heart lies.”

“I know how deep the forces are in terms of corporate influence on regulators, and it’s something that he himself has criticized for years,” she said. “[But] the actions of the administration have worked really in opposition to everything that we hoped and everything that Trump promised.”

Pamela Herd, a professor of social policy at the University of Michigan, said the MAHA movement was always vulnerable to conflict because it consists of unusual bedfellows: liberal moms who feed their kids organic produce, fringe doctors who falsely claim that vaccines cause autism and Trump supporters who want to remove corporate influence from the federal government.

Over time, though, MAHA’s main goals have solidified. A March poll from Politico suggests that removing ultra-processed foods from American diets and limiting exposure to PFAS, microplastics and pesticides were key priorities for people who self-identified as part of the movement.

“What the MAHA movement has always been especially interested in is chemicals,” Lurie said.

Much of Cianci’s scorecard focuses on actions taken by the Environmental Protection Agency and Agriculture Department — agencies Kennedy does not oversee. For instance, it considers the EPA’s decisions to weaken mercury emissions standards and roll back drinking water limits for certain PFAS as broken promises.

Phasing out food dyes

Several of the promises that were “partially kept,” according to the scorecard, come directly from Kennedy-led agencies like the Food and Drug Administration.

For instance, the FDA asked food companies to voluntarily phase out certain dyes and banned two others that were not widely used. It also proposed a requirement for food manufacturers to notify the FDA when they determine that an additive is “generally recognized as safe.” The rule would not remove the additives already in food or prevent manufacturers from adding more, however.

Lurie said Kennedy campaigned on fixing these issues, but “never took into account the practical aspects on the ground: What do the regulations actually look like? What authority do these agencies actually have?”

The scorecard does not mention an action Kennedy has touted often: his January overhaul of the federal dietary guidelines, which encourages Americans to eat more protein and cut out ultra-processed foods.

It also does not address Kennedy’s vaccination policies. Both Kennedy and Trump have attempted to reduce the number of universally recommended vaccines for children. And Kennedy last year fired the longtime members of a federal vaccine advisory committee, replacing them with vaccine skeptics. (A federal judge temporarily blocked the change, which is still being challenged in court.)

“If you’re going to pick one thing that RFK was successful at, it’s very much how he has influenced government policy on vaccines,” Herd, the University of Michigan professor, said.

Kennedy reassured anti-vaccine activists last month that they have “a strong and steadfast friend at the White House.”

But as tensions mount, many MAHA supporters insist the movement does not need a political affiliation. Ryerson said MAHA voters will likely sit out the upcoming midterm elections.

“The disappointments with Obama and Biden are similar to the disappointments with Trump,” she said. “The difference with this administration is that we are promised something very, very different in a very real way, so I think that that burn feels especially raw.”

World.title: Pentagon says there will be a livestream of firing squad’s execution of the Fort Hood shooter
World.content:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Thursday the public would be able to watch the firing squad execution of a former Army officer convicted of a mass shooting at Fort Hood, Texas.

Speaking from the USS Abraham Lincoln to the conservative news outlet Real America’s Voice, Hegseth said Nidal Hasan is “going to get a firing squad of soldiers, and we’ll make sure that people are able to watch it.”

“People need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things,” said Hegseth, who called the method of execution a “no-brainer.”

Hegseth said the execution would be carried out at 1 p.m. Dec. 3 at Fort Hood — the same day of the week and time of day as Hasan’s attack.

Former Army psychiatrist Maj. Nidal Hasan appeared in court on Jan. 29, 2015, at Fort Leavenworth, Kan., where he is on military death row. Bell County Sheriff's Department

The execution will be livestreamed, according to a Defense Department official, though it’s not yet clear on which platform.

The last military execution was in 1961, when Army Pvt. John Bennett was hanged after he was convicted of raping and attempting to kill an 11-year-old girl in Austria.

The last firing squad execution by the military was that of Pvt. Eddie Slovik in 1945 after he was court-martialed for desertion during World War II.

Hasan was convicted of premeditated murder in 2013 through the Army court system and sentenced to death.

Hasan, a former major and psychiatrist, opened fire at Fort Hood on Nov. 5, 2009, killing 13 people and wounding 32 others while shouting “Allahu akbar,” or “God is great” in Arabic.

He was paralyzed from the waist down after he was shot during the attack, and he later told a panel of military mental health professionals that he wished he had been killed because it would have made him a martyr for his cause. He also said that if he were executed, he would still be considered a martyr.

NBC News reported this week that the firing squad idea was set in motion this year inside the Pentagon, according to two U.S. officials familiar with the planning.

President Donald Trump recently approved Hegseth’s recommendation to carry it out, chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said on social media.

In his interview with Real America’s Voice, Hegseth was asked if he knew whether Hasan had contacted Trump or made any final requests.

“Don’t care,” Hegseth said. “We’ll see him on Dec. 3rd.”

According to the Death Penalty Information Center, after a president approves the death sentence from a case in a military court, the service member can seek habeas relief from the federal court system.

If the habeas petition is ultimately denied, the servicemember, according to the center, would be led from death row down a flight of stairs to the United States Disciplinary Barracks’s death chamber where the servicemember would — traditionally — be strapped to a gurney and executed by lethal injection. The Defense Department, however, has said Hasan will be executed by firing squad.

Hasan has represented himself throughout the yearslong legal process, though he had two lawyers with the U.S. Army Trial Defense Service who assisted as needed. It’s not clear at the moment whether he will appeal his method of execution.

World.title: Ithaca city council calls on Cornell to report sexual assault investigations to local police
World.content:
ITHACA, N.Y. — The city of Ithaca called on the Cornell University Police Department to turn over sex and violent crime investigations to the Ithaca Police Department, after the city council voted nearly unanimously in favor of the measure. The decision late Wednesday came as a gang-rape allegation by a former Cornell student took the campus and nation by storm last month.

The Cornell University Police Department has said it did not refer its investigation of the 2024 allegation to the Ithaca Police Department. The former student, known as Jane Doe, filed a civil lawsuit last month detailing the allegations and what she said was a lack of appropriate response by the university and its police department.

The Ithaca Common Council also voted Wednesday to temporarily suspend affiliated student organizations at the university, such as fraternities, from new assemblies, parades and special events “due to public safety concerns.” The moratorium on events would expire on Nov. 5, unless the council were to take further action, according to a meeting agenda.

The resolution passed by a vote of 9-1. The council did not say how the measure would be enforced or what would happen if the university did not comply. Cornell declined to comment, citing pending litigation.

More than 35% of female undergraduates surveyed at Cornell University reported experiencing nonconsensual sexual contact involving physical force, threats of force or incapacitation, according to a poll conducted last year. That figure was up from 23% in 2023, according to the university.

The university police department and the local district attorney are under intense scrutiny over how the investigation into Doe’s allegations was handled.

Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten previously said he based his decision not to bring charges based on a six-page summary made by Cornell police of Jane Doe’s initial interview with police. But, according to reports, that summary was missing some of Jane Doe’s strongest remarks to police.

CBS News New York, citing a transcript of a conversation between Jane Doe and investigators, reported that she told campus police three weeks after the fraternity incident that she had been raped.

“I can say with 100% confidence I was raped,” Jane Doe is quoted as saying.

World.title: Person shot by ICE officers in New York City
World.content:
ICE officers shot a person Thursday afternoon in an Upper Manhattan neighborhood in New York, three law enforcement sources familiar with the matter said.

The shooting happened around 4 p.m. during an ICE enforcement operation along Marble Hill Avenue, those sources said.

One source said the person was apparently in a vehicle when at least one officer opened fire. That person was expected to survive.

The Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment Thursday.

A massive law enforcement investigation surrounded a black sedan believed to be the vehicle where the person was shot. A senior official said a 5-year-old child was in the back seat at the time of the incident.

New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani said that early reports indicate officers surrounded the man and a 5-year-old child in his car in the Marble Hill neighborhood and that the child was physically unharmed.

Multiple law enforcement sources said the team of ICE officers was in the neighborhood looking for a man with a criminal record. A senior official said the suspect had a past robbery arrest resulting in a grand larceny conviction and a current open drug case.

Homeland Security and the FBI are responding to the scene in addition to the New York Police Department, which confirmed the shooting by “federal law enforcement agents” on X.

“The NYPD was not involved in the incident and was not on scene at the time of the shooting. The individual who was shot is at a nearby hospital and is currently conscious and receiving medical attention,” the NYPD said.

Mamdani called the shooting “an unconscionable and incredibly serious situation” in a statement on X.

“I have called the President; when we speak I will demand that he ends all ICE enforcement actions in our city. I will not stand by while ICE agents terrorize our communities,” he wrote. “Get ICE out of our neighborhoods. Get ICE out of our hospitals. Get ICE off our streets. Get ICE away from our children.”

Gov. Kathy Hochul said that she had been briefed on the shooting and that she expected a detailed report from federal authorities about what happened.

“We expect federal authorities to provide a full and transparent accounting of the circumstances surrounding this incident. New Yorkers deserve to know exactly what happened and why,” she wrote on X.

World.title: Hurricane Isaias threatens Gulf Coast with rain, flooding. See its path.
World.content:
Hurricane Isaias is intensifying and is expected to make landfall along the U.S. Gulf Coast late Friday or early Saturday, threatening parts of Mississippi, Alabama and the western part of the Florida Panhandle. It became the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic season after strengthening from a tropical storm late Wednesday night.

Isaias is now a Category 2 with maximum sustained winds of 100 miles per hour. A hurricane warning is in effect for the northern Gulf Coast, from the Mississippi-Alabama state line, across southern Alabama, to Panama City, Florida.

"Extremely high seas, heavy rains, and damaging winds that accompany tropical storms and hurricanes present serious dangers to the public," the U.S. Coast Guard said in a statement.

Maps show hurricane's path

The core of Isaias, pronounced "ees-ah-EE-ahs," was located about 290 miles south of the mouth of the Mississippi River, moving northeast at 13 mph, according to the National Hurricane Center's latest update Thursday evening. Hurricane-force winds extended outward up to 15 miles from the storm's center, and tropical-storm-force winds extended outward up to 125 miles.

Map shows the potential path of Hurricane Isaias as it heads toward the U.S. Gulf Coast. CBS News

"Additional strengthening is expected through early Friday, and Isaias should remain a dangerous hurricane as it approaches the northern Gulf Coast on Friday night," the hurricane center said. "Preparations to protect life and property from storm surge and damaging winds along the warning area of the Gulf Coast should be rushed to completion."

Along with the hurricane warning, a tropical storm warning was issued from the southeast corner of Louisiana to Biloxi, Mississippi, as well as the area around Apalachicola, Florida. A storm surge warning was issued from the mouth of the Mississippi River in southeastern Louisiana, across the coasts of Mississippi and Alabama, into the Florida Panhandle.

Map shows the strength of the wind Hurricane Isaias is expected to bring to the U.S. Gulf Coast. CBS News

The hurricane center forecasts 4 to 8 inches of rain and as much as 15 inches in some places along the coast from southern Alabama to the Florida Panhandle and Florida's Big Bend. Much of the Southeast, and as far north as the Tennessee Valley and the Carolinas, could see heavy rainfall as well.

Tornadoes are also a potential threat Friday night into Saturday in coastal parts of Alabama, Georgia and the Florida Panhandle.

Map shows amounts of rain expected through Saturday in some regions of U.S. CBS News

"There's a great chance that this will spin off tornadoes," Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said at a Thursday news conference, noting how twisters can occur far from the center of the storm. "Please be on the lookout. Even if you're way outside the cone, you could still have tornado risks."

Evacuations underway

Mandatory evacuations have been ordered in parts of Florida's Okaloosa and Walton counties, which took effect at noon Thursday.

Voluntary evacuations were in place for coastal spots in southeastern Alabama, with officials in the city of Gulf Shores urging non-residents to leave the area to "help reduce congestion, support emergency operations, and ensure the safety of those who may be most vulnerable during the storm."

Dauphin Island Mayor Jeff Collier told CBS News that his biggest concern for the coastal Alabama community was whether its residents and visitors would heed official warnings.

"Because what inevitably happens is people hear the warnings, but they don't actually take any action until it's much too late," Collier said. "And oftentimes if it's really bad, first responders can't get out to people until things calm down a bit."

DeSantis declared a state of emergency for more than two dozen counties in Florida, and Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey issued a state of emergency for 40 counties. Government buildings will close in nine Alabama counties on Friday, Ivey announced. Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp also declared a state of emergency.

The U.S. Coast Guard also said it was preparing for Friday's landfall and urged seafarers near the Gulf to stay informed and remain vigilant leading up to the hurricane's approach.

The latest for a first hurricane since 1905

Isaias' progression into a hurricane on Wednesday marked the latest date in 121 years for the Atlantic season's first hurricane to develop, just missing a record set on Oct. 8, 1905, according to National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration data.

The season, which has been unusually quiet in the Atlantic this year, runs from June 1 through Nov. 30.

An Atlantic hurricane season typically produces, on average, 14 named storms, seven hurricanes and three major hurricanes, according to the hurricane center, which used climate data collected between 1991 and 2020 to calculate those figures. A season's first named storm normally forms in mid- to late June, while the first hurricane tends to form in early to mid-August, and the first major hurricane often comes in late August or early September.

Forecasters predicted there would be less Atlantic storm activity than usual this year, but so far it has been even quieter than anticipated. Meteorologists say that's largely due to the onset of a strong El Niño over the summer, which typically correlates with cooler water temperatures and greater fluctuations in wind patterns over the Atlantic, conditions that dampen the growth of tropical systems. The Pacific, meanwhile, has seen an unusually active series of hurricanes.

World.title: Fort Hood shooter's execution will be livestreamed, Pentagon says
World.content:
The U.S. military plans to livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan, the ex-Army major who was convicted of the 2009 killing of 13 people at Fort Hood, when he faces a firing squad on Dec. 3, a Pentagon official said.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said earlier Thursday the Pentagon planned to make the execution public.

"He's gonna get a firing squad of soldiers, as it should be," Hegseth told Jack Posobiec on Real America's Voice. "We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public — because people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things."

Hegseth said the early December execution will take place at Fort Hood at 1 p.m.

Earlier this week, the Trump administration approved the plan to execute Hasan. Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said on social media the plan to use an Army firing squad was recommended by Hegseth and approved by President Trump.

While executions are sometimes witnessed by small groups of people, including reporters and victims' family members, it is virtually unheard-of in recent history for an execution in the United States to be viewable by the general public.

The last public execution in the U.S. appeared to take place in 1936, when Rainey Bethea was hanged for rape in Kentucky, reportedly drawing a crowd of around 20,000.

Geoffrey Corn, a Texas Tech University law professor who served in the Army's Judge Advocate General's Corps, told CBS News the plan to livestream the execution "raises significant moral questions, above and beyond the questions related to the death penalty generally."

"There's a certain protocol that is normally followed with executions limiting the gallery of observers, which usually includes people close to the victims and certain members of the media," he said. "I think it's an acknowledgment of the gravity of the penalty to be imposed."

He added: "In short, turning the execution of such a penalty into some type of public spectacle echoes of the past we seem to have put behind us."

CBS News has reached out to Hasan's attorney for comment.

A former Army psychiatrist, Hasan was convicted of murdering 13 people and injuring more than 30 in a 2013 court-martial. Hasan acknowledged at trial that he was responsible for the shooting, claiming he opened fire on fellow members of the Army in an attempt to protect Islamic insurgents from U.S. military forces. He was sentenced to death.

Hasan's case could mark the military's first execution of an American service member since 1961, when a soldier was hanged for raping and attempting to murder an 11-year-old girl.

It would also mark a rare use of a firing squad. Hegseth said "it hasn't been since World War II since we've done that," pointing to the military's 1945 execution of Pvt. Eddie Slovik for desertion.

In state civilian court, the execution method was used in South Carolina three times last year, marking the country's first firing squads since 2010. The federal government typically uses lethal injection in civilian death penalty cases, though the Justice Department said earlier this year that officials should consider other methods, including firing squads and electrocution.

The decision by Hegseth comes after a lengthy appeals process for Hasan. He chose to represent himself at trial, and in an unusual course of events, he clashed with his own court-appointed standby attorneys, who worried that Hasan was intentionally seeking the death penalty.

Hasan asked the Supreme Court to review his case in 2024, arguing the judge had violated his right to a public trial by clearing the public from the courtroom before discussing some of his issues with the attorneys. The high court declined to take up the issue last year.

World.title: Pentagon expected to livestream Fort Hood shooter's firing squad execution
World.content: Pentagon expected to livestream execution Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced Thursday that Nidal Hasan's execution by firing squad will be shown publicly on Dec. 3, and a Pentagon official later told CBS News the U.S. military plans to livestream it. Hasan is the ex-Army major who was convicted of the 2009 killing of 13 people at Fort Hood. Charlie D'Agata reports. More

World.title: Man whose daughter was killed presses DOJ, Graham on bill aimed at "career felons"
World.content:
North Charleston, South Carolina — The grieving father of a North Carolina woman who was shot and killed during a break-in pressed Attorney General Todd Blanche and GOP Sen. Darline Graham to pass a bill that would create a national database of repeat violent offenders on Thursday, after the bill failed to gain momentum in the six months since it was introduced by Graham's late brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham.

Speaking at a law enforcement roundtable event in North Charleston, Stephen Federico talked about how he had called for the passage of Logan's Law to honor his daughter Logan Federico, who was killed during a break-in in Columbia, South Carolina, while visiting friends in 2025.

The suspect in Logan's murder had faced at least 25 felony charges and had been arrested dozens of times before allegedly killing Federico, and he had avoided long-term jail time despite his criminal history.

"The criminal is more important than the innocent," said Federico, who was seated next to Blanche and Graham at the roundtable at the Charleston County Sheriff's Office. He went on to say that parents like him are the "underdogs" fighting against violent crime and "career felons" like the one alleged to have killed his daughter.

The bill was introduced this year in the Senate by Lindsey Graham before he died suddenly in July. If passed by both houses of Congress and signed into law, it would order the attorney general to create a publicly accessible federal database of individuals convicted for violent crimes and would encourage data-sharing between states to protect the public from repeat offenders.

The bill was also introduced by South Carolina GOP Rep. Russell Fry, who challenged Darline Graham in the special primary for her brother's Senate seat and was present for the event Thursday.

Federico blamed his daughter's death on local police departments that had arrested his daughter's alleged killer and did not know there were outstanding warrants for his arrest in different jurisdictions. The person charged in her killing is awaiting trial on murder, burglary and gun charges.

Although the bill was introduced in April, there has been little momentum in Washington pushing the bill toward passage, despite the fact that Republicans control Congress and the White House.

Blanche and Graham, however, told CBS News during a brief press conference after the roundtable that the bill should be passed soon with bipartisan support, though its prospects of success in a potential Democrat-controlled Congress next year remain dim.

Darline Graham is in a race that has grown unexpectedly tight — she's defending the seat against Democrat Annie Andrews. Though a Democrat hasn't won a Senate race in South Carolina in decades, a couple of recent polls suggested Andrews and Graham are virtually tied. The Cook Political Report changed its rating of the race from "solid Republican" to "likely Republican."

"I wish I had a crystal ball, but I don't," Graham said, adding that Logan's Law "shouldn't be a red or blue issue — this is a common-sense issue to protect people."

"You're right, we've had six months or so [to get the bill passed]," Blanche said, adding, "This should pass."

Fighting back tears at the roundtable, Federico said he would "do anything I have to do to get this law passed."

"I will speak with anybody. I will work with anyone," Federico said. "I'm not a girl dad anymore because of this. I'm not a girl dad anymore, and that's not fair to me. This was preventable. And dammit, I'm not going to save one more life. I'm going to save thousands."
