World.title: Suicide is up among Black Americans. We need to talk about it.
World.content:
Suicide is up among Black Americans. We need to talk about it.

My brother took his own life on May 10, 2010. Rarely a day goes by that I don't think of him. But just because I thought about him, it didn't mean I could talk about him. For a long time, I couldn't.

Sometimes when the subject of suicide came up, I would want to — or literally have to — leave wherever I was. Not helpful if you're in the news business.

I've come to realize that I have to talk about it. We have to talk about it.

Why do we have to? Because our silence is not protecting us.

Sponsor Message

Suicide is a public health crisis for the country — but that crisis is becoming acute in the Black community. Black suicide rates are climbing, increasing more than 50% over about the past 10 years according to CDC data. And the suicide rates among Black youth are increasing particularly dramatically. The rate of Black youth suicides by firearms exceeded that of white youth in 2022.

At a time when government-sponsored public health initiatives are retreating from issues that impact different communities differently, we're going there with care, sensitivity and honesty.

I hosted an NPR's Morning Edition live event called Going There: A Matter of Life and Death. It brought together a panel of clinicians, lawmakers and people who have lived with this pain to talk about this epidemic, in front of a live audience who have also experienced it. Speakers include CEO emerita of BET Debra Lee, Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman, D-NJ, psychiatrist Dr. Paul Nestadt, retired NFL champion Vernon Davis, WWE superstar Ettore "Big E" Ewen and Rev. Johnny Parker, who is both a pastor and a counselor.

It was an attempt to try to find out why this crisis is happening, how it is affecting us, and most importantly, what we can do about it.

Sponsor Message

During the conversation, Super Bowl-winning tight end Vernon Davis shared his struggles with panic attacks and depression.

"I would have these episodes in the game," Davis said, "I would go sit on a bench and breathe hard. I just felt like, for a split second, that I didn't want to be here. I had nothing to live for. It happened so fast, and it was just so sudden."

Davis now says that focusing on his mental health is a daily priority. And, after Davis lost both his brother and sister in quick succession, he started speaking more openly about his experiences with mental health.

"There's people out there who are going through the same thing that I went through," he explained, "they just need to hear that there's someone else out there that is going through the same thing."

Dr. Paul Nestadt is a psychiatrist, medical director of the Johns Hopkins Center for Suicide Prevention, and a national authority on suicide. He notes that white people still account for the majority of suicide deaths, and the suicide rate has decreased slightly among white Americans. Meanwhile, the rate has gone up among Black Americans. Access to guns accounts for at least part of that increase.

"When that trend in young Black people, especially young Black males, started to go up was also a time when we saw a dramatic increase in firearm ownership in the Black community. That was in 2020, in the context of the pandemic, the murder of George Floyd, and a variety of other things," Nestadt said.

As a result, 2025 survey data shows the lowest rate of self-reported suicide attempts among young Black people in America in years. But, Nestadt said, "the death rate has gone higher than it's ever been. And that just comes down to the fact that when an attempt is made, now with so many more guns in the house, that attempt is fatal."

Sponsor Message

Nestadt emphasized that it is crucial to correct several prevailing myths about suicide: chiefly that only people with long-term mental illnesses are vulnerable and that mentioning that you are concerned that someone might take their own life plants the idea. Neither is true. He says suicide is often an impulsive act, and interrupting that thought can work.

Every panelist brought similar words of wisdom. Among the most important advice:



Reaching out to offer support to loved ones who seem like they might be struggling can be lifesaving.



Free and low-cost resources and treatment options are out there, and are effective.



Remembering those we've lost to suicide as the full people that they were can be healing to those left behind.

There's a lot we can do to support each other and take care of ourselves.

And if you or someone you know is in crisis, call or text 988 to reach the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline. You can reach someone 24 hours a day, just to talk or to help get access to care.

World.title: The long-deployed USS Lincoln is returning home to San Diego
World.content:
The long-deployed USS Lincoln is returning home to San Diego

The USS Abraham Lincoln is returning home to San Diego Thursday after supporting the Iran war during a record long deployment of 265 uninterrupted days at sea that included reports of deteriorating conditions among its crew.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth flew out to the carrier on Wednesday to give the crew the Presidential Unit Citation, the highest honor a unit can receive that is typically reserved for significant achievement in combat.

Hegseth pushed back against what he said were efforts to turn the "Lincoln into some sort of a symbol, a symbol of dysfunction or a symbol of low morale or a symbol of a failed mission."

He said that "what makes the U.S. military and the U.S. Navy and all these sailors different is that you adapt and that you're resilient and you overcome — you finish the mission nonetheless."

Hegseth told the crew that President Donald Trump "tracked your activities from day one and couldn't be more proud of what you executed."

The Navy initially downplayed problems on the carrier

The carrier drew national attention following reports of stress among the crew and poor mental health, as well as supply shortages, including food and hygiene products, during its Iran war mission.

Sponsor Message

The Navy initially downplayed any problems, and Trump commented in August that the Lincoln's lengthy deployment was "not nearly long enough."

The carrier had left San Diego in November and arrived in the Middle East in January. U.S. and Israeli forces launched airstrikes against Iran on Feb. 28.

Navy leaders, however, eventually acknowledged there were some issues aboard.

In August, acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao said the Lincoln maintained adequate food supplies, but because combat operations limited resupply opportunities, meal options were reduced from two to one for a short time. He said in a letter to a Democratic lawmaker seeking information that four nutritionally balanced meals were served daily.

After more than 10 months at sea, the Lincoln's crew got a stop in Thailand early last month on the way back from the Middle East.

Long deployments can tax service members

Extended naval deployments can wear on service members who are away from home for long periods and increase strain on the ship and its equipment.

The Navy told lawmakers that eight sailors attempted suicide during the record-setting deployment, though experts say that number is low in a strike group of 6,000 sailors over 10 months.

According to the citation that Hegseth read to the crew, the Lincoln and its strike group executed 3,693 combat missions, delivered 1.37 million pounds of ordnance, launched 450 Tomahawk cruise missiles, shot down 77 one-way attack drones, sank 64 Iranian warships, destroyed 21 anti-ship cruise missiles and defended against four fast-attack craft and explosive-carrying ships.

Sponsor Message

The Lincoln, which set a record for days in between ports of call, is the second carrier to endure an unusually long deployment to support the war against Iran and to receive the Presidential Unit Citation afterward.

Hegseth in May met the crew of the USS Gerald R. Ford during its return from a 326-day deployment — the longest for an aircraft carrier in the past 50 years and a record in the post-Vietnam War era.

Another carrier, the usually Asia-based USS George Washington, relieved the Lincoln in the Middle East in August.

World.title: New U.S. indictment charges former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro with torture
World.content:
New U.S. indictment charges former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro with torture

toggle caption i Ariana Cubillos/AP

NEW YORK — U.S. authorities added new torture charges Thursday to their case against former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, ramping up pressure on the ousted authoritarian leader already fighting drug trafficking allegations.

Maduro and wife Cilia Flores, already charged with participating in a conspiracy to send cocaine into the U.S., now also face allegations of human rights abuses during his time as president of the oil-rich South American nation.

The updated indictment "alleges conduct that is truly unthinkable," New York-based U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald said outside the courthouse where the case is being handled. He said thousands of Venezuelans, and some Americans, were tortured to ensure that Maduro and Flores held onto power.

"This is the epitome of corruption," McDonald said.

The allegations include electric shocks, beatings and asphyxiation at Maduro's behest. Maduro, the indictment claims, signed off on torture methods, sought and got updates on specific victims' treatment, watched a video of a forced confession and personally threatened the killing of one prisoner's child "as a form of psychological torture."

Sponsor Message

Flores, a former legislator and attorney general, helped develop the repressive system and ordered the torture of some specific people, the indictment contends.

A message seeking comment was sent to Maduro's lawyer. Flores' attorney said he hadn't yet had time to review the new allegations.

The couple pleaded not guilty in the U.S. drug case first brought years ago against them and numerous alleged co-conspirators. Their attorneys have asked for the case to be dismissed on the grounds that they have immunity as the leader and first lady of a foreign country.

They face potential sentences of life in prison if convicted.

Maduro, who served as Venezuela's president from 2013 until his capture in January, has been under investigation for years by the International Criminal Court over allegations of crimes against humanity, tied to his crackdown on opponents. He has always denied any wrongdoing.

Both Maduro and Flores have been behind bars in New York since early January, when forces seized them from their Caracas home in a middle-of-the-night raid. Flores' lawyers unsuccessfully asked a judge Thursday to release her on house arrest.

Outside the courthouse, over a dozen demonstrators chanted slogans and held signs supporting her request.

Alleged torture victims included U.S. citizens

The revised indictment includes several mentions of the involvement of Venezuela's feared DGCIM military intelligence agency, which was headed for many years by one of Maduro's co-defendants, Gen. Hugo Carvajal. He broke with Maduro years ago, pleaded guilty last year to drug trafficking charges in New York and has offered to testify against his former boss.

Sponsor Message

While the indictment doesn't name the alleged torture victims, three are described as U.S. citizens. One was punched, subjected to electric shocks and forced to eat his own vomit during eight months of imprisonment, the indictment says. Another was beaten badly enough to necessitate a long hospital stay and had a gun stuck in his mouth. A third was handcuffed, hooded and beaten for two days every half an hour, suffering a permanent eye injury, the indictment said.

Maduro has long ignored lawsuits brought in U.S. courts by Americans who alleged they were beaten while in custody in Venezuela.

Among those who sued is Matthew Heath, a former U.S. Marine corporal from Tennessee. He was arrested at a roadblock in Venezuela in 2020 and held in custody for more than two years.

In May, Heath and another former prisoner won a $300 million default judgment against Maduro and other top Venezuelan officials for overseeing a pattern of torture. The lawsuit, brought under a federal anti-terrorism law, included allegations of waterboarding, electrocution, threats of rape with a nightstick, administration of mind-altering medications and the repeated use of a cramped cell nicknamed "El Tigrito."

"It's incredible to see a dictator in court," Heath said Thursday upon learning of the new charges. "The Maduro prosecution will do more to prevent the kidnapping of Americans by rogue regimes than a hundred press releases from the United Nations."

Former first lady denied release for medical treatment

Meanwhile, Flores' lawyers argued that Flores, 69, has medical problems that cannot be treated effectively in jail. She has lost 25 pounds (11 kilograms) while imprisoned at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn, might have suffered a minor heart attack in July, has "lingering lightheadedness, dizziness and shortness of breath" and has been told that she might need heart surgery, the attorneys said.

Sponsor Message

They also said she suffered permanent scarring when she was "thrown against a wall or dresser" during her capture.

Prosecutors opposed the bail request, saying that Flores was an "extreme" flight risk and has been taken for treatment at a local hospital when needed.

U.S. District Court Judge Alvin Hellerstein denied Flores' request. He noted, among other things, that she's unwilling to undergo catheterization in jail in order to determine the cause of her heart problems and the appropriate steps for treatment.

He also pushed back at the notion that her high blood pressure was life threatening, noting she's already on medication for that.

U.S. President Donald Trump's administration has defended the raid to capture Maduro as a "surgical law enforcement operation." Maduro has called himself a prisoner of war and his capture a kidnapping.

World.title: 4 people on NASA's Crew-12 mission return to Earth after 8 months in space
World.content:
4 people on NASA's Crew-12 mission return to Earth after 8 months in space

toggle caption i NASA via Anil Menon

Three astronauts and a cosmonaut of NASA's Crew-12 mission have safely returned to Earth after an almost eight-month trip to the International Space Station.

The crew, commanded by NASA's Jessica Meir and pilot Jack Hathaway with mission specialists Sophie Adenot of the European Space Agency and Andrey Fedyaev of Russia's Roscosmos, splashed down into the Pacific Ocean off the coast of Los Angeles, Calif., on Thursday, aboard a SpaceX Crew Dragon capsule.

Their trip home started about 45 minutes before, at an orbital speed of 17,500 mph.

The spacecraft lit its thrusters to nudge it out of orbit, causing the capsule to plunge into the atmosphere, its ablative heat shield battling extreme temperatures (up to 3,500 degrees Fahrenheit) during the fiery reentry. Over the course of about half an hour, the capsule slowed to a few hundred miles per hour, and then four orange-and-white parachutes took over, easing the spacecraft to just 16 mph above the cool, blue ocean and a gentle plop into the water.

Sponsor Message

The Crew-12 mission was the 20th time SpaceX had sent humans into orbit, lifting off in February on a Falcon 9 rocket from Cape Canaveral in Florida. It docked with the space station the next day. During the eight months in space, NASA said the crew completed dozens of science experiments and research, including studies of stem cells, how crystals grow in space and bone loss in microgravity.

Not all of their work happened inside the space station. Meir conducted four spacewalks totaling just over 27 hours to perform maintenance and upgrade the aging orbital outpost. Adenot performed three spacewalks.

Before departing, members of the Crew-12 mission were relieved by the three astronauts and cosmonaut of Crew-13, who arrived at the space station last week to start a six-month rotation.

During a pre-departure news conference on the station last month, Meir said she couldn't wait to be reunited with her 3 1/2-year-old daughter.

But there was something else she missed after all this time in orbit. "So looking forward to seeing nature again, feeling the breeze on my face, the wind rustling through the leaves. Experiencing all those things that we don't have up here," she said.

The two-time space veteran said there were two things she'd miss about space: weightlessness and the wonderful views of Earth.

World.title: South Korea to recall its ambassador to Ukraine over North Korean POW dispute
World.content:
South Korea to recall its ambassador to Ukraine over North Korean POW dispute

toggle caption i Seth Wenig/AP

SEOUL, South Korea — South Korea said Thursday it will recall its ambassador to Ukraine, stepping up its protest against Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's recent revelation of a supposedly secret transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea.

The South Korean announcement came days after its President Lee Jae Myung threatened to take unspecified punitive steps if Ukraine refuses to apologize over the revelation.

South Korea's Foreign Ministry didn't say when the ambassador, Park Hee-chang, will be brought back home. A ministry statement said that South Korea will continue consultations with Ukraine, adding it hopes the dispute between the two countries would be resolved smoothly.

Sponsor Message

South Korea and Ukraine became embroiled in a diplomatic row after Zelenskyy spoke about the transfer of the North Korean soldiers during his U.N. speech on Sept. 23. South Korea has accused Ukraine of violating a nondisclosure agreement on their transfer in mid-September, but Kyiv has denied agreeing to such a deal.

The soldiers were among thousands of North Korean troops deployed to support Russia's war against Ukraine. Since their capture in early 2025, the soldiers had expressed their desires to resettle in South Korea, because they could face persecution if repatriated home. South Korea had said it would accept them, because it legally regards the North as part of its territory and has a policy of accepting and financially supporting North Korean defectors.

South Korean officials said the non-disclosure agreement was made because they were concerned about the safety of the North Korean soldiers and their relatives in the North. But many experts say South Korea's liberal government likely also worries the disclosure of their arrival may hurt its efforts to improve ties with North Korea.

North Korea's state media hasn't commented on the soldiers' transfer. But the North previously reacted with fury to major defections of its citizens, accusing South Korea of kidnapping them. North Korea has shunned any talks with South Korea and the U.S. and focused on bolstering its nuclear program since 2019.

Sponsor Message

It's unclear what other steps South Korea would take. Experts say maintaining good relations with Ukraine is in South Korean national interests because Kyiv could provide Seoul with intelligence about North Korea's expanding cooperation with Russia and its battlefield experiences. They say cooperation with Ukraine is important for South Korea's partnerships with many Western countries supporting Ukraine over the war.

Observers say Zelenskyy disclosed the transfer of the North Korean POWs to expose the danger of North Korea's military support to Russia as a way to win more international assistance.

South Korea has provided $445 million in humanitarian assistance to Ukraine since 2022. In July, Lee pledged $100 million in aid to Ukraine in a meeting with Zelenskyy,

World.title: South Korea test-flies its first domestically developed hypersonic weapon
World.content:
South Korea test-flies its first domestically developed hypersonic weapon

toggle caption i Jeon Heon-kyun/EPA POOL via AP

SEOUL, South Korea — South Korea flight-tested on Thursday its first domestically developed hypersonic weapon, designed to fly at least five times the speed of sound and evade missile defense systems, bringing Seoul closer to what it says could be game-changing weapons capabilities.

There was no immediate response from North Korea, which last week tested its own hypersonic missile that landed in the waters near Japan.

South Korean President Lee Jae Myung attended the test, saying it's a major step in strengthening the country's conventional defense capabilities, according to a statement. It did not elaborate where the test took place.

Sponsor Message

The statement said the weapon separated from its booster rocket at the planned altitude, then descended and maneuvered both vertically and horizontally before hitting a test target. It said once developed, the weapon would be able to strike key targets by surprise in the "Korean Peninsula theater of operations."

Lee stressed that South Korea "must secure our security through our own strength," and also inspected the country's most powerful Hyunmoo-5 ballistic missile on Thursday, his office said. It did not mention any direct comments by Lee on the North.

Tensions between the Koreas have increased in recent weeks after three South Korean soldiers were injured in land mine explosions last month near the heavily armed inter-Korean border.

The South's military and the U.S.-led United Nations Command concluded the blasts were caused by devices planted by North Korea, which has denied responsibility and ridiculed the South's demands for an apology.

North Korea has also stepped up weapons testing activity as its leader Kim Jong Un expands his military nuclear program while taking an increasingly hard line toward Seoul.

Kim has so far rebuffed U.S. President Donald Trump's calls to revive their diplomacy that broke down in 2019, with his government demanding that Washington abandon its "hostile" policy toward Pyongyang and drop demands for its denuclearization as a precondition for talks.

Sponsor Message

The tensions have been a setback for Lee, who favors engagement with North Korea and has tempered his rhetoric toward the North even as public anger grows over the mine blasts.

Lee has also called for strengthening South Korea's conventional defense capabilities while reducing its reliance on the United States, which unilaterally decided to scale back a major military exercise with the South in August, with Trump citing his "very good relationship" with Kim.

In its latest weapons test on Oct. 3, North Korea launched what it described as a hypersonic intermediate-range missile that it said flew more than 1,000 kilometers (621 miles). Japan said the missile landed in waters outside of its exclusive economic zone.

South Korea said it detected the missile flying more than 700 kilometers (435 miles), while Japan's Defense Ministry said it assessed that the missile flew about 680 kilometers (422 miles).

Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of the North Korean leader, claimed the differing flight estimates by the two U.S. allies showed they are incapable of properly tracking such a missile during its flight and would therefore not be able to intercept it.

World.title: Isaias intensifies to hurricane. And, judge orders Pike execution evidence preserved
World.content:
Isaias intensifies to hurricane. And, judge orders Pike execution evidence preserved

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

Tropical Storm Isaias intensified into a hurricane overnight and is forecast to make landfall as early as tomorrow night near the Alabama Gulf Coast and the Florida Panhandle. Coastal communities in its path are preparing for high winds and flooding by stocking up on supplies to board up windows and gather sandbags. Residents who live farther inland are also preparing for inches of rain and wind.

toggle caption i Brandon Bell/Getty Images

🎧 State officials have declared states of emergency so they can stage equipment along the Gulf, Lauren Linahan of NPR network station WBHM tells Up First. They're coordinating shelters and warning people to be ready, even though, with landfall more than 24 hours away, the forecast could still change. Some non-essential workers from oil production platforms in the Gulf have been evacuated — a common occurrence during hurricane season. If the storm gets really bad, oil prices could be impacted, Linahan says. Big events are still scheduled for this weekend, including the Alabama-Georgia SEC football game in Tuscaloosa on Saturday night, which President Trump is expected to attend. If the storm maintains its path, its worst impacts will happen that morning.

Sponsor Message

Republicans currently have a slim majority in the House, holding 218 seats to the Democrats' 214. With less than a month until Election Day, an NPR analysis of both parties' campaigns highlights key races that will shape control of the House in 2027. The Cook Political Report lists 43 competitive districts, including 22 toss-ups. But both parties are pouring hundreds of millions of dollars into shaping a much larger electoral landscape.



🎧 Some districts that voted for Trump and a Democratic House representative, or vice versa, in 2024 are expected to be close again in the midterms. But NPR's Stephen Fowler says the political landscape has changed drastically since then. With an unpopular president, rising prices and strong anti-incumbency sentiments, many more districts are now competitive. The unpopularity of the current administration, particularly among Latino voters who supported Trump, could lead to new Republican-drawn districts electing Democrats. There's a massive amount of money involved in these campaigns; AdImpact reports half a billion dollars in House ads leading up to Election Day. Both parties are essentially throwing a huge amount of resources at the wall to see what sticks, Fowler says.

The Davidson County Chancery Court in Nashville has ordered Tennessee prison officials to preserve all evidence related to the botched lethal injection of Christa Pike last week. This includes log books, medical waste and all communications from officials involved in the execution attempt. The court granted Pike's attorneys "liberal access" to her, requiring prison officials to respond to requests for in-person visits within two hours. Pike's attorneys said that she is now awake, speaking and receiving critical medical care after several days of unconsciousness.



Sponsor Message

➡️ Meanwhile, Trump has approved the execution of a former U.S. Army psychiatrist by firing squad. Nidal Hasan killed 13 people in 2009 during a shooting at Fort Hood, Texas. This would mark the first U.S. military execution in more than 60 years and the first by firing squad since World War II. Secretary of the Army Adam Telle announced that Hasan will be executed at Fort Hood on Dec. 3. The Pentagon's decision, including the choice of firing squad, remains unclear, but some experts that NPR spoke with say it may relate to recent concerns over Pike's botched lethal injection.

CNN, MS NOW and Politico are in federal court today to argue that Trump is infringing on their constitutional rights by blocking their access to the White House. The news outlets say that they have the right to determine how, what and where they can cover the president at any given time. A judge last month issued a temporary restraining order preventing the Trump administration from barring the outlets from the White House while the court considered the lawsuit.



🎧 NPR's David Folkenflik says the White House has inconsistently followed the judge's order, including not allowing CNN to do the work it typically does at smaller spaces, like Air Force One. Although the White House has the right to deny access to its grounds, once credentials are granted, they cannot be revoked for dissatisfaction with the speech. The White House has been saying these outlets report fake news and have cited national security concerns, referencing questions from the outlets about the bunker and areas below the East Wing's newly renovated ballroom.

Behind the story

by Cooper Katz McKim , The Indicator from Planet Money associate producer

toggle caption i David Zalubowski/AP Photo/David Zalubowski/AP

The cost of diesel fuel is breaking records left and right. The previous record was $5.85/gallon. A few weeks ago, it hit $6.53/gallon. If I drove a diesel car, I might stay home.

Sponsor Message

At the Indicator, we've been watching whether President Trump would try to lower prices by banning exports of diesel fuel. He did not do that, though he did make diesel cheaper by expanding the use of tax-exempt diesel for highway vehicles through the end of the year. Still, I wondered why diesel prices are so consistently higher than regular gas.

We have a weekly newsletter at The Indicator where we track what's driving the economy and how it affects your life. It was the right platform to ask: Is diesel fuel inherently more expensive than regular gas?

The answer: NO! Before 2004, diesel was actually cheaper. But step by step, the price got higher.

The first domino to fall: taxes. In 1993, the federal excise tax on diesel increased to 24.4 cents, 6 cents more than the regular gas tax.

Soon after, demand for diesel began to skyrocket. China and India were ramping up industrialization, agriculture and new infrastructure to new levels. The world saw diesel vehicles take off.

In the U.S., the last major domino to fall was air quality standards. In 2006, diesel fuel needed to have less sulfur, which required new — and more expensive — refining and distribution methods.

One lesson that stuck with me is how diesel is essential for the modern economy. It's needed in shipping, long-haul trucking, mining and backup generators. Whether the cost is high or low, the demand is there. Regular gasoline? Demand is a little squishier.

You can check out the full segment here. And if you liked this story, subscribe to The Indicator newsletter here!

Life advice

toggle caption i Anton Vierietin/Getty Images/iStockphoto

Are you feeling nervous about facing a high-stakes event, such as a race or a job interview? Well, get ready to face those challenges head-on with the help of psychologist Cindra Kamphoff, the author of The Confidence Habit: 7 Core Practices to Transform Self-Doubt into Self-Belief. She shared with Life Kit some of her creative strategies for managing fear and negativity to overcome anxiety and build confidence before, during and after big tasks.

Sponsor Message

🏃 Practice positive self-talk. Even small affirmations can boost your self-esteem. You can even write them on your arm to remind yourself during events like races.

🏃 Set a range of goals instead of aiming for one perfect outcome. This approach can help to reduce anxiety by lowering the pressure and encouraging you to focus on the present moment.

🏃 When negative thoughts creep in before your task, ask yourself: Is this thought true? Is it serving me? And what empowering statement can I replace it with? This approach pauses negativity and helps you refocus on the present.

For more advice on how to beat performance anxiety, listen to this episode of NPR's Life Kit. Subscribe to the Life Kit newsletter for expert advice on love, money, relationships and more.

3 things to know before you go

Diaa Hadid/NPR

NPR's Diaa Hadid is sending greetings from the Lahore High Court in Pakistan for this week's installment of Far-Flung Postcards. She describes it as "a near-perfect example of British South Asian colonial architecture." Opal Lee, the Grandmother of Juneteenth, celebrated her 100th birthday at the future site of the National Juneteenth Museum in Texas. (via KERA) A remarkably intact fossil discovery has given scientists new evidence about when the ability to chew and swallow food emerged among mammals.

This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

World.title: What we know about Ottawa's $2B rebate plan for heat pumps
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canada's federal government has announced a new $2-billion rebate plan aimed at getting more heat pumps installed in homes across the country in the years ahead.

Initial details of the National Heat Pump Rebate Program were announced Thursday.

Here's what we know so far.

How many households will benefit?

The Government of Canada says up to 820,000 households will be able to take advantage of the rebate program, over an eight-year period.

How soon does it start?

The government expects to launch the rebate early next year. But Ottawa is eyeing making it retroactive to fall.

How does it work?

Homeowners will be able to apply for the rebate when their existing heating system breaks down — or when they plan to replace a heating system that is approaching end of life.

Government data suggests 80 per cent of HVAC replacements occur when current systems break. The new program is trying to cater to this group of individuals — and provide a path to switching over to heat pumps accordingly.

WATCH | Carney talks new home-heating rebate program: Ottawa launching $2B rebate program for home heat pumps | Duration 0:57 The federal government is introducing a $2-billion rebate program to get one million households to switch to heat pumps. According to Prime Minister Mark Carney, the program will help up to 820,000 Canadian homeowners over the next eight years by providing average savings of $1,400 a year when they replace their current heating systems.

Applications for the rebate will be filed via an online portal. The government says approvals will be confirmed within 24 hours.

Homeowners will submit receipts after installation of the pre-approved heat pumps, so that rebates can follow — with payment to be "approved within five days," according to a government document outlining aspects of the new program.

The payments that follow will be made via direct deposit.

How much is the rebate worth?

Up to $10,000 for households below the median income. Other eligible households can claim $2,000.

What kind of heat pumps will be eligible?

Homeowners will be able to look to a list of eligible products, which the government says will include " an extensive selection of over 100,000 options at various price points and configurations, all suited for the Canadian climate."

Will energy audits be required?

No.

What happens next?

The government says it will be consulting with industry and work with HVAC installers to maximize the reach of the pending program.

Government officials who briefed media said that Ottawa wants industry to have the needed inventory on hand to deliver the program as planned. This is one reason why consultations are taking place.

World.title: Will Ottawa really take Stelco to court? Here's what happened last time
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Stelco Holdings has days to share a plan to save hundreds of Ontario steel workers from layoffs already underway — or it risks legal action from the Canadian government.

The clock is ticking on what lawyers say is a test of how foreign investors are held to account as Prime Minister Mark Carney seeks to lure more of them to Canada amid a bitter trade war with the United States.

So, how idle is the threat? And is it likely to save workers' jobs? Here's what we know from the last time the federal government took the U.S. steelmaker to court.

2 decades since Ottawa fought ex-Stelco owner in court

In 2007, Pennsylvania-based U.S. Steel announced a deal to acquire Stelco, then a publicly traded company , for about $1 billion US, and the company was renamed U.S. Steel Canada.

Major foreign investments must benefit the domestic economy, per the Investment Canada Act. So, foreign buyers must give legally binding written commitments — called undertakings — to the federal industry minister to prove the deal provides a "net benefit to Canada."

At the time, U.S. Steel agreed to several such undertakings, including a three-year commitment to maintain Canadian employment levels, and increase steel production in Canada by at least 10 per cent.

However, when the 2008 financial crisis sapped global demand, U.S. Steel closed most of Stelco's Canadian operations and laid off over 1,500 employees.

WATCH | Union says layoffs have begun: Layoffs start at Hamilton Stelco plant, union says | Duration closed caption 7:19 Layoffs at the Stelco steel plant in Hamilton, Ont., are underway and expected to roll out over three weeks, says Ron Wells, president of United Steelworkers Local 1005. Stelco worker Jordan Williams says he received his layoff notice at the end of his shift on Wednesday.

The attorney general of Canada filed a lawsuit against U.S. Steel in July 2009.

"As far as the public record shows, it is the only time Ottawa has gone to court over commitments like this," Toronto-based business lawyer Nassira El Hadri told CBC News.

According to a summary of court filings compiled by a lawyer at Toronto-based Torys LLP, Stelco argued the undertakings only required compliance at the end of their three-year term, not before.

Stelco also said that per Industry Canada guidelines, its investors should not be held accountable for factors beyond their control, like the unfolding financial crisis.

WATCH | Stelco worker speaks about his layoff notice: Layoff uncertainty 'a roller-coaster' for Stelco workers | Duration 1:12 Steelworker Jordan Williams describes the frustration he’s feeling after receiving a layoff notice from Stelco. Cleveland-Cliffs — the Ohio-based company that owns Stelco — started issuing individual layoff notices as it plans to lay off as many as 500 workers and idle production at the Hamilton plant.

Last legal battle ended in deal to keep making steel

The attorney general of Canada formally withdrew the lawsuit in late 2011, ending in an out-of-court-settlement before the court could make a judgment.

U.S. Steel agreed to keep production alive in Hamilton and Lake Erie, and to make $50 million in new capital investments by the end of 2015 to modernize its operations. It agreed to new undertakings with Ottawa, but those did not include minimum worker headcount requirements.

But before then, in 2014, U.S. Steel Canada filed for creditor protection, and the American parent company severed ties with its Canadian operations.

In 2016, a New York-based private equity firm acquired the steelmaker. The Stelco name was revived when the company returned to the Toronto Stock Exchange the next year.

The dispute prompted updates to the Investment Canada Act in 2009 and 2012 to make settlement negotiations easier, and strengthen enforcement. The government later raised daily non-compliance fines to $25,000, and tightened reviews for sensitive industries.

What's happening now at Stelco?

Flash forward to 2024, when Ottawa approved Ohio-based Cleveland-Cliffs' $3.4-billion cash-and-stock deal to buy Stelco.

The conditions included a promise to maintain at least the same number of unionized employees in Canada for five years, as well as the vast majority of non-unionized workers, according to a government statement at the time .

Last week, Stelco announced a plan to idle certain production in Hamilton, resulting in up to 500 layoffs company-wide. The union says layoffs are already underway.

Cleveland-Cliffs CEO Lourenco Goncalves said the cuts are necessary and justified by the Canada-U.S. trade war, arguing that Stelco's ability to sell steel to the U.S. was an "underlying condition" of the deal.

But in a letter Monday to Stelco president Paul Simon, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly gave the company five business days to share a job plan, or face legal action.

And on Tuesday, Joly slammed Goncalves's public support of American steel tariffs.

"He's in favour of these U.S. tariffs against steel," she said. "They cannot say that this is now an act of God or force majeure."

Will Stelco fight Ottawa in court again?

El Hadri says the matter is "most likely going to end up in court."

She points out that Joly's letter does not ask Stelco and Cleveland-Cliffs for an explanation about why they plan to lay off workers. It states the company's commitments "do not cease to apply simply because business strategy or market conditions have changed."

"It may end up in a settlement as well, but it all depends on the economic conditions, like what's going on inside Stelco," El Hadri told CBC News.

The court has "wide powers" at its disposal, she said, including putting a business up for sale.

"We could end up with new commitments, which is what happened with Stelco in 2009."

Sandy Walker, co-chair of the competition and foreign investment review group at the global law firm Dentons, says it's still possible that Stelco could reverse course on its full layoff plans to avoid going to court.

"That depends on how effective the Canadian government’s threats are," she told CBC News.

"There are many reasons why [it] may not end up in court, but may end up with a variation of its undertakings, or otherwise settling with the Canadian government."

At the same time, Walker says those Industry Canada guidelines on factors beyond a company's control may let Stelco "off the hook" to some extent.

What does this mean for PM's agenda?

Both Walker and El Hadri agree the timing is somewhat awkward, given Ottawa's push for $1 trillion worth of investments across the country over the next five years.

Last month, Carney hosted hundreds of deep-pocketed investors at an investment summit in Toronto in a bid to spur deals, and cut reliance on the United States.

"We are giving a signal to the world that ... you have to respect our rules," El Hadri said.

"It's a difficult balance," Walker said. "The government has got to worry about looking weak."

World.title: Sask., Alberta premiers reject Elon Musk's call for provinces to separate from Canada
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The premiers of Alberta and Saskatchewan have rejected a suggestion by one of the world's richest men that the two provinces should separate from Canada.

Elon Musk, a trillionaire tech businessman who was formerly an advisor to U.S. President Donald Trump, weighed in on his social media platform Twitter, now known as X.

On Wednesday, Musk said Quebec would benefit from independence, as would Alberta and Saskatchewan.

The tech tycoon was responding to a quote from Quebec premier-designate Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, who said the province's independence "will be realized one day."

On that same day Premier Scott Moe offered a short, one-word response to Musk in his own social media post: "No."

Moe was not available for an interview on Thursday and his office said he had nothing more to add to the post.

WATCH | Canada's future 'will be decided by Canadians': Carney on foreign interference: Canada's future 'will be decided by Canadians': Carney on foreign interference | Duration closed caption 0:58 Asked about whether he thinks Elon Musk's comments on Quebec sovereignty is an example of foreign interference, Prime Minister Mark Carney says Canada's future will be decided by Canadians' priorities. These priorities include living 'free from interference from foreign governments and large tech firms that think they can tell us what to do,' he says.

According to the Canadian Press, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said she also strongly disagrees with Musk's opinion.

Prime Minister Mark Carney was asked about Musk's comments Thursday while speaking in Quebec.

Carney said the future of Canada will be decided by Canadians, the priorities of Canadians and the people of Quebec.

"A strong Canada means more independent, more sovereign, more prosperous," Carney said, adding that Canada will be "free from foreign interference of foreign governments and large tech firms that think they can tell us what to do."

The state of play in each province

On Oct. 19, Albertans will head to the polls to decide if the province should stay in Canada or whether there should be a second binding referendum on separation.

Smith has said she plans to vote to stay in Canada in the upcoming provincial referendum.

Moe believes Saskatchewan is stronger within a united Canada, but has previously said he would not stop a plebiscite if Saskatchewanians were able to secure enough signatures to trigger a referendum.

Moe has also enjoyed a much better relationship with Prime Minister Mark Carney than with his predecessor Justin Trudeau.

WATCH | Why Saskatchewan's premier says Trump's potash threats are 'not realistic': Why Saskatchewan's premier says Trump's potash threats are 'not realistic' | Duration closed caption 8:40 U.S. President Donald Trump told reporters on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York that his country would stick with Canada as its potash supplier for the time being, while claiming Belarus is offering the U.S. potash at a much lower price. Power & Politics speaks to Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe about whether he thinks it's worth going back to the negotiating table with the Trump administration.

Moe has at various times refused to say Trudeau's name even after his departure from federal politics.

In Quebec, the sovereigntist Parti Québécois is back in power after a securing enough seats to form a minority government in Monday's provincial election.

Soon-to-be premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has vowed to hold a referendum.

World.title: Pentagon says firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter will be livestreamed
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Pentagon says the firing squad execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan will be livestreamed after War Secretary Pete Hegseth said the execution would be "public."

Hegseth, speaking to the conservative TV outlet Real America's Voice News on Wednesday, said the execution of Hasan will take place at Fort Hood on Dec. 3.

Hasan, a former U.S. army officer, was convicted of killing 13 people and injuring 32 others in a shooting at the military base in 2009.

"We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public," Hegseth said.

Hegseth spoke to the outlet aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier while visiting the long-deployed crew, who supported the Iran war, before their arrival at their home port in San Diego.

When asked if Hasan had made any final requests or reached out to the Trump administration, Hegseth simply replied: "Don't care. We'll see him on December 3rd."

Former U.S. major Nidal Hasan, the army psychiatrist convicted in the 2009 Fort Hood shooting, will be executed Dec. 3. (Bell County Sheriff's Office/Getty Images)

Hasan, an army psychiatrist who held the rank of major, walked into a medical building where soldiers were getting checkups, shouted Allahu akbar — Arabic for "God is greater" — and opened fire with a laser-sighted handgun.

During the trial it was revealed that Hasan spent weeks planning the deadly attack, and his preparation included videotaping a sales clerk showing him how to change the magazine on the pistol that he purchased. He would later go to a gun range outside Austin and ask for advice on how to reload with speed and precision from an instructor.

Soldiers later testified that Hasan's rapid reloading made it all but impossible to stop the shooting.

Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell had said Monday that U.S. President Donald Trump had approved the execution of Hasan.

The White House on Thursday immediately referred questions about the plans for the livestreamed execution to the Pentagon.

Officials in the Pentagon clarified Thursday that the execution will be livestreamed and that more details would follow.

Mixed reaction

Deborah Denno, a death penalty expert and law professor at Fordham University, said livestreaming an execution could make the process "much more transparent" and inform the public about all that capital punishment entails. Those are benefits that she said would be useful at a time when Christa Pike's botched execution in Tennessee has raised fresh questions about the manner by which criminal defendants are put to death for their crimes.

"I think it could possibly be a good idea because it would be transparent and the public would be fully aware that it's happening," she said.

When many states have had difficulty carrying out lethal injections due to difficulty accessing drugs or finding medical professionals willing to participate in executions, firing squads are coming to be seen as a less inhumane alternative, said Brenner Fissell, a professor at Villanova Law and vice-president of the National Institute of Military Justice.

"Firing squads can be a quicker, cleaner, more precise way to execute a prisoner," he said. "I don't think that's what's motivating this. There's a perceived masculinity and military-ness to firing squads that is part of the aura Hegseth is trying to emphasize — the ‘lethality culture.'"

Elisabeth Semel, co-director of the Death Penalty Clinic at UC Berkeley Law, said Hegseth's announcement raises a host of legal and public policy questions, including concerns for the dignity of the defendant, who will be eligible to view the execution and what the Trump administration has in mind in opting for an unusual spectacle.

Though there has been long-running discussion about the idea of televising an execution, "I don't recall a situation in which it was instituted by the government. I think that also raises serious questions about what is the motivation of the government," she said.

"This is a president who's about spectacle and that's, I think, precisely the message that he intends to deliver," Semel said, adding that she was skeptical that the administration had given second thought to the legal and social questions being presented by the decision.

The military hasn't executed a servicemember by firing squad since the Second World War. The last military execution took place on April 13, 1961, when Army Private John Bennett was executed by hanging.

World.title: Is it better to buy or rent?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Home prices are dropping and stock markets are surging – so we have to ask: is it better to buy a home, or to rent and invest? CBC's Nael Shiab breaks that down for you.

Buying a property is the largest purchase most Canadians will make in their lifetime. For many, it’s also their biggest investment. But strictly financially speaking, are you better off putting down a large down payment and facing higher monthly costs as an owner, or remaining a renter and investing your savings somewhere else? Who ends up with more money in their pocket at the end of the day?

Don't miss our simulator below. Keep reading to understand how to use it.

To answer this question, we analyzed over two decades of historical data on property prices, rents, inflation and interest rates across 22 Canadian metropolitan areas, alongside long-term stock market returns.

Using this data, we built an interactive simulator. Every time it runs, it calculates the monthly expenses and financial gains for three distinct paths: an owner with a fixed-rate mortgage, one with a variable-rate mortgage and a renter. Whenever the renter's monthly costs are lower than the homeowner's, those savings are automatically invested in stocks and bonds to compound over time.

The simulator projects these financial paths over a 25-year period across 1,000 unique scenarios. Some scenarios feature high rents and low interest rates; others simulate average inflation paired with weak stock market returns.

The calculations factor in mortgage payments, insurance, property taxes, maintenance costs, condo fees, rent and eventual selling fees. Every outcome represents a possible future based on historical patterns and the options you select.

Of course, no one can predict the future. This tool provides probabilities, not guarantees, and should not be used for major financial decisions. Below is a simplified version of our simulator. You can find a more comprehensive version with expanded options and a detailed methodology breakdown at the end of this article.

Home prices decline, while stocks surge

Our simulator is not perfect. The past is no guarantee of the future, and many macroeconomic factors are bound to change. Canada’s population is aging, the immigration outlook remains uncertain, an AI bubble could crash stock markets and countless variables continuously reshape the broader economy and housing markets.

Because comprehensive historical data is limited, our tool is based on the last 25 years, meaning it does not account for Canada's last major housing crash in the early 1990s. Several experts also pointed out that the cost of maintaining a property is often higher than estimated, especially when a roof starts to leak unexpectedly. Furthermore, realistically, few Canadians stay in the exact same home for a quarter-century.

A sandwich board is shown on a street on Quebec's unofficial moving day in Montreal on July 1. (Graham Hughes/The Canadian Press)

Still, home prices have been declining over the last few years, while interest rates, average property taxes and maintenance costs have increased.

Meanwhile, the stock market has been surging. An investment made in 2005 would be worth roughly seven times more today, compared to just three times more for a property bought at the same time.

Based on this, our calculations reveal a clear trend: If you rent an average studio or one-bedroom apartment and aggressively invest the cash you save by not owning a condo, you have a strong chance of pulling ahead.

But as soon as you step up to a two-bedroom apartment or larger, that math changes quickly. Rent prices swallow up the surplus, making it nearly impossible to save and invest meaningfully.

In fact, in many scenarios, the monthly cost of renting eventually eclipses the cost of owning. A homeowner's largest monthly expense is their mortgage, typically locked in for a five-year term. Adjusted for inflation, the real value of that payment actually decreases over time.

Rents, on the other hand, almost always rise, often outpacing general inflation. Eventually, the lines cross. The renter begins paying more per month than the owner, wiping out their monthly savings and halting any new investment contributions.

Location, of course, dictates everything. In some regions, owning a condo loses the least amount of money after all cumulative expenses, compared to renting a two bedroom or bigger. Buying and then selling a condo is not a guaranteed profit. Single-family houses or townhouses offer a higher probability of financial return, but they come with a much steeper upfront purchase price.

'2 housing crises in Canada'

Yet for millions of Canadians, this debate is purely theoretical, and renting is their only option. Half of all couples in the cities we analyzed do not earn enough to qualify for an average condo in the city they live in — a figure that jumps to two-thirds for a house.

The outlook is even starker for the growing demographic of single-income households. Most Canadians are forced to rent, even when doing so is the less financially advantageous path.

“I would argue there are two housing crises in Canada,” said Aled ab Iorwerth, deputy chief economist at the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC).

“One is the housing crisis for the middle class, affording a condo in places like Toronto, Vancouver and increasingly in Montreal, especially since the pandemic. But there's an affordability crisis as well for low-income Canadians, who really need help just finding a place to live.”

Affordability is one factor causing younger generations to live with their parents for longer, a May 2026 Statistics Canada study found. They also tend to settle on a career, form a family and buy property later in life, a phenomenon described as “life-stretching.” And when they do finally leave the family nest, they also typically live alone or with roommates more often than previous generations.

This purchasing delay observed among younger Canadian generations can have massive compounding consequences.

“Timing is everything,” said Jean-Philippe Deschamps-Laporte, assistant director of the Centre for Housing and Income Statistics at Statistics Canada, who was involved with the report. When younger generations buy their first property later in their life compared to their parents, this investment has less time to potentially bear fruit.

“Younger generations could face returns that are not what they would have had if they had been born earlier."

His own research has found that when people graduate during a recession, it carries consequences for the rest of their lives. The same logic applies to the housing and stock markets. If you are lucky, you buy when prices are low and sell when they are high. But more often than not, you do not really get to choose, he notes, as it depends entirely on your current life stage.

So, should you buy or should you rent?

“The calculations done here are very useful for a lot of Canadians, but the most important thing is to do some introspection on how much owning a home will actually improve your life,” said James Macek, assistant professor at the University of Alberta's School of Business.

Kiana Basiri, assistant professor at the Toronto Metropolitan University, had a similar sentiment.

“We are kind of pushing people toward ownership at the expense of them being tighter financially and less resilient, simply because they really want to own something," she said.

"We just assume ownership is the best way for people to accumulate wealth over time, but I feel we need more education for people on how they can invest their savings in different ways.”

Furthermore, when people move to the suburbs to find more affordable properties, they sometimes forget to factor in other costs, like maintaining two cars instead of paying for public transit.

WATCH | Watch out for AI-generated real estate listings: Fact check: Canadian real estate listings use AI-generated images | Duration 1:44 Whether you're looking to rent or buy a home, you might come across AI-generated photos in real estate listings. CBC's Fact Check team takes a look at some recent examples — and what rules realtors are supposed to follow.

As Jean-Pierre Lessard, an economist and partner at Aviseo Conseil, put it: “We are crazy about property ownership in Canada, but there is no link between a nation's economic growth and its homeownership rate.”

A key point he made during a talk in a May 2026 conference was that it’s possible for the average household in Quebec City and Montreal to build more wealth by remaining renters instead of becoming owners.

“Originally, public policies to encourage buying were intended to stimulate construction. We've lost sight of that,” Lessard said. “We need to return to something more rational.”

In some nations, it is entirely normal to be a lifelong renter. Germany and Switzerland, for example, are famous for having populations where more than half of all residents rent, backed by robust regulations that cap rent increases and protect tenants' rights.

“Overall, we need to increase the supply of both homeownership and rental units quite significantly,” said ab Iorwerth. The challenge, he said, is to balance supply with measures that encourage homeownership, such as the first home savings account, which tend to push prices up, while simultaneously ensuring there is enough inventory to keep homes affordable.

In June 2025, the CMHC published a report projecting that around 250,000 new housing units would be started each year over the next decade, whereas twice as many are actually needed to restore affordability.

Methodology

The detailed data sets and calculations used can be found here. Our methodology was shared prior to publication with the experts quoted in the article above, and their suggestions helped inform the analysis.

Do you have data that tells an important story you would like to share? Write to nael.shiab@cbc.ca.

World.title: Class action alleging sexual assaults at Spa Nordik to proceed
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Dozens of people have joined a certified class-action lawsuit alleging they were sexually assaulted at Nordik Spa Village in Chelsea, Que. The CBC’s Matthew Kupfer reports.

Dozens of people have joined a certified class action alleging they were sexually assaulted at Nordik Spa Village in Chelsea, Que., in a lawsuit that implicates dozens of massage therapists who worked there over a 19-year period.

According to the class action, filed in French in Quebec Superior Court, the popular spa just north of Ottawa and Gatineau, Que., is alleged to have improperly handled complaints and not done enough to inform and protect clients.

Lambert Avocats, the lawyers representing the plaintiffs, said 143 people contacted them in the last year saying they’d been sexually assaulted by massage therapists at Spa Nordik. The lawsuit alleges wrongdoing by a total of 36 different massage therapists at the spa between 2007 and 2026.

"People are generally pretty shocked to hear the numbers, but I think they’re also relieved to see something is being done about it and they have a recourse," said lawyer Philippe Brault.

The claims in the class action have not been tested in court.

According to the lawsuit, several of the clients who raised allegations with Spa Nordik’s management were offered gift cards "to return to the establishment where they were sexually assaulted."

'It's disturbing, it's disgusting'

The lawsuit focuses on a representative case that occurred in December 2024. CBC interviewed the woman at the centre of the complaint, who is not identified in court documents. CBC News is also not identifying her to respect the court process.

"It's disturbing, it's disgusting," she said of the number of complaints since the class action was initiated last summer.

"I represent all of the women, so that keeps me going. I want to represent them and let people know this is happening and this needs to be a situation that is managed, and these girls need to be protected and all women need to be protected and all people should be protected."

According to the court documents, the woman paid for a massage and was assigned to a male massage therapist who instructed her to undress. During the massage, he did not ease the pressure he applied despite being asked three times, according to the complaint.

It's also alleged that he touched the woman through his clothes with his stomach and genitals, and after placing a towel over her face began massaging her upper thighs.

The court documents allege Spa Nordik claimed its massage therapists were "independent contractors" and offered no apology or followup, and made no effort to prevent similar abuse following the complaint.

"This is a matter of institutional negligence," said Brault. "We want Spa Nordik and other similar establishments to understand that they have a responsibility to ensure their clients’ safety to prevent these types of events taking place, and when they know about these situations to take the proper measures to stop the situations from happening."

Client safety 'our highest priority,' spa says

The application for the class action argues Spa Nordik would have been aware of previous allegations of sexual assault before the representative case in 2024, including cases that ended up in criminal court.

The class action argues the spa should have taken steps to improve vetting and training of massage therapists, and should have better informed clients about what to expect from its services and how to report any discomfort.

Spa Nordik told CBC News in a statement that the certification of the class action is not a judgment, and it plans to defend itself.

It said the spa has taken "all necessary measures to ensure a respectful, safe and trustworthy environment."

"The safety and well-being of our guests, employees and professionals remain our highest priority," wrote Isabelle Mathieu, general manager of Nordik Spa Village.

She said the spa is unable to comment further given the ongoing legal proceedings.

World.title: A crash course in Anne Carson: the books that won the Canadian author the Nobel Prize
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canadian poet and essayist Anne Carson was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature, the Swedish Academy in Stockholm announced Thursday.

Known for infusing classical philosophy with witty, ironic brilliance, the Toronto-born author and scholar is the first Canadian to win the Nobel Prize in Literature since Alice Munro in 2013.

Carson has also won other major literary prizes, including the Griffin Prize for Poetry (she's the only person to win it twice), a Guggenheim Fellowship, a MacArthur "genius grant," the PEN/Nabokov Award for Achievement in International Literature and the T.S. Eliot Prize for Poetry.

Looking to brush up on her catalogue? We've compiled a list of some of Carson's most important books.

Autobiography of Red

Autobiography of Red is a book by Anne Carson. (McClelland & Stewart)

Autobiography of Red is perhaps Carson's best-known work. The 1998 book is a combination of both a poem and a novel that partially retells the Greek myth of Geryon and Herakles, infusing it with a contemporary coming-of-age story.

As the title suggests, Autobiography of Red is told as Geryon's autobiography. In it, Geryon, a red-winged monster, runs away from his complicated family to find comfort in photography. When he meets a young man named Herakles, he falls into a deep infatuation with him, only to be devastated when he leaves. But when Herakles returns suddenly a year later, Geryon must reckon with his desire and set forth on a major journey of growth.

"Herakles is that person you probably know from Saturday morning cartoons who did the famous labours. Hercules, we call him in American," said Carson in a 2011 interview on CBC's Writers & Company.

"One of his labours was to travel to the island of the supposed monster called Geryon and capture his magic red cattle. So he did that, and killed Geryon, took the cattle and succeeded. So I just changed that story a bit."

Autobiography of Red won the A.M. Klein Prize for Poetry and was nominated for the National Book Critics Circle Award Poetry and the T.S. Eliot Prize.

Eros the Bittersweet

Eros the Bittersweet is a book by Anne Carson. (Deep Vellum)

Eros the Bittersweet is Carson's first book of literary criticism, originally published in 1986.

In the collection of essays, Carson, a classics scholar, adapts her 1981 PhD thesis to examine the concept of "eros" as it appears in classical philosophy and literature.

Eros the Bittersweet was named as one of the best 100 nonfiction books of all time by Modern Library in 1999.

Glass, Irony and God

Glass, Irony and God is a book by Anne Carson. (New Directions Publishing)

Glass, Irony and God, Carson's 1995 book, features the celebrated poem The Glass Essay, which is more than 30 pages long and tells the story of a love affair coming to an end through a reading of Emily Brontë's poetry.

In the Nobel Prize ceremony, it was praised by the Swedish Academy for demonstrating "the potential of the long poem where genre boundaries are seen to blur."

Men in the Off Hours

Men in the Off Hours is a book by Anne Carson. (Vintage)

Carson won her first Griffin Poetry Prize for Men in the Off Hours in 2001. The collection brings together historical figures from Oedipus and Emily Dickinson to St. Augustine, blending the past with the contemporary.

The Beauty of the Husband

The Beauty of the Husband is a book by Anne Carson. (Vintage Canada)

The Beauty of the Husband is a fictional essay told in what Carson calls 29 "tangos" of narrative verse, examining English poet John Keats' idea that beauty is truth, and illustrating a marriage as it falls apart.

"I think beauty is a romantic ideal that works itself out in various ways and various relationships," said Carson in 2011 on CBC's Writers & Company. "It's that myth you're desiring, the one you have invented, rather than the one who exists."

With The Beauty of the Husband, Carson became the first woman to receive England's T.S. Eliot Prize for Poetry. The essay also won the Los Angeles Times Book Prize and the A. M. Klein Prize for Poetry.

If Not, Winter

If Not, Winter is a collection of Sappho's poetry, translated by Anne Carson. (Vintage Canada)

As a scholar, Carson is widely known for her translations of the ancient Greek poet Sappho. If Not, Winter collects her translations of Sappho's poetry fragments and features the ancient Greek on facing pages.

In a 2016 interview on CBC's Writers & Company, Eleanor Wachtel asked Carson about the experience of being immersed in translation.

"It's like being on a surface with a lot of cracks in it, looking down through the cracks to something like another world down there that you can almost see, almost express, but not quite," she said.

Red Doc>

Red Doc> is a book by Anne Carson. (McClelland & Stewart)

The follow-up to Autobiography of Red, Red Doc> returns to the story of Geryon as an adult in the 21st century, now called "G."

Red Doc> follows him as he journeys with his lover, Sad, a war veteran formerly known as Herakles, and the artist Ida, to places near and far, from green pastures to a psychiatric clinic.

"I just wanted to draw them both into that state of mind of turning the page on hope," said Carson about revisiting the characters of Geryon and Herakles in a 2016 Writers & Company interview.

"After you realize hope is there to set your souls on fire, they'll have a different attitude to adventure and entering into new things. So I wanted to make them both a little bit wary, a little bit jaded and with grown-up problems."

Red Doc> won Carson her second Griffin Poetry Prize win in 2014.

"What is taken up again, more significantly than an update of Autobiography, is a daunting writer having her particular way with the language," wrote the Griffin jury in a statement.

Norma Jeane Baker of Troy

Norma Jeane Baker of Troy is a book by Anne Carson. (New Directions Publishing)

Norma Jeane Baker of Troy is a poetry collection that brings together the mythology of Helen of Troy and Marilyn Monroe, two women from different millennia whose beauty brought them power and influence, but ultimately caused them great pain.

Norma Jeane Baker of Troy won the 2020 Governor General's Literary Award for poetry and was lauded by the jury for using "irreverence to lure and wreck our concepts of time, place and subject."

Wrong Norma

Wrong Norma is a book by Anne Carson. (New Directions Publishing)

Carson's most recent title, Wrong Norma, published in 2024, won the National Book Critics Circle Award for Poetry.

Wrong Norma is a collection of prose pieces greatly varying in subject matter, from Joseph Conrad to snow and her dad. As Carson writes in the book, "The pieces are not linked. That’s why I’ve called them ‘wrong.’”

World.title: Official languages commissioner rebukes Air Canada CEO over English-only message
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The commissioner of official languages of Canada is rebuking Air Canada's outgoing CEO for a condolence message he delivered almost entirely in English after a deadly plane crash in New York earlier this year.

The commissioner's annual report says the office received a large number of complaints after Michael Rousseau posted a four-minute video that only included two French words — "bonjour" and "merci."

"The intensity of the reactions and the high volume of complaints received in response to this video show that both of our official languages genuinely matter to the Canadian public and that we must continue to protect them," Kelly Burke told reporters in Ottawa, adding that the complaints are still under investigation.

"This situation illustrates that bilingualism is an essential skill for any leader, whether in politics, federal public service or even in the private sector."

Rousseau's video message came after an Air Canada regional jet that took off in Montreal collided with a fire truck crossing the runway at LaGuardia Airport in New York on March 22, killing two pilots and sending more than 40 people to hospital.

Quebecer Antoine Forest and Mackenzie Gunther, from Ontario, were the two pilots killed in the collision.

Burke's report says it's important for Canadians to hear and see their leaders speaking equally in both official languages in times of crisis, "and not solely through an interpreter or subtitles."

Seven days after Air Canada posted Rousseau's video, the company's board of directors announced that he would retire by the end of the third quarter of 2026 and that it was considering a number of criteria for his successor, including the ability to communicate in French.

The commissioner's office said in an email that it received 2,425 complaints on the video, including 98 that arrived after the end of the current financial year on March 31.

Burke's 31-page report also touched on a number of other issues, including concern over how federal budget cuts could impact the government's language obligations and minority language communities.

"In the past, spending on official languages-related activities has often been targeted during periods of fiscal restraint," the report read.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has promised to cut the size of the public service, relying mainly on attrition.

Burke said it's still too soon to measure the impacts of the 2025 federal budget, which laid out a plan to save tens of billions of dollars over five years in budget cuts and government efficiency measures.

"We're watching the government's actions closely on this subject, and we're waiting to see how the cutbacks will actually play out within the administration, so we can then assess how the government has addressed the concerns we raised at the beginning," Burke said.

WATCH | Carney 'very disappointed' in English-only message: Carney 'very disappointed' by Air Canada CEO's English-only message | Duration 0:56 Prime Minister Mark Carney said Air Canada CEO Michael Rousseau's English-only message showed 'a lack of judgment and a lack of compassion,' after an Air Canada Express passenger jet collided with a fire truck at New York's LaGuardia airport, killing both pilots.

The report also cited what it saw as positive developments, including $150 million in additional funding announced for CBC/Radio-Canada in the 2025-26 fiscal year and a Supreme Court decision in June that ruled New Brunswick's lieutenant-governor must be bilingual.

This decision "represents a step forward for the province's language rights and a major victory for official language minority communities," the report read.

The report also dedicated several pages to the use of artificial intelligence.

It noted that AI has potential to be used as a tool for translation and interpretation, as well as promoting bilingualism and language learning.

But Burke noted that AI is prone to errors, and has a "language bias" toward English due to the predominance of English-language "content and perspectives" on the internet.

The commissioner recommended that the Treasury Board of Canada Secretariat incorporate official languages to its artificial intelligence strategy and other documents by March 2027, "so that they are systematically taken into account during the development, implementation and use of any tools, training, programs, policies or guidelines aimed at deploying artificial intelligence across the public service."

There are moments when a government reveals more by what it does not say than by what it does. For Foreign Minister Anita Anand, that moment came last week after what happened aboard Flydubai Flight 1073. The flight was travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv on Sept. 30 with 174 passengers onboard. During the flight, the Omani co-pilot allegedly attacked and stabbed the Indian captain, Smit Machchhar. Because people acted, everyone aboard survived. So what did Canada’s foreign minister have to say? Anand expressed concern about the “incident” aboard a Flydubai flight “bound for Israel.” She spoke about the safety of “air passengers,” said she was relieved that everyone was safe and commended the “swift action and courage of those on board.” All true. But something was missing. The word “attack” was missing. So were “stabbing,” “hijacking,” “terrorism,” “Israelis” and, most strikingly, “Jews.”
