Construction company BAM announced on Thursday that it had purchased Geldermalsen-based pipelines company A.Hak for more than half a billion euros.

A.Hak specialises in underground infrastructure, including heat networks and transport pipelines.

BAM said in a press release that it had acquired the company to better position itself in the growing Dutch energy market.

The acquisition “complements our existing capabilities with specialist expertise in transport pipelines and trenchless techniques,” BAM CEO Ruud Joosten said in a statement.

The construction giant paid €504 million for the acquisition.

A.Hak operates primarily in the Netherlands but also in Belgium and the United Kingdom. It earned nearly €18 million in profits in 2025.

World.title: Alkmaar mayor defends ban on Israeli club’s fans at AZ match
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

The mayor of Alkmaar is facing scrutiny over her decision to bar all supporters of Israeli club Hapoel Be’er Sheva from a Europa League game set to be played against AZ at the city’s AFAS Stadium on October 15.

The decision was taken, mayor Anja Schouten said, to prevent public disorder in and around the city. It follows violence surrounding Maccabi Tel Aviv’s match against Ajax in Amsterdam in November 2024, which spurred Amsterdam mayor Femke Halsema to call on Alkmaar to prevent a similar situation.

Some local councillors criticised the decision in an emergency debate on Monday, NRC reported.

The Lawfare Project, a US-based pro-Israel legal group, told Dutch News it is examining possible legal action, arguing the ban is discriminatory.

Schouten told councillors last week the decision was based on public order, “not on political considerations”. Keeping groups apart was possible “with heavy deployment” around the stadium but “virtually impossible” elsewhere, particularly as visiting fans were expected to stay in Amsterdam hotels, she said.

Lawfare said that UEFA rates Hapoel’s supporters as only medium risk, and that if security cannot be guaranteed for them, then no one should be allowed to attend.

The ban is not on Israeli nationals, only on Hapoel ticket holders and on displays of support for the opposing club in the stadium, according to AZ. A spokesperson from AZ confirmed to Dutch News that no ticket sales had been made before the decision was taken.

Banning away fans from home games is common in Dutch football when authorities judge the risk too high.

In December 2024, Amsterdam barred Lazio fans from a Europa League match against Ajax over the risk of anti-Semitic and racist incidents. Enschede’s mayor reversed a similar ban on Besiktas supporters after the Turkish club called it discriminatory.

Schouten also barred Ajax fans from a cup match in January 2025 after hooligans stormed an AZ supporters’ café. UEFA normally requires clubs to offer 5% of tickets to visitors but generally accepts such bans, broadcaster NOS reported.

Dutch fans have often been on the receiving end of one-way bans. In October 2024, French authorities barred PSV fans from a Champions League match in Paris a week before kick-off, after 2,000 had already bought tickets.

Feyenoord supporters have been barred from several matches in Rome since riots in 2015 caused €8 million of damage in the Italian capital.

They were also kept out of Lille in January 2025 after a legal challenge failed at France’s highest administrative court.



Other tactics

Other host cities facing Hapoel this season have used different routes to avoid trouble.

Leuven’s mayor Mohamed Ridouani refused to host Union Saint-Gilloise’s match against the club “not even behind closed doors”, saying people could still flock to the stadium. The game will instead be played without spectators in Düsseldorf on October 22.

Turkish club Besiktas will play its home match against Hapoel in Batumi, Georgia, on November 26 with spectators present, club president Serdal Adalı said last week.

Of the three, only Alkmaar is keeping the match in its own stadium while excluding one set of fans.

World.title: Heavy showers usher in the autumn weather
World.content:
Thursday will continue to be wet after heavy rains on Wednesday evening, which have driven down temperatures across the country and ushered in the autumn weather.

The rain will continue throughout the day, and the west of the Netherlands will likely see thunderstorms.

Temperatures will reach highs of 15°, lower than usual for this time of year, according to the weather institute KNMI.

The sun will come out in most places in the afternoon but winds will keep the air chilly.

Friday will be cloudy with periods of heavy rain. The west will see highs of 17°, owing to warm ocean air. The rest of the country will only reach around 14°.

Autumn holidays for schools start at the weekend and the weather will be cloudy and cool. The north of the country is likely to see rain but the days will get drier as the weekend goes on. The highs will be between 15° and 19°.

World.title: Polish man suspected of helping Russian plot to assassinate Zelensky sentenced to 5.5 years
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A Polish man has been sentenced to five and a half years in prison for spying on behalf of Russia. The tasks assigned to him included reconnaissance of Rzeszów-Jasionka airport as part of a possible plan to assassinate Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky while he travelled through Poland. The sentence was handed down by the court of appeal in Lublin on Thursday, increasing by two years a jail term issued by a lower court earlier this year. The ruling is now final and binding. The 51-year-old former Polish soldier, who has been named only as Paweł K. under privacy law, was detained by Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW) in April 2024. Investigators found that the suspect had declared his willingness to collaborate with Russian intelligence and, between December 2022 and March 2024, had established contact via email and instant messaging with Russians involved in military operations against Ukraine, including army officers. Prosecutors determined that Paweł K. had been assigned tasks including gathering and transmitting information regarding security at Rzeszów airport, which is the main hub for goods and people being transported in and out of Ukraine. “These activities could have been used by Russian intelligence services, including in the context of planning a possible assassination attempt on the head of a foreign state, that is, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelensky,” wrote Poland’s National Prosecutor’s Office earlier this year. Poland and Ukraine have revealed further details of a foiled plan to assassinate @ZelenskyyUa at Poland's Rzeszów airport. A Polish man was last month indicted in relation to the incident, which he is accused of seeking to carry out on behalf of Russia https://t.co/Lrp99vH4s2 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 23, 2025 Last year, the head of the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) said that Paweł K. had been “recruited decades ago and firmly believed in the Soviet cause”. Polish prosecutors have not commented on that claim. However, they did find that the suspect had declared his willingness to join Russian “sabotage structures”, including the Wagner mercenary group and Unit 29155 of the GRU, Russia’s military intelligence agency, which is tasked with carrying out destabilisation activities. Paweł G. denied the accusations against him and claimed that he had actually been trying to help capture Russian war criminals by deceiving them into trusting him, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP). His defence attorney argued that the information Paweł G. had transmitted regarding Rzeszów airport was “trivial and publicly available”, according to news website Onet. In January this year, Paweł K. was found guilty of espionage and illegal possession of ammunition by the district court in the city of Zamość, which sentenced him to three and a half years in prison. However, prosecutors appealed against that ruling, arguing that the suspect deserved a longer jail term of seven and a half years. In a judgement issued on Thursday, the Lublin appeals court agreed that Paweł G’s initial sentence had been “grossly lenient” and increased it by two years, reports PAP. “Submitting an offer to work for…the intelligence service of a country that is at war with a country directly neighboring Poland, a country that is making quite extensive unfriendly gestures towards Poland, cannot be treated leniently,” said judge Artur Achrymowicz. Poland has charged three of its own citizens with working on behalf of Russian intelligence. They are accused of spreading disinformation, conducting reconnaissance of NATO troops, and undergoing firearms training in preparation for acts of sabotage https://t.co/maYd0kb9HW — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 20, 2026 Poland has become a primary target for acts of espionage, sabotage and disinformation conducted by operatives working on behalf of Russia. In many cases, they are so-called “disposable agents”: individuals already on the ground, often amateurs hired and paid through messaging apps such as Telegram, rather than professional spies or soldiers. The AWB last year launched 48 investigations related to espionage, more than twice as many as in 2024. Over those two years, there were more espionage investigations than over the previous three decades combined A report published earlier this year by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism found that Poland is the “primary focus” of Russia’s sabotage operations in Europe. Poland is the "primary focus" of Russia's sabotage campaign in Europe, finds a new report by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism. Among 151 incidents identified since 2022, 31 of them took place in Poland – more than in any other country https://t.co/QXfSI00FD6 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 3, 2026 In January, Polish prosecutors indicted five people – four Ukrainian citizens and one Russian – accused of carrying out a plot on behalf of Russia to plant explosives in packages that were then dispatched by courier services across Europe. In April, prosecutors charged a soldier from Poland’s Territorial Defence Force with seeking to spy on behalf of Russia. The following month, three Polish citizens were charged with working on behalf of Russian intelligence to spread disinformation and conduct reconnaissance of NATO troops. In July this year, a Russian married couple who had been studying in Poland were jailed for spying on behalf of Moscow and involvement in a plot to send a parcel bomb. World.title: Beavers destroy sign warning about beavers
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A sign installed to warn the public about damage caused by beavers has been destroyed by the beavers themselves, according to the Polish foresters who erected it. The incident was reported in a post on social media by the forestry district of Lubliniec in southern Poland, which shared photos of the sign, which read “Warning! Damage caused by beavers”. The wooden post it was displayed on had been destroyed in an apparent beaver attack. “We wanted to warn you about the potential consequences of beaver activity at the pond and the surrounding area – since beavers dig burrows under the road and fell trees near the pond – but the beavers didn’t want you to be warned, so…they cut down the oak post displaying the hazard notice,” wrote the foresters. “So, if you are around the pond, please exercise caution; and if you spot a piece of wood sticking out of the ground that has been gnawed by beavers, just imagine there was a sign there reading ‘Warning! Damage caused by beavers’.” Beavers were once almost hunted to extinction in Poland. By 1928, it was estimated that only 235 remained in the country. However, thanks to postwar efforts to reintroduce the animals into the Polish wilderness, the beaver population has grown and is currently estimated at around 150,000. Ecologists note that beavers play an important role in tackling drought by retaining water through the dams they build. Those dams also create “oases of biodiversity”, notes the state water agency PGW WP. However, the rodents can cause damage to roads, houses and farmland, which has led some to call for culls to keep beaver numbers down. World.title: One person killed in second school knife attack in Poland in two days
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. One person has been killed in a knife attack on a primary school carried out today by a 15-year-old former pupil. It comes just a day after another knife attack by a 19-year-old on a different school in Poland, which left eight people injured. The assailant was also carrying a homemade explosive device that failed to detonate. Meanwhile, police also announced today the arrest of a 17-year-old who had reportedly threatened to attack a school and was found to be in possession of knives. The developments have caused shock in Poland, a country where such violent incidents are normally rare. “We are seeing a radicalisation of young people,” warns the education minister, who has called for tougher controls on online content. W rękach Policji jest już 15-latek, który około godziny 9 wszedł do szkoły w miejscowości Leszczydół-Nowiny, w powiecie wyszkowskim i ostrym narzędziem ranił 3 pracowników placówki. Wśród rannych jest dyrektor, który ujął 15-latka. Policja była na miejscu już po kilku minutach od… pic.twitter.com/EV1RPP7LA5 — Policja Mazowsze (@PolicjaMazowsze) October 8, 2026 The latest attack took place in a primary school in the village of Leszczydół-Nowiny, around 60 km (37 miles) northeast of Warsaw, on Thursday morning. A 15-year-old former pupil of the school entered the facility and stabbed three members of staff, including the principal, who managed to subdue him. One of the victims, a 37-year-old female caretaker, died from her injuries. The other victim, a teacher, was hospitalised. The attacker was detained and will appear before a family court, reports the Gazeta Wyborcza daily. The incident comes just a day after another similar tragedy only 50 km away, in the town of Ostrołęka. On Wednesday morning, a 19-year-old attacked a vocational high school, leaving four students, two teachers and two bystanders injured before being captured. The assailant, who has been named only as Jakub Z. under Polish privacy law, is a student at the school. On Wednesday evening, national prosecutor Dariusz Korneluk told broadcaster TVN that the attacker had a homemade explosive in his backpack “that almost detonated”. “The backpack was already in the computer room and, only due to the responsible actions of the teacher and the students, was it thrown out of the window” after smoke had begun to billow out of it, he said. Justice minister Waldemar Żurek pledged that “prosecutors will ensure that the perpetrator answers for every blow inflicted and faces the legal consequences…There is no tolerance for violence in Polish schools”. Policjanci z Ostrołęki w pobliżu plaży miejskiej zatrzymali 19-letniego mężczyznę podejrzewanego o zaatakowanie ostrym narzędziem osób w pobliżu i na terenie szkoły w Ostrołęce. Ze wstępnych informacji wynika, że mogło dojść do zranienia 7 osób. Policjanci na miejscu wykonują… pic.twitter.com/cRzqMs36rD — Policja Mazowsze (@PolicjaMazowsze) October 7, 2026 On Thursday morning, around the same time as the attack in Leszczydół-Nowiny was unfolding, interior minister Marcin Kierwiński announced that a 17-year-old boy had been detained by police after threatening to attack another school. The suspect, who resides in the same Masovia province where Wednesday and Thursday’s attacks took place, “was found with two knives”, said Kierwiński, quoted by news website Interia. His internet history also showed that “he was looking for information on how to carry out this type of bloody act”, added the minister. The potential incident was prevented after fellow pupils reported to teachers that the suspect announced he wanted to “do something bad at school”. Last week, a 13-year-old was detained by police after telling a fellow online gamer that he was planning an attack on his school in the village of Książki, north-central Poland. He reportedly confessed to having killed cats and said that he wanted to attack random people with a cleaver in the school halls. Dzięki przytomnej reakcji uczniów, nauczyciela oraz błyskawicznej akcji policjantów z Sierpca powstrzymano 17-latka, który zapowiadał, że „zrobi coś złego w szkole”. Policjanci zatrzymali nastolatka i zabezpieczyli należące do niego noże, a w jego telefonie natrafiono na historię… pic.twitter.com/oUkwKbHmNr — Policja Mazowsze (@PolicjaMazowsze) October 8, 2026 The Polish authorities have recently warned of growing concern over radical ideas spreading among young people. Last month, the security services detained three teenagers accused of being part of online groups promoting neo-Nazism and violence. One was charged with planning an attack on a school and a mosque. Last year, a 19-year-old student was detained after it was determined he was planning an Islamic State-inspired attack on a Christmas market. In August, he was indicted to stand trial. In February, an 18-year-old was indicted over claims he planned to attack a school, also inspired by the Islamic State. Speaking on Wednesday, after the Ostrołęka incident but before today’s events, education minister Barbara Nowak warned that “we are seeing a radicalisation of young people”, reports the Onet news website. She called for “much greater control over what happens on the internet”. Earlier this year, Poland introduced a new law banning online content depicting illegal acts or other forms of abusive and degrading behaviour. The government is also working on measures to block children from social media and has banned the use of smartphones in schools. Poland’s state-owned National Development Bank (BGK) has announced the launch of the country’s first fund to support companies developing space technologies. Vinci Space Tech Fund will be worth 500 million zloty (€114 million), investing up to 100 million zloty each in 15-20 firms in the sector. The brainchild of finance minister Andrzej Domański, the fund aims to foster the growth of Polish space technologies and bolster the country’s technological independence. Kosmos to nie tylko gospodarka i innowacje. Kosmos to także bezpieczeństwo Polski. 🇵🇱 Dziś w Krakowie uruchamiamy pierwszy w Polsce fundusz dla sektora kosmicznego – Vinci Space Tech Fund. 500 mln zł na rozwój sektora @BGK_pl Vinci. Mamy ambitne spółki, znakomitych naukowców i… pic.twitter.com/NQBy8HYOcY — Andrzej Domański (@Domanski_Andrz) October 6, 2026 According to the growth and technology ministry, one of the fund’s strategic partners, BGK will invest between 10 and 100 million zloty in companies with a potential for rapid growth and expansion into international markets through its Vinci investment vehicle. The fund’s other partners are the Polish Space Agency and Kraków Technology Park (KTP), where the launch took place, along with ICEYE, a world-leading Finnish microsatellite manufacturer and operator co-founded by Pole Rafał Modrzewski. Announcing the fund, Domański highlighted the space sector’s role in responding to threats, protecting critical infrastructure, strengthening energy security and monitoring Poland and its surroundings. “The money from the Vinci fund is an investment in Poland’s capacity to build its own strong companies and develop competences that will be strategically significant for our economy and security,” he said. Warsaw has been chosen as the location for a new European Space Agency security centre, as Poland takes another step in its ambitions to become a bigger player in the space sector The facility will be the @esa's first outside its 11 founding member states https://t.co/WnHIbrW3ze — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 13, 2026 Mirosław Czekaj, president of the BGK management board, also noted that the development of the space industry would help “to build Poland’s technological sovereignty”, as one of the projects that are “vital to the Polish economy”. The fund is expected to invest in 15 to 20 companies, mainly Polish, although companies from elsewhere in Europe may also qualify if they have their main business operations in Poland, the ministry said. Its key investment areas include satellites, optics and Earth observation, satellite communications, electronics and photonics, rockets and propulsion systems, and artificial intelligence. In addition to funding, companies will benefit from advice and support from the fund’s partners. KPT, the city of Kraków and the Faculty of Space Technologies at AGH University are expected to provide much of the initiative’s academic, research and technical expertise. ICEYE, meanwhile, will share its experience of growing a space company and expanding into global markets. Last month, the company opened a satellite technology centre in Warsaw, and it plans to invest more than 120 million zloty in Poland by 2028, reports industry website Space News. Modrzewski said that raising capital in Poland was difficult when the company was founded 12 years ago, but that it has become easier as space has emerged as one of the country’s “strategic domains”. “The availability of capital in Poland will allow our companies to build their position on the global market without needing to leave the country at an early stage,” Modrzewski said, quoted by financial news site Bankier.pl. Vinci has previously invested in ICEYE as part of its private equity fund. Astronaut @astro_slawosz's recent trip to the International Space Station highlighted the Polish space industry's growing importance. Once limited to making components for others, Poland is now building its own spacecraft and participating in missions https://t.co/TmQiD91IzZ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 6, 2025 Poland’s space sector has expanded rapidly since the country joined the European Space Agency in 2012, moving from supplying components for foreign missions to developing its own satellites and space systems. A key milestone came in 2024 with the launch of EagleEye, Poland’s largest satellite, which was designed and built by a consortium of Polish companies and research institutions. In 2025, a Pole went to space for the second time in history, 50 years after the first Polish astronaut’s flight. The sector is now taking on larger international projects, while Russia’s war in Ukraine has highlighted the importance of domestic space capabilities for national security. In July this year, Warsaw was chosen as the location for a new European Space Agency centre focusing on civil security and resilience. World.title: Warsaw records EU’s highest employment rate
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The Warsaw region, which includes Poland’s capital and its suburbs, had the highest employment rate in the European Union last year, according to new Eurostat data. The employment rate among people aged 20-64 in the region stood at 86.9%, more than 10 percentage points above the figure for the EU as a whole. It was also the highest recorded for Warsaw since data began to be collected in 2013. Last year, only four EU regions had employment rates of at least 85%. Warsaw was followed by Prague in the Czech Republic at 86%, Finland’s Åland Islands at 85.5%, and Utrecht in the Netherlands at 85.4%. The EU average stood at 76.1%, slightly below the target of 78% the bloc set for itself for 2030. At the other end of the scale, 64 of the EU’s 244 regions had employment rates below 74% last year. The lowest was recorded in France’s overseas departments of Mayotte (36.9%) and French Guiana (50%), followed by Italy’s Calabria (50.3%), Campania (50.8%) and Sicily (51.4%). After Warsaw, the second-highest employment rate in Poland was recorded in the central Łódź province (80.8%) while the lowest was in the southeastern Subcarpathian province (73.2%). The figure for the country as a whole was 78.8%, which was only the 13th highest in the EU. In addition to topping the overall employment rate ranking, Warsaw also had the third lowest rate of youth employment (for people aged 15-29) at 3.9%, higher only than Yugozapaden in Bulgaria (3.8%) and Zeeland in the Netherlands (3.6%). And it had the third-highest rate of employment among people with tertiary education (93.5%), behind only Portugal’s Região Autónoma dos Açores (94.6%) and Yugozapaden (93.6%). Poland's unemployment rate of 2.6% in January is the lowest ever recorded in the country by @EU_Eurostat and was the joint-lowest that month among all EU member states For more, read our full report here: https://t.co/eP5A9JT4eg pic.twitter.com/A9oHu2zLZ6 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 7, 2025 The most recent Eurostat figures, from August, show that Poland’s unemployment rate (3.3%) was the second-lowest among all member states and well below the EU-wide figure of 6.2%. The strong labour market reflects years of economic growth, rising wages and increased employment. However, Poland’s ageing and shrinking population is creating labour shortages and encouraging companies to invest more heavily in automation. At the same time, job creation is slowing, while some industries – including manufacturing, automotive, furniture and construction materials – are coming under pressure, according to experts. World.title: Ukrainian refugees raised Poland’s GDP by 2.4% in 2025, finds UN study
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Ukrainian refugees boosted the size of Poland’s economy by 2.4% last year, the equivalent of 94 billion zloty (€21.5 billion), according to a new report by the UN refugee agency (UNHCR) and accounting firm Deloitte. The refugees’ level of employment has now also surpassed that of Polish citizens, but their growing presence in the labour market has had no negative impact on employment or wages for other workers, finds the study. “Refugees from Ukraine in Poland have entered a new phase characterised by deeper economic integration, increasing labour market participation, and a gradual transition from emergency support mechanisms towards long-term integration into public institutions,” wrote the UNHCR and Deloitte. 📉Facts matter. Refugees from Ukraine contributed 2.4% of Poland’s GDP in 2025, says new analysis by UNHCR and Deloitte. This is what happens when people forced to flee are given the opportunity to rebuild their lives with dignity. The full report: https://t.co/egUp8jjCwc pic.twitter.com/CSNONqdKGU — UNHCR Polska (@UNHCRPoland) October 1, 2026 The findings come in the latest edition of an annual report analysing the economic impact of Ukrainian refugees, almost one million of whom were living in Poland in 2025. Modelling carried out by Deloitte showed that their presence is having an increasingly positive effect: in 2025, Ukrainian refugees raised Poland’s GDP by 2.4%, compared to 2.3% in 2024, 2.0% in 2022 and 1.5% in 2022. Deloitte forecasts that the figure will rise to 2.8% by 2035 as Ukrainians integrate further. The company’s latest figures for 2023 and 2024 differ from those published in last year’s report, with Deloitte saying that it now uses a modelling strategy that is “similar to” but “improved” from before. The report also notes that the figure for 2025 likely understates the economic impact of Ukrainians who arrived in Poland as refugees, given that many – especially the most economically integrated – have shifted from refugee status to other forms of residency, meaning they do not count towards Deloitte’s data. The employment rate among Ukrainian refugees in Poland rose from 61% in 2023 to 76% in 2025. The latter figure was slightly higher than the rate among Polish citizens. However, the report notes that Ukrainian refugees are far more likely to be employed on a more precarious basis than native workers: only 42% have standard employment contracts, compared to 80% among Polish citizens. Ukrainian refugees also much more often work in positions they are overqualified for, while their median wage is only around 85% of the figure among all workers in Poland. Meanwhile, the report finds that, “contrary to concerns that a large increase in labour supply would negatively affect Polish workers, there is no evidence of deterioration in employment outcomes or wages”. In fact, employment among Polish citizens has continued to rise. The number of foreign workers in Poland rose 7.2% last year to reach 1.14 million. Immigrants now make up almost 7% of all workers. While Ukrainians remain by far the largest group, the fastest-growing nationalities last year were Colombians and Indians https://t.co/E0LNJXyyTx — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 9, 2026 Through their high levels of employment, Ukrainian refugees also contribute to Poland’s public finances via taxes and social security contributions. The report estimates that general government revenues are 2.6% higher because of refugee-related economic activity. Meanwhile, although “the arrival of refugees from Ukraine represented a major stress test for the Polish healthcare system…healthcare expenditures on refugees remain substantially lower on a per-capita basis than expenditures on Polish residents”. Indeed, in 2025, they paid around 2.8 billion zloty more in health-insurance contributions than the cost of the services they received. At the same time, Poland’s understaffed hospitals have been boosted by the arrival of thousands of Ukrainian doctors, dentists, nurses and midwives. Ukrainians do have access to Polish social benefits, such as grants for children, but these account for only 10% of income in Ukrainian refugee households. The vast majority, 87%, is earned through work. Ukrainian immigrants pay more in taxes than they receive in benefits, a report by Poland's National Development Bank has concluded. The research also indicated that Ukrainians contribute between 0.5% and 2.4% to Poland's annual GDP growth https://t.co/KhXxLtif5W — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 15, 2025 The report notes that the status of Ukrainian refugees in Poland is becoming increasingly normalised, pointing to changes in Polish government policy introduced earlier this year that meant they no longer had special status. Meanwhile, surveys show a weakening of refugees’ intentions to eventually return to Ukraine. Research by the National Bank of Poland (NBP) found that the proportion who plan to settle permanently in Poland rose from 21% to 25% between 2024 and 2025. However, UNHRC’s report also highlights the negative shift in attitudes towards Ukrainian refugees in recent months, with a July poll showing for the first time that a majority of Poles are opposed to accepting refugees from Ukraine. Poland will examine whether Paramount Skydance can take control of TVN, one of the country’s leading broadcasters, following its acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, which owns TVN. The review is being conducted under a law that requires state approval for ownership changes of companies designated by the government as strategic and protected from takeovers deemed to threaten the national interest. TVN was added to the list in 2024, following reports of its possible sale. Minister Aktywów Państwowych zajmie się przejęciem TVN przez grupę Paramount Skydance#PAPinformacjehttps://t.co/FxxDnozx9i — Polska Agencja Prasowa/Polish Press Agency (PAP) (@PAPinformacje) October 6, 2026 Paramount Skydance’s $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, one of the largest mergers in the global media market, brings together major US media assets including Paramount’s CBS and MTV and Warner’s HBO, CNN and Discovery Channel. After the deal was completed on Tuesday, Poland’s state assets ministry told the Polish Press Agency (PAP) that, because the acquisition would give Paramount Skydance indirect control of TVN, the new owner must notify the ministry of the takeover. The ministry then has 90 days to “conduct an administrative investigation into this matter to verify the impact of the transaction on security or public order in Poland”. The ministry can either approve the change of ownership or block the new owner from controlling TVN. In the latter case, the state assets minister, Wojciech Balczun, may order the sale of TVN’s shares. “I assure you that it will be an entirely substantive and objective administrative procedure, carried out in fulfilment of a statutory obligation, and nothing more,” Balczun told broadcaster Kanał Zero on Tuesday. The procedure is necessary because the Polish government added TVN and another large private broadcaster, Polsat, to its list of strategic companies in December 2024, bringing them under state protection against takeovers considered aggressive or contrary to the national interest. That move came amid reports that Warner Bros. Discovery was considering selling TVN and that a businessman linked to Hungary’s then-Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, an ally of Poland’s conservative opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party, was seeking to buy it. 🎙️Minister @wbalczun w @OficjalneZero o przeprowadzeniu postępowania ws. przejęcia TVN przez grupę Paramount Skydance: bardziej bym skupił się na organie, czyli ministrze aktywów państwowych. To jest odpersonalizowana procedura administracyjna, która wynika z ustawy o kontroli… pic.twitter.com/jp3J9zC0jh — Ministerstwo Aktywów Państwowych 🇵🇱 (@MAPGOVPL) October 7, 2026 Prime Minister Donald Tusk said at the time the move was intended to protect the broadcaster from hostile foreign takeovers and prevent foreign interference in Poland’s media and elections. TVN, which was originally founded in 1995, has been in American hands since 2015, when it was bought by US broadcaster Scripps, which was in turn acquired by Discovery in 2018. The station, which is known for taking a liberal position on many issues, has long been a target for Polish conservatives. In 2021, the then-PiS government passed a law that would have forced Warner Bros. Discovery to sell its majority stake. However, that was vetoed by then-President Andrzej Duda. Poland is adding the country’s two largest private TV stations, Polsat and TVN, to its list of “strategic companies” under special protection. That allows the government to block the sale of the firms to owners from “hostile states”, says PM @donaldtusk https://t.co/TwK9IFRPrs — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 11, 2024 Some in Poland have expressed fear that Paramount could push TVN in a more conservative direction, as it has been accused of doing with other media outlets it has acquired, notably US broadcaster CBS. Paramount’s owner, David Ellison, is a Trump ally, as are PiS and Poland’s current president, Karol Nawrocki. On Sunday, the Journalists’ Association, a Polish organisation representing journalists, called on TVN’s management to establish an editorial independence council similar to those being created at CNN and CBS under the settlement deal that paved the way for the merger in the US. Media reports claim that President Trump tried to persuade Poland's defence minister to leave the government and form a coalition with the right-wing opposition. We outline what is known so far and how the government, including PM @donaldtusk, has reacted https://t.co/m04H8VgoSF — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 5, 2026 In July, Reporters Without Borders (RSF) also raised concerns about the potential impact of the merger on TVN’s editorial independence, citing the new ownership structure and the risk of political interference. The NGO called for guarantees protecting the channel as a condition of approval for the takeover from the European Commission. The EU executive, however, approved the deal in July without imposing such conditions, following an antitrust review. The commission’s approval covered the entire European Union, meaning that national competition authorities have no grounds to challenge the deal, Tomasz Chróstny, head of Poland’s consumer protection authority UOKiK, told news service Wirtualna Polska before the transaction was completed. World.title: Poland launches new combat uniforms, including first designed for female soldiers
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has launched new combat uniforms for its army. It is the first time that the designs have been updated in 33 years, and also the first time that they include a version specially created for women, who now make up around 16% of soldiers. “A soldier’s safety and comfort during service are paramount,” said defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, announcing the new uniforms, which have been undergoing testing by various branches of the military, “[They are] adapted to the needs of women and men serving in the Polish army, because both deserve not only respect and gratitude, but also the creation of conditions that will encourage service as much as possible,” he added. The new tactical uniform features new camouflage patterns that are intended to better reflect the colours and shadows found in natural environments, “allowing the soldier to remain invisible for as long as possible”. According to the armed forces, testing shows it provides 30% better camouflage effectiveness. The defence ministry says that the outfits, which will be produced completely in Poland, are created from “lighter, more flexible and durable materials” than before. The women’s version features a more “closely fitted shape” with a “choice of tops and bottoms to suit women’s figures”, allowing “greater freedom of movement”. Wreszcie mamy mundur dedykowany dla kobiet – żołnierzy! Dzisiaj w polskiej armii 16% żołnierzy to kobiety, a Wojskach Obrony Terytorialnej to ponad 20%. Nie pozwolę nikomu obrażać i zbijać kapitału politycznego na tym, że próbuje się dyskredytować kobiety w mundurach.… pic.twitter.com/GzJOhkwgTO — Magdalena Sobkowiak (@magdasobkowiak) October 5, 2026 “For the first time in the history of the Polish military, female soldiers will no longer have to choose the size that fits them from men’s uniforms,” said deputy defence minister Magdalena Sobkowiak. She noted that women now make up 16% of soldiers in the army, and as much as 20% of those serving in the Territorial Defence Force (WOT), a volunteer reserve formation. Kosiniak-Kamysz says that the new uniforms, which cost around 1,000 zloty (€228) each, will be rolled out gradually, with 7,500 delivered this year. The defence ministry recently signed an agreement with logistics giant InPost to use its parcel lockers to deliver uniforms to soldiers. Poland has dramatically increased the size of its armed forces in recent years. NATO figures show that the number of Polish military personnel has risen from 101,600 in 2016 to an estimated 263,600 this year. That means Poland now has the alliance’s largest armed forces in continental Europe, ahead of France (202,000), Italy (191,600) and Germany (183,200). In NATO as a whole, only the United States (1.3 million) and Turkey (395,800) have more military personnel. Meanwhile, both the number and proportion of women serving in the armed forces have increased dramatically. In 2015, there were only 4,000 professional female soldiers in Poland, a number that has now risen to almost 37,000. Poland has NATO’s third-largest military and the alliance’s largest in Europe, new figures show. For more, see our full report here: https://t.co/QBBVQ9cqzS pic.twitter.com/TA34KQrJ4k — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 16, 2024 “Women soldiers contribute significant value to the functioning of the armed forces,” said General Wiesław Kukuła, chief of the general staff of the Polish armed forces, earlier this year. “They successfully perform not only support tasks, but increasingly often stand alongside male soldiers in strictly combat roles,” he added. “They pilot aircraft and helicopters, serve on ships, operate missile systems, and serve in special units.” “Their service is guided by the overarching principle that it is not gender, but physical attributes, competence and determination that define a soldier ready to succeed.” Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Prague 7 Turns Streets Into Outdoor Art With Designs by Local Children
World.content:
Prague 7 has transformed several streets around local schools with large-scale colorful paintings created with the help of local schoolchildren.

The new artwork can be seen on Rajská, Plynární, Jablonského and Antonínská streets, as well as part of Bubenská Street. The municipality placed the designs mainly near schools and along busy pedestrian routes.



On Antonínská Street, students from grades five through eight at Strossmayerovo Square Elementary School helped create the artwork. They produced the original drawings, which artist Jakub Karlík then combined into the final design.

Several other educational institutions are located close to the painted streets, including Bratrská Elementary School, the Holešovice Business Academy, the Higher Vocational School of Fashion Design and the Secondary Industrial School of Fashion Design.

The new designs have received mostly positive reactions from local residents. Comments on Prague 7’s Facebook page described the streets as more cheerful and said the artwork had made the area more interesting.

There has also been criticism, particularly over the cost and the practical impact of painting the asphalt. Some residents questioned whether the project was necessary and raised concerns about the roughness of the surface, pedestrian movement and whether the paint could become slippery.

Prague 7 said anti-slip paint was used, similar to materials applied to cycle paths and sports surfaces.

The project cost 755,000 CZK, covering the designs, preparation, materials and application. According to Prague 7 spokesperson Martin Vokuš, each of the two phases took around 20 days.

The municipality awarded the contract directly to Karlík. Before selecting his proposal for the Antonínská and Bubenská sections, Prague 7 compared three offers and chose his as the most advantageous.

World.title: Beer Consumption in Czech Republic Falls to Lowest Level on Record
World.content:
Czech beer consumption fell to its lowest level on record in 2025, with the average resident drinking 121 liters during the year, according to data from the Czech Association of Breweries and Malt Houses (ČSPS).

Total domestic consumption reached 14.86 million hectoliters, down 3.2% from 2024. The figure is the lowest recorded since nationwide beer consumption statistics began.

Overall beer production in the Czech Republic also declined last year. Breweries produced 19.96 million hectoliters of alcoholic and non-alcoholic beer, 4.3% less than in 2024.



The decline affected nearly every category, with non-alcoholic beer the main exception. Production of non-alcoholic and flavored non-alcoholic beer increased by 4% to 1.68 million hectoliters.

Demand for non-alcoholic beer has been rising steadily for more than a decade. Between 2019 and 2024 alone, production increased by around 50%.

Pubs lose ground as more Czechs drink at home

The shift in drinking habits is particularly visible in restaurants and pubs. Draft beer accounted for 28% of beer sold on the Czech market in 2025, down one percentage point from the previous year.

The longer-term decline is more significant. Draft beer represented 35% of sales in 2019 and 51% in 2008.

The ČSPS said the figures reflect changes in consumer behavior, including greater interest in moderation and healthier lifestyles. When Czechs do go out for beer, they are increasingly looking for quality and variety rather than simply drinking larger quantities.

Czech beer exports also decline

Exports followed the domestic market downward. Czech breweries exported 5.48 million hectoliters of beer in 2025, an 8.2% decrease compared with the previous year.

European Union countries accounted for around 90% of Czech beer exports, with Germany and Slovakia among the largest buyers.

Imports also declined, falling by 18.3% year on year. Foreign beer accounted for only 2.5% of total beer consumption in the Czech Republic, down 0.5 percentage points from 2024.

World.title: Nearly Half of Czechs Spend More Than 30% of Their Income on Housing
World.content:
Nearly half of people in the Czech Republic spend more than 30% of their net income on housing, while around one in 10 spends more than half.

Housing is generally considered financially burdensome when rent, utilities and other related costs exceed 30–40% of household income. The EU average is around 24%.



The findings come from a survey by Česká spořitelna and Evropa v datech, conducted with Ipsos among 1,000 respondents in February.

Housing affordability remains particularly difficult for young Czechs. Among people aged 18 to 29, 58% live with their parents at least part of the time, while 29% live with friends or a partner.

The survey found that 60% of people under 30 who are dissatisfied with their housing situation have postponed a major life decision because of it. For around one-third, this has happened repeatedly. Starting a family is among the decisions affected by housing conditions.

Homeowners were considerably more likely to be very satisfied than renters, with 41% of owners describing themselves as very satisfied compared with 18% of renters.

Czechia still has the least affordable housing in the EU

The Czech Republic improved by six places in this year’s housing conditions ranking, reaching 17th among the 27 EU member states. The improvement was linked to increased investment in residential construction, fewer households facing excessive housing costs or difficulties paying for heating, and relatively favorable rental conditions.

Buying a home, however, remains more difficult than elsewhere in the EU.

An average-sized Czech apartment costs 13.3 average annual gross salaries, compared with 13.6 a year earlier. The figure has improved only slightly, while other countries have made faster progress. In Hungary, the ratio fell from 13.6 to 11.9 annual salaries, while Slovakia improved from 13.2 to 11.7 and Slovenia from 13.4 to 11.4.

Ireland has the most affordable housing by this measure, with an average home costing 6.2 annual salaries, followed by Belgium and Finland.

An average apartment in Czechia costs roughly the equivalent of 29 years of average rent. In city centers, the figure is close to 31 years, compared with less than 13 years in Ireland.

High housing costs are changing household decisions

Housing expenses are also forcing some households to reduce other spending. Last year, 40% cut their budgets because of housing costs. Nearly one-quarter reduced spending on holidays, hobbies and entertainment, while 16% cut spending on essentials such as food, clothing and personal-care products.

Around 38% of Czechs see living with parents as an economic necessity caused by high property prices. Another 26% consider it a reasonable temporary solution, while 9.4% see multigenerational living as a viable long-term model.

At the same time, 46% of young people expect to inherit property from their families.

World.title: Famous Dancing House Photo Spot in Prague Is Set for a Major Makeover
World.content:
Jiráskovo Square in Prague is set for a major redesign that will change one of the city’s best-known photo spots near the Dancing House.

The project, estimated to cost around CZK 35 million, will replace part of the damaged lawn with paving, restore a historic fountain and move the monument to writer Alois Jirásek.



The Prague 2 district plans to carry out the transformation over the next two years. The redesign is based on a 2022 study prepared by archiF studio.

The square’s lawn has long been a problem. Its location directly opposite the Dancing House makes it a popular stopping point for tourists, many of whom step onto the grass to take photographs with the distinctive building in the background.

One of the most common poses involves visitors appearing to support the Dancing House with their foot or kick it. The repeated foot traffic has left the grass heavily damaged, despite attempts to restore it.

Under the new plans, part of the lawn will be replaced with a paved surface. This will create a more durable area for visitors to take photographs while reducing pressure on the remaining greenery.

Historic fountain to return to operation

The redesign will also restore the Cubist fountain created by architect Vlastislav Hofman. The area around the fountain will be repaved, while the fountain itself will be returned to its original appearance and function.

Water is expected to flow through the fountain again after decades.

Architect Soňa Formanová, one of the project’s authors, said the team was able to locate Hofman’s original documentation, including plans covering the fountain and the approaches to the nearby bridge.

The project will also introduce a raised edge around the lawn that can be used for seating. New flowerbeds and trees are planned for the northern part of the square, while existing shrubs considered unsuitable for the area will be removed.

The monument to Alois Jirásek, the Czech writer after whom the square is named, will be relocated to the center of the small park.

World.title: Queer Arts Festival PINKBUS Returns With New Performances and International Guests
World.content:
The PINKBUS Festival will return to Prague on November 3-14 with several days of theatre, dance, drag, music, visual art and performance.

This year’s edition, titled Forward March!, will focus on the need to keep moving forward amid an uncertain social and political climate.

Organised by the PINKBUS queer arts platform, the festival aims to create a space for artists and audiences to meet, experiment and share experiences. The programme combines established artists with new projects and will also mark the beginning of a new season for the platform.



One of the highlights of this year’s festival will be the premiere of two original works developed through the PINKBUS open call First Ride.

Richard Eliáš, an Academy of Arts, Architecture and Design in Prague (AVU) student, will present the interdisciplinary drag fantasy I Guess It’s Kind of My Fault, or What?. The second project, by the performative art collective Izbová teplota & Alejandra, is Štúrovci Went to Devín and Had Some Fun, offering a new and unconventional take on the group of Slovak national revival figures known as the Štúrovci.

The festival will also feature international guests. French artists Nicolas Poggi and Giselle Hauscarriaga will present SUDOR (Sweat), a Czech premiere performed with a local cast. The post-performative work explores physical exhaustion, sweat and the limits of the body.

Another premiere, Lipsync Her Name… Because It’s Precious, is being created in collaboration with the Italian festival RAINBOW.IT and Slovak organisation DRAMA QUEER. The performance focuses on three figures from European LGBTQIA+ history: Lucy Salani, Romina Cecconi and Ota Tasinata.

Directed by Tomáš “Grófka” Procházka, the production combines three monodramatic sketches exploring identity and the determination to remain true to oneself. The cast includes Italian actor Antonello Foddis and his drag alter ego La Trave Nell’Okkio, as well as Czech performer Venice, also known as Martin Talaga.

The programme will also include the PINKPANEL discussion series. This year’s edition, titled (The Tinsmith’s) Hammer Against Queerness, will examine the potential impact of current cultural policy on LGBTQIA+ artistic production and discuss possible forms of resistance.

The festival will conclude with a special BEST OF edition of the PINKBUS variety show, featuring Venice, Just Karen, La Cuntessa, Tonic Garbáge, Helena Araujo and other performers, alongside special guests.

World.title: Roger Waters Brings New Pink Floyd Show to Prague in June 2027
World.content:
Roger Waters will bring a new Pink Floyd concert production to Prague next year, with LEGACY – A Pink Floyd Show scheduled for June 8, 2027, at O2 universum.

The new production has been created under Waters’ direction and will feature a ten-piece band led by his son, Harry Waters. The Prague show will focus on music from what is widely regarded as Pink Floyd’s most influential period, spanning 1971 to 1979.



The setlist will draw from four of the band’s best-known albums: The Dark Side of the Moon, Wish You Were Here, Animals and The Wall.

The music will be accompanied by a new visual production featuring high-resolution LED screens and imagery inspired by Pink Floyd’s original artwork and stage concepts.

Harry Waters will serve as the show’s musical director, performing on Hammond B3 organ and piano while also contributing vocals. He has a long history with the band’s music and spent more than 15 years performing alongside his father on major tours, including The Dark Side of the Moon and The Wall.

His connection to Pink Floyd goes back even further. As a child, Harry’s voice appeared on “Goodbye Blue Sky” from The Wall. He also saw the original The Wall concert production at a young age.

The band includes drummer Graham Broad, guitarist Edo Scordo, bassist and backing vocalist Dahniel Knight, saxophonist and multi-instrumentalist Ryan Saranich, keyboardist Matt Riddle, lead vocalist Clifton David Broadbridge and backing vocalists Eva Avila and Genevieve Little.

Roger Waters co-founded Pink Floyd in 1965 and became the band’s principal lyricist and conceptual leader following Syd Barrett’s departure. He played a central role in the creation of albums including The Dark Side of the Moon, Wish You Were Here, Animals and The Wall.

Ticket prices start at 1,600 CZK

Live Nation Club and O2 presale starts October 8, 2026, at 10:00 AM

World.title: GALLERY: Vltava Philharmonic Reveals Its Interiors for the First Time
World.content:
Prague’s planned Vltava Philharmonic has offered the first detailed look inside the building, releasing visualizations of its main foyer and the spaces serving its three principal concert halls.

The interior design will combine wood, glass and stone, with flowing shapes inspired by the Vltava River and the building’s distinctive sloping roof. The plans also emphasize open public spaces designed to connect the concert halls with the rest of the building.



The main foyer will be dominated by a large glass wall extending across several floors. Its curved geometry is intended to echo the movement of the Vltava and will separate the open foyer from other areas of the building.

Light-colored solid wood panels will cover the ceilings, following the contours of the roof above. Stone elements will be used in areas connecting the public foyer with the foyer of the main concert hall, including spaces designed for both seating and standing around bar counters.

´

The project has become significantly more expensive

The cost of the Vltava Philharmonic has increased sharply since the project was first estimated.

In 2021, the projected construction cost was CZK 6.1 billion. After the Danish architecture studio Bjarke Ingels Group (BIG) won the international competition in 2022, the estimate rose to CZK 9.4 billion.

A more detailed architectural study completed in 2024 put the figure at CZK 11.65 billion. The latest estimate is CZK 11.98 billion for the building itself.

Once improvements to the surrounding area are included, the overall project is expected to cost almost CZK 17 billion.

Construction could begin in 2028

The city expects to obtain the permit in the first quarter of 2027. A general contractor would then be selected, with construction currently scheduled to start in the first quarter of 2028.

Trial operations are planned to begin in 2033.

The Vltava Philharmonic will occupy three underground and six above-ground floors. In addition to five concert halls, the complex will include facilities for the Czech Philharmonic and the Prague Symphony Orchestra (FOK), a music department operated by the Municipal Library of Prague, a creative hub, a restaurant and publicly accessible terraces.

The building is being designed by Bjarke Ingels Group, whose proposal was selected in the international architectural competition in 2022.

World.title: Up to 80 Startups to Pitch Investors at Prague’s Engaged Investments Conference
World.content:
The international Engaged Investments conference, taking place on October 21 and 22, 2026, is significantly expanding its scope this year.

The event, which brings hundreds of startup investors from all over Europe to Prague, is now fully opening its doors to tech founders and the broader innovation ecosystem.



Alongside the main program, the two-day event will feature two specialized industry tracks focusing on fintech and defense, pitches from up to 80 startups, and an extended accompanying program.

Real defense instead of geopolitical theories

The defense track is being organized in collaboration with the Invest in Bravery initiative, which is deeply involved in the Ukrainian ecosystem, alongside the European EUDIS Matchmaking program for defense and Cassini Matchmaking for space technologies.

A special guest will be Senior Lieutenant Mykyta Puz, Defense Industry Liaison Officer of the Azov Brigade of the National Guard of Ukraine. He previously worked in business and AI product management before volunteering for the front lines in 2024.

He will shed light on what a modern army truly and urgently needs from the defense industry. Alongside him, speakers will include Erin Hallock, Managing Partner of the NATO Innovation Fund, a representative of the renowned Ukrainian fund Brave1, and others.

Fintech that solves business, not theory

The UnBundled Fintech track, which will run throughout the second day of the conference, is being prepared by The FinTechers in collaboration with Mastercard. The goal is to connect the traditional banking sector with technology companies and investors. The program will focus on stablecoins and tokenization, operational resilience of banks, liability for fraudulent payments, and the deployment of artificial intelligence in financial services.

In addition to new technologies, it will address what European companies need to grow into global players without relying on American capital and infrastructure.

Speakers will include Michal Vodrážka, Director of the Payment Systems Regulation Division at the Czech National Bank. In a debate with Jiří Raška, Chief Technology Officer of Partners Banka, he’ll raise the question of who takes the hit when a payment ends up in a fraudster’s hands. It’s a timely topic, with mandatory payee verification coming in 2027.

The block dedicated to stablecoins and new financial infrastructure will be opened by Dorothea Ysenburg, Vice President of Global Partnerships for Digital Assets and Blockchain at Mastercard. Maryna Muntian from J.P. Morgan will also present, discussing why Central European banks and investors still lack mutual trust when looking at the same deals.

A place where startups find real investors

Closing investments is one of the core components of the conference, which last year attracted investors from more than 20 countries. Up to 80 selected startups, ranging from early-stage to Series A, will have the opportunity to pitch their companies in three minutes to investors actively investing in their respective segments. This year will introduce new dedicated pitching blocks for startups in the fields of financial technology, defense, and space.

On October 22, the best fintech projects from the two-day “Coding the Future of Finance” hackathon—organized on October 19 and 20 by The FinTechers together with Deloitte, AWS, and other partners—will also be presented to investors.

World.title: Orbán-era oligarchs reportedly seek immunity deals as corruption arrests grow
World.content:
Some members of Hungary’s former economic elite are reportedly looking to make deals with the new Tisza government, with one wealthy oligarch allegedly offering to return assets and money in exchange for protection from prosecution.

Oligarch reportedly offers assets in exchange for immunity

Some members of the economic elite associated with the former Orbán era are already seeking ways to reach an agreement with Hungary’s new government as several prominent figures face criminal investigations and arrests, according to the latest edition of the VSquare newsletter Goulash.

A senior member of the Tisza government told VSquare that one unnamed, wealthy and influential oligarch has reportedly been sending messages to the government through intermediaries. According to the source, the businessman would be prepared to return assets and money in exchange for immunity from prosecution.

The source did not identify the oligarch or specify the amount of money or assets allegedly involved. It is also unclear whether the government led by Prime Minister Péter Magyar is willing to consider such an arrangement.

Never miss a headline: join our Messenger group!

Another oligarch reportedly chooses a different strategy

According to the same source, another member of the former economic elite has chosen a different approach. Rather than attempting to negotiate immunity, the oligarch is reportedly keeping a low profile, returning whatever the government demands and trying to remain in business through bids from foreign subcontractors.

The source compared this strategy to that previously used by Austrian construction company Strabag, which operated while being placed on a blacklist by the previous Orbán government. The reports come amid a series of high-profile arrests involving figures linked to Hungary’s former political and economic establishment.

High-profile arrests shake former elite

In September, Dániel Jellinek, Hungary’s seventh-richest person and CEO of property company Indotek, was detained together with former state asset manager chief Norbert Szivek over alleged bribery linked to public transport bus purchases.

A court ordered Jellinek to remain in pre-trial detention for a month. His company has denied wrongdoing on his behalf, and the detention order is under appeal.

Two weeks later, former ministers Balázs Hankó and Miklós Seszták were arrested within hours of Parliament lifting their immunity. Courts subsequently ordered 30 days of detention for both men in separate corruption-related cases.

The arrests have contributed to growing uncertainty among members of the economic elite who built their fortunes or political connections during the previous governing era.

Will the new government make deals?

The VSquare source said it remains unclear how willing Magyar’s government will be to negotiate with former oligarchs and potentially spare them from prosecution in exchange for the return of assets. Any such agreements would raise significant questions about accountability and the treatment of wealth accumulated during the previous political era.

World.title: Wizz Air cancels several Eastern flights for the entire winter season
World.content:
Wizz Air has scrapped its planned winter return to Abu Dhabi and Dubai, citing ongoing airspace restrictions that have made the routes commercially unviable.

Wizz Air postpones Middle East return

Wizz Air will not resume its planned flights to Abu Dhabi and Dubai this winter after cancelling all services to and from the two UAE destinations for the season. The airline had originally planned to operate the routes between 25 October and 27 March, following an earlier announcement that it would return to the UAE alongside services to Jeddah in Saudi Arabia and Amman in Jordan.

The latest decision comes just days after Wizz Air initially announced that some Abu Dhabi routes would be postponed until January following updated safety guidance from Europe’s aviation regulator. The airline has now cancelled the Abu Dhabi and Dubai services for the entire winter season.

Longer routes make flights too expensive

Wizz Air said the decision was prompted by regional airspace restrictions that were extended on 30 September. The restrictions mean aircraft would have to take significantly longer routes to reach their destinations, increasing both flight times and operating costs.

According to the airline, the resulting costs make operating the routes commercially unviable under current conditions, including with its Airbus A321neo and A321XLR aircraft.

“We regret the disruption to travel plans and will continue to monitor developments, reassessing operations as safety guidance and operating conditions evolve,” Wizz Air said in a statement to The National.

The airline also confirmed that its planned flights to and from Amman are affected by the latest conflict-zone guidance from the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA), which recommends that airlines do not operate within Jordanian airspace.

Have you heard? Wizz Air rethink could reshape ticket prices and routes across Europe

Wizz Air had planned a major Middle East comeback

The cancelled UAE services were part of a much bigger planned return to the Middle East. For the winter season, Wizz Air had announced plans for 12 routes and 49 weekly flights connecting nine European cities with destinations in the UAE, Saudi Arabia and Jordan.

The planned network would have offered around 470,000 seats across the three countries. Wizz Air had suspended its European-operated Middle East services in late February following the escalation of the regional conflict.

The planned return came after the airline’s low-cost subsidiary Wizz Air Abu Dhabi ceased operations in September 2025. The continuing airspace restrictions have also forced other international airlines to adjust their schedules and routes across the region.

For passengers who had been planning to fly Wizz Air to Abu Dhabi or Dubai this winter, the latest announcement means the airline’s much-anticipated return will have to wait.
