World.title: UN Human Rights Council adopts resolution on Georgia’s occupied territories
World.content:
UNHRC resolution on Georgia’s occupied territories

On 7 October, the UN Human Rights Council adopted a resolution in Geneva concerning Georgia‘s occupied regions.

According to Georgia’s Foreign Ministry, the resolution, entitled “Cooperation with Georgia”, addresses the human rights situation in Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region (South Ossetia).

The UN Human Rights Council calls for unhindered access to the occupied territories for the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, as well as international and regional human rights mechanisms.

The resolution also condemns Russia’s actions aimed at annexing Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region, and reaffirms support for Georgia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity within its internationally recognised borders.

It expresses concern over discrimination and human rights violations against ethnic Georgians in the Russian-occupied regions.

The document also highlights the importance of the Geneva International Discussions, established under the ceasefire agreement of 12 August 2008.

The resolution, submitted by Georgia, was adopted by consensus, as it was last year.

World.title: ‘No right to enter classroom’: Teacher beats pupil at Armenian school
World.content:
Teacher beats pupil at school in Armenia

A video showing a teacher beating a second-grade pupil at a school in the Armenian village of Vardadzor has shocked people across Armenia. A relative of the girl told journalists that she was so frightened by the incident that she had refused to return to school.

The girl’s parents appealed to the Gegharkunik regional administration, demanding that the teacher be dismissed. However, they were told that this would only be possible if complaints were filed by at least seven parents.

Social media users responding to the video called on the Interior Ministry to investigate the incident and launch criminal proceedings.

The Education Ministry said it had contacted the Interior Ministry, the Education Inspectorate and the National Centre for Educational and Psychological Support to ensure a thorough investigation.

“Relevant legal procedures will begin shortly to strip this teacher of the right to teach,” the ministry said.

Armenia’s Human Rights Defender, Anahit Manasyan, described the violence against the schoolgirl as “unacceptable and deeply concerning”.

The Investigative Committee opened a criminal case over allegations of “inflicting severe physical pain or serious mental suffering on a minor”.

By the time of publication, reports had emerged that the teacher had been detained.

What happened

A relative of the second-grade pupil told Shamshyan.com that the class teacher had first beaten the girl in the classroom. The violence continued in the corridor after the pupil left the classroom. The girl returned home with swollen eyes and marks from the blows on her neck and arms.

“There had been slaps before, but never beatings like this – with hands and a pointer,” the relative said.

The girl has not attended school since the incident. According to family members, she later encountered the teacher by chance in the street and ran home in terror.

The girl’s mother said she did not want the teacher to face criminal prosecution but insisted that she be dismissed.

Armenian media reported that the incident was discussed at the school the following day.

“The teacher admits her guilt. She submitted a written statement acknowledging what she had done and asked not to be punished. As a result, I issued her a written reprimand,” school headteacher Gevorg Nersesyan said.

He also said such incidents were unacceptable and expressed surprise that a teacher with 30 years of experience could have treated a second-grade pupil in this way.

‘Schools must be a safe environment for children’

Armenia’s Human Rights Defender, Anahit Manasyan, stressed that schools must provide a safe environment for children.

“Any form of violence against a child or any other form of inappropriate treatment is fundamentally incompatible with respect for the child’s dignity, safety and rights,” she said.

According to Manasyan, children must be protected not only through responses to individual incidents, but also through effective measures to prevent and address potential cases of violence.

Manasyan also questioned the effectiveness of mechanisms designed to protect pupils in schools, particularly the work of pupil protection groups.

“The effectiveness of these mechanisms should be assessed primarily on the basis of how they work in practice,” she said.

Pupil protection groups were established in all schools on 1 September 2026 by order of the Minister of Education, Science, Culture and Sport. They were specifically set up to prevent violence, bullying and other high-risk situations. Following the incident at the school in Vardadzor, the pupil protection group held a meeting. However, according to the girl’s relatives, no steps were taken to help her return to school.

The Office of the Human Rights Defender said it had launched an investigation into the incident.

Not the first case of violence since start of school year

Two weeks ago, a maths teacher at a school in the village of Berdavan in Armenia’s Tavush region slapped a 13-year-old boy across the face. He also pushed the pupil, forcibly made him sit at his desk and hit him on the head with a notebook, striking the child’s eye with its edge.

According to the boy’s mother, the teacher’s wife, who is the school’s deputy headteacher, also treated him harshly. She slapped him across the face, pushed him into her office and made him stand in the corner.

Although the boy continues to attend school, his mother told journalists that he had been left psychologically distressed by the incident.

The teacher has also been charged with “inflicting severe physical pain or serious mental suffering on a minor”. He has been released on an undertaking not to leave the country and suspended from his duties.

Social media reactions

“A written reprimand is not enough. A teacher like this should be barred from working in education.”

“If people like this were prosecuted, teachers would think twice before raising a hand against someone else’s child.”

“Someone who displays such aggressive and unacceptable behaviour simply has no right to call themselves a teacher. What can such a person teach children – respect, kindness or compassion for others?“

“If a similar incident had happened in Germany, for example, the teacher could have faced up to five years in prison. Moreover, if the headteacher had seen the footage – had seen a child being beaten – but failed to take appropriate action, questions would also arise about his professional responsibility.“

“If the teacher behaves so brazenly in front of a camera, it is frightening to imagine what she might have done in a classroom without cameras. She should be dismissed, made to apologise to the child and permanently banned from teaching.”

“The situation is much the same in almost every school. In some, there is physical violence; in others, psychological pressure; and in some, children are simply ignored. At parents’ request, cameras should be installed not only in school corridors but also in classrooms.”

“When such incidents become public, headteachers condemn the teacher’s actions and express utter surprise that someone with more than 30 years of teaching experience could behave this way. But before things reach that point, when we ask for cameras to be installed, those same headteachers come up with a thousand excuses to prevent it.”

“They just don’t want teachers to be embarrassed or parents to see how often a teacher talks on the phone during lessons.“

World.title: Opinion from Tbilisi: ‘Everything is in place for Prime Minister Kobakhidze’s resignation’
World.content:
Political analyst Gia Khukhashvili predicts that Georgia’s Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze could resign soon. The analyst focuses on Kobakhidze’s remarks at a government meeting on 7 October, where he spoke about projects completed and currently under way during his time as prime minister.

Also on 7 October, Kobakhidze appointed Economy Minister Mariam Kvrivishvili as deputy prime minister. Khukhashvili sees this as a possible signal of upcoming changes in the government. He believes Kvrivishvili could eventually replace Kobakhidze.

On 7 October, the government held its first meeting in a month. Irakli Kobakhidze spoke about projects completed and currently under way in various sectors during his time as prime minister. Kobakhidze spent more than half an hour reviewing the government’s record.

Gia Khukhashvili: “Everything is in place for his [Kobakhidze’s] resignation. In fact, he has been powerless for a long time. No minister in the executive branch feels accountable to him. A purely technical government has been formed.

I would not rule out the possibility that [his lengthy speech at today’s government meeting] means exactly that. I can support this with the fact that Mariam Kvrivishvili has been promoted to deputy prime minister. That also happened today, and it is another sign that the end of his premiership is near.

It is possible that during the transition period, Mariam Kvrivishvili could become acting prime minister to ensure continuity until a new prime minister takes office. However, I would not rule out the possibility that Kvrivishvili herself could become the new prime minister.”

“Anything is possible — these are games at the royal court, after all. I do not see either Kobakhidze or [former prime minister] Garibashvili as real actors in the political process. There have been periods when they were given more room to manoeuvre, but they are not real players.

Anything is possible. The main and most important decisions, the fundamental ones, are made elsewhere. Someone else decides whom to hang and whom to pardon, and we all know his first and last name [Bidzina Ivanishvili, founder of Georgian Dream — JAMnews].

And this is just some petty squabbling among small-time people.”

Gia Khukhashvili on possible resignation of Kobakhidze

World.title: EU prepares to expand without Georgia: what ‘candidate status on paper’ means
World.content:
The European Union is preparing for a new round of enlargement and drawing up concrete roadmaps for four leading candidates — Montenegro, Albania, Moldova and Ukraine.

Georgia is no longer part of this process. The European Commission does not mention it at all in its main communication. An accompanying 149-page document explicitly says that Georgia’s EU accession process has effectively been put on hold.

Against this backdrop, the political conflict between Tbilisi and Brussels has become increasingly clear. So has their different understanding of European integration itself. The European Commission says democratic reforms and alignment with EU foreign policy form part of the conditions for membership. Leaders of the ruling Georgian Dream party, meanwhile, have increasingly openly portrayed some of Brussels’ demands as pressure that harms the country’s interests.

“A candidate only on paper”

On 6 October, the European Commission published a communication titled “Communication on Pre-Enlargement Policy Reviews – Preparing for a Wider Union” (“Pre-Enlargement Policy Review — Preparing for a Wider Union”).

The document outlines how the EU itself should prepare for future enlargement. One of the main areas involves gradually integrating candidate countries before they achieve full membership.

At the same time, the European Commission is considering stronger safeguards in case a new member violates the EU’s fundamental principles after joining. In the most serious cases, such a mechanism could even suspend the member state’s voting rights in the Council of the EU.

The European Commission will prepare roadmaps for four countries — Montenegro, Albania, Moldova and Ukraine.

The main 25-page communication does not even mention Georgia.

On 6 October 2026 in Brussels, European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos described Georgia’s position in response to a question from a Georgian journalist:

“As you know, Georgia is a candidate country only on paper. I regret that. I would like Georgia, with the huge support of the Georgian people, to be at the same level as Moldova and Ukraine today.

How we continue working with the country will depend to a large extent on how the member states assess its future. But much of what is happening in the country [in Georgia] will appear in the enlargement reports at the end of October. You can imagine which direction things will take.”

The working document accompanying the communication does mention Georgia among the enlargement countries, but it adds an important caveat:

“Georgia’s accession process has been de facto halted in line with the conclusions of the European Council.”

This is an important point: the EU has not revoked Georgia’s candidate status, and it did not take any new decision to do so on 6 October.

However, despite retaining its formal status, Georgia does not rank among the candidates for which the European Commission is now planning the next stage of accession.

A common starting point, different trajectories

Georgia applied to join the European Union in March 2022, at the same time as Ukraine and Moldova.

It received candidate status in December 2023, subject to fulfilling nine steps set out by the European Commission.

The three countries then took sharply different paths.

The EU opened accession negotiations with Ukraine and Moldova in 2024. In Georgia’s case, however, EU documents state that steps taken by the authorities since 2024 have harmed the country’s European path and effectively halted the accession process.

On 28 November 2024, Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze said the government would not put the opening of EU accession talks on the agenda until the end of 2028 and would reject all EU budget grants.

The new 2026 package makes the difference even clearer: Moldova and Ukraine now rank among the four leading candidates, while Georgia does not.

“Moldova listens to Brussels, while we don’t”

Statements by Georgian Dream show that relations between Tbilisi and Brussels have become increasingly confrontational.

Georgian authorities respond to criticism from the EU not only by defending their policies, but also by openly rejecting and criticising Brussels’ demands themselves.

Government representatives also frame compliance with some EU demands as a question of protecting Georgia’s national interests.

Georgian Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili contrasted Marta Kos’s statement about Moldova’s progress with economic indicators. He said Georgia’s economic growth was higher.

Papuashvili linked this difference to Georgia’s approach to Brussels’ recommendations:

“[Moldova] deserves more and more praise, but our experience tells us that the more Brussels praises you, the more its decisions and imposed directives harm you.”

Papuashvili also compared poverty rates in the two countries and linked the differences to their respective approaches to Brussels’ policies.

*“What is the difference? Moldova listens to Brussels, while we don’t. […] The conclusion is clear: those who listen to Brussels suffer; those who do not listen to Brussels but listen to their own people come out ahead economically. The only thing Moldova is really ahead of us in is Brussels’ beautiful words.

We certainly do not need such beautiful words if those words only mean that we suffer from policies imposed by Brussels,”* Papuashvili said.

Parliamentary majority leader Irakli Kirchkhalia gave a similar response.

He said the Georgian authorities were ready to carry out the reforms needed for European integration, but that Georgia had “red lines” and national interests that it could not sacrifice to join the EU.

He compared compliance with Brussels’ political demands to “blind obedience” and said Georgia wanted EU membership “not at any cost”.

“If Brussels now considers a country’s ‘progress’ to depend on how blindly it follows specific political demands, then this is no longer merit-based European integration, but an assessment of blind obedience. […] So when we are told that Georgia is ‘lagging behind’ Ukraine and Moldova, our answer is simple: Georgia chooses dignity and peace!” Kirchkhalia said.

What the European Commission says

The European Commission’s 2026 document sets out very different criteria. Alongside economic development, the central issues in the accession process include the rule of law, democratic standards and alignment with the EU’s Common Foreign and Security Policy (CFSP).

According to the document, Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro and North Macedonia fully align with the CFSP, while Moldova and Ukraine demonstrate a high level of alignment. Georgia and Serbia need to make significant progress in this area, while Georgia and Turkey have low levels of alignment.

The European Commission sees this as an indication of a candidate country’s strategic choice and says these issues must be resolved before accession.

The document also gives Russia a separate focus. According to the European Commission, enlargement directly counters Russian influence because the accession process requires countries such as Georgia and Serbia to fully align with EU foreign policy and legislation. This includes sanctions, energy, trade, foreign investment and visa policy.

The document also states:

“At present, the Georgian authorities are not actively pursuing EU and NATO membership, while Ukraine is making changes to achieve full compatibility with NATO.”

This ranks among the strongest formulations in the new document because the assessment concerns not just the implementation of a specific reform, but the authorities’ overall political course.

The opposition on Moldova’s example

Salome Samadashvili, one of the leaders of the opposition Lelo — Strong Georgia alliance, contrasts Moldova’s example with Georgian Dream’s narrative about a so-called “second front”.

She says Moldova did not open a “second front” against Russia. Instead, the EU is helping Moldova strengthen its security and defence capabilities in response to threats from Russia.

Samadashvili also links Moldova’s European progress to its efforts to tackle oligarchic influence, arguing that Georgia has gone in the opposite direction.

“Unfortunately, Georgia has gone in the opposite direction: an oligarch has taken complete control of the government, destroyed all state institutions, and as a result, our EU accession agenda has been cancelled,” Samadashvili says.

Ban on opposition parties

The political context of Georgia’s relations with the EU is also visible in the European Parliament’s current agenda.

On 7 October, the European Parliament is due to hold a debate officially titled “Attempts by the ruling Georgian Dream party to ban opposition parties in Georgia”. A vote on the corresponding resolution will take place on 8 October.

This is a separate procedure from the European Commission’s enlargement package, and it would be incorrect to directly link the two.

However, the two processes also illustrate the different political contexts between Georgia and the other leading candidates. The EU is working on the next stages of integration with four countries, while the European Parliament is discussing the possible banning of opposition parties in Georgia.

The next important assessment of Georgia will come at the end of October, when the European Commission publishes its enlargement reports.

EU enlargement without Georgia

World.title: Ex-German intelligence chief arrested as investigators probe links to Azerbaijani intelligence
World.content:
German intelligence passed information to Azerbaijan

Former German foreign intelligence chief August Hanning has been arrested on suspicion of obtaining information constituting state secrets, attempted treason and acting on behalf of a foreign intelligence service.

Germany’s Federal Prosecutor’s Office has not specified which foreign country is involved. However, according to Der Spiegel, investigators are examining Hanning’s possible links to an Azerbaijani intelligence officer and whether he prepared analytical materials for the officer using classified information.

Hanning has also served for many years on the board of the German-Azerbaijani Forum.

Hanning, 80, who headed Germany’s Federal Intelligence Service (BND) from 1998 to 2005, was detained on 6 October. His former chief of staff, Manfred D., was also arrested as part of the same investigation.

According to the Federal Prosecutor’s Office, Hanning is under strong suspicion of espionage involving treason, obtaining information constituting state secrets, attempted treason and acting as an agent for a foreign intelligence service. Manfred D. is suspected of attempted treason and aiding and abetting espionage.

The investigation is ongoing, and the allegations have yet to be considered by a court on their merits. No final judicial decision has been made in Hanning’s case.

Around 2,000 BND documents

According to investigators, several years after leaving the BND, Hanning reached an agreement with his former employee to provide him with classified information.

The Federal Prosecutor’s Office believes that around spring 2010, Hanning and Manfred D. struck an agreement under which D. would regularly provide his former boss with important information obtained from the BND in exchange for payment.

Manfred D. worked with Hanning at the BND before following him to Germany’s Federal Ministry of the Interior. In 2012, he returned to the BND, where he held a senior position in the offices of subsequent heads of the intelligence service until March 2026. In this role, he had access to classified information.

According to preliminary findings by investigators, between 2010 and 2022, Manfred D. provided Hanning with around 2,000 documents. A significant proportion contained classified information and were intended exclusively for internal use within the BND.

Some of the materials contained information intended for the BND leadership, as well as for regular meetings of intelligence service representatives at the German Federal Chancellery. According to an investigation by WDR, NDR and Süddeutsche Zeitung, the documents included material on Iran’s nuclear programme and the Russian military, as well as information obtained from Germany’s partner intelligence services.

Prosecutors say Hanning intended to use the information for commercial purposes as part of his private consultancy work.

How did Azerbaijan connection emerge?

The Federal Prosecutor’s Office does not mention Azerbaijan or any other country in its official statement.

According to the official account, Hanning once used classified information obtained from Manfred D. to prepare an analysis for “an employee of a foreign intelligence service”. Investigators have so far been unable to establish whether the analysis was actually passed to its intended recipient.

The possible Azerbaijan connection emerged in reports by German media citing sources familiar with the investigation.

According to Der Spiegel, investigators are examining Hanning’s possible links to an Azerbaijani intelligence officer. The magazine also reports that the analysis Hanning prepared using classified BND information was intended for this individual. The same information has also been reported by WELT, t-online and other German media.

Hanning sits on board of German-Azerbaijani Forum

Another factor drawing attention to the possible Azerbaijan connection is Hanning’s longstanding public ties with the country.

He has for many years served on the board of the Deutsch-Aserbaidschanisches Forum (German-Azerbaijani Forum).

In an announcement about the election of the forum’s new leadership in August 2025, Hanning was again listed as a board member. The same list also included Elmar Mammadov, a representative of Azerbaijan’s state oil company SOCAR in Germany.

The forum describes itself as an independent platform promoting political, economic, academic and cultural ties between Germany and Azerbaijan. LobbyControl, a German organisation that monitors lobbying in Germany, has previously described the forum as one of the lobbying organisations with close ties to the Azerbaijani authorities.

Hanning has served on the forum’s board for many years. As early as 2017, Tagesspiegel reported that the former BND chief was a member of the organisation’s board. It said that even then, the forum’s structures included former ministers, MPs and senior government officials.

Previous ‘Azerbaijan case’ in Germany

The current espionage investigation is not the first major scandal in Germany involving Azerbaijan.

In recent years, German authorities have investigated a number of criminal cases involving the alleged bribery of politicians in Azerbaijan’s interests.

In July 2025, a Munich court gave former CSU MP Eduard Lintner a nine-month suspended prison sentence for his role in transferring funds originating from Azerbaijan in an effort to influence decisions by the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE). The court explicitly described this as vote-buying.

In January 2026, former CDU MP Axel Fischer was given a 14-month suspended prison sentence. According to the court, while serving in PACE, Fischer received tens of thousands of euros from Azerbaijan and, in return, made positive statements about the country and passed on confidential documents.

Legally, these cases are unrelated to the current investigation into Hanning. The Lintner and Fischer cases concerned political corruption and lobbying on behalf of the Azerbaijani government’s interests. The Hanning case concerns state secrets and suspected activity on behalf of a foreign intelligence service.

Classified documents discovered during unrelated investigation

Suspicions of espionage involving Hanning emerged under unusual circumstances.

In September 2025, German law enforcement officers searched Hanning’s home and offices as part of a separate criminal investigation into the kidnapping of the children of businesswoman Christina Block. Hanning also denied the allegations in that case.

During the searches, investigators reportedly discovered classified BND material. The documents were subsequently handed over to federal authorities, and in May 2026 a covert investigation into Hanning and Manfred D. was launched.

The findings of the investigation could have serious implications for Germany’s intelligence service. BND chief Martin Jäger said an internal review was also under way and that the initial suspicions had been further substantiated. German lawmakers responsible for overseeing the intelligence services have called for a comprehensive investigation into what happened.

If reports of Hanning’s links to Azerbaijani intelligence are confirmed, the case would go beyond previous scandals involving Azerbaijani lobbying in Germany: this time, the issue is not political influence but the possible transfer of classified German intelligence to a foreign intelligence service.

World.title: Azerbaijani para-taekwondo athlete wins silver medal at Grand Prix in Paris
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 9. Azerbaijani representative Sabir Zeynalov has won a silver medal at the Para Taekwondo Grand Prix in Paris.

This was reported by the National Paralympic Committee of Azerbaijan.

According to the information, Azerbaijani para taekwondo athlete Sabir Zeynalov, competing in the K44 category in the up to 58 kg weight class, faced Israel’s Asaf Yasur in the final. Zeynalov lost to his opponent in the decisive bout and claimed the silver medal.

It should be noted that at the Paris Grand Prix, which brings together the world’s top-ranked athletes, Azerbaijan is represented by three para taekwondo athletes under head coach Farid Taghizade — Imamaddin Khalilov (70 kg), Sabir Zeynalov (58 kg), and Amin Aliyev (63 kg).

World.title: Chronicles of Victory: October 9, 2020
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 9. The Azerbaijani Army launched a counter-offensive operation, later called the "Iron Fist", on September 27, 2020, in response to the large-scale provocation of the Armenian armed forces along the frontline.

The erupted 44-day Second Karabakh War ended with liberation of Azerbaijan’s territories from nearly 30-year Armenian occupation.

Trend presents the chronicle of the 13th day of the Second Karabakh war:

- President of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev addressed the people. The Supreme Commander of the Armed Forces announced that the Azerbaijani army liberated the village of Hadrut and several villages from occupation and destroyed a large number of military equipment of the Armenian armed forces.

- The Ministry of Defense of Azerbaijan announced the destruction of another headquarters of the Armenian army, the elimination of the chief of artillery of the regiment, and also presented a list of destroyed and captured equipment.

World.title: Milli Majlis Speaker chairs coordination meeting of Non-Aligned Movement Parliamentary Network (PHOTO)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 8. On October 8, a coordination meeting of the Non-Aligned Movement Parliamentary Network (NAM PN) was held in Arusha, Tanzania, on the sidelines of the 153rd Assembly of the Inter-Parliamentary Union (IPU). The meeting was chaired by Speaker of the Milli Majlis and Chair of the NAM PN Sahiba Gafarova.

Sahiba Gafarova stated in her speech that coordination meetings held in parallel with IPU Assemblies are crucial for collective action and making the most effective use of this platform. These meetings create opportunities for constructive dialogue among member parliaments, further strengthening cooperation among them.

The Speaker of the Milli Majlis and Chair of the NAM PN stated that the Parliamentary Network continues to expand its scope and strengthen its international role. Sahiba Gafarova emphasized that, as Chair, she considers promoting the role and activities of this organization a priority during her foreign visits, bilateral meetings, and participation in international conferences, and provided information on the measures taken in this direction.

Noting that developing institutional dialogue and strengthening cooperation with other organizations remain priorities for the Parliamentary Network, Sahiba Gafarova pointed out that the NAM PN currently has observer status with six organizations, while eight organizations have observer status with the Network. In addition, concluding memorandums of understanding with partner organizations expands the organization's involvement in international cooperation.

Sahiba Gafarova noted that since the founding of the Network in Madrid in November 2021, five conferences have been held in Baku, Manama, Geneva, Tashkent, and Istanbul in 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025, and 2026, respectively. Each conference has been of great significance for the institutional development of the Parliamentary Network.

The discussions focused on the agenda, including the institutional development of the Non-Aligned Movement Parliamentary Network.

World.title: Man who allegedly crashed into Newcastle Knights fans granted bail
World.content:
The 18-year-old accused of driving a car that hit and injured 10 Knights fans in Newcastle has been granted bail at a review hearing, after spending six nights in custody.

Indika Bambrick Samarasinghe is facing a total of nine charges, including three counts of dangerous driving occasioning grievous bodily harm, three counts of negligent driving occasioning grievous bodily harm and three counts of causing bodily harm by misconduct.

He appeared via audiovisual link in Newcastle Local Court today, after his lawyers lodged a bail review application earlier this week.

Thousands of fans had lined the streets of Wallsend to wave the Newcastle Knights off to their first NRL grand final in 25 years, before a car rammed into the crowd at a roundabout on Link Road.

Ten people were hospitalised after the incident and two victims, including a 5-year-old girl, were left in a critical condition at the time.

Indika Bambrick Samarasinghe faced a bail review hearing today. (Source: Facebook)

The court heard Mr Samarasinghe, a P-plater, was seen driving erratically before the crash.

He was arrested soon after the incident and faced court less than 24 hours later.

In his first appearance on October 4, Mr Samarasinghe did not apply for bail, which was formally refused.

He has since undergone a medical assessment in custody.

Hunter New England Health confirmed the conditions of the 10 patients had improved since the incident, and three remain in care in a stable condition.

Calls have been growing for a state-led trauma response to assist the thousands of potential witnesses to the crash.

World.title: Nurse says hospital parking fix needed after being chased to her car
World.content:
A Hobart-based nurse who was chased by a group of young men while she walked to her car after work says a lack of parking options in the city continues to put health workers at risk.

The incident occurred on Monday night when Audrey McAllister had just finished her shift at the Royal Hobart Hospital.

It was late, just past 11pm, but not an unusual time for the nurse to clock-off.

Loading...

However, as Ms McAllister walked to her car, which was parked at Queens Domain — a roughly one-kilometre walk from the hospital — she was chased by a group of about seven young men who began to yell at her as she walked past.

Ms McAllister ran to her car and locked the doors, before calling the police.

While she made it back to her vehicle safe and physically unharmed, Ms McAllister said the experience had left her shaken.

"I don't ever want to park up there again," she told 936 ABC Hobart.

" It doesn't feel safe, it doesn't feel appropriate, so I'm probably going to park in the Market Place car park and have to fork out that fee. "

The area around Queens Domain is where many nurses, midwives and other shift workers park their cars to save money on expensive inner-city car park fees, or where they are forced to park due to the lack of options close to the hospital.

There is no dedicated parking for hospital workers in Hobart's CBD.

While only a short walk from the city centre, the Queens Domain area is poorly lit and predominantly bushland.

Securing safe and affordable parking for health staff is an issue that the Australian Nursing and Midwifery Union (ANMF), of which Ms McAllister is a delegate, wants to see addressed.

"Unfortunately, that's not an isolated incident," ANMF Tasmania branch secretary Emily Shepherd said of Ms McAllister's experience.

"We don't want to wait until one of our members has some serious adverse outcome or, worse, loses their life in this type of scenario."

Union wants dedicated staff parking

The Royal Hobart Hospital is centrally located in Hobart's CBD and is the largest hospital in the state.

Often, however, staff are unable to access nearby parking.

The closest option, Argyle Street car park, closes at 10pm.

Emily Shepherd says the union is extremely concerned about Audrey McAllister's experience. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

The nearby Market Place car park is open 24/7 but can quickly become expensive or unaffordable if access is needed several times per week.

Ms McAllister said she would like to see private car park providers create dedicated and safe hospital staff parking for shift workers.

"There's no subsidised rates for healthcare workers," Ms McAllister said.

" I've also heard of many colleagues, nurses and midwives who have experienced harassment or assault within [Market Place] car park as well. "

The ANMF said it had put up a raft of requests to the Tasmanian government to try and encourage it to provide better safety measures for health staff as part of ongoing enterprise agreement negotiations.

These included introducing a shuttle service or security to escort staff back to their vehicles after their night shifts, and for a roof to be built over the bike storage area at the hospital so that staff can ride to work without fear of theft.

A Tasmanian government spokesperson said any violence or threatening behaviour towards health staff was completely unacceptable, "regardless of whether they are on duty, or travelling to and from their place of work".

The spokesperson said "violence prevention risk assessments" of all entrances to the hospital were being undertaken, and the government remained committed to delivering fair pay rises and improved conditions for nurses and midwives.

"We are continuing to negotiate in good faith," they said.

World.title: Students run hairdressers and cafe at remote Indigenous school
World.content:
There is more than meets the eye when you look inside the collection of green buildings nestled at the rear of the Wadja Wadja High School.

The front donga has been kitted out as a cafe, with a counter space for taking orders, a coffee machine and a dining area.

Just next door is a hair salon, complete with mirrors, wash basins and styling tools.

Across the corridor, fishing rods hang on the wall, with tables arranged into a study room.

Student Lataya Skeen taking coffee orders in the training cafe. (ABC Capricornia: Vanessa Jarrett)

The services might be commonplace in other communities, but for the 1,000 people who call Woorabinda home, these spaces are a rarity.

"We looked at the community and what we needed in community," school principal Cherie Blinco said.

Filling a gap in local services

The Aboriginal community, 170 kilometres south-west of Rockhampton, only has a handful of shops, with the nearest place to order a coffee about 40 kilometres away.

The new facilities allow the senior students at the school to study vocational certificates that also go towards their year 12 graduation.

"These spaces are about much more than training; they are about creating opportunities for our young people here in Woorabinda, building confidence and employment skills," Ms Blinco said.

Wadja Wadja High School principal Cherie Blinco with former teacher Hector Costello. (ABC Capricornia: Vanessa Jarrett)

The idea to offer vocational education and training (VET) subjects at the school was the brainchild of retired principal Hector Costello, who did advisory work at the school in 2019.

"What I discovered was the standard curriculum they were delivering just wasn't working for the kids here," he said.

"In VET you can achieve much more tangible things and it's got much greater real-life applicability for students here.

"A lot of schools are doing it but for this community it has worked perfectly. "

Enrolments at the Wadja Wadja High School have grown over the past 12 months to now 110 students. (ABC Capricornia: Vanessa Jarrett)

Attendance rates at the school have "skyrocketed" over the last few months since the VET programs were introduced, principal Cherie Blinco said.

"It gives them a purpose to come to school … learning something that they can use within their community and it means that they don't have to leave to get that education," she said.

Future hair salon students Juu'garr Bamboo, Jahlaila Beckett, Virginia Finlay and Carol Oakley. (ABC Capricornia: Vanessa Jarrett)

Kuku Yalanji woman and year 10 student Jahlaila Beckett plans to study a certificate in salon services next year.

"I was pretty excited … The commitment we want to put into doing hairs and stuff. I think it's a big opportunity to go out there and explore more," Jahlaila said.

Wadja Wadja woman and year 11 student Juu'garr Bamboo is also enrolled next year and said she had already learnt some things that might help her to become a hairdresser in the future.

"We've just been practising hairstyles and how to start a conversation with some of the locals here in Woorabinda," Juu'garr said.

Kulgoodah Dancers, led by Terrence Adams Snr, performing at the grand opening ceremony for the new VET training spaces at the Wadja Wadja High School. (ABC Capricornia: Vanessa Jarrett)

An official grand opening of the space was held this week.

Students opened the cafe for trial runs over term three, before an official grand opening of the space this week, which welcome community members.

Community members of Woorabinda supporting the new cafe. (ABC Capricornia: Vanessa Jarrett)

"Now that we've got it in Woorabinda, it's going to be so great," local Woorabinda resident Renee Hill said.

"It's so wonderful seeing the kids having a go at everything.

"We don't put the kids down, we encourage them so it's really good to come and pop in and have a coffee and just see their smiling faces."

World.title: State government takes control of Sydney Town Hall Square project
World.content:
The NSW government has moved to take control of the City of Sydney's Town Hall Square project.

Planning Minister Paul Scully last month forced a pause on work to create a 4,500-square-metre civic plaza outside the CBD's Town Hall, while the Independent Planning Commission (IPC) provided advice on the proposal.

Plans for the square were put on display for community feedback in August after council unanimously resolved in February to move ahead with the design and construction of the square.

The council has said the plaza, which will require the demolition of several buildings the city has obtained since the 1980s, was necessary to create a gathering point for community events, music events and markets.

Mr Scully said he accepted an IPC recommendation the proposal be declared a State Significant Development (SSD), a development approval process reserved for large or sensitive projects, paving the way for a council development application.

"This process will allow for a rigorous whole-of-government assessment by the department and provide an opportunity for individuals, the community, and other stakeholders to have their say on any development application before its determination by the IPC," he said in a statement.

The City of Sydney has allocated $150 million to the project. (Supplied: City of Sydney)

The IPC assessment only considered whether the project should be declared a SSD and did not grant development approval.

In advice to the minister, IPC member Richard Pearson said the square could deliver "significant" public and economic benefits and given state-owned public transport infrastructure, its significance extended beyond the council area.

The City of Sydney council has been contacted for comment.

The council has previously said while the project would be delivered in coordination with the state government and a SSD designation could lead to "unnecessary costs or delays".

Council has estimated the project would cost $94 million with $150 million allocated to allow for cost overruns.

World.title: Man found dead by police after 'serious incident' in Perth's south
World.content:
Homicide detectives are investigating the death of a man at a house in Perth's southern suburbs.

WA Police say they were called to a residence on Nye Way in Orelia about 2:20pm yesterday after "reports of a serious incident".

Officers found the man dead at the house.

In a statement, police said another man "known to the deceased" was found inside the house and taken into custody.

Detectives and forensic pathologists were among those sent to the scene. (ABC News: Samantha Goerling)

The investigation is being led by the Homicide Squad and remains ongoing.

The street was still blocked off this morning, with three police vehicles on the scene, along with a forensic van.

Officers appeared to be working in the backyard of the property.

Earlier, police said detectives and forensic specialists were among those at the scene.

"The incident is contained; there is no threat to public safety," they said in a statement.

World.title: Powderfinger confirm reunion, 16 years after breaking up
World.content:
Powderfinger, one of the most celebrated acts in Australian music history, have confirmed they are reforming, 16 years after breaking up.

In a video posted to the band's social media this morning, frontman Bernard Fanning said they would "do some shows all around Australia from September next year".

"We always said that if we were going to get back together to do some shows, that you guys would be the first to know," he said.

"We're going to build something pretty special just for you guys," guitarist Darren Middleton said. "We'll see you from the stage."

The video confirmed what fans had already suspected: They were behind a series of cryptic teasers that had appeared around the country over the past week.

Internet sleuths took no time figuring out Powderfinger's connection to the posts.

They identified references to the band embedded in opaque imagery shared via a new account named The Return of the Electric Horsemen, and projected onto landmarks across the country.

Loading Instagram content

The rumour mill has been in overdrive ever since, with some fans predicting a full-scale reunion, while others are picking something less dramatic, like reissues of classic albums.

Yesterday, the band's official account, which had recently been wiped clean, posted the tease for the first time.

"Add enough time to enough variables and something extraordinary happens…" the caption read.

Who are Powderfinger?

Formed in Brisbane in 1989, Powderfinger spent their first few years as just another local rock band, until their second album, 1996's Double Allergic, brought them their first taste of national acclaim.

Double J — a place for music lovers Double J gives you the new music you'll actually love, alongside the classic tracks you keep coming back to. Give your playlist a rest and join us here.

By the time they released Odyssey Number Five in 2000, they were one of the biggest bands in the country.

That record peaked at the top of the charts and won six ARIA awards, including Album of the Year and Record of the Year for My Happiness.

They are an especially decorated act in the triple j Hottest 100, winning the 1999 and 2000 countdowns, making the annual polls 22 times, and picking up three entries in last year's Hottest 100 of Australian Songs, including a spot in the top 10.

There have been two semi-reunions over the years. Four members played together at Splendour in the Grass in 2017, and the band's virtual performance during 2020's COVID-19 lockdowns raised more than $450,000 for Support Act and Beyond Blue.

When are they touring?

The band confirmed they would head back on the road from September next year, but stopped short of sharing further details.

Whenever and wherever those shows take place, Powderfinger will not be the only Australian legacy act fans have been clamouring to see this year.

The news comes just a week after Powderfinger's peers Silverchair responded to calls for them to reform for the NRL grand final.

"Thanks to everyone who's asked if we're playing before the game. We're way too rusty, so sorry, no can do," the statement read.

Powderfinger embarked on a mammoth farewell tour of the country before splitting in 2010, selling more than 200,000 tickets across 34 shows.

Get prepared for the Powderfinger reunion by listening to the Powderfinger J Files.

World.title: No end in sight for multi-million-dollar Cable Beach development
World.content:
One of Australia's most-famous beachfronts continues to remain a construction site with a timeline for the multimillion-dollar redevelopment of Cable Beach blowing out.

The landmark beach in Broome, 2,000 kilometres north of Perth, is a major state and national tourists drawcard with its famous camel rides and sunsets a feature of West Australian tourist campaigns.

But the long-term redevelopment of the precinct, which will see a water park, amphitheatre, new beach access and other features added, has left access to much of the area restricted since 2023.

Keen tourists and locals were promised the final stage of the project would be complete by the mid to late-2026.

Camel rides are a staple of Cable Beach tourism. (ABC Kimberley: Ruby Littler)

But as that deadline approaches the Shire of Broome says the project's official opening will not occur until 2027.

They were unable to confirm whether construction work would be complete by the end of this year.

Restricted access frustrating

The development has drawn a mixed reception from locals, with many frustrated by the ongoing restrictions to parking and beach access.

Jemma Vincent and Giles Fresher grew up in Broome, enjoying everything Cable Beach has to offer.

Ms Vincent said she was not surprised to hear about delays to the opening.

"Sounds about right, everything takes a long time to do here," she said.

" Some of my friends just left town and said 'we'll come back when Cable Beach is done'. "

Jemma Vincent and Giles Fresher grew up in Broome and say the redevelopment delays impact the lifestyle. (ABC Kimberley: Ruby Littler)

Among Ms Vincent's circle of friends, being denied car access via ramp to the northern side of Cable Beach was the biggest concern.

"People didn't really care about [the construction] as long as you could get down onto the beach and have car access," she said.

" I feel like they [the shire] honestly fed us a lie. "

But fellow Broome local Grant Garrett said he believed the redeveloped foreshore would be great for tourism.

Grant Garrett has lived in Broome for two decades and is supportive of the project. (ABC Kimberley: Ruby Littler)

"Any kind of progress for Broome is good, but I think it's come along very slowly, unfortunately," he said.

"Overall, when it's all done, it will be a great improvement for the community and tourism industry."

Impact on surrounding businesses

While supportive of the redevelopment overall, Spinifex Brewing chief executive Leanne Andrews said the road closures had reduced foot traffic and spontaneous visits to its Cable Beach venue.

"Probably the biggest thing is not knowing when it's going to finish and the prolonged staffing impacts," she said.

"I've no doubt it will be positive in the end but it would be good to know when it's actually going to finish."'

The chief executive of Broome's Spinifex Brewing said road closures had impacted their Cable Beach business. (ABC Kimberley: Andrew Seabourne)

Ms Andrews said a lack of communication around progress and timelines had proven disruptive for Cable Beach businesses.

"It's still on the website as mid to late-2026. It's been one of those developments that's just kept on keeping on," she said.

"We're one community and I guess we all just want to see each other succeed."

Cable Beach is known for its four-wheel drive access. (ABC News)

A Shire of Broome spokesperson said it was committed to providing updates as key milestones were confirmed.

"We know there is strong community interest in the redevelopment," they said.

"The shire is working closely with the contractor and reviewing the latest project information to ensure the information we provide to the community is accurate and up to date.

"Planning is also underway for an official launch event which is expected to take place next year."

World.title: Michael Robotham's latest novel sat in his bottom drawer for 35 years
World.content:
Michael Robotham was a 22-year-old journalist working for a Sydney newspaper when he began writing his first novel in the early 1980s.

"[It] was going to be my great Australian novel … [and] win me every prize in the world," Robotham tells ABC Arts.

He finished it six years later, when he was living in London. It came very close to being published.

Set in a small country town based on his hometown of Gundagai in the Riverina region of NSW, the novel had the working title Blessed Are the Meek.

"I missed out by a single vote in an acquisitions meeting for a major publisher," Robotham says.

"I was told that it was really the setting … They just felt it was a little bit too hard for them to market, because this was obviously well before Jane Harper and Liane Moriarty and few Australian-set books had ever done well internationally."

He consigned the manuscript to his bottom drawer and spent the next decade working as a journalist and then as a ghostwriter.

Count down the Top 100 Australian Books ABC Radio National's annual Top 100 Books countdown is on! Tune in on October 17-18 to hear how the nation voted.

Robotham returned to Australia in the 90s, but when he eventually began writing a new novel he recalled the advice he'd been given and set it in the UK.

That book, The Suspect — the first instalment of what would become the popular Joe O'Loughlin series — triggered a bidding war at the London Book Fair before it was published in 2004. It has since sold more than 1 million copies worldwide and was adapted for television in 2022.

Now, two decades later, Robotham has finally set a book in Australia.

Tell Me Something True, Robotham's 20th novel, is a "seriously rewritten and re-imagined" version of that first manuscript.

"All the story and the characters remain the same, but it's been in the bottom drawer since the 1980s," he says.

A tale of brotherhood

Robotham wrote the first version of Tell Me Something True on a Remington typewriter, so the first step of the rewriting process was transferring it to a computer.

When he cast an appraising eye over the original story, he recognised both strengths and weaknesses in his work.

"I read some sections and thought, 'Wow, that guy could really write! Whatever happened to him?!' And then I read other sections that I thought, 'Oh, that's so naive. That was a 20-year-old … who was very self-indulgent and full of himself.'"

Robotham says his latest novel, Tell Me Something True, leans into the tradition of small-town mysteries. (Supplied: Hachette Australia)

He also found that the world had moved on in many ways.

"There was no such thing as a sensitivity reader all those years ago," he says.

"It's amazing how you'd put things in books 20 years ago that you wouldn't put in a book today."

But the most significant change was structural. The original story unfolded chronologically.

"Back then, it was the story of Arlo Hackett and his brother Luke … and into their life I dropped this very feisty, opinionated teenage girl, Saxon, who arrives in a stolen car," he says.

" I wasn't writing it as a crime novel. I saw it as a coming-of-age novel and a story about brotherhood and family. "

In the published version, Robotham created a second storyline set in the present as Arlo returns to his hometown of Yulara after his release from prison.

To contemporary readers, Tell Me Something More belongs to a well-established tradition in Australian publishing of mysteries set in the bush, also known as outback noir, kicked off by Jane Harper's 2006 novel, The Dry.

But, as Robotham good-humouredly points out, his novel predates the trend by decades.

"I did this first," he says. "Well before the others did it, I'd done it."

Small-town secrets

Robotham describes Tell Me Something True as his most autobiographical work.

"It's my most personal book in a sense," he says. "There are scenes in it that are lifted straight out of my childhood."

Robotham's father was a teacher, and the family moved often when he was a child.

His primary school years were spent in Gundagai, a town of 2,000 people on the Murrumbidgee River known, among other claims to fame, as the resting place of 19th-century bushranger Captain Moonlite.

Robotham says the novel's protagonist, Arlo Hackett, "pleads guilty because he believes he should have stopped the crime happening". (ABC Radio - Conversations)

While Robotham says the town is easily recognisable to anyone familiar with its geography and history, he chose not to use its name in print, renaming it Yulara instead.

"In small towns there is only one high school and one high school principal and only one senior police officer," he says.

"I didn't want people playing a guessing game as to whether I based any of this on real-life characters."

As the popularity of outback noir attests, a small town is a fertile setting for a fiction writer.

"Small country towns are very slow to forgive," Robotham says.

"They're full of secrets and yet they're places where it's almost impossible to keep a secret."

Why Australian readers love outback noir There's a literary crime spree underway in Australia thanks to authors such as Jane Harper and Chris Hammer.

In Tell Me Something True, the newly freed Arlo attempts to resume life in Yulara, but encounters hostility from the town's residents, many of whom he's known his whole life.

His mother is in a nursing home and the house he grew up in is in disrepair.

With nowhere else to go, he sets about fixing up the house.

As he reflects on his past, told in flashbacks, he begins to question the events that led to his imprisonment.

"Initially you're asking readers to accept a narrator who spent 12 years in prison for being an accessory to a terrible rape and murder," Robotham says.

"And you're thinking, 'How am I going to go along with this? Do I want to spend time with this man?'

"But as his story unfolds, you realise how badly wronged he's been."

Literary influences

Robotham says he can see his early literary influences in Tell Me Something True, from John Irving's The World According to Garp (1978) and Hotel New Hampshire (1981) to John Steinbeck's 1937 novella, Of Mice and Men.

Also an enthusiastic reader of Australian fiction, Robotham's number one choice in the Top 100 Australian Books was Illywhacker by Peter Carey.

Shortlisted for the 1985 Booker Prize, the novel tells the story of the memorable and idiosyncratic Herbert Badgery.

"He's a 139-year-old con man who relates the story of his life, and you can't believe a word of what he says … and I loved that," Robotham says.

" I read that in my 20s and thought Peter Carey was a genius. "

Robotham is also an admirer of Year of Wonders by Geraldine Brooks, his former colleague-turned-fellow novelist.

"It's an astonishing piece of research," he says.

"I'm in awe of people who write historic fiction. The idea of capturing that period of history of the plague years in that tiny, isolated village in Britain — I thought she did a remarkable job."

September's best books The latest new releases from some of the world's biggest literary stars, including Emily St John Mandel, RF Kuang and Kate Atkinson, are among this month's best books.

Robotham acknowledges we're at a crucial moment in global publishing thanks to the encroachment of AI.

"There was something like a million extra books published in the last year because they've been generated by AI. There's going to be a tsunami of AI slop," he says.

"But I'm a realist … It might make mistakes now, but AI will get better."

Robotham is currently part of a lawsuit in the US accusing tech companies of stealing authors' work to train their language models.

"I hate the idea that we're going to probably cave into the AI companies and give them some sort of right to Australian copyrighted material," he says.

"To me, it's like someone robbing your house and then saying to you, 'Don't worry about it, I'll give you your toaster back'."

Michael Robotham will be at Sydney Writers' Festival's Homegrown at the State Library of NSW on October 10.

ABC Radio National will count down the Top 100 Australian Books on air on October 17 and 18.

World.title: ATO credit card ban delayed after backlash
World.content:
Breaking PoliticsFederalCredit cards ATO credit card ban delayed after backlash Nick Newling October 9, 2026 — 11:26am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The Australian Taxation Office’s controversial banning of credit card payments will no longer come into effect at the end of next month, after the government negotiated with the independent agency to delay the change. Treasurer Jim Chalmers will allocate additional funds to the agency to support a year-long transition period, after the ban – which was set to come into effect on November 30 – came under heavy criticism. Treasurer Jim Chalmers. Louie Douvis The announcement comes after fierce pushback from the business community, opposition parties and some members of the Labor backbench that saw the ATO’s decision as damaging to the cash-flow management of small businesses. Appearing on morning television on Friday, Environment Minister Murray Watt said the ATO’s plan to ban credit car payments for tax bills so as not to burden all taxpayers with the associated costs was a completely “independent decision”.



“When they made clear that they intended to proceed with this, we insisted on them having a good transition plan with the business community and to consult with the business community about that,” Watt told Seven’s Sunrise. “We expect them to do that consultation properly. I mean, I think we need to keep it in perspective that when it comes to payments to the ATO, it’s only a very small number of taxpayers who pay their tax payments by credit card, it’s about 5 per cent for small businesses and about 2 per cent for individuals.” Deputy Liberal leader Jane Hume during a doorstop at Parliament House in Canberra. Dominic Lorrimer Following the October 1 introduction of bans on credit card surcharges, the tax office surprised small business owners in announcing a November 30 cut-off date for credit card payments. The government produced mixed messaging on the topic on Thursday, when Housing Minister Clare O’Neil shared the government’s “real concerns” about the plan, countered by Assistant Minister Andrew Charlton who said the government supported the decision.



The government offered a more unified message on Friday, with Watt joined by Foreign Minister Penny Wong, who encouraged the tax office to perform meaningful consultation on the ban, while Defence Industry Minister Pat Conroy said the ATO should “do their job and talk to small businesses”. Related Article Credit cards Labor ministers contradict each other over ATO credit card surcharge ban Wong also reiterated the independence of the tax office, as deputy Liberal leader Jane Hume questioned “who is in charge”. “You can change this with a stroke of a pen. You can change this with a decision. Small businesses are crying out for a change. They are asking for your help,” Hume told Sunrise, “You just have to have the will, and you can’t blame the ATO. They’re your agency. You’re the government. You should do this”. Several Labor MPs speaking to this masthead on the condition of anonymity shared their concerns over the way the government’s relationship with small business was being framed, but stressed the ATO had blindsided the government but were difficult to wrangle because of their independence.



“It’s just alarming that were seeing this sort of behaviour from the ATO. It’s overreach, it’s hostile they need to remember who they serve. I’m hoping that they reverse this and find efficiencies elsewhere to cover the cost,” one senator said, questioning why the Reserve Bank had not foreshadowed such moves. Another said the ATO had likely made the right decision in finding value for the taxpayer, but had botched the transition and needed to “pull its head out of the sand”. “People probably don’t realise how completely totally independent the tax office is of the government of the day, for good reasons, but yes, sometimes it is completely infuriating,” they said. Concern in the Labor ranks that the party is failing to meet small business owners appears to be growing, with one particularly strident MP laying the blame directly at the feet of cabinet. “I don’t think it’s acceptable for us to say it was the ATO’s decision not ours. If that’s the case, then there’s something seriously wrong with our government. If the ATO can dictate policy like this without government oversight and agreement, I don’t quite understand that government,” the MP said.



“I just think there is no one in cabinet with any small business experience. We have a small business minister that knows nothing about small business. We need someone with some guts to stand up to the tax office. I think it’s very, very disappointing”. Small Business Minister Anne Aly was the first government minister to raise concerns over the ATO’s move on Wednesday, urging the tax office to consult more widely about the ban’s implementation. One MP, who is factionally unaligned with Aly, dismissed the criticism of cabinet, saying: “This is an argument as old as representative democracy itself. I get that having that background is good, but you can’t have a government made up of experts”. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. World.title: A Room With a View is fun … but we’re told too much instead of being allowed to work it out
World.content:
Belvoir St Theatre, October 7, until November 1

Knowing if you’ve fallen in lust is straightforward; knowing if you’ve fallen in love, more elusive. In E. M. Forster’s novel A Room with a View, Lucy Honeychurch is even confused by lust, so has little chance with love – at least not without wise counsel. But then, she lives in starched Edwardian England, where pretence and hypocrisy rule, and therefore, as the Reverend Mr Beebe says, “It can be so difficult to understand people who speak the truth.”

Star of A Room With A View Nathalie Morris. Steven Siewert

Grace Chapple’s new stage adaptation, directed by Hannah Goodwin, is a brave undertaking. In 1985, Merchant Ivory threw a galaxy of stars at their film version, and even the peerless Daniel Day-Lewis struggled as Cecil, the man with whom Lucy thinks she’s fallen in love.

Forster’s prose and view of humanity share an airiness, and his characters are cheapened by excessive caricature. Underscoring his work is a benevolence best encapsulated by Mr Emerson, a humanist and socialist who believes in maximising life’s potential.

World.content:
Exclusive Eating outJust open Join Yum Club – Ama’s new restaurant serves Thai food unlike anywhere in Sydney “You’ll feel it as soon as you come in: the music, the vibe, the distinct smell of the herbs and spices.” A first look at the latest venture from the team behind Good Food Guide’s 2026 Critics’ Pick. Bianca Hrovat October 9, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. 1 / 7 The courtyard at Yum Club. STEVEN SIEWERT 2 / 7 Laos sausage, pork meat balls and beef skewers; corn fritters; green mango and crispy anchovy, pork nam tok and kee ga chilli relish. STEVEN SIEWERT 3 / 7 Owners Alisa (‘Nana’) Luangpaseuth, Rowena Rangwan Chansiri, and Rujirada Wongswadiwat. STEVEN SIEWERT 4 / 7 Green mango and crispy anchovy som tum and corn fritters with a chrysanthymum frozen margarita and fresh coconut juice vodka cocktail. STEVEN SIEWERT 5 / 7 Yum Club, Surry Hills. STEVEN SIEWERT 6 / 7 Head chef Min Poohmin has come over from Ama. STEVEN SIEWERT 7 / 7 Yum Club, Surry Hills. STEVEN SIEWERT Previous Slide Next Slide Prepare to join Yum Club – a new Surry Hills restaurant capturing the bold colours, flavours and fun of the Isan region, near Laos in north-eastern Thailand. “Isan food is all about fun. You’ll feel it as soon as you come in – the music, the vibe, the distinct smell of the herbs and spices,” said Rowena Chansiri, who co-founded Yum Club with Alisa “Nana” Luangpaseuth and Rujirada “Mild” Wongswadiwat. Yum Club will open on Monday, October 12. It’s Chansiri’s third venture, following the success of Ickle, her specialty coffee roastery and cafe in Kingsgrove, and Ama, a casual Thai-Chinese restaurant in Surry Hills, awarded the Good Food Guide Critics’ Pick of the Year in 2025. Yum Club. STEVEN SIEWERT



The Yum Club concept was born out of post-shift hangs at Wongswadiwat’s home, where the three women gathered over a charcoal barbecue to grill Isan-style dishes. They met while working at Ickle, when Chansiri was head roaster and Luangpaseuth and Wongswadiwat were baristas, and connected over their love of Isan cuisine. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up While there are several Sydney restaurants with Isan dishes on the menu (such as Nua Lao Thai Kitchen in Haymarket and Kim Yum at World Square) Chansiri is confident that Yum Club is only restaurant in the city serving only Isan food. That means you won’t find some of Thailand’s most popular dishes, including pad Thai and pineapple rice. Instead, there’ll be lots of small share plates, with dishes like crispy corn fritters with sweet chilli sauce, skewers of saucy marinated scallops, and char-grilled pork neck with a side of garlicky rice – perfect for warm evenings in the outdoor courtyard, with an ice bucket of Singha or Chang beers. “For Thai people, Isan food is the go-to for social catch-ups,” Chansiri said. “It’s not fancy, it’s very approachable, a bit like tapas.” Grilled meat skewers, pork nam tok and an icy coconut vodka cocktail. STEVEN SIEWERT



The cuisine was born out of necessity, she explained: small freshwater fish caught from local canals, fermented and made into sauces; sticky rice wrapped in bamboo leaves for easy portability; and the ready availability of fresh produce, such as green papaya and chilli. “It’s very summery food,” said Chansiri. Only proteins are grilled. Yum Club divides the menu into six main categories of Isan cuisine: fried, grilled, skewered, soupy, som tum (aromatic salads) and yum (dishes tossed with fresh chilli and sour-savoury dressing). Head chef Min Poohmin, who moves over from Ama, adapted many of the recipes from Wongswadiwat’s Laotian mother Muay Nattapon. “Isan food is very similar to Laos food, just twisted with Thai taste and ingredients,” said Chansiri, who recommends ordering at least one dish from four categories for the full experience. The pork larb, Laos sausage skewers, tum mua (green papaya and Vietnamese pork with pickled vegetables and crackling) and om (a fragrant chicken or beef stew) are a good place to start. Head chef Min Poohmin in the kitchen. STEVEN SIEWERT Most seating is outdoors, in a shady courtyard out the back, but there’s capacity for 10 inside and a few more on the footpath. Yum Club will take bookings, while reserving a few tables for walk-in diners.



“The thing I really enjoy about running a restaurant is being able to communicate through food and do something that’s kind of new for local people,” Chansiri said. “It’s our pride to tell you about our food and culture, and people connect through food easily because you can talk about it, taste it, feel it – it’s a joyful experience for me.” Shop 1/265 Crown Street, Surry Hills, instagram.com/yumclub.sydney

World.title: Chaos in Sydney’s CBD after alleged carjacking, crash outside Queen Victoria Building
World.content:
Updated NationalNSWCrime Chaos in Sydney’s CBD after alleged carjacking, crash outside Queen Victoria Building Daniel Lo Surdo Updated October 9, 2026 — 11:07am ,first published October 9, 2026 — 6:58am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. A South Australian man visiting Sydney will be charged after allegedly carjacking a Mazda and driving erratically down George Street, hitting a pedestrian and crashing into a police car in front of stunned Thursday-night shoppers. The 36-year-old man appeared covered in blood and dressed only in his underwear when he was arrested outside the Queen Victoria Building about 9pm on Thursday, shocking onlookers leaving work and enjoying late-night shopping. A man was arrested outside the Queen Victoria Building after an alleged carjacking. TNV The man who was arrested on October 8 after a police pursuit ended in a major collision at the corner of Market and George streets in Sydney’s CBD after 9pm. TNV He allegedly bundled a woman in her 20s out of her Mazda sedan after approaching the parked car at the intersection of King and Pitt streets in Sydney’s CBD, climbing over the roof and bonnet before throwing out the driver.



Police believe it was a random attack, and had fielded calls about the man’s erratic behaviour before the alleged carjacking. Detectives are investigating whether he was affected by drugs at the time of the crash. The man drove along George Street before crashing into a ride-share vehicle near the intersection of Market Street, hitting the driver and female passenger in her 20s. Both were unharmed. The vehicle then allegedly crashed into a marked police car parked near the light rail tracks at the Queen Victoria Building, occupied by two officers uninjured in the collision. They arrested the man, who was treated by police and paramedics on the nearby footpath. Footage from the scene shows the Mazda crashed head-on with the vehicle, next to the light rail stop, while onlookers gathered. A woman walking past the Queen Victoria Building was struck by a bollard dislodged in the collision, suffering injuries to her head. The woman in her 50s, who had been shopping at the precinct before the crash, suffered head injuries and was hospitalised in a stable condition. Police arrest the bloodied man after the collision in the Sydney CBD on October 8. TNV



The alleged carjacker, known to SA Police but not NSW law enforcement, was taken to St Vincent’s Hospital under police guard. He is expected to be charged over the carjacking in the coming hours, once he is discharged from hospital. He may face additional driving offences, pending the results of drug and alcohol testing. Sydney City Police Area Commander Adam Solah described a “chaotic scene” confronting officers on Thursday, and praised first responders at the scene. “There were people out, late-night shopping outside the Queen Victoria Building, it was very crowded, we were very lucky that no one was seriously injured,” Solah said. “A number of bystanders came in to offer medical assistance to everyone who was involved, and they did a really good job.” The police car parked on George Street is regularly stationed by the QVB for officers conducting proactive patrols, who are tasked with assisting the flow of traffic in the busy pedestrian area.



The young woman allegedly bundled from her car was shaken by the incident, according to Solah, and was helping police with the investigation. The scene has been cleared, and the light rail is running at normal servicing on Friday morning. World.content:
