The Australian sharemarket has risen at the open with banks driving gains despite falls on Wall Street, with technology stocks slumping after a report said OpenAI’s revenue may be lower than forecast. The S&P/ASX 200 was up 38.7 points, or 0.5 per cent, to 8699.6 in early trade, with six of 11 industry sectors in positive territory. Tech stocks weighed down Wall Street. Bloomberg Financial stocks advanced across the board with Westpac rising 1 per cent while Commonwealth Bank, National Australia Bank and ANZ Bankadded 0.9 per cent. Technology stocks are higher despite sharp falls for technology stocks on Wall Street. Codan added 0.9 per cent, WiseTech gained 1.6 per cent, Xero advanced 2.2 per cent, Technology One climbed 1.2 per cent and NEXTDC gained 0.8 per cent.



Related Article AI Oliver Curtis’ bid to float Firmus for $44 billion falls over Meanwhile, data centre start-up Firmus has withdrawn its plans for a blockbuster listing on the ASX after investors balked at the price and terms, scrapping an initial public offering that would have valued the Australian company at about $43.7 billion. Mining stocks are mixed. BHP lost 0.3 per cent, Fortescue shed 0.6 per cent while Rio Tinto was 0.3 per cent higher. Gold miners are higher after the price of the precious metal rose from a two-month low, with traders assessing the outlook for energy prices after President Donald Trump said the US would not attack Iran before the midterm elections. Bullion climbed as much as 0.9 per cent to trade near $US4146 an ounce. Northern Star added 0.5 per cent and Evolution Mining was 0.7 per cent higher. Energy stocks are mixed as oil prices eased in early Asian trade after Trump’s Iran announcement. West Texas Intermediate dropped toward $US91 barrel while Brent closed above $US104. Woodside Energy dipped 0.3 per cent and Santos added 0.2 per cent in early trade while Ampol was flat and Viva Energy shed 0.9 per cent. The Australian dollar was trading at US69.59¢.



Overnight, the S&P 500 dipped 0.5 per cent for its second-straight loss after setting its all-time high. The Dow Jones closed flat and the Nasdaq finished 1.3 per cent lower. Related Article Analysis

IPO Oliver Curtis’ transformation from jailbird to corporate kingpin has gone awry Nvidia, the chip company that’s ridden the tidal wave of demand created by the artificial-intelligence technology frenzy, fell 2.9 per cent and was one of Thursday’s heaviest weights on the S&P 500. Tech and AI-linked stocks fell around midday amid multiple bearish headlines. The Financial Times reported OpenAI’s annualised revenue is $US20 billion ($28.7 billion) less than previously signalled. Oracle slid following a report it was trucking natural gas to server farms as a workaround to power bottlenecks. That was even though a bellwether for the chip industry, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., reported growth for September that suggested its revenue for the latest quarter was strong enough to top analysts’ expectations. TSMC’s stock that trades in the United States fell 1.4 per cent. Wall Street also felt pressure from more sharp swings within the bond market.



The yield on the 10-year Treasury veered from 5.28 per cent late on Wednesday to 5.35 per cent early on Thursday morning. It then fell back to 5.26 per cent. Despite all the back and forth, it remains near its highest level since 2002 and well above its 3.97 per cent level from before the war with Iran began because of worries about high inflation, big government debt loads and other factors. Also helping to support yields was the latest report to suggest the US economy is continuing to chug along. Fewer US workers applied for unemployment benefits last week, which may mean companies are laying off fewer workers. Higher yields can slow the economy by making it more expensive for everyone to borrow money. High yields also put downward pressure on prices for stocks and other investments, and those seen as the most expensive often feel the brunt. That raises the pressure on companies to deliver big growth in profits, which can offset the downward push on their stock prices from higher bond yields. A big reason for the S&P 500’s rally to a record is that analysts expect companies in the index to deliver nearly 30 per cent growth in earnings per share this upcoming reporting season.



Related Article Opinion

Trade wars Europe raids Trump’s tool box for new ‘trade bazooka’ against China Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist That’s a high bar. Levi Strauss reported a bigger profit for its latest quarter than analysts expected, while raising its forecast for profit over its full fiscal year. But its stock nevertheless fell 2.4 per cent after its growth in revenue fell short of analysts’ expectations. PepsiCo, in contrast, added 3.7 per cent after reporting stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected and highlighting strength outside of North America. It, though, cut its forecast for an underlying measure of profit this fiscal year. Expectations are likely not as high for PepsiCo as for other companies because its stock came into the day with a drop of nearly 14 per cent for the year so far. That compares with gains of nearly 15 per cent for the S&P 500 and 27.3 per cent for Nvidia over the same time, which are both near their records.



In stock markets abroad, South Korea’s Kospi fell 2.6 per cent for one of the world’s larger losses. It was hurt by a 2.4 per cent drop for Samsung Electronics, one of its two dominant stocks. The tech giant said its operating profit for the latest quarter likely soared to $US107.4 trillion Korean won ($110 billion) from $US12.17 trillion won a year earlier, but that wasn’t enough to satisfy investors. Indexes fell across much of the rest of Asia and Europe. With AP, Bloomberg The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. World.title: ‘Not all hope is lost’: Troye Sivan, pop’s ultimate party boy, is just looking for love
World.content:
Troye Sivan after the Rush: “A lot of this album was me trying to figure out… how do I want the next 10 years of my life to look?”

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Troye Sivan is lonely. Across much of his fantastically strange new album She’s the Best the Aussie pop star is in a funk, alienated in hotel rooms and yearning (often quite desperately) for The One. I have a theory on all this, I tell Sivan. I’m trying to explain it to him while a record label publicist sternly messages me to “keep the discussion focused on music”, as though it isn’t all the same thing. It’s the weddings, I say. He was there at his bestie Charli XCX’s lavish Sicilian wedding, right? “Yes,” says Sivan. Was he at Taylor Swift’s wedding? “No …” he replies. (My bad, I should’ve known that, considering Charli and Swift’s icy detente. Pop stars have to pick sides, too.) Was he at Dua Lipa’s wedding? “I was,” he replies. That’s what I’m saying: it’s a lot of weddings to go to within a year. And big weddings, too. Probably, in fact, the biggest weddings, judging by tabloid attention. All those weddings can get to a singleton’s head; leave you wondering what you’re doing wrong. Especially at the tender age of 31, which Sivan turned in June. “I think that’s definitely part of it,” says Sivan. “I grew up in suburban Perth and then lived in a very tight-knit Jewish community in Melbourne. Everyone turns 26-ish and gets married. That’s just what we do! But I felt no pressure from that because I had other-ised myself so much by moving overseas and being gay and whatever, so I was like, OK, I don’t need to follow the same timeline as everyone else.



“And then, all of a sudden, my music industry friends who are busier than me are getting married and it’s like, OK, that’s not an excuse any more. They have crazier work schedules than I do and they managed to get married, so I’m like, f---! What do I do? Maybe I do need to get on it. I definitely started to feel the normal kind of societal pressure, where I’m like, oh, it’s time, for sure.” Sivan, ever the jet-setter, is speaking from a hotel bed in Austin, Texas. Later that evening he’ll take the stage at the Austin City Limits festival, where headline act Charli XCX has gifted him several minutes of her stage time to debut songs from his new album. Much of She’s the Best looks to reset the public perception that attached itself to Sivan following the wild success of his chart-topping 2023 album Something to Give Each Other. That album, with its clubby hedonism and post-lockdown celebration of Melbourne’s queer nightlife, established Sivan as pop’s ultimate party boy. His subsequent Sweat tour – a co-headlining gig with Charli XCX at her “Brat summer” peak – found Sivan deftly at pop culture’s apex, where slime-green celebrity cameos and Apple cam-dances went viral every night. From an outside perspective it seemed crazy: non-stop parties, glitz and decadent glamour. Each time we’d see Sivan he’d be at a Met Gala or walking at Paris Fashion Week or, yes, at a wedding, with another beautiful celebrity from my fantasy list of famous friends. “Oh, really?” says Sivan. “Like who?” I mean, Charli, obviously. Rachel Sennott and Lily-Rose Depp (his co-stars in the much-maligned The Idol; the latter also sings in French on She’s the Best’s closing track). Is pop icon Addison Rae in his crew? “Yep,” he says.



Who else, The Bear’s Ayo Edebiri? “She’s part of it, too, yeah. Love Ayo,” says Sivan. See what I mean? “Yeah, all very, very funny women.” What’s it feel like being in those spaces? When Sivan’s doing the Sweat tour, for example, does he realise he’s sitting in on a generation’s coolest party? “Definitely,” he says. “That was a special time, and I think we were all very aware of how special it was while it was happening. It was this kind of ‘stars aligning’ moment. [Sivan’s single] Rush came out and it started to do better than most of my other stuff, and then Brat came out and it was this absolute tsunami in our lives. It was magical.” Sivan onstage at Madison Square Garden during his sold-out Sweat tour with Charli XCX. Getty Images for MSG Entertainment Holdings, LLC She’s the Best feels like the natural, inevitable, discombobulating comedown. Across the album Sivan paints a picture of himself alone in fancy hotel rooms in a post-gig high, self-pleasuring while dreaming of the special boy he’s yet to meet (or worse, an ex he won’t forget). You can practically see him staring into the vanity mirror, humming The Smiths’ I Know It’s Over to himself: “If you’re so very entertaining … why do you sleep alone tonight?” How heavy did he get with those thoughts? Were there dark nights of the soul amid the comedown? “I think that, you know, it’s easy to not really know how to process stuff like that,” Sivan says of his sudden disillusionment with his post-Rush frenzy. “One also kind of exacerbates the other, where you just get busier and start leaving less time for things that might ground you, and then it can be a bit of a spiral.



“I think I needed to take some time off, to try to fill my cup in ways other than work. But it became easier to isolate and hide behind the work and just keep going, rather than addressing all the feelings. I think a lot of the writing process for this album was me trying to work through that tension and figure out, OK, what do I actually want? How do I feel about what’s been happening? How do I want the next 10 years of my life to look?” That process takes Sivan to some nakedly vulnerable places. On the sample-delic highlight I Do This for You he’s vamping onstage in line with his hedonistic persona, before literal pop-up ads – “Find hot singles in the Los Angeles area!” – interject with a hard dose of reality. “It’s a pop-up ad I’m getting on my computer while I’m trying to get to a porn site,” Sivan explains. “It made me laugh but it was also unfortunately so true – the idea that I’m performing on stage, like, ‘Hey, I’m the best’, and then going home to the reality of it. It sums up the whole album in one song.” ‘I think if I felt the need to ask the person to sign an NDA, I’m on a date with the wrong person.’ On Sex Star, another album highlight, he mocks his own oversexed image – “Got a fake tan and a trainer/Got a six-pack and coconut skin” – as the song devolves into lusty desperation. “That song literally started with me getting a personal trainer and getting a spray tan,” Sivan says, laughing. “I was like, I’m really trying to become what I think guys want. I’m skinny and pale but maybe if I was ripped and tanned, things would be different. “It comes back to the disconnect I was feeling. I was on stage promoting this very hypersexual image and album [Something to Give Each Other], and for a time that felt true. But I just didn’t feel like that in my everyday life any more.” Unlike the casual libertine of yore, much of the album – Cowboy, Le Boy, FF, Love So Big It Hurts – finds Sivan yearning for true love. It begs the question: what’s it like going on dates now as Troye Sivan? Does the other person have to sign an NDA or something?



Sivan laughs, and the publicist’s warning pops up again. “No NDAs. I think if I felt the need to ask the person to sign an NDA, I’m on a date with the wrong person,” he says. “I’ve been living in New York for a couple of months now for the first time in my life and I’m finding it really easy to meet people in real life. So not all hope is lost, I would say.” It’s odd seeing such discomfort in pop-star life from Sivan, who just an album ago was relishing the spotlight. It must be the Australian in him; we’re not built for such self-aggrandisement. I ask him if he’s ever seen the documentary In Bed with Madonna. “I haven’t,” he says, shockingly. Sivan, all dressed up on his way to this year’s Met Gala in May. Charles Sykes/Invision/AP To me, that film feels like the ultimate instructional guide on how a pop star should live. Set during her 1990 Blond Ambition world tour, Madonna revels in all of it. In one scene, talking to her then-bestie Sandra Bernhard, Madonna casually decides she’s attracted to Antonio Banderas and that she’s going to fly to Madrid to hook up with him. Barely a scene later she’s flirting with Banderas at dinner, right in front of his then-wife, Spanish actress Ana Leza. What’s stopping Sivan from living like that? “Wow, OK, I should watch that and take some tips,” Sivan says facetiously. He was onstage with Madonna at the MTV VMAs just last week, when she chanted his instantly viral catchcry – “Party in the bush!” – from his new single, Party (the song samples Madonna’s Music). “Immediately my mind went to Australia,” says Sivan. “I was so proud of that, the queen of the dance floor saying, ‘Party in the bush!’” One of the fun things around this album’s rollout has been watching Americans trying to decipher Sivan’s heavy Australianisms. Most are clueless, but I’d imagine Madonna knows what a bush doof is. “I think so, yeah,” says Sivan.

World.title: No such thing as a free lunch: Doctors ‘heavily influenced’ by pharma freebies, major review finds
World.content:
NationalHealthcare No such thing as a free lunch: Doctors ‘heavily influenced’ by pharma freebies, major review finds Rachel Rasker October 9, 2026 — 11:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Money and meals given to doctors by pharmaceutical companies increased inappropriate prescribing, leaving patients with drugs that were more expensive, had fewer benefits or were not clinically necessary, a major global review finds. The first-of-its-kind Cochrane review – considered the gold standard in healthcare research – analysed millions of doctors’ prescribing practices across 93 studies to understand how visits from sales representatives, sponsored educational opportunities and covered travel influenced prescribing. The first Cochrane review into pharmaceutical marketing has revealed clinicians are heavily influenced. Matt Willis The review, published on Friday, found that pharmaceutical company gifts and payments to doctors increased inappropriate prescribing and the number of prescriptions they wrote, and likely affected how much patients spent on prescriptions. “Doctors often think that … they can’t be bought for the price of a sandwich but the data shows this is an effective marketing strategy,” said the review’s lead author, University of Sydney professor in pharmacy Barbara Mintzes.



“The more free meals a doctor receives, the more likely they are to prescribe less appropriate or more expensive drugs,” Mintzes said. The studies compared doctors who received payments and gifts or met with sales representatives with other doctors who did not meet with representatives, or who had fewer of these interactions. Most of the studies included in the review were US-based because of the availability of vast amounts of detailed data, with pharmaceutical companies publicly reporting all payments to prescribers that could be compared with individual doctors’ prescribing data. While it also included European reports, no Australian studies were included in the review because this granular-level data isn’t available. But co-author Associate Professor Geoff Spurling at the University of Queensland said these marketing tactics were “all around the world, in every country … including Australia”, despite its national medical code of conduct setting clear restrictions on gifts, inducements and hospitality that could influence prescribing.



Related Article Exclusive

Healthcare Healthcare workers champion green alternative to multibillion-dollar industry Pharmaceutical lobbying was “totally commonplace” in Australia, said Spurling, also a GP. “A lot of doctors will say, ‘Oh, a cheap meal’s not going to be an issue’, or, ‘a pen’s not going to be an issue’. But of course it is an issue, and the review found that even $13 meals influence prescribing,” Spurling said. “The problem for doctors is that they think … they’re too smart to be influenced, and that may even make them more vulnerable.” Measures of appropriate prescribing differed across papers. One study found clinicians prescribed more antibiotics for coughs and colds if they were more exposed to promotional interactions. Another measured how often doctors prescribed opioids at a dangerous dose level.



“[On] the flip side, the doctors who were having [fewer] interactions with pharmaceutical companies were prescribing more appropriately,” Mintzes said. Environments with strong conflict-of-interest policies also had more appropriate prescribing, she said. Dr Adrian Pokorny, a Sydney-based medical oncologist and co-author of a separate, Australian-based report published earlier this year, said the review’s findings were “completely unsurprising”. His study found that more than 104,000 payments to attend educational meetings, worth $164.4 million, were made to about 23,500 Australian healthcare professionals between 2015 and 2024. “There’s a really small percentage [1 per cent] of clinicians who receive the lion’s share of these payments from industry,” Pokorny said.



Almost 86 per cent of specialists in Pokorny’s specialty – haematology and oncology – received at least one payment from a pharmaceutical company between 2015 and 2024. Pokorny said doctors’ involvement with the pharmaceutical industry was, in some ways, unavoidable, given their sponsorship of clinical trials and conferences. “It’s a difficult one because … you can’t say that we should have absolutely no interaction with the pharmaceutical industry whatsoever,” he said. “It’s not like anybody else has put up their hand to do adequate education for clinicians. “But the research is driven by profit and … when it becomes a financial relationship, it becomes very murky because, as the Cochrane review rightly shows, those financial relationships can affect prescribing.”



Royal Australian College of General Practitioners president Dr Michael Wright said the review raised legitimate concerns about the influence of commercial relationships on prescribing behaviour but said Australia has protections in place under the medical code of conduct. Related Article Exclusive

Healthcare ‘Patients want answers’: Why the health practitioner watchdog needs to show it’s working A spokesperson for the Medical Board of Australia said it took regulatory action when practitioners failed to appropriately manage conflicts of interest, including by accepting gifts or inducements that could affect, or be seen to affect, their professional judgment. Medicines Australia’s disclosure log provides the public with a searchable database of significant payments and transfers made to healthcare professionals by its pharmaceutical company members. Australian Medical Association vice president Associate Professor Julian Rait said doctors must manage relationships with pharmaceutical companies appropriately.



“The overriding principle guiding doctors’ relationships with industry is the primacy of patient care,” Rait said in a statement. “Patients and the wider community expect doctors to uphold this duty and put patients’ interests above their own personal interests or the interests of industry.” Mintzes said implementing stronger conflict-of-interest policies across hospitals, government and medical schools would improve prescribing and protect patients. World.title: ATO credit card ban delayed after backlash
World.content:
Breaking PoliticsFederalCredit cards ATO credit card ban delayed after backlash Nick Newling October 9, 2026 — 11:26am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. The Australian Taxation Office’s controversial banning of credit card payments will no longer come into effect at the end of next month, after the government negotiated with the independent agency to delay the change. Treasurer Jim Chalmers will allocate additional funds to the agency to support a year-long transition period, after the ban – which was set to come into effect on November 30 – came under heavy criticism. Treasurer Jim Chalmers. Louie Douvis The announcement comes after fierce pushback from the business community, opposition parties and some members of the Labor backbench that saw the ATO’s decision as damaging to the cash-flow management of small businesses. Appearing on morning television on Friday, Environment Minister Murray Watt said the ATO’s plan to ban credit car payments for tax bills so as not to burden all taxpayers with the associated costs was a completely “independent decision”.



“When they made clear that they intended to proceed with this, we insisted on them having a good transition plan with the business community and to consult with the business community about that,” Watt told Seven’s Sunrise. “We expect them to do that consultation properly. I mean, I think we need to keep it in perspective that when it comes to payments to the ATO, it’s only a very small number of taxpayers who pay their tax payments by credit card, it’s about 5 per cent for small businesses and about 2 per cent for individuals.” Deputy Liberal leader Jane Hume during a doorstop at Parliament House in Canberra. Dominic Lorrimer Following the October 1 introduction of bans on credit card surcharges, the tax office surprised small business owners in announcing a November 30 cut-off date for credit card payments. The government produced mixed messaging on the topic on Thursday, when Housing Minister Clare O’Neil shared the government’s “real concerns” about the plan, countered by Assistant Minister Andrew Charlton who said the government supported the decision.



The government offered a more unified message on Friday, with Watt joined by Foreign Minister Penny Wong, who encouraged the tax office to perform meaningful consultation on the ban, while Defence Industry Minister Pat Conroy said the ATO should “do their job and talk to small businesses”. Related Article Credit cards Labor ministers contradict each other over ATO credit card surcharge ban Wong also reiterated the independence of the tax office, as deputy Liberal leader Jane Hume questioned “who is in charge”. “You can change this with a stroke of a pen. You can change this with a decision. Small businesses are crying out for a change. They are asking for your help,” Hume told Sunrise, “You just have to have the will, and you can’t blame the ATO. They’re your agency. You’re the government. You should do this”. Several Labor MPs speaking to this masthead on the condition of anonymity shared their concerns over the way the government’s relationship with small business was being framed, but stressed the ATO had blindsided the government but were difficult to wrangle because of their independence.



“It’s just alarming that were seeing this sort of behaviour from the ATO. It’s overreach, it’s hostile they need to remember who they serve. I’m hoping that they reverse this and find efficiencies elsewhere to cover the cost,” one senator said, questioning why the Reserve Bank had not foreshadowed such moves. Another said the ATO had likely made the right decision in finding value for the taxpayer, but had botched the transition and needed to “pull its head out of the sand”. “People probably don’t realise how completely totally independent the tax office is of the government of the day, for good reasons, but yes, sometimes it is completely infuriating,” they said. Concern in the Labor ranks that the party is failing to meet small business owners appears to be growing, with one particularly strident MP laying the blame directly at the feet of cabinet. “I don’t think it’s acceptable for us to say it was the ATO’s decision not ours. If that’s the case, then there’s something seriously wrong with our government. If the ATO can dictate policy like this without government oversight and agreement, I don’t quite understand that government,” the MP said.



“I just think there is no one in cabinet with any small business experience. We have a small business minister that knows nothing about small business. We need someone with some guts to stand up to the tax office. I think it’s very, very disappointing”. Small Business Minister Anne Aly was the first government minister to raise concerns over the ATO’s move on Wednesday, urging the tax office to consult more widely about the ban’s implementation. One MP, who is factionally unaligned with Aly, dismissed the criticism of cabinet, saying: “This is an argument as old as representative democracy itself. I get that having that background is good, but you can’t have a government made up of experts”. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. World.title: A Room With a View is fun … but we’re told too much instead of being allowed to work it out
World.content:
Belvoir St Theatre, October 7, until November 1

Knowing if you’ve fallen in lust is straightforward; knowing if you’ve fallen in love, more elusive. In E. M. Forster’s novel A Room with a View, Lucy Honeychurch is even confused by lust, so has little chance with love – at least not without wise counsel. But then, she lives in starched Edwardian England, where pretence and hypocrisy rule, and therefore, as the Reverend Mr Beebe says, “It can be so difficult to understand people who speak the truth.”

Star of A Room With A View Nathalie Morris. Steven Siewert

Grace Chapple’s new stage adaptation, directed by Hannah Goodwin, is a brave undertaking. In 1985, Merchant Ivory threw a galaxy of stars at their film version, and even the peerless Daniel Day-Lewis struggled as Cecil, the man with whom Lucy thinks she’s fallen in love.

Forster’s prose and view of humanity share an airiness, and his characters are cheapened by excessive caricature. Underscoring his work is a benevolence best encapsulated by Mr Emerson, a humanist and socialist who believes in maximising life’s potential.

World.content:
Exclusive Eating outJust open Join Yum Club – Ama’s new restaurant serves Thai food unlike anywhere in Sydney “You’ll feel it as soon as you come in: the music, the vibe, the distinct smell of the herbs and spices.” A first look at the latest venture from the team behind Good Food Guide’s 2026 Critics’ Pick. Bianca Hrovat October 9, 2026 Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. 1 / 7 The courtyard at Yum Club. STEVEN SIEWERT 2 / 7 Laos sausage, pork meat balls and beef skewers; corn fritters; green mango and crispy anchovy, pork nam tok and kee ga chilli relish. STEVEN SIEWERT 3 / 7 Owners Alisa (‘Nana’) Luangpaseuth, Rowena Rangwan Chansiri, and Rujirada Wongswadiwat. STEVEN SIEWERT 4 / 7 Green mango and crispy anchovy som tum and corn fritters with a chrysanthymum frozen margarita and fresh coconut juice vodka cocktail. STEVEN SIEWERT 5 / 7 Yum Club, Surry Hills. STEVEN SIEWERT 6 / 7 Head chef Min Poohmin has come over from Ama. STEVEN SIEWERT 7 / 7 Yum Club, Surry Hills. STEVEN SIEWERT Previous Slide Next Slide Prepare to join Yum Club – a new Surry Hills restaurant capturing the bold colours, flavours and fun of the Isan region, near Laos in north-eastern Thailand. “Isan food is all about fun. You’ll feel it as soon as you come in – the music, the vibe, the distinct smell of the herbs and spices,” said Rowena Chansiri, who co-founded Yum Club with Alisa “Nana” Luangpaseuth and Rujirada “Mild” Wongswadiwat. Yum Club will open on Monday, October 12. It’s Chansiri’s third venture, following the success of Ickle, her specialty coffee roastery and cafe in Kingsgrove, and Ama, a casual Thai-Chinese restaurant in Surry Hills, awarded the Good Food Guide Critics’ Pick of the Year in 2025. Yum Club. STEVEN SIEWERT



The Yum Club concept was born out of post-shift hangs at Wongswadiwat’s home, where the three women gathered over a charcoal barbecue to grill Isan-style dishes. They met while working at Ickle, when Chansiri was head roaster and Luangpaseuth and Wongswadiwat were baristas, and connected over their love of Isan cuisine. Restaurant reviews, news and the hottest openings served to your inbox. Sign up While there are several Sydney restaurants with Isan dishes on the menu (such as Nua Lao Thai Kitchen in Haymarket and Kim Yum at World Square) Chansiri is confident that Yum Club is only restaurant in the city serving only Isan food. That means you won’t find some of Thailand’s most popular dishes, including pad Thai and pineapple rice. Instead, there’ll be lots of small share plates, with dishes like crispy corn fritters with sweet chilli sauce, skewers of saucy marinated scallops, and char-grilled pork neck with a side of garlicky rice – perfect for warm evenings in the outdoor courtyard, with an ice bucket of Singha or Chang beers. “For Thai people, Isan food is the go-to for social catch-ups,” Chansiri said. “It’s not fancy, it’s very approachable, a bit like tapas.” Grilled meat skewers, pork nam tok and an icy coconut vodka cocktail. STEVEN SIEWERT



The cuisine was born out of necessity, she explained: small freshwater fish caught from local canals, fermented and made into sauces; sticky rice wrapped in bamboo leaves for easy portability; and the ready availability of fresh produce, such as green papaya and chilli. “It’s very summery food,” said Chansiri. Only proteins are grilled. Yum Club divides the menu into six main categories of Isan cuisine: fried, grilled, skewered, soupy, som tum (aromatic salads) and yum (dishes tossed with fresh chilli and sour-savoury dressing). Head chef Min Poohmin, who moves over from Ama, adapted many of the recipes from Wongswadiwat’s Laotian mother Muay Nattapon. “Isan food is very similar to Laos food, just twisted with Thai taste and ingredients,” said Chansiri, who recommends ordering at least one dish from four categories for the full experience. The pork larb, Laos sausage skewers, tum mua (green papaya and Vietnamese pork with pickled vegetables and crackling) and om (a fragrant chicken or beef stew) are a good place to start. Head chef Min Poohmin in the kitchen. STEVEN SIEWERT Most seating is outdoors, in a shady courtyard out the back, but there’s capacity for 10 inside and a few more on the footpath. Yum Club will take bookings, while reserving a few tables for walk-in diners.



“The thing I really enjoy about running a restaurant is being able to communicate through food and do something that’s kind of new for local people,” Chansiri said. “It’s our pride to tell you about our food and culture, and people connect through food easily because you can talk about it, taste it, feel it – it’s a joyful experience for me.” Shop 1/265 Crown Street, Surry Hills, instagram.com/yumclub.sydney

World.title: Chaos in Sydney’s CBD after alleged carjacking, crash outside Queen Victoria Building
World.content:
Updated NationalNSWCrime Chaos in Sydney’s CBD after alleged carjacking, crash outside Queen Victoria Building Daniel Lo Surdo Updated October 9, 2026 — 11:07am ,first published October 9, 2026 — 6:58am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. A South Australian man visiting Sydney will be charged after allegedly carjacking a Mazda and driving erratically down George Street, hitting a pedestrian and crashing into a police car in front of stunned Thursday-night shoppers. The 36-year-old man appeared covered in blood and dressed only in his underwear when he was arrested outside the Queen Victoria Building about 9pm on Thursday, shocking onlookers leaving work and enjoying late-night shopping. A man was arrested outside the Queen Victoria Building after an alleged carjacking. TNV The man who was arrested on October 8 after a police pursuit ended in a major collision at the corner of Market and George streets in Sydney’s CBD after 9pm. TNV He allegedly bundled a woman in her 20s out of her Mazda sedan after approaching the parked car at the intersection of King and Pitt streets in Sydney’s CBD, climbing over the roof and bonnet before throwing out the driver.



Police believe it was a random attack, and had fielded calls about the man’s erratic behaviour before the alleged carjacking. Detectives are investigating whether he was affected by drugs at the time of the crash. The man drove along George Street before crashing into a ride-share vehicle near the intersection of Market Street, hitting the driver and female passenger in her 20s. Both were unharmed. The vehicle then allegedly crashed into a marked police car parked near the light rail tracks at the Queen Victoria Building, occupied by two officers uninjured in the collision. They arrested the man, who was treated by police and paramedics on the nearby footpath. Footage from the scene shows the Mazda crashed head-on with the vehicle, next to the light rail stop, while onlookers gathered. A woman walking past the Queen Victoria Building was struck by a bollard dislodged in the collision, suffering injuries to her head. The woman in her 50s, who had been shopping at the precinct before the crash, suffered head injuries and was hospitalised in a stable condition. Police arrest the bloodied man after the collision in the Sydney CBD on October 8. TNV



The alleged carjacker, known to SA Police but not NSW law enforcement, was taken to St Vincent’s Hospital under police guard. He is expected to be charged over the carjacking in the coming hours, once he is discharged from hospital. He may face additional driving offences, pending the results of drug and alcohol testing. Sydney City Police Area Commander Adam Solah described a “chaotic scene” confronting officers on Thursday, and praised first responders at the scene. “There were people out, late-night shopping outside the Queen Victoria Building, it was very crowded, we were very lucky that no one was seriously injured,” Solah said. “A number of bystanders came in to offer medical assistance to everyone who was involved, and they did a really good job.” The police car parked on George Street is regularly stationed by the QVB for officers conducting proactive patrols, who are tasked with assisting the flow of traffic in the busy pedestrian area.



The young woman allegedly bundled from her car was shaken by the incident, according to Solah, and was helping police with the investigation. The scene has been cleared, and the light rail is running at normal servicing on Friday morning. World.title: Banks boost ASX, Wall Street slides after OpenAI warning
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets Banks boost ASX, Wall Street slides after OpenAI warning Staff writers Updated October 9, 2026 — 11:01am ,first published October 9, 2026 — 5:20am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. The Australian sharemarket has risen at the open with banks driving gains despite falls on Wall Street, with technology stocks slumping after a report said OpenAI’s revenue may be lower than forecast. The S&P/ASX 200 was up 38.7 points, or 0.5 per cent, to 8699.6 in early trade, with six of 11 industry sectors in positive territory. Tech stocks weighed down Wall Street. Bloomberg Financial stocks advanced across the board with Westpac rising 1 per cent while Commonwealth Bank, National Australia Bank and ANZ Bankadded 0.9 per cent. Technology stocks are higher despite sharp falls for technology stocks on Wall Street. Codan added 0.9 per cent, WiseTech gained 1.6 per cent, Xero advanced 2.2 per cent, Technology One climbed 1.2 per cent and NEXTDC gained 0.8 per cent.



Related Article AI Oliver Curtis’ bid to float Firmus for $44 billion falls over Meanwhile, data centre start-up Firmus has withdrawn its plans for a blockbuster listing on the ASX after investors balked at the price and terms, scrapping an initial public offering that would have valued the Australian company at about $43.7 billion. Mining stocks are mixed. BHP lost 0.3 per cent, Fortescue shed 0.6 per cent while Rio Tinto was 0.3 per cent higher. Gold miners are higher after the price of the precious metal rose from a two-month low, with traders assessing the outlook for energy prices after President Donald Trump said the US would not attack Iran before the midterm elections. Bullion climbed as much as 0.9 per cent to trade near $US4146 an ounce. Northern Star added 0.5 per cent and Evolution Mining was 0.7 per cent higher. Energy stocks are mixed as oil prices eased in early Asian trade after Trump’s Iran announcement. West Texas Intermediate dropped toward $US91 barrel while Brent closed above $US104. Woodside Energy dipped 0.3 per cent and Santos added 0.2 per cent in early trade while Ampol was flat and Viva Energy shed 0.9 per cent. The Australian dollar was trading at US69.59¢.



Overnight, the S&P 500 dipped 0.5 per cent for its second-straight loss after setting its all-time high. The Dow Jones closed flat and the Nasdaq finished 1.3 per cent lower. Related Article Analysis

IPO Oliver Curtis’ transformation from jailbird to corporate kingpin has gone awry Nvidia, the chip company that’s ridden the tidal wave of demand created by the artificial-intelligence technology frenzy, fell 2.9 per cent and was one of Thursday’s heaviest weights on the S&P 500. Tech and AI-linked stocks fell around midday amid multiple bearish headlines. The Financial Times reported OpenAI’s annualised revenue is $US20 billion ($28.7 billion) less than previously signalled. Oracle slid following a report it was trucking natural gas to server farms as a workaround to power bottlenecks. That was even though a bellwether for the chip industry, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., reported growth for September that suggested its revenue for the latest quarter was strong enough to top analysts’ expectations. TSMC’s stock that trades in the United States fell 1.4 per cent. Wall Street also felt pressure from more sharp swings within the bond market.



The yield on the 10-year Treasury veered from 5.28 per cent late on Wednesday to 5.35 per cent early on Thursday morning. It then fell back to 5.26 per cent. Despite all the back and forth, it remains near its highest level since 2002 and well above its 3.97 per cent level from before the war with Iran began because of worries about high inflation, big government debt loads and other factors. Also helping to support yields was the latest report to suggest the US economy is continuing to chug along. Fewer US workers applied for unemployment benefits last week, which may mean companies are laying off fewer workers. Higher yields can slow the economy by making it more expensive for everyone to borrow money. High yields also put downward pressure on prices for stocks and other investments, and those seen as the most expensive often feel the brunt. That raises the pressure on companies to deliver big growth in profits, which can offset the downward push on their stock prices from higher bond yields. A big reason for the S&P 500’s rally to a record is that analysts expect companies in the index to deliver nearly 30 per cent growth in earnings per share this upcoming reporting season.



Related Article Opinion

Trade wars Europe raids Trump’s tool box for new ‘trade bazooka’ against China Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist That’s a high bar. Levi Strauss reported a bigger profit for its latest quarter than analysts expected, while raising its forecast for profit over its full fiscal year. But its stock nevertheless fell 2.4 per cent after its growth in revenue fell short of analysts’ expectations. PepsiCo, in contrast, added 3.7 per cent after reporting stronger profit and revenue for the latest quarter than analysts expected and highlighting strength outside of North America. It, though, cut its forecast for an underlying measure of profit this fiscal year. Expectations are likely not as high for PepsiCo as for other companies because its stock came into the day with a drop of nearly 14 per cent for the year so far. That compares with gains of nearly 15 per cent for the S&P 500 and 27.3 per cent for Nvidia over the same time, which are both near their records.



In stock markets abroad, South Korea’s Kospi fell 2.6 per cent for one of the world’s larger losses. It was hurt by a 2.4 per cent drop for Samsung Electronics, one of its two dominant stocks. The tech giant said its operating profit for the latest quarter likely soared to $US107.4 trillion Korean won ($110 billion) from $US12.17 trillion won a year earlier, but that wasn’t enough to satisfy investors. Indexes fell across much of the rest of Asia and Europe. With AP, Bloomberg The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion. World.title: ‘Not all hope is lost’: Troye Sivan, pop’s ultimate party boy, is just looking for love
World.content:
Troye Sivan after the Rush: “A lot of this album was me trying to figure out… how do I want the next 10 years of my life to look?”

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Troye Sivan is lonely. Across much of his fantastically strange new album She’s the Best the Aussie pop star is in a funk, alienated in hotel rooms and yearning (often quite desperately) for The One. I have a theory on all this, I tell Sivan. I’m trying to explain it to him while a record label publicist sternly messages me to “keep the discussion focused on music”, as though it isn’t all the same thing. It’s the weddings, I say. He was there at his bestie Charli XCX’s lavish Sicilian wedding, right? “Yes,” says Sivan. Was he at Taylor Swift’s wedding? “No …” he replies. (My bad, I should’ve known that, considering Charli and Swift’s icy detente. Pop stars have to pick sides, too.) Was he at Dua Lipa’s wedding? “I was,” he replies. That’s what I’m saying: it’s a lot of weddings to go to within a year. And big weddings, too. Probably, in fact, the biggest weddings, judging by tabloid attention. All those weddings can get to a singleton’s head; leave you wondering what you’re doing wrong. Especially at the tender age of 31, which Sivan turned in June. “I think that’s definitely part of it,” says Sivan. “I grew up in suburban Perth and then lived in a very tight-knit Jewish community in Melbourne. Everyone turns 26-ish and gets married. That’s just what we do! But I felt no pressure from that because I had other-ised myself so much by moving overseas and being gay and whatever, so I was like, OK, I don’t need to follow the same timeline as everyone else.



“And then, all of a sudden, my music industry friends who are busier than me are getting married and it’s like, OK, that’s not an excuse any more. They have crazier work schedules than I do and they managed to get married, so I’m like, f---! What do I do? Maybe I do need to get on it. I definitely started to feel the normal kind of societal pressure, where I’m like, oh, it’s time, for sure.” Sivan, ever the jet-setter, is speaking from a hotel bed in Austin, Texas. Later that evening he’ll take the stage at the Austin City Limits festival, where headline act Charli XCX has gifted him several minutes of her stage time to debut songs from his new album. Much of She’s the Best looks to reset the public perception that attached itself to Sivan following the wild success of his chart-topping 2023 album Something to Give Each Other. That album, with its clubby hedonism and post-lockdown celebration of Melbourne’s queer nightlife, established Sivan as pop’s ultimate party boy. His subsequent Sweat tour – a co-headlining gig with Charli XCX at her “Brat summer” peak – found Sivan deftly at pop culture’s apex, where slime-green celebrity cameos and Apple cam-dances went viral every night. From an outside perspective it seemed crazy: non-stop parties, glitz and decadent glamour. Each time we’d see Sivan he’d be at a Met Gala or walking at Paris Fashion Week or, yes, at a wedding, with another beautiful celebrity from my fantasy list of famous friends. “Oh, really?” says Sivan. “Like who?” I mean, Charli, obviously. Rachel Sennott and Lily-Rose Depp (his co-stars in the much-maligned The Idol; the latter also sings in French on She’s the Best’s closing track). Is pop icon Addison Rae in his crew? “Yep,” he says.



Who else, The Bear’s Ayo Edebiri? “She’s part of it, too, yeah. Love Ayo,” says Sivan. See what I mean? “Yeah, all very, very funny women.” What’s it feel like being in those spaces? When Sivan’s doing the Sweat tour, for example, does he realise he’s sitting in on a generation’s coolest party? “Definitely,” he says. “That was a special time, and I think we were all very aware of how special it was while it was happening. It was this kind of ‘stars aligning’ moment. [Sivan’s single] Rush came out and it started to do better than most of my other stuff, and then Brat came out and it was this absolute tsunami in our lives. It was magical.” Sivan onstage at Madison Square Garden during his sold-out Sweat tour with Charli XCX. Getty Images for MSG Entertainment Holdings, LLC She’s the Best feels like the natural, inevitable, discombobulating comedown. Across the album Sivan paints a picture of himself alone in fancy hotel rooms in a post-gig high, self-pleasuring while dreaming of the special boy he’s yet to meet (or worse, an ex he won’t forget). You can practically see him staring into the vanity mirror, humming The Smiths’ I Know It’s Over to himself: “If you’re so very entertaining … why do you sleep alone tonight?” How heavy did he get with those thoughts? Were there dark nights of the soul amid the comedown? “I think that, you know, it’s easy to not really know how to process stuff like that,” Sivan says of his sudden disillusionment with his post-Rush frenzy. “One also kind of exacerbates the other, where you just get busier and start leaving less time for things that might ground you, and then it can be a bit of a spiral.



“I think I needed to take some time off, to try to fill my cup in ways other than work. But it became easier to isolate and hide behind the work and just keep going, rather than addressing all the feelings. I think a lot of the writing process for this album was me trying to work through that tension and figure out, OK, what do I actually want? How do I feel about what’s been happening? How do I want the next 10 years of my life to look?” That process takes Sivan to some nakedly vulnerable places. On the sample-delic highlight I Do This for You he’s vamping onstage in line with his hedonistic persona, before literal pop-up ads – “Find hot singles in the Los Angeles area!” – interject with a hard dose of reality. “It’s a pop-up ad I’m getting on my computer while I’m trying to get to a porn site,” Sivan explains. “It made me laugh but it was also unfortunately so true – the idea that I’m performing on stage, like, ‘Hey, I’m the best’, and then going home to the reality of it. It sums up the whole album in one song.” ‘I think if I felt the need to ask the person to sign an NDA, I’m on a date with the wrong person.’ On Sex Star, another album highlight, he mocks his own oversexed image – “Got a fake tan and a trainer/Got a six-pack and coconut skin” – as the song devolves into lusty desperation. “That song literally started with me getting a personal trainer and getting a spray tan,” Sivan says, laughing. “I was like, I’m really trying to become what I think guys want. I’m skinny and pale but maybe if I was ripped and tanned, things would be different. “It comes back to the disconnect I was feeling. I was on stage promoting this very hypersexual image and album [Something to Give Each Other], and for a time that felt true. But I just didn’t feel like that in my everyday life any more.” Unlike the casual libertine of yore, much of the album – Cowboy, Le Boy, FF, Love So Big It Hurts – finds Sivan yearning for true love. It begs the question: what’s it like going on dates now as Troye Sivan? Does the other person have to sign an NDA or something?



Sivan laughs, and the publicist’s warning pops up again. “No NDAs. I think if I felt the need to ask the person to sign an NDA, I’m on a date with the wrong person,” he says. “I’ve been living in New York for a couple of months now for the first time in my life and I’m finding it really easy to meet people in real life. So not all hope is lost, I would say.” It’s odd seeing such discomfort in pop-star life from Sivan, who just an album ago was relishing the spotlight. It must be the Australian in him; we’re not built for such self-aggrandisement. I ask him if he’s ever seen the documentary In Bed with Madonna. “I haven’t,” he says, shockingly. Sivan, all dressed up on his way to this year’s Met Gala in May. Charles Sykes/Invision/AP To me, that film feels like the ultimate instructional guide on how a pop star should live. Set during her 1990 Blond Ambition world tour, Madonna revels in all of it. In one scene, talking to her then-bestie Sandra Bernhard, Madonna casually decides she’s attracted to Antonio Banderas and that she’s going to fly to Madrid to hook up with him. Barely a scene later she’s flirting with Banderas at dinner, right in front of his then-wife, Spanish actress Ana Leza. What’s stopping Sivan from living like that? “Wow, OK, I should watch that and take some tips,” Sivan says facetiously. He was onstage with Madonna at the MTV VMAs just last week, when she chanted his instantly viral catchcry – “Party in the bush!” – from his new single, Party (the song samples Madonna’s Music). “Immediately my mind went to Australia,” says Sivan. “I was so proud of that, the queen of the dance floor saying, ‘Party in the bush!’” One of the fun things around this album’s rollout has been watching Americans trying to decipher Sivan’s heavy Australianisms. Most are clueless, but I’d imagine Madonna knows what a bush doof is. “I think so, yeah,” says Sivan.

World.title: No such thing as a free lunch: Doctors ‘heavily influenced’ by pharma freebies, major review finds
World.content:
NationalHealthcare No such thing as a free lunch: Doctors ‘heavily influenced’ by pharma freebies, major review finds Rachel Rasker October 9, 2026 — 11:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Money and meals given to doctors by pharmaceutical companies increased inappropriate prescribing, leaving patients with drugs that were more expensive, had fewer benefits or were not clinically necessary, a major global review finds. The first-of-its-kind Cochrane review – considered the gold standard in healthcare research – analysed millions of doctors’ prescribing practices across 93 studies to understand how visits from sales representatives, sponsored educational opportunities and covered travel influenced prescribing. The first Cochrane review into pharmaceutical marketing has revealed clinicians are heavily influenced. Matt Willis The review, published on Friday, found that pharmaceutical company gifts and payments to doctors increased inappropriate prescribing and the number of prescriptions they wrote, and likely affected how much patients spent on prescriptions. “Doctors often think that … they can’t be bought for the price of a sandwich but the data shows this is an effective marketing strategy,” said the review’s lead author, University of Sydney professor in pharmacy Barbara Mintzes.



“The more free meals a doctor receives, the more likely they are to prescribe less appropriate or more expensive drugs,” Mintzes said. The studies compared doctors who received payments and gifts or met with sales representatives with other doctors who did not meet with representatives, or who had fewer of these interactions. Most of the studies included in the review were US-based because of the availability of vast amounts of detailed data, with pharmaceutical companies publicly reporting all payments to prescribers that could be compared with individual doctors’ prescribing data. While it also included European reports, no Australian studies were included in the review because this granular-level data isn’t available. But co-author Associate Professor Geoff Spurling at the University of Queensland said these marketing tactics were “all around the world, in every country … including Australia”, despite its national medical code of conduct setting clear restrictions on gifts, inducements and hospitality that could influence prescribing.



Related Article Exclusive

Healthcare Healthcare workers champion green alternative to multibillion-dollar industry Pharmaceutical lobbying was “totally commonplace” in Australia, said Spurling, also a GP. “A lot of doctors will say, ‘Oh, a cheap meal’s not going to be an issue’, or, ‘a pen’s not going to be an issue’. But of course it is an issue, and the review found that even $13 meals influence prescribing,” Spurling said. “The problem for doctors is that they think … they’re too smart to be influenced, and that may even make them more vulnerable.” Measures of appropriate prescribing differed across papers. One study found clinicians prescribed more antibiotics for coughs and colds if they were more exposed to promotional interactions. Another measured how often doctors prescribed opioids at a dangerous dose level.



“[On] the flip side, the doctors who were having [fewer] interactions with pharmaceutical companies were prescribing more appropriately,” Mintzes said. Environments with strong conflict-of-interest policies also had more appropriate prescribing, she said. Dr Adrian Pokorny, a Sydney-based medical oncologist and co-author of a separate, Australian-based report published earlier this year, said the review’s findings were “completely unsurprising”. His study found that more than 104,000 payments to attend educational meetings, worth $164.4 million, were made to about 23,500 Australian healthcare professionals between 2015 and 2024. “There’s a really small percentage [1 per cent] of clinicians who receive the lion’s share of these payments from industry,” Pokorny said.



Almost 86 per cent of specialists in Pokorny’s specialty – haematology and oncology – received at least one payment from a pharmaceutical company between 2015 and 2024. Pokorny said doctors’ involvement with the pharmaceutical industry was, in some ways, unavoidable, given their sponsorship of clinical trials and conferences. “It’s a difficult one because … you can’t say that we should have absolutely no interaction with the pharmaceutical industry whatsoever,” he said. “It’s not like anybody else has put up their hand to do adequate education for clinicians. “But the research is driven by profit and … when it becomes a financial relationship, it becomes very murky because, as the Cochrane review rightly shows, those financial relationships can affect prescribing.”



Royal Australian College of General Practitioners president Dr Michael Wright said the review raised legitimate concerns about the influence of commercial relationships on prescribing behaviour but said Australia has protections in place under the medical code of conduct. Related Article Exclusive

Healthcare ‘Patients want answers’: Why the health practitioner watchdog needs to show it’s working A spokesperson for the Medical Board of Australia said it took regulatory action when practitioners failed to appropriately manage conflicts of interest, including by accepting gifts or inducements that could affect, or be seen to affect, their professional judgment. Medicines Australia’s disclosure log provides the public with a searchable database of significant payments and transfers made to healthcare professionals by its pharmaceutical company members. Australian Medical Association vice president Associate Professor Julian Rait said doctors must manage relationships with pharmaceutical companies appropriately.



“The overriding principle guiding doctors’ relationships with industry is the primacy of patient care,” Rait said in a statement. “Patients and the wider community expect doctors to uphold this duty and put patients’ interests above their own personal interests or the interests of industry.” Mintzes said implementing stronger conflict-of-interest policies across hospitals, government and medical schools would improve prescribing and protect patients. World.title: Northern Marianas lacks land to host new major US military base, governor says
World.content:
The Northern Mariana Islands (CNMI) says it does not have enough land to accommodate a massive new United States military base, despite its growing strategic importance in Washington's defence plans for the Pacific.

CNMI's Governor David Apatang said the US Department of War has invited states and territories to identify possible locations for what it calls the next "Great American Base".

However, Apatang said the Northern Marianas would struggle to meet the land requirements.

The total land area of the CNMI is approximately 179 square miles (464 sq km), with a population of under 50,000.

"We just don't have the land requirement that they are looking for in the Commonwealth," he told reporters on Thursday.

Edward Camacho, special assistant to the governor for the Commonwealth Bureau of Military Affairs, said the proposal requires between 100,000 and 250,000 acres of contiguous land, meaning one large, connected area.

The proposed installation would also need adequate electricity, water, schools, healthcare facilities, and housing for military personnel and their families.

Camacho said those requirements would be difficult for the territory, which is already seeking billions of dollars in federal assistance to repair aging infrastructure damaged by successive typhoons.

"So the kind of stuff that we went to ask for is also what they need already," he said.

However, Camacho said the Northern Marianas could still play an important role in the US military's strategy in the Western Pacific through smaller facilities spread across its islands.

"So we may not be a base. We may be a place," he said.

Camacho said military annexes could potentially be established on Saipan, Tinian, Rota, and the Northern Islands.

These could serve as staging areas and logistics hubs, allowing US military vessels to obtain supplies, equipment, and replacement parts without returning to Hawaii or the US mainland.

Camacho said the territory's three airports and three seaports make it strategically valuable, although major infrastructure improvements would be needed to support expanded military operations.

The proposal comes amid an expanding US military presence in the Northern Marianas, particularly on Tinian, where the Pentagon is developing facilities to support military aircraft and operations.

Camacho said the administration intends to respond formally to the Department of War, outlining the territory's land and infrastructure limitations while identifying possible alternatives.

He said the response could be submitted within approximately 10 days, subject to further federal guidance.

World.title: Police puzzled by grisly discovery in Wellington pedestrian tunnel
World.content:
Police want to hear from anyone who has information about a large pool of human blood discovered in a Wellington pedestrian tunnel over the weekend.

Police were called to Coutts Street in Rongotai on Sunday night at 10.40pm after the blood was found. The scene was cordoned off while police conducted a scene examination.

Detective Senior Sergeant Steve Wescott said testing shows it was human blood but they didn't locate anybody in the nearby area.

Police are now asking for the public's help to identify anyone who may have been involved.

The tunnel runs under Wellington Airport. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

"If there is a person involved, our priority is to check on their welfare," Wescott said.

Police want to hear from anyone who was in the area near the tunnel, which runs under the Wellington Airport from Coutts Street, Rongotai, to Miro Street in Miramar, on Sunday evening prior to 10.40pm.

World.title: 'Should not be available': Calls for political support to axe sugary drinks from schools, ECE centres
World.content:
Nineteen public health organisations are calling for cross-party political support to make schools and early childhood education centres sugary drink free.

They say sugary drinks can cause unhealthy weight gain, type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, dental caries, and have negative impacts on concentration, behaviour, and learning.

"Sugar is the biggest driver of that and about 26 percent or over a quarter of the sugar children consume is from sugary drinks," lead author Dr Gerhard Sundborn from the University of Auckland and FIZZ Public Health Advocacy group said.

"This issue warrants cross-party support, the evidence is clear that sugary drinks, which can contain up to 16 teaspoons of sugar in a single serving, harm children's health and undermine their learning. These products should not be available in schools."

Under the proposed policy, drinks that have more than 5g of sugar per 100 millilitres would not be available in schools and childcare centres.

It allowed water, unflavoured milk and zero sugar alternatives.

Sundborn said the policy would improve the health of students and also lower the burden on the health system.

"If we get sugar out of schools it's a step in the right direction and there'll be a lot less harm incurred on children in terms of dental caries but also other health issues and it's going to improve learning as well, so we think it's a no brainer.

"We've been advocating around reducing sugary drink availability of sugary drinks for around 10 years now and we think that there's not much opposition in terms of the public to a policy like this."

Co-author Professor Bodo Lang said the proposed policy still allowed for choice, with alternatives that included more than just water.

"Debate over sugary drinks in schools has become unnecessarily politicised," he said.

"The policy we propose is practical, evidence-based, and still preserves choice through the availability of zero-sugar alternatives and other healthy options.

"Removing high-sugar drinks from schools is one of the simplest and most effective steps we can take to create healthier learning environments for all New Zealand children.

"Fewer sugary drinks means fewer children experiencing preventable health problems."

The letter concluded, should it be implemented by the next government: "A healthier next generation of New Zealanders will surely thank them for it."

World.title: Youth unemployment at 'crisis level' and AI may mean recovery is tough, NZIER says
World.content:

Can my landlord put a political billboard on my home? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 9m

Young people facing "crisis-level unemployment" aren't likely to get any relief simply from the economy improving, the NZ Institute of Economic Research (NZIER) says.

It says the emergence of AI and other technological changes have added another layer of uncertainty that is likely to affect young people's unemployment even as the landscape improves.

It has released an update that notes that unemployment among 15 to 19-year-olds has increased to 25.3 percent and among 20 to 24-year-olds it has risen to 12 percent, while the overall unemployment rate has stayed relatively stable.

It said while young people were always more exposed to downturns because they had less experience, the current situation was different because while the 15 to 19-year unemployment rate was near historical highs the overall employment rate was well below 1990s levels.

Senior economist David Hamill and principal economist Sarah Hogan said young people were facing "crisis level" unemployment, underutilisation and rates of being not in employment, education or training.

They said policy decisions during and after Covid had played a role.

The current government had prioritised fiscal restraint over support, they said, and policies that focused on strengthening the incentives to work overlooked the shortage of job opportunities.

They said the current push to move young people off benefits and into work would only be successful if there were jobs to go to.

NZIER said the solution might not be as straightforward as economic recovery.

"AI uncertainty can affect both employers and young people. Employers may be putting hiring on hold, especially for the workers they expect are most replaceable by AI, and young people are likely to be questioning the value of investment in education and training. "The education and training sector has always been slow to adapt," Hogan said.

"But the impacts of that are worse when technology is moving very fast and in ways that make it unclear what skills employers and workers will need in the near future."

It said the share of migrants filling low-skill jobs had been increasing before Covid and the government had eased restrictions allowing employers to bring more migrants in for minimum wage jobs even though the advice from officials was that a wage premium was needed to minimise the displacement of young New Zealanders.

They said construction and retail, food and accommodation had both significantly shifted the composition of their workforce in a way that favoured migrants on temporary work visas over young New Zealanders.

"Many young people may be locked out in a perfect storm," Hamill said.

"We can't be certain about the role of each individual factor, but there appears to be a complex combination of cyclical and structural risks at work, including a sluggish recovery, business uncertainty, unhelpful policy responses, pre-existing structural problems, accelerating technological change, and increasing reliance on temporary migrant workers in some sectors where young people are also concentrated."

Given the likely role of structural factors, the crisis may persist to some extent even during an economic recovery. Young people currently in the labour market need greater support, and the government needs a workforce strategy fit for the future, be successful if there were opportunities and little had been done to create those.

The Reserve Bank has also indicated it is watching the emergence of AI as a factor for youth unemployment rates.

World.title: 'Enough is enough': New Zealand First wants to ban fireworks
World.content:
New Zealand First has made a fresh push for a ban on backyard fireworks after the leaders of National and Labour shot the idea down in a recent debate.

The party wants to ban the public sale and private use of fireworks, blaming them for frightening animals, starting fires and causing havoc for emergency services.

"Enough is enough," the party said in its announcement.

"The abuse and misuse of fireworks has far outgrown any of the benefits."

In a statement, a spokesperson said the legislation was already written and ready to be introduced to Parliament within the first 100 days of the next government.

NZ First lodged a member's bill proposing a ban in November last year.

The proposed ban would also stop the manufacture and import of fireworks for private use, but professionally organised public displays would still be permitted.

"This is not about being 'nanny state'," the statement said. "This is about bringing some common-sense into what is a desperately needed conversation about the future of fireworks in our community."

Speaking to RNZ, NZ First leader Winston Peters said politicians who considered the matter a "freedom issue" did not appreciate the true damage fireworks caused.

"It's not a freedom issue," he said.

"It's a right to peaceful and harmonious living for both the community and for animals."

Peters said his own dog spent all of Guy Fawkes Night in a panic.

"A lot of people making comments have never seen the damage to animals, like to dogs and cats and particularly horses... cut to the bone and having to be put down because of the injuries they've sustained being panicked by fireworks."

In Tuesday night's TVNZ leaders' debate, National's Christopher Luxon and Labour's Chris Hipkins both answered "no" when asked whether fireworks should be banned from public sale.

Tuesday night's TVNZ leaders' debate. TVNZ/Harley Peters

ACT leader David Seymour also opposed a ban. In July, he told media: "Just for a few days a year at the start of summer, let's just keep something of the Kiwi childhood, please?"

Also in July, Green Party co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick said restricting private sales was a "common sense position", citing animal welfare and environmental concerns.

Parliament's Petitions Committee this term considered three petitions on the topic backed by more than 95,000 signatures.

Its report, released in April, concluded the evidence of harm made it difficult to recommend anything other than a ban.

But in July, the coalition government rejected the recommendation, arguing a ban would remove access to a long-standing legal activity.

It said existing rules struck an appropriate balance between preventing harm and protecting individual choice.

At the time of the government's rejection in July, Peters vowed the issue would be back on the table after the election.

Under current rules, fireworks can be sold to people aged 18 and over for just four days a year, from November 2 to 5. There is no nationwide restriction on when they can be used.

World.title: US to livestream Army execution of Fort Hood shooter, Pentagon official says
World.content:
The US will livestream the Army's upcoming firing squad execution on 3 December of Nidal Hasan, who killed 13 people at Fort Hood, Texas, in a 2009 shooting spree, a Pentagon official says, in what would be an unprecedented move.

Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, is set to become the first person to be executed by firing squad by the US military since 1945, shortly after the end of World War Two.

The Pentagon official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, did not offer more information and said details would follow.

US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth earlier told the Human Events Daily podcast he planned to make Hasan's execution public, according to video of his comments posted on social media on Thursday (local time).

Hegseth said deciding to execute Hasan by firing squad at Fort Hood on a Thursday at 1pm - the approximate time, day of the week and location of Hasan's shooting - was a "no brainer".
