World.content:
A new poll shows the coalition has slightly extended its lead over the left bloc thanks to a surge in support for New Zealand First, while both the major parties remain languishing in the 20s.

The Taxpayers' Union Curia poll has National and Labour neck and neck: since its September results, National dropped to 28.5 percent (down 0.5 percentage points), while Labour rose to 28.2 percent (up 2.3).

On Thursday Labour accused National of painting beneficiaries as "bludgers" in the hope it translates to a bounce in the polls.

National on Thursday vowed to introduce random drug testing for those receiving Jobseeker support, arguing they should take "reasonable steps to remain work-ready".

World.title: Fijian Teachers Association head's threat to 'roast' critics in earth ovens sparks political storm
World.content:
Controversial, profanity-laden remarks made by the head of the Fijian Teachers Association (FTA) while defending Indigenous chiefs and threatening to "roast" critics in earth ovens have sparked a major political storm.

On Monday, FTA general-secretary Paula Manumanunitoga made a Facebook post weighing in on the constitutional reform debate currently dominating the country.

It comes as Fijians prepare to mark their 56th Independence Anniversary on Saturday.

Manumanunitoga specifically challenged those who he believed questioned the place and role of iTaukei chiefs in the governance of Fiji.

"Saying they do not have a place in the administration of this country, didn't anyone tell you how and why you're here in this country instead of your original country?," he wrote in all capital letters in the post.

"How quickly you have forgotten how you have come to exist here in Fiji? You and your kind are here because of the decision our chiefs made to cede Fiji to Queen Victoria of Great Britain in October 1874.

"So shut the [expletive] up and mind your own business before we catch you and roast you in earth ovens !!!! You're free to go anywhere, do whatever business you like but do not be disrespectful to belittle our chiefs or become thick-headed by whatever you've achieved in this country."

Paula Manumanunitoga made a Facebook post threatening non-indigenous people in Fiji of roasting them in earth ovens for questioning the place and role of iTaukei chiefs in the governance of Fiji. Screengrab / Facebook/Paula Manumanunitoga

His post, which is public, remains online and has attracted widespread criticism from political figures and the public.

Major political leaders have condemned Manumanunitoga's remarks, calling them "disgraceful", "disturbing" and "racially divisive".

The Fijian government has remained silent on Manumanunitoga's comments with no statements made by Prime Minister Sitiveni Rabuka or his Information Minister Lynda Tabuya, who is usually vocal against harmful and divisive digital communications.

However, Fiji's Women and Children's Minister Shashi Kiran has called for his resignation, to which Manumanunitoga has also hit back, saying Kiran had not released any statements when "they were swearing at our chiefs".

Fiji's parliamentary opposition leader Inia Seruiratu and the National Federation Party leader Biman Prasad have both called for Fiji Police to investigate his statements.

Seruiratu wants police to determine whether Manumanunitoga has committed any offences under Fiji's laws relating to threats, incitement to violence and communal antagonism.

"No individual, regardless of their position, ethnicity or standing in society, should be above the law," he said.

Social Democratic Liberal Party (Sodelpa) leader Aseri Radrodro said while Manumanunitoga is entitled to his views "freedom of expression must be exercised with responsibility, maturity, and respect".

"There comes a time when we must draw a clear line between standing up for our traditional leaders and resorting to hostility, vulgarity, and explicit threats against our fellow citizens," Radrodro said.

He warned that such rhetoric risks creating deep ethnic divisions among Fijians.

World.title: Khawaja's 'Sandpapergate' book does not worry Cummins
World.content:
Pat Cummins says he is not fazed by the prospect of the so-called Sandpapergate incident being raised in Usman Khawaja's autobiography, which will be the first from any Australian player who played in that 2018 Cape Town Test.

Cummins confirmed today Khawaja had called to inform him he was writing the book, which will be released days after the end of Australia's first Test tour of South Africa since the infamous match.

How much will be written about the ball-tampering scandal that rocked Australian cricket remains to be seen.

Khawaja is a childhood friend of former opening partner David Warner, who copped a 12-month ban for the ball-tampering scandal.

How Sandpapergate rocked Australian cricket In 2018, Sandpapergate rocked Australian cricket to its very core. Here's how a febrile atmosphere colluded with a team persistently testing the limits of acceptability to change the game.

At the time, Warner was painted as the architect of the ploy, with captain Steve Smith also suspended for a year and Cameron Bancroft nine months.

There was a report at the time that Khawaja had suggested the team should take joint responsibility for the incident, rather than just the three players.

However, a Cricket Australia investigation found no other player had knowledge of the plan to apply sandpaper to the ball, a point that has long been maintained.

Australia's bowlers have also previously issued a statement saying they did not know a "foreign substance" would be taken onto the field.

There is no suggestion Khawaja's autobiography, which has been penned without a ghost writer, will suggest anything other than what the investigations found.

Usman Khawaja's (left) upcoming autobiography book may mention the 2018 South Africa tour and Sandpapergate. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney, file photo)

Cummins was asked ahead of Friday's first Test in Durban if Khawaja had specified how much detail he would go into and if he would agree with his former teammates' version of events.

"You would have to ask him," Cummins responded.

"It's obviously a long time ago. All the investigations, everything was done back then. Answered every question a million times.

"It was dealt with then. All I can say is as a group we've moved on. [I'm] very happy with the last eight or nine years, how we've been as a group and evolved.

"He didn't go into too much detail … As always, it was, 'No worries. You can tell your story. That's fine.'"

It has been hard to escape talk of the 2018 series in the lead-up to the first Test.

Question over Connolly for Aussie Test XI South Africa is going in with two spinners for the first Test in Durban, but the Australian line-up is still unclear with illness and pitch questions still to be answered.

Cummins noted on Thursday there was a larger-than-normal media turn-out in Durban, with this also the battle between the world's top-two sides.

Beyond the ball-tampering scandal, the 2018 series was littered with clashes between the two teams from the middle of the pitch to dressing-room stairwells.

But tensions have thawed significantly since, with neither side expecting similar dramas.

"It was quite a big series that 2018. It was pretty full on," Cummins said.

"After that, I think pretty much every Test team in the world felt like they'd made some adjustments.

"This group is quite a different group in how we approach playing and I'm really proud of how the guys have been since that 2018 series."

AAP

World.title: Brisbane Lions slump a long time coming for AFLW powerhouse
World.content:
Brisbane enters its round nine match against Hawthorn in an uncomfortable position.

Already two games out of the top eight, a loss would make a finals series mathematically impossible for the perennial contender.

Across AFLW history the Lions have missed finals just once, 2019, and made seven of nine grand finals.

So the come-down this year with just two wins from eight starts across the opening two months seems like a stark fall.

They have been caught in the eye of a perfect storm, making the 2025 Grand Finalist a bottom-eight side, and maybe that's not such a bad thing.

The personnel problem

Across the opening decade of the AFLW the Lions have been durable, with coach Craig Starcevich regularly enjoying his pick of the list each week.

High-performance manager Matt Green has been a driver of this.

This year things have been different. Two-time premiership forward Taylor Smith was traded to Sydney over the off-season, as were premiership duo Poppy Boltz and Ellie Hampson to Greater Western Sydney and Port Adelaide, respectively.

The Lions lost plenty of talent in the off-season, including Taylor Smith to the Sydney Swans. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Mark Metcalfe)

All-Australian forward Courtney Hodder has been unavailable this year due to pregnancy, stalwart Ally Anderson missed the opening four rounds of the season, her first ever absence, with a hamstring concern.

And throughout the year a number of other players have spent time on the sidelines nursing injuries.

This all adds to an aging playing list with a heavy reliance still on those senior players to set the tone.

For the first time in its history, Brisbane has been challenged for depth and player availability and it has exacerbated already emerging issues in its game style.

Game style gaps

Brisbane has always been a hard-running, super fit team, relying on that to plug any holes that its game style might offer.

Unfortunately, this is the growth area for most other clubs in recent years, closing the gap on Brisbane at the top of the pack.

The AFLW's attacking revolution AFLW games are becoming faster, higher-scoring and more entertaining, and the stats and numbers behind the scenes prove it.

No longer will long bombs toward the front half into space for its runners beat the best teams. The increasing defensive strategy and organisation across the competition plans for this attacking style.

The Lions have struggled to establish more nuance across their ball movement.

Many of their players have been recruited based on their athletic attributes given the game style they were expected to play, but are struggling to adapt toward more of a precise ball movement game.

The area of the ground where this hurts most is with the Lions' forward 50 entries. 82.8 per cent of their entries turn into opposition rebounds, the fourth-highest rate across the AFLW this year.

The only sides conceding higher rebound rates are Port Adelaide (85.1 per cent), Collingwood (85.6 per cent), and St Kilda (87 per cent).

Blazing away through the middle of the ground and either kicking to an outnumber, or putting the ball out of their forwards' advantage, has been a common theme of the Lions this year, but it's not a brand-new problem.

Brisbane's goal efficiency, goals per inside 50, has been steadily dropping since its premiership season of 2023, hitting a club-low of 15.1 per cent this year.

It simply isn't getting bang for buck up forward and hasn't for a while.

Inefficiencies in attack

Year Shot efficiency (%) Goal efficiency (%) 2026 39.2 15.1 2025 43.7 17.9 2024 45.9 19.6 2023 45 20.3

Some of this can be the result of personnel with no Smith, Hodder, or Neasa Dooley. But more of this is due to haphazard attacking movement.

The club boasts the second-lowest disposal efficiency in the AFLW this year, using the ball at just 59.0 per cent, ahead of only contested beasts Port Adelaide, and this is another metric that has steadily dropped for the Lions over recent years.

Their ball use is getting more panicked, less considered, and less effective over time.

What they're giving up

Where the Lions have typically been strongest is in defence. They've prided themselves on squeezing the ground, minimising opposition inside 50s, and making life hard for forward lines when they do get into attacking positions.

This has been another steady shift, now conceding a club-high 36.1 inside 50s per game. While some of this has been due to the aforementioned poor ball use and, therefore, turnovers, another large piece has been weakening control around stoppage.

The Lions are losing clearance by 6.3 per game this year, the second-greatest average deficit behind 2017. They are giving up 20.6 points from the source per game. This is an increase of more than a goal compared to its 12.0 points conceded from stoppage on average last year.

They are being burnt at stoppage, and burnt badly.

It means more pressure on the back line to defend more inside 50s and ultimately greater scores conceded each week.

Lions' weakening defence

Clearance differential Inside 50s conceded Points conceded 2026 -6.3 36.1 44.5 2025 -0.4 29.4 35.6 2024 +1.9 30.1 31.3 2023 -1.8 28.6 33.6 2022 (S7) +3.1 24.2 19.8

All of this has contributed to an unfamiliar feeling for the Lions: not being considered a contender for finals.

But it's not necessarily a bad thing as it's a chance to regenerate, get some rare games into the kids.

Claudia Wright, Marlo Graham, Sophie Peters, Evie Long, and Asher Fearn-Wannan have all played a lot more footy than they would have expected and load up with their highly-rated academy prospects in December's draft.

Before that, however, they'll be considering Sunday's clash with the Hawks as one last throw at the stumps.

Against former midfield coach Daniel Webster, and as inaugural Lion Kaitlyn Ashmore brings up game number 100 wearing the brown and gold, they will be hunting a win to remain a narrow chance at yet another finals series.

World.title: Live: Butters edges closer to sealing Dogs move as Saints prepare Blakey offer
World.content:
Following on from Essendon's likely draft with the first pick, what's the current thinking for Richmond with the second? Earlier in the year all the hype around Richmond circles was for Harry Van Hattum, but given he's dropped on some mock drafts and the tigers now signing Briggs, who are they likely to target instead? - Adam

(Getty Images)

In many ways the Tigers will shape the top five or six picks in this draft with their selection. Like Chris, I expect Essendon will take Ethan Drever with the first pick in the open pool, leaving Richmond with a strong group to pick from.

I certainly wouldn't be counting out Harry van Hattum with that pick. He may not have had the season he had hoped for and has slipped in some rankings around the place, but not in mine. He remains a unique and exciting ruck prospect, and he has spent a fair bit of time talking with Richmond already, going so far as sitting down and discussing ruck craft with Ivan Maric.

If van Hattum gets past Richmond, I don't think the Eagles take him as they went with Cooper Duff-Tytler early last year (even though I think HVH is more likely to be a leading AFL ruck than CDT), so he could end up a steal for someone like Melbourne, depending on how the top 10 shakes out after trades.

If not van Hattum, Richmond would look closely at Arki Butler. I would wonder if he is not a little too similar to the style of player they have taken early in previous years already.

Heath Mellody should come under strong consideration too, as I think he would balance out the young Richmond midfield really well. There's more than a little Trent Cotchin in Mellody.

World.title: Illness uncertainty as Australia weighs up Test XI
World.content:
Cooper Connolly has had to travel separate to Australia's team while wearing a mask, as the tourists weigh up his potential return to the Test team in South Africa.

Connolly was spotted leaving Kingsmead in a van after training on Thursday (Friday AEDT) afternoon on the eve of the first Test against South Africa, while the rest of the side moved back to the Durban team hotel on a bus.

It is understood the 23-year-old has a head cold and Australia opted for caution after he trained normally through the afternoon session.

Still, it comes at an interesting time for the West Australian ahead of the first Test.

Australia is already without regular number five Cameron Green due to an abdominal strain, while Josh Inglis is back in Perth with a fractured finger.

Aussies dealt injury blow Australia will have to reshuffle its line-up for the series opener against the Proteas in Durban after one of its stars is ruled out with an injury.

The tourists will wait to see how dry the pitch is on Friday before announcing their side at the toss, with Connolly and Nic Maddinson in contention to come in for Green.

Connolly has not played a Test since his debut against Sri Lanka last February, while Maddinson's last appearance came way back in December 2016.

One potential option would be for that to come at the expense of Beau Webster, who batted at number seven in the recent Test series against Bangladesh.

The South Africans has already confirmed they will play two spinners in Keshav Maharaj and Simon Harmer, in a clear sign of how they believe the wicket will play.

"Everyone brings something a little bit different to it, and it's just trying to work out what we think the best combo is," Australia captain Pat Cummins said.

Green is a chance to return for Australia in the second Test, while Inglis is recovering well and is expected to fly back to South Africa before the series ends.

Australia is also confident Marnus Labuschagne has shown signs he can return to form at number three, after a century in a warm-up game last weekend.

The 32-year-old has not reached three figures in any of his past 39 completed Test innings, and was briefly dropped for last year's tour of West Indies before fighting back.

"He doesn't need to go searching for something that he doesn't already have," Cummins said.

"I think it's him finding his way back to when he was at his best, and we've seen that in the last six months.

Labuschagne makes timely century Marnus Labuschagne makes his case to keep the number three spot in Friday's first Test against South Africa, with a timely century in a warm-up match.

"I know a lot of it hasn't translated into Test runs, but we love what he's bringing, we love his approach.

"He's hitting the ball beautifully in the nets, I know it doesn't guarantee success out in the field, but we think he's really well placed."

Australia has spoken about the need to potentially play this Test at a different tempo to many recent ones, which have been dubbed as "fast-forward cricket".

"We've got to get a little bit better, and we can get a bit better at, getting to the grind," Cummins said.

"It might not be the glamorous stuff, but it's that grinding out a session, going for two runs an over, not these major falls or not these whirlwind innings at the time.

"We haven't played too many of those Test matches in the last few years, particularly in Australia, they've been quite fast-paced.

"A lot of our success has come off these big moments, with a Travis Head hundred or Starcy [Mitchell Starc] running through the top order."

AAP

World.title: Everything you need to know as Australian Test cricket returns tonight
World.content:
Australia is back in South Africa for one of the most eagerly anticipated Test series in recent history.

It has been eight long years since Australia last toured South Africa in red-ball cricket, in a series that will forever be remembered for its ignominy.

Sandpapergate is what that contest will be remembered for, but even before that, it was crossing a red line in despicable behaviour unbecoming of the sport.

Here's everything you need to know ahead of the three-Test series.

When are the Test matches?

Newlands is one of the world's most picturesque cricket grounds. (Getty Images: Dave Rogers)

The two teams will play three Tests.

The first is at Kingsmead in Durban from October 9 to 13.

The second is at St George's Park in Gqeberha from October 18 to 22.

And Newlands in Cape Town will host the third from October 27 to 31.

What time are the Test matches?

The Durban Test starts at 6:30pm AEDT and will likely run through to 2am AEDT.

That AEDT time relates to New South Wales, the ACT, Victoria and Tasmania.

In Queensland, the action begins at 5:30pm.

In South Australia, at 6pm.

In the Northern Territory, at 5pm.

And the first ball will be bowled at 3:30pm in Western Australia.

How can I watch the Test series?

Unless you're lucky enough to be on the Kingsmead hill like Wiaan Mulder, you'll have to watch on Fox Sports or Kayo. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Darren Stewart)

The entire series is live on Fox Sports and Kayo.

ABC Sport will also have live radio commentary on the ABC Listen App or online.

You can also follow every ball in our live blog on the ABC Sport website.

Who is playing in the series?

Australia's squad: Pat Cummins (c), Scott Boland, Alex Carey (wk), Cooper Connolly, Cameron Green, Sam Harper (wk), Josh Hazlewood, Travis Head, Matthew Kuhnemann, Marnus Labuschagne, Nathan Lyon, Nic Maddinson, Michael Neser, Matt Renshaw, Steven Smith, Mitchell Starc, Beau Webster.

South Africa's squad: Temba Bavuma (c), Marques Ackerman, David Bedingham, Corbin Bosch, Gerald Coetzee, Tony de Zorzi, Simon Harmer, Marco Jansen, Keshav Maharaj, Aiden Markram, Wiaan Mulder, Senuran Muthusamy, Anrich Nortje, Dane Paterson, Kagiso Rabada, Ryan Rickelton (wk), Tristan Stubbs (wk), Kyle Verreynne (wk).

Australia's record against South Africa

Australia has historically had great success against the Proteas in South Africa. (Getty Images: Morne de Klerk)

Australia has won 54 of the 102 Test matches between the two teams, with 21 draws and 27 defeats since their first meeting in 1902.

On South African soil, Australia also has a winning record, with 29 victories against 16 defeats and nine draws.

Australia has won six of the 11 Tests played at St George's in Durban, including winning each of the last three Tests it has played there, while South Africa has won three with two draws.

The two teams also drew a Test at the city's old Lord's ground in 1921, before the venue's demolition in 1922.

South Africa has a much better record at St George's Park in Gqeberha though, winning four of the seven matches played there, including the last two.

Before 2021, Gqeberha was Port Elizabeth, but is now known by its Xhosa name, and this is the first time Australia will play in the city under its new name.

Australia will play in Gqeberha for the first time. Australia's previous trips to St George's Park came when the city was known as Port Elizabeth. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Richard Huggard)

Australia has a great record at Newlands though, winning 10 of the 14 Tests played in the shadow of Table Mountain. However, it has only won one of its last four Tests at the ground considered one of the most beautiful in the world.

The two teams last played a Test in June 2025, when South Africa shocked Australia at Lord's to win the World Test Championship.

In the 2022/23 summer of cricket, Australia claimed a 2-0 Test series victory over South Africa on home soil.

The last time Australia played a Test series in South Africa was 2018, and it's safe to say things were … complicated.

The fiery 2018 series

Cameron Bancroft and Steven Smith were hauled over the coals for the ball tampering scandal. (Getty Images: Gallo Images/Ashley Vlotman)

It is fair to say the 2018 series was combative, fiery, febrile and chaotic.

Australia won the first Test at Kingsmead in Durban, but not before David Warner and Quinton de Kock almost came to blows in a stairwell at the end of the fourth day.

South Africa won the second Test in Gqeberha, but man of the match Kagiso Rabada, who took 5/96 and 6/54, was subsequently banned for barging into Steve Smith after dismissing him in the first innings.

Rabada was then handed a reprieve after an appeal involving one of South Africa's highest-profile lawyers, freeing him to play the next two matches.

The third Test was in Cape Town where, in the shadows of Table Mountain, Australia's descent into the dark arts was exposed.

Sandpaper gate scandal explained Cameron Bancroft was charged with ball tampering in Cape Town — here's how the dark day for Australian cricket unfolded.

On the third day, host broadcaster Supersport captured Cameron Bancroft rubbing the ball with a square of sandpaper to help encourage the prodigious reverse swing that had featured throughout the series thus far.

While South Africa romped to a 322-run win and a series lead, the full extent of Australia's cheating was exposed, leading to a moral reckoning about the team's approach back home, with then-prime minister Malcolm Turnbull leading the criticism of the offending players.

Smith, Bancroft and Warner were all sent home in disgrace, and an under-manned Australian team was thumped by 492 runs at the Wanderers in Johannesburg.

What's happened since?

South Africa stunned Australia at Lord's to win the World Test Championship. (Getty Images: Gareth Copley)

Australia has toured South Africa twice since the 2018 Test series, in 2020 and 2023 for limited-overs matches, with Smith and Warner both involved.

The two teams also just completed a three-match ODI series, which South Africa won 2-1.

The Proteas also toured Australia for a Test series in 2022/23, Australia winning 2-0 with a draw in the third Test in Sydney.

South Africa are the current World Test champions, beating Australia in the final in 2025, but haven't played a match in this format for 11 months.

By the time the first ball is bowled in Durban, it will have been 641 days since South Africa last played a Test on home soil.

Australia, the world number-one-ranked Test team, is coming off a humbling defeat to Bangladesh in Darwin.

Hopefully the febrile atmosphere of eight years ago has dissipated.

Because, unencumbered by the extracurricular issues, the cricket should be of the highest quality.

World.title: Katie Lynch wants to see AFL 'harness the momentum' of Pride Round
World.content:
The Gold Coast Suns' Katie Lynch says Pride Round comes at exactly the moment needed every season.

Two weeks out from the men's season finishing and a month before the women start finals, it provides an injection of enthusiasm, celebration and joy.

"A different energy comes into the competition on Pride Round," Lynch told ABC Sport.

"Because so many of our players connect with the movement and understand the power of the round for the community and who we represent," Lynch told ABC Sport.

However, Lynch would like to see that movement grow beyond the AFLW competition and across the whole AFL, to include not just the men's teams but all club staff and fans of the game.

Katie Lynch and Lily Mithen wanted the Suns' Pride guersney to represent celebration of the queer community. (Supplied: Gold Coast Suns)

The dedicated league-wide Pride Round was introduced annually in 2021.

It celebrates inclusion and diversity over two weeks, while honouring the contributions of the LGBTQ+ community to the game and providing a platform for education on queer issues, particularly those entwined with the game.

"I think that can be perhaps transferred across more of the whole code essentially," Lynch said.

"A pride round in the men's would be awesome to see, and I know from my experience, it's nothing but a positive experience, and so I can see that going enormously well and being enormously helpful for the entire code."

AFLW has had a dedicated league-wide Pride Round since 2021. (Getty: Michael Willson/AFL Photos)

Some LGBTQ+ Australian Rules fans and community members have felt the pang of exclusion from the sport in recent years.

The AFL is cracking down on homophobic language in the game, with CEO Andrew Dillon stressing "homophobia has no place in Australian football", at any level or under any circumstances, which has come as a reaction to the prevalence of slurs.

In the past three years, there have been 10 cases of AFL-listed players or coaches sanctioned for homophobic language, including Suns players Max Knobel this year and star defender Wil Powell in 2024.

Inaugural AFLW player Aliesha Newman designed the official match ball for Pride Round 2026. (Getty: Michael Willson/AFL Photos)

When put to Lynch whether an extended Pride Round would help in this regard, she said the game of Aussie Rules had always been excellent at creating a space for people to connect, converse and interact, and that Pride Round was an incredible vehicle to do that around LGBTQ+ issues and experiences.

"We know that the players and the code have significant ability to influence, of course, and we've seen that probably have a negative effect on our fans more recently," she said.

"So I think for me, it's how do we shift that dial to come back the other way?

"And that's why I talk about things like visibility and representation."

She said it was also a great opportunity to connect more fans to the game, and have them feel seen within it.

This year Lynch helped design the club's Pride guernsey alongside her teammate Lily Mithen and good friend and tattoo artist Mady Peters.

It resembles patchwork tattoos and stickers, including a tramp stamp on the back, which Lynch says is proof they had a lot of fun putting it together.

Katie Lynch with Mady Peters, who helped craft the Pride guernsey. (Supplied: Gold Coast Suns)

But more than that, Lynch said it felt special to have her friend Peters "who doesn't even know what a drop punt is" now have an attachment to the game of AFLW through the Pride movement, where she is represented as a queer person.

Lynch said she noticed the boost in attendance during Pride Round, including within her own friend group.

"My friends are great, very supportive of me … but if they're going to come to a game, it's Pride Round," she said.

" Pride Round has the power to bring people, even loose fans of AFL, to the game … and not only to experience the joy of it but they're there because they feel like they belong there. "

Pride Round is a big celebration every year in the AFLW. (Getty: James Wiltshire/AFL Photos)

She wants that "special feeling" to reach even further.

"That's what I've felt, particularly this year, is the support for us and this Pride Round has been enormous, and it's growing," she said.

"The opportunity now is to harness the momentum we've got and use it in a growth capacity.

"We'll probably never know the enormity of pride and visibility, particularly as players … I feel there's so much impact that I don't see, but I know is there."

World.title: The duality of Australia's newest cricket captain Sophie Molineux
World.content:
There are two sides to Sophie Molineux.

The everyday version. Quiet, composed, down-to-earth. Calmly answering questions, even the difficult ones, unfazed.

Those level-headed qualities come in handy when she's on the field, allowing her to think clearly and execute at critical points in the game.

Then there's Molineux's alter ego. The outgoing, bubbly personality that her teammates know well and us outsiders get a glimpse of every now and then.

Katy Perry performs on stage with Sophie Molineux at the MCG in 2020. (Getty: Cameron Spencer)

Whether it be dressing up as 80's icon Jane Fonda in neon lycra to lead a stretch session on tour, opening the batting in a game of street cricket outside the Old Mates pub in New York, or celebrating hard after a T20 World Cup win … It's fun and it's rather infectious.

In 2020, Molineux danced on stage with Katy Perry at the MCG. In 2026, she channelled Shane Warne on the Lord's balcony, holding a stump aloft as a beer was poured over her head.

During her six months in the job as the nation's newest captain, this contrast has made a real impact to the team environment. And it speaks volumes that two of her peers that watched from the sidelines in July as Australia reclaimed the T20 crown were filled with pride.

Loading Instagram content

Instead of feeling bitter they'd been left on the bench while the rest of the side beat England in the final by seven wickets, Grace Harris and Megan Schutt reflected on how much this victory meant to the entire group. The first with Molineux in charge.

"That was good fun," Harris remarked.

"It's not unlike Soph to get amongst the celebrations and it's great to see an Aussie captain kind of relax a bit too — you've got to enjoy the wins.

"To go through the World Cup and not even look like losing was really cool and a real answer to the criticism we've had in recent times," Schutt added.

"It was a euphoric feeling for Soph. There were so many people that doubted the decision to make her captain, when we knew internally why she was picked for that role. To be able to put it to them a bit felt good and we're so proud of her.

"Following the game when the crowd had dispersed, it was late at night, and we were sitting on the ground with the trophy basically having a gratitude session for the last six weeks.

"It felt really deserving for Soph."

Molineux has suffered a range of injuries during her career. (Getty: Jonathan DiMaggio)

When it was announced that skipper Alyssa Healy would retire in March and Molineux would be her successor, even the most diehard cricket fans were shocked.

Most had thought the experience of vice-captain Tahlia McGrath or all-rounder Ash Gardner would put them next in line. McGrath had even filled in for Healy 15 times previously. Perhaps even 24-year-old Annabel Sutherland would have been a good pick, as a long-term nod to the future?

All three had certainly played more international matches than Molineux, whose career has been hampered by a string of injuries since her debut in 2018. Due to serious foot, knee and shoulder issues, Molineux had only accumulated a total 58 caps when she was appointed.

Social media was rife with criticism. Were others more worthy? Would she be able to stay fit and be a consistent presence in the team?

Those concerns are still a question mark now, as a hip injury rules Molineux out of the ODI series beginning on Friday against Bangladesh on home soil. The selectors are hopeful she'll be back to play the three T20Is scheduled at North Sydney Oval against New Zealand in late October.

Vice captain Tahlia McGrath was an obvious choice as the next skipper, having already filled in the role when Alyssa Healy was unavailable. (Getty: Matt Roberts)

"I was aware of the criticism, and I understood completely why it came and why people wouldn't have expected my appointment," Molineux tells ABC Sport.

"I would have loved to have played another 100 games for Australia by now but that hasn't been my journey and I can't change that.

"I wouldn't even want to change that because through those injuries and setbacks I learned a whole lot about myself — what's important to me and a big part of that was leading.

"Making sure that whatever environment I was in, that I could contribute and make others feel safe. It set me up, in a way, to be able to do this job.

"At the same time, I was pretty determined to prove it all wrong, and it probably fuelled me to nail the preparation for the T20 World Cup."

Australia lifts the ICC Women's T20 World Cup for a seventh time. (Getty: Alex Davidson)

After two consecutive semi-final exits at ICC tournaments, there was extra pressure on Australia to perform. Despite this, Molineux excelled.

The left-arm orthodox bowler finished in the top three wicket-takers (11 in 7 innings with best figures of 2/6) and was credited by her teammates for spearheading their most consistent and dominant campaign yet.

Which is saying something, as this was their seventh T20 title. The result felt like vindication for her family too, who have supported her through every one of her setbacks.

Loading Instagram content

"They ride it with you, the highs and the lows," Molineux said.

"Throughout the World Cup they were in the stands watching and for them to be able to experience it was really special to me.

"They were the first ones to the games and the last ones to leave.

"I'm forever grateful for my family's support and Mum and Dad were so excited and happy when I was appointed as captain … Their opinions to me were most important."

As the summer of cricket approaches, with next year's Women's Ashes on the horizon, we wonder, what kind of leader does Molineux want to be?

"I just want to be authentic. I want to be me," she responds.

"I've played under some amazing captains in Meg Lanning and Alyssa Healy. They were strong players who wanted to take the team on their shoulders and lead through their actions. I've learned a lot from them, but I don't want to lose too much of who I am.

"I am from country Victoria. I play cricket because I love the challenge and the people. The memories and the experiences. So, I don't really want to lose that sense of fun.

"Although the job can be serious at times, it's getting that balance right."

This article was written for the ABC Cricket Magazine, available online, or in local newsagents from November.

World.title: Matildas coach backs Mary Fowler's absence from friendlies
World.content:
Coach Joe Montemurro has said the Matildas support Mary Fowler's decision to miss upcoming friendlies for personal circumstances and is adamant they have the creative players available to cover her.

Fowler, 23, withdrew this week from the squad to play world number three Germany on Saturday (AEDT) and Haiti on Wednesday.

"It's really important that we create an environment that is important for the player, and as the circumstances are private, I'm not going to elaborate," Montemurro said.

Fowler out of Matildas internationals Mary Fowler will be replaced by Leah Davidson for the upcoming friendlies, with the Matildas star withdrawing due to personal circumstances.

"But yes, absolutely, discussions were had with Mary, with the club (Manchester City), and with the relative people, and we believe that we've made the right decision and I think everyone's in support of the situation."

There has been speculation that Fowler has returned to Australia to support her partner, Nathan Cleary, which Football Australia has not confirmed.

The Penrith rugby league star required emergency surgery after suffering a career-threatening badly broken leg in the Panthers' NRL preliminary final loss in late September.

Players opting out of windows for personal reasons is not rare, especially given the intense schedules of club and international football.

"At the end of the day, we're all human. You can't always base your life around football," Australian goalkeeper Mackenzie Arnold said.

"I have never personally been in that experience, so I don't really know how to put it into words.

"But I would say if I had that situation that I felt the need to go home and I asked the coach for that and I had full trust in him that he was going to give me that permission — then of course, it's important.

"But I think the the bottom line is, at the end of the day we're all human, so if we need to make that decision, then that's what we need to go with."

The Matildas are without three of their best creative outlets — Fowler, Kyra Cooney-Cross and Katrina Gorry — for this window.

But Montemurro backed Australia's "very, very talented" midfield depth.

Montemurro name-dropped Vittsjo gun Dani Galic, Nottingham Forest midfielder Alana Murphy and uncapped Valerenga playmaker Hana Lowry.

"They're names I want you to remember, because I really do believe that they're going to be the next generation of midfielders," he said.

AAP

Tech.title: US plans livestream of execution by firing squad
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The United States’ execution of the Fort Hood shooter will be livestreamed, anonymous officials from the Defense Department told the BBC and Associated Press. The planned execution of Nidal Hasan, the former US Army major convicted of killing 13 people at the Texas military base, was announced this week. He is scheduled to be executed by firing squad on December 3rd at 2PM ET.

The Verge contacted YouTube, Twitch, TikTok, Meta, Rumble, and Kick to ask if they plan to allow the livestream to be aired on their platforms. None responded before publication.

“We’ll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it’s public, because people need to understand that there’s serious consequences for these types of things,” US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said in an interview with Real America’s Voice.

Tech.title: Anthropic launches free AI security scans for open-source projects
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Anthropic’s offering to help open-source projects track down security vulnerabilities with a new service called OSS Scanner. It says open-source projects that opt-in will get “thorough, periodic security scans by our strongest models at no cost.” That could mean open-source projects get alerted about possible security issues sooner, but the trade-off is that OSS Scanner’s reports don’t come with human review:

The outputs of this opt-in vulnerability scanner will be fully model-generated, without human review or triage. This will enable faster and more frequent scanning, but means that it is possible reports will be incorrect or invalid. These reports will be generated by our strongest models (including Claude Mythos) to give open-source projects the largest defensive advantage.

OSS Scanner is far from the first AI bug hunting helper out there. AI tools have helped find some major security flaws in open-source software over recent months, like the “Copy Fail” bug that impacted nearly every Linux distro in May. At the same time, some open-source projects are struggling to keep up with the sudden onslaught of AI-generated bug reports, including Linus Torvalds and even Google.

Tech.title: SpaceX announces plan to become a ‘major mobile carrier’
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

SpaceX has acquired a portfolio of low-band spectrum licenses — a move the company says “will pave the way” for its Starlink Mobile service to become a “major” US carrier. When the Federal Communications Commission signs off on the deal, SpaceX says it will deploy its new architecture that combines its satellite-to-mobile constellation with a terrestrial mobile network, directly competing with T-Mobile, AT&T, and Verizon.

The licenses include up to 14 megahertz of paired spectrum in the 800 MHz band, which SpaceX says will allow Starlink Mobile’s signal to penetrate through walls and buildings. SpaceX previously acquired 2GHz spectrum from EchoStar as part of efforts to bolster its direct-to-device service.

The FCC has also approved plans to deploy 15,000 V2 Starlink Mobile satellites that will offer more than 100 times the bandwidth than the current generation, according to SpaceX. “With this new low-band spectrum and our Gen2 constellation, Starlink Mobile can now become the first network operator to deploy both satellite and terrestrial spectrum,” SpaceX says. “One network that provides Americans with a reliable service indoors, outdoors, in cellular dead zones, and everywhere in between.”

Tech.title: AMD will bring FSR 4 to handhelds by the end of 2026
Tech.content:
is a senior editor and founding member of The Verge who covers gadgets, games, and toys. He spent 15 years editing the likes of CNET, Gizmodo, and Engadget.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

It’s already possible to get AMD’s framerate-enhancing FSR 4 boost on handhelds as old as the Steam Deck — but in June, AMD reserved the right to disappoint handheld gamers by not officially bringing FSR 4 to older handhelds. Now, AMD consumer chip boss Jack Huynh says he will bring the tech to some handhelds by the end of the year.

Which handhelds? It’s still not clear if it will come to existing handhelds, or if you’ll need a new one to get it — because it comes alongside news that AMD is releasing a new FSR4-capable chip.

“We will expand the machine learning AI-based FSR4 technology, which was first introduced to existing external graphics cards, to the entire product line including APUs, gaming laptops, and handheld devices by the end of this year,” Huynh told Korean publication The Elec (via Google Translate). “We plan to respond in two directions: launching existing APUs and new product lines.”

The Elec says that means both a new APU, and a lightweight FSR4 model for APUs, are coming by year’s end. (Previously, AMD had only promised FSR4 for desktop graphics cards, not APUs bound for laptops and handhelds.) But The Elec doesn’t seem to say if that lightweight FSR4 model is coming to handhelds specifically. Perhaps it’ll require AMD’s leaked upcoming Ryzen Z3 and/or “Gainsborough” handheld chips.

Back when AMD threw a little cold water on the idea of FSR 4 for existing handhelds, exec David McAfee told Tom’s Guide that “we want to make sure the experience and the quality is right” and that AMD would need “a sufficient amount of compute within that product” for FSR 4 to make sense. Perhaps some older laptop chips will qualify, while some older handheld chips don’t.

Valve has said it is working with AMD to bring FSR 4 to the Steam Machine’s console-grade AMD APU, but it hasn’t yet committed to the same for the Steam Deck handhelds.

AMD didn’t immediately respond to a request to clarify Huynh’s statement.
